Rates of autism have been rising in the U.S. over the past few decades, largely due to advanced screening. One in 45 adults are diagnosed with autism, according to non-profit Autism Speaks.

There are several known risk factors, including genetic history, exposure to air pollution or certain pesticides, low birth weight or birth complications, advanced parental age and maternal obesity, diabetes or immune system disorders, the group says.

Autism Speaks has also pointed out that no research has proven taking Tylenol causes autism and says vaccines do not cause autism, either.

“Autism is often diagnosed around the same time children receive routine vaccinations, which has led to concerns about a connection — but decades of scientific research have confirmed that vaccines do not cause autism,” Autism Speaks says.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump has claimed without proof that the MMR vaccine and Tylenol are linked to autism. Research shows that’s not the case ( AFP via Getty Images )

Trump’s claims

The survey’s findings come over a year after President Trump claimed without proof that Tylenol was linked to autism. He’s also tied autism to the use of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine.

In August, he signed an executive order that would split up the shot, alleging that it could “have a huge impact on autism.”

But research shows no link between the MMR vaccine and autism and public health experts say splitting the MMR vaccine could actually make people less safe.

When “vaccines are split and more doses or visits are needed,” Andrew Pollard, director of the Oxford Vaccine Group at the University of Oxford, said. “[T]he result is that doses are missed and protection in the population drops.”

He added: “This is very dangerous in the cases of these viruses, not least with outbreaks of measles already [ongoing].”

News.title: Monty Don bids farewell to Gardeners’ World in moving final episode
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Monty Don has hosted his final episode of Gardeners’ World, bringing to a close a run of more than two decades on the BBC programme.

The 71-year-old signed off from Longmeadow, the garden that has served as the show’s base for 16 years, in an episode broadcast on Friday.

His dog Ned was alongside him as he thanked viewers on the programme.

Don said: “From myself, Ned, and Longmeadow it’s the final goodbye.

“I first began presenting Gardeners’ World 23 years ago at Berryfields and we came here to Longmeadow 16 years ago and, in that time, things have changed.

Monty Don poses in the RHS and BBC Radio 2 Dog Garden at the RHS Chelsea Flower Show, which opens at the Royal Hospital Chelsea in London next week. ( PA )

“The garden has grown, Nigel has been and gone, and Nellie and Patty [his previous dogs], but there has been one constant factor, and that has been the incredible privilege and pleasure of sharing my garden and my gardening life with you here, as well as working with so many superb people.

“So, thank you. Thank you for coming on that journey with me and good luck with your own gardens in the future. So, for the last time. Goodbye.”

His departure from the weekly series does not take him off BBC screens entirely.

During the episode, Don confirmed he would remain part of the presenting line-up for next year’s Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) Chelsea Flower Show.

He will also feature in two winter specials, which are expected to air between now and Christmas.

One celebratory episode will see him reflect on his years presenting the series and the changes he has seen at Longmeadow during his time on the show.

Details of the next series of Gardeners’ World will be announced at a later date.

Don took over the programme in 2003 from fellow TV gardener Alan Titchmarsh, at his predecessor’s request.

Before Gardeners’ World, his television roles included hosting Tomorrow’s World and Holiday, as well as a gardening segment on This Morning.

He stepped away from the programme for three years after suffering a minor stroke in 2008.

The show moved to his private garden when he returned.

Don’s final episode of Gardeners’ World is available to stream on BBC iPlayer.

News.title: AI saw its worst day on Wall Street after midterms blue wave. What that means for you and your 401(k)
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

AI stocks plummeted Thursday - the worst day on Wall Street in more than a year - in the wake of Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories that saw the party regain control of Congress.

AI hardware maker Nvidia’s stock slid 8 percent while Advanced Micro Devices plummeted 16 percent. CoreWeave, which rents access to AI chips through the cloud, tumbled 15 percent.

Investors appear to fear that Democrats’ regained control of Congress may bring more federal oversight of the AI data-center industry. According to one financial report, more federal involvement could slow down data-center construction by as much as 30 percent by 2028.

And it’s not just lawmakers - voters pushed back on data centers in the midterms. Of the 41 data-center measures on ballots, voters shot down or restricted data centers in 35 of the measures, according to Ballotpedia.

Stocks rebounded Friday but with AI companies now making up half of businesses in the S&P 500, The Independent explores what consequences major drops in AI firm values could have on Americans’ personal finances.

open image in gallery After Republicans lost the House and Senate in Tuesday’s midterm elections, AI stock prices plummeted as investors feared that Democrats would hamper attempts to build data centers across the country ( AFP via Getty Images )

401(k) fears

Most 401(k)s - retirement funds offered by employers - are invested in the S&P 500, the largest, publicly-traded companies on U.S. stock exchanges. But not every 401(k) is invested the same way.

Stocks, also known as “equities,” can go through big swings, as AI-company equities proved Thursday.

People in their 60s are likelier to invest more of their 401(k) in low-risk assets like bond and money market funds than equities to reduce the risk of decimating their retirement savings just as they need them.

A 401(k) investment in stocks starts at 89 percent, on average, when the account-holder is in their 20s and falls to 57 percent when in their 60s, according to a 2024 study from research and analysis firm Employee Benefit Research Institute.

This means that it’s more likely that younger people’s 401(k)s will be hurt by the AI stock slide because their portfolios are more high-risk, high-reward. But if a retiree, for example, needs to pull money from the 401(k) now because of a financial emergency or to pay for the daily costs of retirement.

“We tend to talk about retirement as though everyone reaches a certain age, stops working, and immediately starts living off their investments, but retirement looks different for everyone,” Nicole Carlon, a financial advisor with financial firm WiseOak Wealth, told The Independent in an email.

“Someone who needs to start withdrawing money during a market downturn faces a different set of risks. Having to sell investments when they're down to cover living expenses can have longer-term consequences for a retirement portfolio.”

If your retirement plan includes withdrawing from your 401(k) now or in the next few months, work with your brokerage to replace your tech stocks with low-risk mutual funds, Dr. Leo Chen, an assistant professor of finance at the University of South Florida, told The Independent in an email. Known as “rebalancing,” this move can help soften the blow of the AI stock slide.

“One of the biggest [risks] is a large drop just before or just after you start withdrawals,” Chen said. “Using this current sell-off as an example, rebalance now so a tech slide can’t wreck your timeline.”

However, this week’s volatile stock market shouldn’t be a long-term problem because time typically evens out a stock’s highs and lows.

“Time is on your side,” Chen said. “A slide lets you buy at lower prices with every paycheck. Keep contributing, capture the full employer match, and rebalance once a year.”

AI stock prices should return to normal by next summer, he said.

“This has appeared to be a market-wide panic sell-off, since the midterm outcomes may delay the data center buildout instead of cancelling,” Chen said.

“I’d expect several weeks of volatility, and a return to pre-midterm levels in roughly three to six months if AI spending guidance holds up.”

For those who are decades from retirement, a patient approach should guide decisions this week, Carlon said.

“And that's really the goal, making investment decisions based on what you're trying to accomplish with your money, rather than reacting to whatever is happening in the market that day,” she said.

Tech troubles

For investors who buy tech stock outside of their retirement account, Tuesday’s blue wave likely left them awash in pessimism.

AI is intimately intertwined in the tech sector, as it requires a wide range of companies to turn a piece of land into a thriving data center.

Those companies range from AI leaders Alphabet and Meta to software platforms such as Adobe, semiconductor firms like Broadcom, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, Marvell Technologies, and tech giants like Nvidia.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump fields questions from reporters after a meeting with AI leaders in September at the White House. Trump’s cooperative relationship with the AI industry helped keep investors optimistic about the future of AI data centers, but that optimism faded fast after this week’s midterms ( Getty )

And when AI stocks drop like they have this week, Silicon Valley also takes a hit. That’s reflected in the performance of the Nasdaq, a stock index made up of many of the country’s biggest tech firms such as Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft and Meta.

The Nasdaq was down 5.42 percent Thursday afternoon, a full 2 percent lower than the Dow Jones, which includes a range of stocks beyond tech firms.

One key race in Tuesday’s midterms that amplified concerns about a slowdown in data center construction was in Texas after Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Republican Governor Greg Abbott.

open image in gallery Sprawling data centers like this one in Virginia have not only encroached on the fringes of neighborhoods, but they’ve stoked the ire of voters. Some 41 data center measures were on midterm ballots across the country. By Wednesday, voters shot down or approved restrictions on 35 of 41 measures ( Getty )

Her win sent shockwaves not only through political circles, but in the tech world because of Hinojosa’s distaste for data centers. Texas is expected to account for nearly 30 percent of the country’s data center capacity set to go live in 2028, Bloomberg reported this week.

“Hinojosa is a known anti-data center politician and negative on the AI buildout, which makes worries around the future of the data-center buildout in Texas a real issue for tech investors,” financial strategist David Ives said in a Morningstar analysis piece published Thursday.

Morningstar maintains a 4-star rating for 11 top AI firms - the firm believes the companies are undervalued and will generate returns. That list includes Nvidia, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, Broadcom, Meta, Alphabet, Tencent Holdings, Alibaba Group, Marvell Technology, Oracle, Adobe, Baidu and CoreWeave.

Morningstar also notes that its Morningstar Global Next Generation Artificial Intelligence Index, a group of the top 50 AI firms in the market, is up 20.2 percent this year even with this week’s AI-stock downturn.

“Don’t sell everything in a panic, because panic selling turns a temporary drop into a permanent loss,” Chen said.

News.title: Tuchel: Bellingham and I were up and down – now we are in a good place
News.content:
Jobe never wanted to be a carbon copy of his brother. He wanted to write his own story. The club, too, has resisted direct comparisons. They just wanted Jobe, not the younger brother of a world-class star. Now the brothers will be reunited in the England squad. For Jude, it is a dream come true. He previously said: “We’ve played together on the streets for so long. Playing for England alongside my brother would be the greatest dream of my life. That would mean more to me than any trophy.”

Dortmund have never fought harder for a player in recent years than Bellingham. The club’s executives first met him in person in the summer of 2020, when Jude signed. Jobe accompanied his brother to Germany. From that moment on, the club monitored every step of his development: his progress through the youth ranks at Birmingham City, the family club of the Bellinghams, and the evolution of his positioning on the pitch. After all, as a child, Jobe was still playing as a centre-forward. Over time, however, he gradually moved into deeper roles.

In May 2025, BVB decided to make their move. Word had reached Dortmund that Eintracht Frankfurt were interested and had already invited Bellingham to their training facilities. The pressure was on. Dortmund responded by pulling out all the stops. President Hans-Joachim Watzke, the man who shaped the club for more than two decades and led it to the top of German football, stepped in. He flew to England and met Bellingham face to face. It was a secret mission. Watzke was determined not to attract any attention that could jeopardise negotiations.

The problem: Sunderland, Bellingham’s former club, had secured promotion to the Premier League only a day earlier. Hundreds of supporters were gathered outside the hotel where Watzke and Bellingham were due to meet. To avoid being recognised, Watzke put on sunglasses and a cap before making his way through the crowd. He brought two gifts with him. Firstly, a BVB shirt with Jobe’s name on the back. Secondly, a handwritten note from Kovac expressing his desire to work with the midfielder. A few days later, Watzke received a phone call. It was Jobe. His decision had been made. He was joining Dortmund.

News.title: A tech editor’s guide to finding genuine Black Friday discounts
News.content:
The Black Friday shopping season is here. The world’s biggest technology brands, including Amazon, Samsung, Apple and Sony, are all expected to drop their prices, with British retailers such as John Lewis, Currys and Argos throwing their hats in the ring as we speed towards the new year.

While you might already have your eye on a gadget or two in the hope they drop in price during the sales, it’s important to shop wisely – and, crucially, manage expectations.

As Telegraph Recommended’s tech editor, who has been covering the Black Friday sales for well over a decade, I have picked up a number of must-know tips.

Whether that’s buying last year’s iPhone for less than the latest model, or accepting the sad truth that game consoles won’t be discounted ahead of the Grand Theft Auto VI launch, here’s everything you need to know – including early discounts.

News.title: White House postpones tech boss meeting after AI crash
News.content:
The White House has postponed a meeting of Silicon Valley tech bosses including Meta chief Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia boss Jensen Huang following Thursday’s stock market sell-off.

Donald Trump’s administration was scheduled to convene a session on Friday with an industry panel known as the “President’s Council ​of ⁠Advisers on Science and Technology”, which advises Mr Trump on tech matters.

However, the meeting was cancelled by the White House and is yet to be rescheduled. Thursday’s tech rout, which saw the Nasdaq 100 fall the most in six years, wiped more than $1 trillion off the Magnificent 7.

The tech ​panel also includes top Silicon Valley bosses such as AMD’s ‌Lisa Su and Marc ​Andreessen, co-foudner of Andreessen ​Horowitz.

The move comes after the President reaffirmed his commitment to the buildout of data centres, saying that “only foolish leadership will say “NO” to the riches they bring.”

Tech shares fell sharply on Thursday over fears the Democratic “blue wave” will halt the construction of data centres, which have fuelled the AI boom

It comes as US stocks staged a small rebound, with the Nasdaq Composite up 1.77pc.

Meta shares were up 2.5pc on Friday following a 4pc fall on Thursday, while Nvidia rebounded 3.6pc after a drop of 9.3pc a day earlier.

News.title: Cheap version of game-changing HIV preventive drug granted approval by US authorities
News.content:
Millions of people in low and middle income countries are set to get access to a game-changing HIV prevention drug within weeks, after US health authorities green lit a cheap form of the product.

Earlier this week the US Food and Drug Administration granted tentative approval to a generic form of the drug lenacapavir, made by Indian manufacturer Dr Reddy’s Laboratories.

Under an agreement hammered out between drug manufacturers and philanthropic donors in 2025 120 low and middle income countries across Africa, Asia, the Middle East and the Caribbean, will get access to the generic drug, at just $40 per patient per year – compared to the US list price of $28,000.

Lenacapavir, a long-acting injection administered twice a year, was hailed as the scientific breakthrough of 2024 and a potential turning point in the fight against HIV. Clinical trials have shown it provides almost 100 per cent protection against catching the HIV virus for six months and it is more effective and convenient than taking daily pre-exposure prophylactic (PrEP) pills.

Last year, Gilead Sciences, which developed lenacapavir, signed royalty-free, non-exclusive voluntary licencing agreements with six generic manufacturers to enable the production and supply of a generic. Dr. Reddy’s is the first to get FDA approval and it is hoped the first batches will be ready by the end of the year.

Jessica Burry, HIV technical officer at Unitaid, which in conjunction with the Clinton Health Access Initiative and Wits RHI supported Dr Reddy’s in its bid to manufacture the generic, said it normally takes 10 years for a generic form of a drug to be launched.

“So we’re celebrating this milestone,” she said. “There’s a lot of demand in the countries where we’re working and we think having an affordable generic could make a real difference.”

Standard PrEP involves daily pills which some people find difficult to stick to.

“You can overcome the stigma, you can overcome the potential adherence difficulties so it’s really a game changer in terms of things to have in the toolbox,” she said.

News.title: The perilous road to parenthood: Mongolia’s fight to make childbirth safer
News.content:
As the 4x4 raced south, bouncing across Mongolia’s rocky valley roads and dusty forest steppes, an obstetrician was doing her best to ease Otgonbayar Odbayar’s pain and panic.

Hours earlier, the reindeer herder’s waters had broken. But Otgonbayar was six weeks early – and almost 250 miles away from the doctors who could provide the caesarean she knew she needed.

She contacted the nearest clinic, kicking off a relay of calls that spanned the length of Khuvsgul, a region bordering Russia. Soon, a plan came back through the chain: one health team would collect the 26-year-old and sprint south, while doctors from the provincial hospital in Murun would hurtle north. They’d meet in the middle.

Otgonbayar Odbayar with her new baby Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

But Otgonbayar’s three-hour journey was touch and go. “Halfway through, her contractions got very intense and very close together,” said Dr Baasanjargal Tsogbadrakh, the obstetrician who collected her. “She was in a lot of pain. We put her on an IV and were driving so fast.”

They made it to the small clinic in Tugul a little after 11pm, but then faced an excruciating 90 minute wait for the team from Murun, who had further to travel on Mongolia’s rutted roads. Dr Tsogbadrakh didn’t have a Plan B: the baby was in breech position, and the scar from Otgonbayar’s previous c-section still hadn’t fully healed.

Khuvsgul Province in northern Mongolia Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“When [the doctors] arrived, I felt relief,” said Dr Tsogbadrakh. “If we had waited only 30 more minutes to start surgery, no one could tell what would have happened.”

Yet Otgonbayar’s ordeal is now the exception in Mongolia, underscoring just how far the vast country has come in its three-decade drive to tackle the childbirth risks posed by geography.

In 1990, 200 women died for every 100,000 births, but that ratio plunged to 47 by 2015 – making Mongolia one of only nine countries to hit global targets to reduce maternal mortality by 75 per cent over the 25-year period, according to analysis in the Lancet.

Strides have slowed but continued, and the rate now hovers at around 37. By contrast, other countries with a similar maternal mortality ratio in 1990, including Algeria, Brazil, the Philippines and Kiribati, still see more than 70 deaths per 100,000 births, according to Our World in Data.

In a country as vast and sparse as Mongolia – which is more than six times the size of the UK, but home to just 3.5 million people – health gains have been reliant “on overcoming the distance between women and the care they need”, said the health minister Batshugar Enkhbayar.

That has meant introducing telemedicine initiatives to bring specialist advice to remote clinics, waiting homes where pregnant women can stay in the final weeks before delivery, and better trained staff to spot risks before they become acute. In the last year, the country has also started to trial portable ultrasounds.

Northern Mongolia near the Russian border Credit : Simon Townsley

“We cannot always eliminate that distance,” said Mr Enkhbayar, “so we have to plan around it.”

The Telegraph spent a week in Mongolia to find out what this looks like in practice, driving hundreds of miles to meet pregnant women and new mothers in provincial hospitals, village clinics and remote herder communities.

There are also lessons for other countries: the latest data shows that globally, 260,000 women died during pregnancy and childbirth in 2023 – one death every two minutes. In the UK, around 250 women died in childbirth between 2022 and 2024, equal to more than one expectant mother a week.

Obstetrician Otgongerel Uvgii with Otgonbayar Odbayar following her recent birth Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

But in low and middle income countries, the vast majority of fatalities are due to infection, haemorrhage and hypertensive disorders such as preeclampsia, which are all entirely preventable. Reducing these risks does not require expensive or hi-tech kit – instead access to antenatal care, emergency obstetric care and postnatal follow up could all help save women’s lives.

And, when a mother survives childbirth – like Otgonbayar eventually did – her child is significantly more likely to live, receive an education, and break out of generational poverty, strengthening the community around him or her.

Otgonbayar’s third child, a little boy Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

At 2:10am on October 4, the doctors safely delivered Otgonbayar’s third child, a little boy weighing 2.3kg. The family hadn’t yet decided on a name when we visited the stuffy maternity room a day later – but they were already thinking about his future.

“It was very scary and painful, everything was going wrong,” said Otgonbayar, swaddling her newborn in a pink Peppa Pig blanket. “But I feel lucky now. I’m just so glad I’ve been able to meet my baby.

“He doesn’t look like me, [he looks] exactly like his father,” she added, smiling. “I hope in the future he grows to be a good person, and to be healthy.”

Almost 150 miles south in Murun, two expectant mothers are staying in the waiting home that Otgonbayar had planned to use. It’s a simple space: six single beds line the walls of the light and airy room, and there’s a basic kitchen next door.

More than 300 of these facilities are dotted across the country, attached to village clinics and provincial hospitals. Women can stay for free, for as long as they need – in Murun, 147 expectant mothers used the waiting home between January and September, for an average of eight days.

Dr Nyam-Ulzii Odkhuu, one of eight gynaecologists at Murun provincial hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Giving birth is actually very difficult here – just imagine the road they have to take and the distances they have to travel, just to give birth to their babies,” said Dr Nyam-Ulzii Odkhuu, one of eight gynaecologists at Murun provincial hospital. “So it’s important to have maternity waiting homes, especially in Khuvsgul, as we have so many remote villages. It’s a necessity.”

The idea is not a new one. In the 1970s and 1980s, an ad-hoc system saw some towns and villages set up specific gers – Mongolia’s traditional, circular tents – so pregnant women from remote herder families could be close to a clinic before their due date.

But then the Soviet Union fell. Although not officially part of the USSR, Mongolia was considered almost a “satellite state” – a socialist nation that was heavily dependent on Russia. When the bloc broke apart, Mongolia faced a “violent economic crisis” and social turmoil that researchers have called the “lost decade”.

Dr Baasanjargal Tsogbadrakh and midwife Byambasuren Ulziijargal making house calls on horseback Credit : Simon Townsley

In this climate the pregnancy gers almost disappeared, fertility rates dropped and the maternal mortality ratio rose, said Dr Buyanjargal Yadamsuren, a former director of medical services at the ministry of health. Until 2001, when the government – which was keen to boost its population size – decided to prioritise maternal health.

“[Waiting homes] were an approach that made sense,” said Dr Yadamsuren. “But when we reintroduced them nationwide, we really focused on strategy – the referral system, the criteria for who should use them, the funding mechanisms, and so on.”

This formalised approach included sending all women with high-risk pregnancies to give birth in provincial hospitals, which are better equipped and able to perform caesareans.

Khaliun Lkhamsuren in the maternal waiting room at Murun provincial hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

News.title: The perilous road to parenthood: Mongolia’s fight to make childbirth safer
News.content:
As the 4x4 raced south, bouncing across Mongolia’s rocky valley roads and dusty forest steppes, an obstetrician was doing her best to ease Otgonbayar Odbayar’s pain and panic.

Hours earlier, the reindeer herder’s waters had broken. But Otgonbayar was six weeks early – and almost 250 miles away from the doctors who could provide the caesarean she knew she needed.

She contacted the nearest clinic, kicking off a relay of calls that spanned the length of Khuvsgul, a region bordering Russia. Soon, a plan came back through the chain: one health team would collect the 26-year-old and sprint south, while doctors from the provincial hospital in Murun would hurtle north. They’d meet in the middle.

Otgonbayar Odbayar with her new baby Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

But Otgonbayar’s three-hour journey was touch and go. “Halfway through, her contractions got very intense and very close together,” said Dr Baasanjargal Tsogbadrakh, the obstetrician who collected her. “She was in a lot of pain. We put her on an IV and were driving so fast.”

They made it to the small clinic in Tugul a little after 11pm, but then faced an excruciating 90 minute wait for the team from Murun, who had further to travel on Mongolia’s rutted roads. Dr Tsogbadrakh didn’t have a Plan B: the baby was in breech position, and the scar from Otgonbayar’s previous c-section still hadn’t fully healed.

Khuvsgul Province in northern Mongolia Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“When [the doctors] arrived, I felt relief,” said Dr Tsogbadrakh. “If we had waited only 30 more minutes to start surgery, no one could tell what would have happened.”

Yet Otgonbayar’s ordeal is now the exception in Mongolia, underscoring just how far the vast country has come in its three-decade drive to tackle the childbirth risks posed by geography.

In 1990, 200 women died for every 100,000 births, but that ratio plunged to 47 by 2015 – making Mongolia one of only nine countries to hit global targets to reduce maternal mortality by 75 per cent over the 25-year period, according to analysis in the Lancet.

Strides have slowed but continued, and the rate now hovers at around 37. By contrast, other countries with a similar maternal mortality ratio in 1990, including Algeria, Brazil, the Philippines and Kiribati, still see more than 70 deaths per 100,000 births, according to Our World in Data.

In a country as vast and sparse as Mongolia – which is more than six times the size of the UK, but home to just 3.5 million people – health gains have been reliant “on overcoming the distance between women and the care they need”, said the health minister Batshugar Enkhbayar.

That has meant introducing telemedicine initiatives to bring specialist advice to remote clinics, waiting homes where pregnant women can stay in the final weeks before delivery, and better trained staff to spot risks before they become acute. In the last year, the country has also started to trial portable ultrasounds.

And, when a mother survives childbirth – like Otgonbayar eventually did – her child is significantly more likely to live, receive an education, and break out of generational poverty, strengthening the community around him or her.

“It was very scary and painful, everything was going wrong,” said Otgonbayar, swaddling her newborn in a pink Peppa Pig blanket. “But I feel lucky now. I’m just so glad I’ve been able to meet my baby.

“He doesn’t look like me, [he looks] exactly like his father,” she added, smiling. “I hope in the future he grows to be a good person, and to be healthy.”

Almost 150 miles south in Murun, two expectant mothers are staying in the waiting home that Otgonbayar had planned to use. It’s a simple space: six single beds line the walls of the light and airy room, and there’s a basic kitchen next door.

News.title: US stocks plummet as Democrat victory sparks investor panic
News.content:
Wall Street suffered its worst sell-off since Donald Trump’s tariff rollout amid fears the Democrats will derail the AI boom.

The Nasdaq 100 plunged more than 6pc on Thursday - the biggest fall since April 2025 - with shares in semiconductor makers the hardest hit.

The downturn was the worst since Mr Trump’s so-called “liberation day”, when he rolled out tariffs to countries around the world.

Investors fear the Democrats’ midterm election victory will usher in tighter restrictions on AI companies, whose valuations have grown rapidly under Mr Trump.

Nvidia, which is the world’s most valuable listed company, fell by more than 6pc while rivals including AMD and Micron plummeted 13pc and 11pc, respectively.

News.title: Can the UK handle an Ebola infection?
News.content:
A British man who has tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is being flown back to the UK for treatment.

The patient, whose identity has not been revealed, but is believed to be a healthcare worker, is said to be in a stable condition.

They will be transferred to a specialist ambulance and then on to the Royal Free hospital, a rare diseases specialist hospital in north London, which houses the UK’s primary high level isolation unit.

Yesterday, a UK government spokesperson said there were “well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this” and that the risk to the public “remains low”.

It is the first confirmed case of a UK national contracting Ebola during the most recent outbreak of the rare but deadly virus in DRC. The first cases of the Bundibugyo strain of the disease were reported in May, and there have so far been more than 10,000 cases and 5,000 deaths, making it the second largest outbreak in history.

How will the British patient be treated?

The immediate priority will be to assess their condition.

On average, symptoms appear between eight to 10 days after exposure, but they can arise as soon as two days and as many as three weeks after infection. Doctors will have to determine how far the virus has progressed and identify any complications that require treatment.

Ebola can cause severe fluid loss, through profuse vomiting and diarrhoea, electrolyte imbalances and in serious cases organ failure. Experts will closely monitor his vital signs and fluid balance, bloods and organ function, providing intravenous fluids and other supportive treatment.

Sports.title: Nuno was a good man who paid ultimate price in unforgiving climate… but Parker can galvanise West Ham’s promotion push
Sports.content:
Next

THERE is something rather sad about the way Nuno Espirito Santo’s time at West Ham ended.

I liked Nuno. I thought he was a decent appointment, a good man and a manager with a proven track record.



But football is unforgiving and ­sentiment has never been an effective way of climbing a league table.

Nuno arrived in September last year with a difficult job.



West Ham were struggling, ­confidence was low and the club was heading in the wrong direction.

He brought some organisation and initially gave supporters reason to believe the season could be rescued.

Ultimately, he could not prevent ­relegation and the challenge of getting West Ham straight back into the Premier League proved as difficult as many had warned.

I don’t think it is fair to put all of that ­failure at his door. West Ham’s problems were bigger than one manager.

There were issues with recruitment, squad balance, confidence and consistency.

A manager can organise the ­furniture but cannot always change the shape of the house.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

When relegation was confirmed, Nuno agreed to stay and lead the fight for an immediate return.

But West Ham were not entering the Championship as an ordinary club with modest expectations.

There were encouraging moments. At times, West Ham looked capable of overwhelming Championship opposition, and Nuno had his team challenging towards the top of the table.



But defeats by Southampton and West Brom, both at the London ­Stadium, were particularly damaging.

Returning to a club where he is so well regarded gives him the chance to write a different chapter.

Sports.title: ‘It’s not fair on him’ – Robbie Savage hasn’t spoken to son Charlie all week ahead of facing off in FA Cup

ROBBIE SAVAGE admits it is going to feel “horrible” if he were to face son Charlie in tomorrow’s FA Cup first round.

Peterborough host Reading at The Weston Homes Stadium with both League One sides dreaming of a deep run in the competition.



More than a month into the job, new Posh boss Robbie, 52, concedes it has felt strange plotting for Reading’s downfall given that his son could be selected to play for the opposition.

Understandably, the pair have chosen not to talk this week – normally they would speak in the build-up to a match – because they feel it would be unfair to either team.



Midfielder Charlie, 23, was an 84th-minute sub in Reading’s 2-0 loss at rivals Oxford on Wednesday but due to this weekend’s unique circumstances, they have not had a debrief chat.

From an emotional perspective, it has not been an easy week for proud dad Robbie, whose other son Freddie is also involved in football.

Speaking to SunSport, Savage Snr said: “I’ve played against him in the garden numerous times – where I used to always beat him, and Freddie, too.

“He used to get aggressive. I always used to beat him in a one-v-one situation! But it’s going to be horrible. If he does start, it’s not going to be a nice feeling.

“Because we’re trying to beat Reading, who’re flying in the league. I’ve not been able to speak to him all week. After his last match, as a dad, I’ve not been able to say to him: ‘How did you do?’

“I always speak to him in a positive way. And this is only the first occasion since his loan time at Forest Green Rovers where I’ve not been able to speak to him for the week.

“Listen, my two sons are my life.

“Regardless if he plays or not, we need a win to progress in the competition. I know there’s a lot being made about Savage vs Savage, but it’s not.

“It’s Peterborough United vs Reading and Charlie might not play. We’ve just got to put a team out there to beat Reading. But it’s going to be a horrible situation.”



Robbie is proud of how Charlie left the family home three years ago for the Royals, having been a Manchester United trainee, and coped on his own as he pursued his footballing ambitions.

The former Leicester, Derby, Birmingham and Wales midfielder – who could blood some young Posh teenagers on the bench on Saturday – admires the way Charlie dealt with the adversity.

AFTER six qualifying rounds, we have finally reached the first round proper of the FA Cup!

Clubs from League One and Two are now joining the competition as 40 ties will take place this weekend.



Premier League and Championship clubs don’t enter the FA Cup until the third round, which takes place on the weekend of Saturday, January 9 2027.

2021 winners Leicester are in the first round of the competition this year after dropping down to the third tier last season – they face Oxford City tonight.



It is the first time the Foxes will face a non-league side since 2008, when they beat Stevenage 3-0.

Wigan, who won the FA Cup in 2013 against Manchester City, face a trip to National League Boreham Wood this weekend as the Tics look to keep their dream of returning to Wembley alive.



Do FA Cup 1st round ties go to extra-time or straight to penalties?

FA Cup first round ties go to extra-time if the scores are level after 90 minutes.

The rules come from replays being scrapped in the 2024/25 season as part of an agreement between the FA and the Premier League.

Replays were an integral part of the competition for over 150 years, but after the expansion of Uefa‘s club competitions, fixture congestion was a key reason for them being removed.

It was a controversial decision when announced, with the traditions of the competition being changed and smaller clubs arguing that replays could be a vital source of income if they were drawn a trip to a big stadium.



It means every game must be decided on the day, and so extra-time is utilised throughout the FA Cup.

Sports.title: ‘The message was clear’ - Vasseur holds Hamilton-Leclerc meeting after clash
Sports.content:
Ferrari boss Frederic Vasseur says he reminded Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc that the team comes first after their first-lap clash in Mexico in a meeting ahead of this weekend's Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

The lap-one incident between the Ferrari drivers in last Sunday's race, which saw both cars run wide track at Turn Four in battle for the lead, ultimately opened the door for Red Bull's Max Verstappen to win the race.

Hamilton has subsequently been critical of Leclerc in interviews and said that discussions were required to more clearly define their rules of combat to avoid costly repeats in future.

Vasseur confirmed talks did take place on Thursday evening at Interlagos.

"We did it [talked] yesterday evening because I had to fly back to Europe between the two races, but it went well," said Vasseur in Friday's team principals' press conference.

"It was good to discuss, good to clarify my position and their position - that it was good to do.

"Now we turn the page and we are focused on the next one."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Craig Slater outlines what's been the aftermath at Ferrari after Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc's controversial opening lap incident at Mexico City

Asked about the detail of the meeting, Vasseur said: "The guidelines is still the same. They accumulated perhaps a bit of frustration because they are starting each weekend side by side, and you have a kind of accumulation of fact.

"But at the end of the day, the guideline is always the same - it's that they need to respect each other.

"They are two competitors with the fighting spirit for sure, but they need to have a respect for the other one.

"But mainly and firstly, they need to respect the brand, the team, the people working at home, the people working at the on track.

"I think we are putting a lot of effort on this, and the message was clear and will stay clear."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton was left furious after Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc overtook him on the opening lap while leaving the track but was only given a five-second penalty for the infringement

Pressed on whether the drivers had agreed in the meeting that they would be able to work together in future to ensure Ferrari win races, Vasseur replied: "When I said that the message was clear, it's that overall, I think it's true for Ferrari, but it's true for every single team on the grid is that they are working for the team and the team has to come first.

"For sure, in this situation, we failed collectively because that we were one-two and we didn't win the race at the end. It's clear that we failed, and we have to react, but the conclusion of the meeting yesterday evening was clear, that it was a clear reminder that the Ferrari is coming first, coming first for the brand, for the employees, for the Tifosi and this we have to keep it in mind."

'I will deal with the negative' - Vasseur happy to manage competitive pairing

After a difficult first year in red for Hamilton in 2025, the Ferrari team-mates have proved one of the most closely-matched on the grid this year with little to choose in their head-to-head records.

Leclerc leads qualifying 10-9 while Hamilton is ahead by the same score for race-day results.

Third-placed Hamilton is 14 points ahead of Leclerc in the Drivers' Championship with four races to go, with the team set to finish second to Mercedes in the constructors' standings - a two-place improvement on last year.

And while Vasseur acknowledges that the events of Mexico were probably a "downside" to having two fast drivers in the same team, he said he would prefer to have that situation and to deal with the flashpoints.

"We have two experienced guys, two competitive guys," he said. "Now it's four or five races in a row that we are at the front, scoring the highest number of points after Monza or Madrid.

"For sure, you have a kind of escalation that you all want to win races, and I think it's probably the downside of the system is that we have two competitive guys starting each weekend next to each other.

"But I think if we are P2 today [in the Constructors' Championship], it's also because we have two guys very, very close, and we have to manage it.

"But it's a choice. It's a choice in the line-up, and I have the positive and the negative. But I will deal with the negative."

He also played down Hamilton's suggestion on Thursday that Leclerc raced him harder than drivers at rival teams.

"He said that he was fighting a bit harder with him than with some other [drivers]," said Vasseur.

"But if you have a look on what Charles did in in Austin in the first section, everybody said that he was magic.

"The line is fine between the two, but he didn't crash into the other car, also. That was not an aggression."

Sports.title: Ex-NFL receiver Brown avoids prison after pleading guilty to reduced charge
Sports.content:
Former Pittsburgh Steelers, New England Patriots and Tampa Bay Buccaneers wide receiver Antonio Brown could have faced up to 30 years in prison if convicted of the original attempted murder charge; Brown, 38, says he wants to "get back to life" and his family

Former NFL wide receiver Antonio Brown has avoided jail time after pleading guilty to aggravated assault with a firearm in connection with a 2025 shooting outside a celebrity boxing match Miami.

Judge Marisa Tinkler Mendez sentenced the 38-year-old to three years of probation, during which time he will have to attend weekly counselling sessions and not possess a firearm, among other conditions.

Speaking outside the court, Brown said he wanted to "get back to life" and his family.

His lawyer, Mark Eiglarsh, said: "My client was facing 30 years in prison with a 20-year minimum mandatory, and he was given an offer he just couldn't refuse. Probation was too good to turn down, and we're both very excited about the outcome."

The plea to the reduced charge means the All-Pro wide receiver - who played for the Pittsburgh Steelers from 2010-2018 before spells with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, where he won the Super Bowl in 2021, and the New England Patriots - has avoided a criminal conviction.

He had had initially been charged with attempted murder after police say he grabbed a handgun from a member of security at the boxing event and fired two shots at a man he had been in a fistfight with earlier.

Brown insisted he was defending himself from an attack as others were trying to steal jewellery from him.

Florida's Stand Your Ground law allows people who believe they face death or serious injury to use deadly force to defend themselves without a duty to retreat.

Prosecutor Howard Rosen said his office was seeking to reduce the charge against Brown because there was "a question" of whether he was actually attempting to shoot the victim, who had been walking away from the altercation at the time.

He noted the victim Zul-Qarnain Kwame Nantambu, who was grazed in the neck, was in court for the hearing and has said publicly that he did not want to press charges.

Rosen said: "Rather than the entire case going away and there being no opportunity for Mr Brown to receive what's ultimately going to be therapeutic treatment, we all came together - the defense and the state - and decided this was in the best interest of everybody."

The victim's lawyer, Richard Cooper, said in a statement: "We are grateful to the court for ratifying this carefully crafted agreement. We have maintained we wish Mr Brown healing."

Sports.title: Billam-Smith stares down Clarke and promises 'violent' fight
Sports.content:
Chris Billam-Smith and Cheavon Clarke finished the ceremonial weigh-in with a wide-eyed staredown.

Billam-Smith maintained a steely, unblinking glare until Clarke looked away.

They box on Saturday night at the Copper Box Arena, live on Sky Sports, and Billam-Smith pledged simply that the fight would be "a violent one".

Does that mean he intends to end it inside the distance? "Absolutely."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ahead of Chris Billam-Smith's Zuffa Boxing 12 main event against Chev Clarke, here's a look back at The Gentleman's best moments.

Clarke though has beaten Billam-Smith before, defeating him twice in amateur bouts a decade ago.

"Twenty-five-year-old me will be very happy tomorrow night," Billam-Smith said.

"[Clarke] is going to be confident, he's come off a good win but I know what I'm capable of and that's all that matters."

He might have beaten the Bournemouth man as an amateur, but Clarke has been overshadowed by Billam-Smith as a pro. He wants to change that on Saturday.

"After tomorrow night you guys will be talking my name," Clarke said. "It's going to be explosive.

"It's been a very, very tough camp. Come tomorrow night you guys will see."

Mosley missed weight on first attempt

Shane Mosley Jr missed weight on the first attempt for his middleweight clash with Denzel Bentley.

Mosley fights Bentley in the chief support to Billam-Smith vs Clarke on Saturday.

The son of boxing legend Shane Mosley, the American contender took to the scales on Friday morning for the official weigh-in.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Shane Mosley Jr produced the performance of his career as he floored Serhii Bohachuk in the sixth round before forcing an impressive stoppage win.

Tall and big for the weight, Mosley looked gaunt as he stepped on to the scales. Stripping to shave off some additional weight, he stepped on to the scales behind a screen but was still one pound over the middleweight limit for his first attempt.

London's Bentley looked in fine condition as he hit the 160lb limit exactly. He stayed to watch Mosley return to the scales. The American took almost the full hour to shed the final pound but did so, having to strip again. The fight is on.

"He's made the weight now, hopefully rehydrates nice and healthy and we have a good fight tomorrow," Bentley told Sky Sports. "It's not his first time making middleweight. I feel fit and well that gives me confidence, the fact that I feel so good.

"That's what makes it a good fight, both of us are confident. We haven't got to be at each other's throats to make a fight. We're both respectful but we're letting each other know I think I'm coming out the victor."

Mosley Jr dismissed the weight miss as a 'miscalculation'.

"I just miscalculated a little bit but we got it done," he said later. "I win this fight on points, outclass him.

"You know I'm ready, I can't wait."

Image: Shane Mosley Jr on the scales on Friday morning (Photo: Zuffa Boxing)

Clarke made weight easily, scaling 198.8lbs. For Billam-Smith it was a harder cut but he came in at 199.5lbs.

Both Billam-Smith and Clarke are coming off thrilling wins, beating Ryan Rozicki and Jack Massey respectively in barnstorming bouts in Bournemouth in June. That put the two on a collision course.

Zuffa Boxing promoter Dana White told Sky Sports: "It's always about putting on the best fights with the best fighters. After his showing in the main event in Bournemouth was incredible. Every time you have a fight a different storyline is built and different guys that build to bigger and better fights.

"Styles make fights and stylistically that should be a fun fight. CBS and Rozicki was one of the craziest fights I've ever seen and it really put those two on the map now in the boxing scene. So hopefully we get another one of those."

Watch Billam-Smith vs Clarke on Saturday live on Sky Sports.

Sports.title: George: England players hurt by 'shocking' report of rift with Borthwick
Sports.content:
Jamie George says England's players were "hurt" by a newspaper report of a rift with head coach Steve Borthwick in the summer, calling the timing of the article "shocking" ahead of Sunday's Nations Championship clash with Australia.

The Times reported that some England players lost faith in Borthwick during a summer campaign with included a 45-21 defeat to world champions South Africa and a nervy win over Argentina.

It is alleged players objected to Borthwick's treatment of them, that he was involved in a training ground bust-up with Ellis Genge and that they wanted RFU chief executive Bill Sweeney - who this week unequivocally backed the head coach - to listen to their gripes.

Speaking to Sky Sports News on Friday, hooker George, captain for the July tour with Maro Itoje rested and named in the starting XV to face the Wallabies this weekend, says the squad addressed the article and will use it to "galavanise" them.

Image: George (left) says everyone in the England squad is behind Borthwick

The 36-year-old, who insisted England are "all massively behind Steve in every way possible" said: "I'm really disappointed with the article that's been written. There's not a huge amount of truth to any of it, really.

"I think the timing of it is shocking, to be completely honest. Releasing it two days before a Test match is always trying to be divisive, in my opinion.

"I think that we're all quite hurt. We have made sure that we aren't distracted by it, but also allowing us to be galvanised by it, in a way, because we want to defend Steve.

There was a review process, as there always is with a tour, or the Six Nations or an Autumn Nations series, like there will be in six weeks. There were really good chats in and around the environment that we want to have, the team that we want to be, the key learnings that we took away from the tour and we're a better team for it.

"We are all massively behind Steve in every way possible. I think probably, unfortunately for them, it won't be divisive and it might be quite galvanising for us."

'We have to look after Steve in every way we know how'

George continued: "We had to address it. I spoke to [captain] Maro [Itoje] last night. I don't like elephants in rooms.

"I just think that everything is much better out in the open. And we did exactly that. Maro spoke brilliantly, opened it up. George Ford then spoke brilliantly. It's done now.

"We're upset by it. We are disappointed with it.

"At the same time, we're seeing it for what it is and understanding that we've got a really important role to step up now and look after Steve in every way that we know how.

"The best way to do that is by putting out a brilliant performance on Sunday."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player England head coach Borthwick says his contract extension has not changed the focus on the 2027 World Cup

'Baxter one of best I have played with'

Harlequins' Fin Baxter, who has only played two games since returning from 10 months out with a foot injury, will start at loosehead prop against Australia, with George lavishing praise on the 24-year-old.

George added of Baxter: "I am going to be very careful as I don't want to give too many superlatives to Fin but I honestly think he is one of the best props I have played with.

"He is physically incredible with a baby face, which I love. He is strong. But the thing about Fin I love the most is his game-feel, his understanding.

"As a loosehead prop, there aren't many in the world that are able to do it in the way he does. He is a huge asset to our team."

Image: Fin Baxter will start at loosehead prop against Australia on Sunday

After facing Australia on Sunday (3.10pm kick-off), England go on to play Japan and New Zealand on November 14 and November 21 respectively, before the Nations Championship finals weekend across November 27-29.

England XV to face Australia: 15. George Furbank; 14. Tommy Freeman, 13. Henry Slade, 12. Seb Atkinson, 11. Immanuel Feyi-Waboso; 10. Fin Smith, 9. Jack van Poortvliet; 1. Fin Baxter, 2. Jamie George, 3. Joe Heyes, 4. Maro Itoje, 5. Alex Coles, 6. Ollie Chessum, 7. Ben Curry, 8. Ben Earl.

Replacements: 16. Luke Cowan-Dickie, 17. Ellis Genge, 18. Will Stuart, 19. George Martin, 20. Greg Fisilau, 21. Henry Pollock, 22. Ben Spencer, 23. Marcus Smith.

Sports.title: Everton v Coventry City: Premier League – live
Sports.content:
now 14.59 EST It’s that time … … so here come the players. No sounding of the usual siren, as a mark of respect on remembrance weekend. Everton in their royal blue, Coventry in second-choice white tops. We’ll be off once the Last Post has sounded. RIP the fallen. Share

6m ago 14.54 EST Mr 592 II talks to Sky. “I’m really proud of [equalling Harry Catterick’s record] to be honest … it’s not easy for any manager to manage one club for 592 games … the world we’re in now, managers don’t get that long … so I’ve been really privileged to work under really good people who gave me the opportunity to manage this club … the first time here was a lot longer … this time has been just a couple of years but I'm enjoying it … Coventry are a good side … they won the Championship well … they started slow in the Premier League but they’re back in it now … I want to see if [Tyler Dibling] can do it on the main stage … see more from him … it’s a good opportunity to give him.” Share

11m ago 14.48 EST Pre-match postbag: Evertonians Telling It As They See It edition. “Greetings from almost liberated California. The thrashing of a certain ‘orange’ gentleman has allowed me to have zero anxiety about today’s Everton tilt. I’m happy no matter what happens” – Mary Waltz “I admire the optimism of Everton potentially going into fourth with a five-goal margin of victory today. I watch almost every single game and I struggled to recall the last time they scored five in the league; turns out it was the famous 5-1 win at Brighton in May 2023 that helped them stay up that season. At home, we have to go back to September 2020 when they beat West Brom 5-2 behind closed doors at Goodison. The last time in front of home fans? Their 6-3 win over Bournemouth in February 2017 when Romelu Lukaku scored four. Let’s just say Everton aren’t generally banging in goals for fun” – Matt Burtz Share Updated at 14.49 EST

21m ago 14.39 EST Coventry boss Frank Lampard - who having managed Everton 44 times, sits just 548 games behind the total David Moyes will be hitting tonight – speaks to Sky Sports. “I saw [the Hill Dickinson Stadium] in its early stages … it’s amazing to see the end product … what a stadium for a great football club … good to be here … but it’s more about the game … [Everton] are a strong team … [Coventry] are in a good moment … a good feeling [after the Sunderland win] … we have to show it consistently … reproduce good things … be on our game … [Jack Rudoni] believes in his talent … he’s got a lot of it … he’s said ‘give me the ball and I’ll show you what I can do at this level’ … hopefully that rubs off on other players.” Share Updated at 14.39 EST

45m ago 14.15 EST To the excited chatter of playgrounds up and down the country members of a certain jaded generation, this fixture is a re-run of the 1987 General Motors FA Charity Shield. Coventry, who had won the FA Cup just nine weeks previously, took 35,000 fans to Wembley, a record for the season curtain-raiser, while Everton supporters, making their eighth appearance at the grand old pile in four years, were comparatively thin on the ground. But the latter were the ones who got to celebrate, Wayne Clarke scoring the only goal just before the break, while Kevin Ratcliffe popped Cov’s new £750,000 record signing David Speedie in his pocket. All the post-match talk was of Everton retaining their First Division title: they ended the season in fourth; City, hoping to build on their breakthrough cup win, finished tenth. Both clubs were slightly disappointed with those returns back then; they’d deal on them for this season, right here, right now. View image in fullscreen Will Coventry City finally put the ghosts of the 1987 Charity Shield defeat to rest? Photograph: Mark Leech/Offside/Getty Images Share Updated at 14.55 EST

55m ago 14.05 EST Moyes: 592 up! David Moyes = Harry Catterick. Well, not quite: Top Catt did win two league titles (1963 and 1970) and Everton’s first FA Cup in 33 years (1966) after all. But in another way: yes! Our man Tom Garry reports. double quotation mark With David Moyes tonight set to equal Harry Catterick’s all-time record of 592 matches in charge of Everton across his two spells at the club, his colleague, the Everton women’s team head coach Scott Phelan, has spoken of his fond memories of his role as a ball boy on the day of Moyes’ first match at the helm at Goodison Park in 2002.



Phelan, now aged 38, is a former Everton academy player and he said: “The opportunity to be a ball boy was a big thing. I think I was 14, 15 years of age. Just seeing the players close up, with the best seat in the house, was something I’ll always remember. The sense of occasion, the atmosphere and [Moyes] starting on a positive footing is what I remember.



“What he is about to achieve is really important in his own career but, for this club as well, he’s brought stability in his first and second phase. I have massive respect for him and what he has achieved here.



“He’s had an amazing career. Hopefully he can celebrate with a win.” Everton’s Harry Catterick is the forgotten great of British managers Read more Share Updated at 14.08 EST

1h ago 13.57 EST Coventry City are in If It Ain’t Broke mode. They’re unchanged following last weekend’s 3-1 home win over Sunderland. Bobby Thomas is getting back up to speed after a calf issue but is not risked. Sakamoto sparks Coventry win to keep 10-man Sunderland rock-bottom Read more Share Updated at 14.07 EST

Sports.title: Bellinghams celebrate ‘beautiful story’ as Jobe joins Jude in Tuchel’s England 2.0
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel has given a first England call-up to Jobe Bellingham, admitting the midfielder’s older brother, Jude, had nagged him to do so, as he set up the prospect of their family dream being realised.

Tuchel’s inclusion of the younger Bellingham for the Nations League ties against Croatia and Spain was further evidence of his shift away from the squad that served him well at the World Cup last summer and towards a fresh dynamic for the mission to win Euro 2028. The manager has named a 25-man group for the game against Croatia at Wembley on Thursday and the one against Spain in Madrid three days after; of the 22 outfield players, only 11 were at the World Cup.

Jobe Bellingham, the England Under-21s captain, has impressed for Borussia Dortmund this season and Jude is on record as saying how much it would mean if they could play together for their country, especially at a major tournament. “It would be the biggest dream of my life,” he said. “It would mean more than any of the trophies I have won.”

Tuchel said the brothers coming together in his England squad was a “beautiful story” and he wondered whether Jobe’s presence could inspire Jude to even greater heights. “Let’s see what the effect is,” Tuchel said. “Jude always behaves like a big brother, taking care of his younger brother. I think that helps Jobe now in camp. And it will be beautiful for Jude to have his brother close.

“Me and Jude spoke about his brother because I was aware it was always his dream [to play for England with Jobe]. Jude was always like: ‘Watch him, watch him, he’s good, he can make it.’ I would say: ‘Yeah, we are watching him.’ And we know, of course, [about him] from Lee Carsley [the under-21s manager].”

Tuchel described Jobe as “maybe more a No 8 than a classic 6 and less of a 10”. He noted that with Myles Lewis-Skelly suspended against Croatia, Jobe’s chances of being involved were higher. It has been 19 years since Gary and Phil Neville were the last brothers to play together for England.

Quick Guide England squad Show Goalkeepers Jordan Pickford (Everton), Jason Steele (Brighton), James Trafford (Leeds United) Defenders Trent Alexander-Arnold (Real Madrid), Jarrad Branthwaite (Everton), Marc Guéhi (Manchester City), Lewis Hall (Newcastle United), Ezri Konsa (Arsenal), Jarell Quansah (Bayer Leverkusen), Djed Spence (Inter), Ben White (Arsenal) Midfielders Elliot Anderson (Manchester City), Jobe Bellingham (Borussia Dortmund), Jude Bellingham (Real Madrid), James Garner (Everton), Josh King (Fulham), Myles Lewis-Skelly (Arsenal), Declan Rice (Arsenal) Forwards Dominic Calvert-Lewin (Leeds United), Eberechi Eze (Arsenal), Morgan Gibbs-White (Nottingham Forest), Anthony Gordon (Barcelona), Harry Kane (Bayern Munich), Rio Ngumoha (Liverpool), Morgan Rogers (Chelsea) Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Tuchel accidentally referred to Jobe as “Jube” at one point, a slip that will doubtless be made by others, and said it was a special moment to break the news of the call-up to him on a video call. “He couldn’t stop smiling,” Tuchel said. “He has the same beautiful smile as Jude.”

It is clear that Tuchel’s relationship with Jude Bellingham is on a secure footing, as opposed to this time last year when the player’s place in the squad was in doubt – and certainly his spot in the XI. “It was a bit of an up and down [relationship] but we are in a good place,” Tuchel said. “I hope we have finished with the down. You never know as a coach!”

More broadly, Tuchel looked reinvigorated after the success of the September/October camp when his team won three out of four Nations League ties to all but guarantee a place in the quarter-finals. Tuchel had been tense at the start of the get-together as he was assailed by the fallout from the World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina.

View image in fullscreen Thomas Tuchel also gave a call-up to Fulham’s 19-year-old playmaker Josh King for the matches against Croatia and Spain. Photograph: Tiego Grenho/Every Second Media/Shutterstock

He made some ruthless decisions in September, discarding Noni Madueke, Ollie Watkins and Ivan Toney from the squad he took to the World Cup. Dean Henderson, Dan Burn and Jordan Henderson, picked in the summer and fit again, have been left out, while Kobbie Mainoo and Nico O’Reilly, who is a managing an injury, were also not selected. He overlooked Cole Palmer and Phil Foden. Missing through injury are Reece James, Tino Livramento, John Stones, Trevoh Chalobah, Alex Scott, Bukayo Saka and Marcus Rashford.

Tuchel has placed an emphasis on youth in his post-World Cup selections and he added Josh King to the squad on Friday. The 19-year-old attacking midfielder’s only previous involvement was at the pre-World Cup training camp in Florida. Tuchel has also given a recall to the more experienced right-back Ben White.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It was put to Tuchel that his squad had the look of an England 2.0. “It has to be like this,” he said. “We said at some point that we need to take the next step, otherwise you’re left behind. You need to bring in new players for competition; young players, fresh energy. I was a bit worried in the last camp because we were missing so many internal leaders but the group did excellently in a new style, in a new leadership way but in their style. Now there’s a little bit of proof of concept. We give the players the opportunity and responsibility.”

Tuchel namechecked his current leaders as Harry Kane, Saka, Jude Bellingham, Elliot Anderson, Declan Rice, Ezri Konsa and Marc Guéhi. He said he had spoken to them on day one of the last camp – although not Rice, because he had withdrawn – about the need for them “to make sure we have the same standards as at the World Cup”.

Were the seven players the leadership group? “Per se,” Tuchel replied. “I said straight away that I want to have a group that starts matches regularly. These were the players – without having a guarantee. But I said: ‘I want you to start these matches and you make sure that the energy, attitude, the standards within the group are at the highest level.’ That has not changed. So they are basically a leadership group on the field.”

Tuchel said Palmer’s exclusion was “not personal … but the competition is on. It’s about the ones who walk the walk and come to camp”. He made it sound as if Foden was closer to a recall.

“Phil is always an option because I’m in love with him as a player,” Tuchel said. “It was very close. It’s also close for Eberechi Eze to keep his place with us. He’s not starting for Arsenal. The advantage was maybe that Eberechi and Morgan Gibbs-White were in camp last time. They need to fight for it. That’s what we want. And Phil is always close.”

Tuchel also commented on Mainoo’s omission. He took the midfielder to the World Cup but did not play him. “He was hugely disappointed from the World Cup and deservedly so,” Tuchel said. “I said in front of the team and the staff: ‘Sorry, I didn’t pick you. You did nothing wrong. That is on me.’ I think it cost him a bit of confidence. Then he pulled out of the last camp when I was desperate to include him in this new start. And then he entered a difficult spell. He was injured and Man United fell off a cliff a little bit performance-wise.”

Sports.title: Premier League news: United’s Baleba out for weeks, Maresca backs Donnarumma
Sports.content:
1. Baleba facing weeks out in blow for Carrick Michael Carrick has revealed Carlos Baleba will be out for weeks with the hamstring injury the Manchester United midfielder sustained in Tuesday’s 3-2 victory over Roma. Baleba’s absence is a considerable blow to Carrick as he attempts to turn around United’s form and results. The 22-year-old Cameroonian was signed from Brighton in the summer for £70m and had made a promising start. But before Tuesday’s injury he had managed only seven appearances, the first on 10 October after recovering from an ankle problem he had when he joined. “It’ll be a number of weeks,” Carrick said. “It’s definitely not this week and it won’t be any time over the international break [which starts on Monday]. It’ll be a little bit longer than that. Carrick also gave an update on Patrick Dorgu, who has been unavailable since sustaining a hamstring problem with Denmark during the last international break. “He trained with us at the start of the week, so we’ve got to be patient with Pat,” said Carrick. “He’s had a good period of time now with a couple of hamstrings that we need to manage. But he’s slowly getting back with us, so we’ll have to see whether he can be involved at the weekend.” Friday marked the 40th anniversary of Alex Ferguson’s appointment as United manager. Before Sunday’s visit of Aston Villa, Carrick was asked whether it was possible for him to reach the standards achieved by Ferguson at Old Trafford. United are 17th, separated from the relegation zone by goal difference. “It’s not impossible,” said Carrick. “Anything’s possible. You’ve got to build, you’ve got to be realistic. You’ve got to put things in perspective as well, [with] the recent history that we’ve had and where we want to get to. It’s not going to happen in a blink of an eye. Success does take time, and we don’t like having to spend time, but it does take a period of time to build.” Jamie Jackson

2. Maresca backs Donnarumma to bounce back Gianluigi Donnarumma has been backed by Enzo Maresca to rediscover his best form after high-profile mistakes in recent games. The Manchester City goalkeeper has made three errors leading to goals this season, notably against RB Leipzig on Wednesday when he was badly caught out of position. Donnarumma will keep his place when City travel to Nottingham Forest on Saturday evening, aiming to end a run of two Premier League defeats in a row. The hosts are yet to score at home and sit second from bottom. “Overall he’s good,” Maresca said of his compatriot. “He’s quite relaxed, in terms of he recognises that he has done some mistakes but at the same time, as I said after the last game, also he has made some good saves. So it’s just a matter of balance, try to avoid mistakes and continue to do the right things.” Donnarumma’s position is not under threat from his deputy, Gerónimo Rulli. “There are players that when they make some mistake you need a conversation with them, and there are players that when they make some mistake you just need eye contact to understand that he recognises, he knows,” Maresca said. “With Gigio it’s quite easy because every time he has made some mistake or something that was not correct, he recognises immediately. I spoke with Gigio, but again sometimes you don’t need to be so deep with some players.” Nico O’Reilly is available but was left out of the England squad on Friday because he is not fully fit. The left-back will have treatment over the next fortnight for a back problem. Will Unwin

3. Rice determined to hit ‘another level’, says Arteta Mikel Arteta has lauded Declan Rice’s “desperate” determination to improve after the midfielder was one of five Arsenal players called up to Thomas Tuchel’s England squad. Rice has contributed five Premier League assists this season – the most of any player – and a Champions League goal. Asked what had changed in Rice’s performance, Arteta said: “The mentality to go out and win football matches and to add another level to his game, another kind of threat and be much more unpredictable, and we’ve been working a lot on that. “He’s desperate to improve every part of his game, and we need to do that while we maintain so many incredible things that he’s already done, but he’s on the right trajectory.” View image in fullscreen Declan Rice is one of five Arsenal players in the England squad. Photograph: Kieran McManus/Shutterstock Arteta agreed Rice had strengthened his ball progression, and explained his thinking behind dropping the 27-year-old deeper. “We cannot restrict his qualities and his capacities,” Arteta said. “He can drop back, he can progress play. He can drop back, he can carry the ball, he can be incredible in transition. “He can win duels. He can produce passes by arriving, by playing far, by crossing the ball left or right, it doesn’t matter. On set pieces [too], he’s got a lot to offer. His shooting ability from long range as well is something that we need to use more.” PA

Sports.title: Matthias Jaissle caught in the storm as Newcastle struggle without European fix
Sports.content:
At least Matthias Jaissle has a sense of humour. “There’s a lot of storm at the moment,” reflected Newcastle’s head coach on Thursday. A wry smile suggested he was not referring to the north-east weather. Jaissle has seen his tactics, team selection, man management and entire philosophy rubbished in recent days but, on current evidence, appears to be holding his nerve. After all, it is not Jaissle’s fault that his appointment has coincided with supporters, players and directors struggling to adjust to life without Champions League involvement.

A disappointing 12th-place finish under Eddie Howe last season dictates that there are no more exciting trips to Barcelona, Paris and Marseille and, significantly, no much-needed boost to club finances. Indeed, Newcastle are finding life without last term’s continental fix so tricky that they travel to Fulham on Saturday with the disgruntled mindset of a passenger accustomed to flying business class who suddenly finds themselves stuck in a cramped, mid-row economy seat.

Even worse, many fans regard the trip to Craven Cottage as a full-blown relegation six-pointer. Given Newcastle are 13th on 11 points that, ostensibly, is somewhat hysterical. Yet anyone who has watched the bulk of Newcastle’s games this season will understand the reasons underpinning the sense of panic. And if Jaissle bears some responsibility for a run of four defeats in the past five games in all competitions, Newcastle’s unwanted club record-breaking run of 14 home league matches without a clean sheet stretches back into last season.

While Jaissle’s bloody-mindedness in persisting with a 4-2-3-1 formation when he lacks both a natural No 10 and pace and mobility in central midfield merits scrutiny, he was not responsible for close-season recruitment. Ross Wilson, the sporting director, signed eight players all aged 24 or under for a combined £262.9m. Only three – Amar Dedic, Nico González and Lukas Hornicek – are likely starters at present. A fourth, Sean Steur, an 18-year-old acquired from Ajax looks potentially top-drawer but Jaissle refuses to overplay him and risk attendant physical overload.

Fingers are duly being pointed at Wilson but the need to comply with football’s spending rules explains why Newcastle sold their three best players – Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães – last summer. The resultant vacuum left Wilson taking calculated gambles on inexperienced youngsters, including Matias Fernandez-Pardo, a £51m forward signed from Lille, Bazoumana Touré, a £42m winger signed from Hoffenheim, and Aladji Bamba, a £30m midfielder from Monaco. Newcastle’s Saudi Arabian owners hope they will prove unpolished gems with high resale values, but only one of those eight new faces, González, possesses Premier League experience. Throw in a youthful, relatively inexperienced manager and the risk is obvious.

View image in fullscreen Matias Fernandez-Pardo arrived on Tyneside from Lille. Photograph: Richard Lee/Shutterstock

While football’s financial regulations have triggered such wholesale player trading at a moment when Newcastle’s commercial revenues fail to match their ambitions, it did not help that Howe hoarded first-teamers, consistently resisting the opportunity to sell stars at peak value. Indeed, Alexander Isak only joined Liverpool for £125m last year after going on strike. The absence of a sporting director at that time left Howe and his nephew, Andy Howe, then a senior Newcastle recruitment executive, heavily involved in reinvesting the cash. The best part of £225m was poured into signing Nick Woltemade, Yoane Wissa, Anthony Elanga and Jacob Ramsey, but that quartet have collectively underwhelmed.

When a disillusioned, burned-out Howe quit three weeks before the new season, Wilson and Newcastle’s chief executive, David Hopkinson, had already lined up his successor. Jaissle’s much-vaunted attacking brand of so-called vertical football had secured two Asian Champions Leagues at Al-Ahli. On Tyneside, though, such ‘verticality’ has frequently turned into a series of optimistic long balls punctuating matches that frequently see Newcastle’s midfield overrun, forwards isolated and defenders exposed. Given that possession retention has long been a problem for a team arguably at their best when choreographed in contain-and-counter mode, Jaissle’s blueprint appears overly ambitious.

View image in fullscreen Matthias Jaissle criticised his Newcastle players for disobeying orders in their 1-0 defeat by Everton. Photograph: Richard Sellers/Allstar Picture Library/Sportsphoto

Newcastle’s formidable attacking pace menaces on the break but the manager’s plan during the 1-0 home defeat against Everton last Monday was to bisect the visiting lines courtesy of sharp incisive passing along the ground. It did not work and afterwards Jaissle criticised his players for disobeying orders, insisting “shooting long balls” had never been on the agenda. “It was not the plan and that is something you need to clearly mention,” he told reporters.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

By Thursday Jaissle looked considerably happier, insisting there was no discord between management and players. “Everyone believes in the long-term project,” he said. Jaissle had apparently been encouraged by his shot-shy players’ willingness to 

One thing remains clear: after describing Jaissle as “fire” and a “rock star” – not to mention paying Al-Ahli £9.5m to release him – Hopkinson will not sack the 38-year-old German lightly. He and Wilson are standing resolutely by their man.

“Everyone’s aware of, and realistic, about the journey ahead and where we are right now,” said Jaissle. “The nice part is that I get even more the feeling from the club of how committed they are.”
