Sports.title: "Exhausted" Russell set for Brazilian F1 grid penalty
Sports.content:
Mercedes driver George Russell will lose five places on Sunday's Formula 1 Brazilian Grand Prix grid as he takes his sixth internal combustion engine of the season.

Following a brace of power unit related issues earlier this year, the latest arriving after a failure at the Bahrain GP in Malaysia, Russell was always going to require a sixth ICE before the end of the year.

With Lewis Hamilton's spectacular sprint recovery from 20th to fifth in mind, which he pulled off at the 2021 edition with Mercedes, the team felt Interlagos was as good a place as any to take it.

As Russell had already exceeded his initial allowance of four units for the season in Singapore, his additional engine only costs a five-place grid penalty.

"We always had to take a grid penalty at some point between Singapore and the end of the year and we felt like a good place to take it," Russell said on Mercedes' social media channels.

"Obviously, Lewis took a very big penalty here a number of years ago and did pretty well. Five places isn't that bad."

George Russell, Mercedes, Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

Planned or not, it's Russell's latest setback after a nightmarish 2026 campaign in which he was never able to build up momentum and ended up being outperformed by newly crowned world champion Kimi Antonelli.

Speaking on Thursday, Russell admitted that the number of times he has had to bounce back after a disappointing weekend, of which there were many, had been wearing on him.

"I probably just feel a bit exhausted this season of constantly picking myself back up. When you get kicked to the ground you pick yourself back up, then you get kicked down again, you pick yourself back up. I was hoping to do that maybe twice in the season, not every other weekend," he said with a wry smile.

Russell, who has dropped to fourth in the standings behind Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton, always insisted the 2026 power unit regulations punished his natural driving style, having chased his tail across the season to try and adapt. But with the rules reducing the share of electric power next year, amid other tweaks, Russell backed himself to overcome his down year.

"The power unit changes next year. The tyres are changing slightly for next year," he said. "I've had a lot more good years than bad years. I don't think there's a single athlete or just individual in the world that [only] goes through great years every single year.

"It's the way you bounce back from those years to continue having the belief and courage to return to those positive ways, and that mental resilience. What this year has taught me is that I still believe in myself and next year we fight again."

Sports.title: Ferrari set for crunch meeting as Hamilton and Leclerc tension reaches Brazil
Sports.content:
Ferrari arrived at Interlagos facing a problem that, until just a few weeks ago, would have been difficult to imagine in quite this form. After a long season spent chasing competitiveness, the team finally appears to have found many of the answers that had been missing with its SF-26 Formula 1 car.

The results from the last few grands prix confirm that progress, but just as the Scuderia has regained the ability to fight for victories, a delicate issue has emerged: the relationship between Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc on track.

What happened in the opening corners of the Mexico GP continues to dominate the conversation. The flashpoint between the two Ferrari drivers compromised a Sunday that could have delivered a very different result for the team and, more importantly, exposed a tension that does not appear to have dissipated after the race.

Speaking to the media at Interlagos yesterday, Hamilton reaffirmed the position he had expressed on Sunday evening in Mexico City. There was no backtracking and no attempt to play down what happened. It is a sign that the issue remains unresolved.

Read Also: Formula 1 Hamilton backs claims Leclerc races him harder than F1 rivals

There has been no opportunity for the two drivers and team boss Fred Vasseur to sit down together since Mexico. Vasseur returned to Maranello, while Leclerc went to be with his family ahead of the birth of his child with his wife, Alexandra. The discussion has therefore been postponed until today, when the Monegasque arrives in the Interlagos paddock.

It will be an important meeting. Not so much to establish who was right or wrong in Mexico, but to define a principle that both drivers must respect: when a Ferrari is in a position to win, the team's interests cannot be put at risk by an internal battle.

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

But why have two drivers who are no longer in contention for the world championship reached such a high level of tension? The answer is not straightforward and inevitably involves a degree of speculation. Hamilton has spent much of his career in a very particular position. Following Nico Rosberg's retirement at the end of 2016, the British driver enjoyed many years at Mercedes with a team built around him. It was a situation in which his position was never genuinely in question.

His move to Ferrari brought him into a very different environment. Hamilton found himself alongside a team-mate who not only knows the organisation inside out, but has also built a very strong relationship with the Scuderia over the years. For a driver accustomed to being the reference point within his team, sharing that role can be an unfamiliar experience.

On the other side is Leclerc, who has worn Ferrari colours since 2019. The Monegasque has endured difficult seasons, accepted the technical limitations of cars that have often fallen short of expectations and continued to be one of the team's cornerstones. It is understandable that he now feels he has earned a position he has no intention of surrendering, even in the face of a seven-time world champion.

These are two different journeys, two strong personalities and two drivers with more than enough motivation to not give ground. A world championship does not necessarily have to be at stake to fuel a rivalry. Sometimes, it is precisely the absence of an immediate shared objective that makes finding a balance more difficult.

The paradox is that this situation has emerged just as Ferrari appears to have overcome many of the problems that have hampered its season. Over the last three races, the Scuderia has scored more points than any other team in the constructors' championship, marking a significant turnaround compared with the first part of the campaign.

The SF-26 has once again become a car with which Hamilton and Leclerc can target pole positions and wins. Yet, at precisely this moment, the team must contend with the risk that an internal battle could compromise the collective result. What happened in Mexico showed just how fine the line can be between a rivalry that helps drive performance and one capable of turning a potential victory, or even a 1-2 finish, into a missed opportunity and what ended up being second and fourth.

Frederic Vasseur, Ferrari Photo by: Michael Potts / LAT images via Getty Images

Vasseur's role

The French team principal faces one of the most delicate challenges of his tenure. Until now, he has consistently defended his drivers' freedom to race each other on track, believing that two champions should be allowed to compete without excessive restrictions. It is a philosophy that makes sense, but it requires one fundamental condition: both drivers must understand and respect the point beyond which individual rivalry becomes detrimental to the team.

That is precisely what today's meeting at Interlagos must address. Hamilton has already made it clear that he has no intention of changing his interpretation of events. Leclerc's position remains to be heard, as he was absent from yesterday's media commitments. Vasseur's task will be to listen to both drivers and, above all, establish rules that leave no room for interpretation.

To achieve that, however, the team principal must have the full backing of Ferrari's leadership. This is not simply about giving him the support he needs to make decisions, even unpopular ones, but ensuring that there is a single voice when dealing with the drivers – one that everyone recognises as the ultimate authority.

This is a fundamental principle in running a team, particularly one with drivers of Hamilton and Leclerc's calibre. If instructions come from different people, or if there is even the possibility of seeking confirmation and support elsewhere, the authority of the person responsible for leading the team inevitably risks being undermined. Ferrari's leadership must support Vasseur, but, more importantly, it must allow him – and him alone – to represent the team's position to its drivers. That is the only way to give decisions full authority and ensure they are respected.

Managing two drivers of this calibre cannot be influenced by the weight of their respective reputations or by the potential external repercussions of a decision. If the objective is to return Ferrari to a position where it can consistently fight for world championships, the team's needs must take precedence over any individual ambition. That does not necessarily mean introducing predetermined driver hierarchies. Rather, it means ensuring that decisions taken in the Scuderia's best interests are recognised and respected by both drivers, without exception.

There is one final aspect that makes the Interlagos meeting even more important. The 2026 season is now entering its closing stages, but Ferrari is already working towards next year's championship, with the ambition of arriving at the season opener in a position to fight for the biggest prizes.

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari, Charles Leclerc, Ferrari Photo by: Manuel Eletto / Getty Images

That prospect requires not only a competitive car, but also a harmonious environment and an organisation in which everyone understands their role. A potential battle for the world championship would inevitably make managing a rivalry even more difficult – one that has already shown signs of tension despite there being no title at stake this season.

For that reason, the meeting between Vasseur, Hamilton and Leclerc will be about more than simply clearing the air over what happened in Mexico. It could mark the moment when Ferrari establishes the ground rules for how its drivers will work together in the future.

The SF-26 finally appears to have rediscovered the path to competitiveness. Now it is up to the team to ensure that, when the opportunity to win comes, its own drivers do not turn it into another missed opportunity.

Sports.title: Permane signs new Racing Bulls F1 deal
Sports.content:
Red Bull has given Alan Permane a new contract as the Racing Bulls Formula 1 squad’s team principal.

Permane will retain the reins of the Faenza-based outfit until the end of the 2031 season.

A stalwart of the current Alpine squad, where he worked from 1989 to 2023 in various capacities including race engineer and sporting director, Permane joined Racing Bulls (then known as RB) ahead of the 2024 campaign as its racing director, before being promoted to the team principal role when incumbent Laurent Mekies replaced Christian Horner at Red Bull.

Oliver Mintzlaff, CEO Corporate Projects and Investments Red Bull, said: “Alan is doing a tremendous job, and the progress the team has made is a direct reflection of his experience, commitment and competitive mindset. He brings clarity, composure, and a deep understanding of what it takes to perform in Formula 1, while creating an environment where people can consistently deliver at their best.

“The results Visa Cash App Racing Bulls has achieved in recent seasons underline the strength of the team and the work being done throughout the organisation. Alan has played a key role in that progress, and we are very pleased that he will continue to lead the team as we look to build on this momentum in the years ahead.

“Together with Peter Bayer as Co-CEO Commercial, Alan forms a strong and experienced leadership team. They complement each other exceptionally well, bringing different strengths and perspectives to the organisation. I am delighted that we have this stability and continuity in place, providing a clear platform for the team’s future development and long-term ambitions.”

Arvid Lindblad, Racing Bulls, Alan Permane, Racing Bulls, Liam Lawson, Racing Bulls, Peter Bayer, Racing Bulls Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

Permane added: “I am immensely proud to be continuing this journey with VCARB, and I would like to thank everyone at Red Bull for the trust and support they have given me. What makes this team special is the shared spirit of everyone; trackside, in Faenza and in Milton Keynes, and it is a privilege to lead such a talented and committed group every day.

“Fighting for fifth in the championship is something we should all be very proud of, but it is the result of years of hard work from a lot of people, and we are not done yet. We have the right people, the right culture and a clear sense of where we want to go, and I am excited to keep pushing together.”

The Italian team has made steady progress under Permane, having scored 46 points in 2024, 92 last year and already 108 so far this season, with the outfit all but certain to clinch fifth place in the constructors’ championship – its highest finish ever since it was founded as Minardi in 1985.

Asked about Racing Bulls’ progress back in Baku, Permane told Sky Sports F1: “What we've done through the year is we've just put load on the car. We've just put downforce on, and every time we've brought an upgrade, it's worked.”

Sports.title: Hamilton backs claims Leclerc races him harder than F1 rivals
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton maintains Ferrari needs further talks to iron out its rules of engagement, backing claims Charles Leclerc races him harder than drivers from rival teams.

Hamilton and Leclerc came to blows on lap one of last weekend's race in Mexico with both drivers going off the track at Turn 4, which eventually handed Max Verstappen a golden opportunity to snatch away the win and costing Ferrari a possible 1-2 victory, instead the duo finishing second and fourth.

Hamilton was incensed by how hard Leclerc raced on the opening lap, only for the Monegasque to permanently stay ahead as he cut the track at Turn 4. Leclerc only received a five-second penalty for gaining a lasting advantage, with mitigation bringing that punishment down from 10 seconds.

Their Mexico fight further fed suggestions that Leclerc appears to race his teammate harder than anyone else, having come after a Singapore Grand Prix in which Leclerc backed off at the start despite being fully on the inside of polesitter Max Verstappen. Leclerc did race the Dutchman hard at the subsequent US Grand Prix in Austin, however, overtaking the Red Bull man around the outside of COTA's Esses.

When asked if the idea of Leclerc racing him harder than other drivers is something Hamilton has also noticed, the seven-time world champion replied: "Yes. I see what you see. In Singapore, he was fully on the inside into Turn 1, he had won the lead, and he backed off. It was definitely different.

"But I mean, if you look at the team-mates, it was the same with Sebastian [Vettel]. It was the same with Carlos [Sainz].

Photo by: Colin McMaster / LAT Images via Getty Images

As emotions ran high, Hamilton demanded talks to clarify the team's rules of engagement and warned of "big problems" for the squad. Autosport understands team principal Fred Vasseur has spoken briefly to both drivers, albeit separately, after feeling the events of Mexico showed a lack of respect towards the team's 2000 people staff.

But with Vasseur having travelled back to Europe in between races and Leclerc spending time with his family following the birth of his daughter, Hamilton welcomes further talks with Leclerc and their boss in Sao Paulo on Friday. "Naturally I was frustrated, and I'm still frustrated," he said when asked by Autosport if he views the events of Mexico in a different light now they have had time to cool off. "So, conversations need to be had. We will have those when the time permits.

"We had an opportunity to win for the team. The team has done such an amazing job in bringing upgrades this year and I think they've done an incredible job. We've scored more points than any other team in the last three or four races. We could have easily had a one-two, so we definitely have to work towards making sure that doesn't happen again."

Hamilton drew criticism, too, for openly lobbying for his team-mate to get a bigger penalty than the five seconds he was held at his pitstop, as cutting the track handed Leclerc a much bigger advantage than that on a circuit where overtaking proved extremely difficult. But the 41-year-old said he "will not be silenced". "I don't really care how everyone feels about what I've said. I wear my heart on my sleeve, and I say how I feel in the moment," he said.

"I did see something that someone was saying that the things that I'm saying are calculated, and I just want to combat that with the fact that when you're in the race, your heart rate is like 170. You're driving 200 miles an hour. You don't have time to be calculated in what you're saying and thinking about what the media are going to write about, you don't think about that.

"Of course, there's some times you say things and maybe you might regret it afterwards, but I don't, and I'm never going to apologise for being authentic and real. I'm not gonna be silenced. I've never ever been silenced. I have not been asked to not say anything [by the team], and that's just the way it is."

Sports.title: How rough diamond Camara feels ahead of 'very surprising' F1 home debut
Sports.content:
If Rafa Camara felt any nerves about making his F1 debut earlier than expected, on home soil no less, then he didn't show it.

The Ferrari junior has been drafted in to replace Esteban Ocon at Haas next year, and already starts that journey this weekend after Ocon's high-profile split with the team halfway through the Mexico weekend.

Counting against Camara this weekend, the 21-year-old Brazilian has never driven a 2026 F1 car before with all its quirks, has never raced at Interlagos before and is coming into the weekend with few opportunities to prepare. Camara was actually slated to conduct FP1 for Ferrari, so he had at least completed some simulator work in Maranello.

What's counting for the current F2 championship leader is his immense potential. During a private test with Haas in Portimao, Camara was so quick that regular driver Oliver Bearman struggled to match his times and that blew Haas team boss Ayao Komatsu away enough to hand him the keys for next season. Camara has always been seen as a future star by Ferrari, perhaps the biggest raw talent coming through the driver program but one needing a layer of polish.

Whether or not that varnish has had a chance to set remains to be seen. But in front of throngs of international and local media, both in his print huddle and in the FIA's press conference, the somewhat shy Camara looked anything but overawed by the occasion.

"I was very surprised," Camara said when asked by Autosport about receiving the phone call to jump into the VF-26 this weekend. "Definitely not a place where I would expect to make my debut in Formula 1, but just very happy for the opportunity, very grateful as well for the team to put trust in me this week. So I'm just trying to enjoy the home race and have some fun out there."

A home debut, especially on short notice with little preparation time, is always a baptism of fire. It wasn't all that long ago when recently crowned world champion Kimi Antonelli crashed in Friday practice at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix, and was left drained by the attention around his Imola homecoming last season.

Rafa Camara, Ferrari Photo by: Davide Cavazza

"There will be a lot of things going on," Camara acknowledged the surge in media and attention since his drive was announced. "But I think it should be all right. Whatever people are speaking [about] or what's happening outside, it's never been a real problem. I always try to just focus on my side, focus on things that I can control, and whatever is happening outside is not really under my control. So I just really try to go there and do what I know what to do."

What helps is that with a 2027 drive already in the bag, Camara knows he can focus on kickstarting his preparation for next year, rather than feeling the urge to go out and prove himself, or be tempted to do too much.

"I'm just really trying to learn as much as I can," the reigning FIA F3 champion said. "There will be a lot of things going on, but I think on my side I just try to see it as a positive note. Just driving at home is something that I didn't do for a long time. So I'm just really trying to enjoy this weekend and just have some fun. Obviously it will be not easy, but I think what always helps for me is just really focus on my side, focus on my job, and make sure that every time you're learning and moving forwards."

As well as filling his experience bank for 2027, Camara is trying to make sure he doesn't forget to stop and soak it in the occasion, too.

"Once I joined F3, where you get more exposed, the support from the Brazilian fans was really big. And it's always been nice to see how much they cheer and how much they support you," he said.

"Just being able to do my first F1 race here in front of everyone, would be something very special. For sure, I'll try to give them a nice weekend."

Sports.title: Mora Warns Joshua Buatsi: Stop Brawling with Hutchinson
Sports.content:
Sergio Mora argues Joshua Buatsi can simplify his rematch with Willy Hutchinson by sticking to a disciplined jab and compelling the counterpuncher to initiate the action. The difficulty lies in implementing that strategy without muting the devastating rib attack that defines Buatsi, or getting dragged into brawling the moment Hutchinson scores.

Two knockdowns secured the verdict for Buatsi in their first encounter, yet Mora insists the Londoner gave away unnecessary openings by working inside the telephone booth. The former world champion urges Buatsi to command distance, bag rounds on the scorecards, and make the Scotsman gamble.

“Buatsi can make it so easy for himself. I know he’s a great body puncher, and he makes fights entertaining. But he can make this fight so easy if he uses more boxing than fighting, and he fights a little bit longer. If he pops behind the jab. Let Hutchinson make the mistakes because Hutchinson, he’s a good fighter, he’s a good counter-puncher, but he’s a reactive fighter. He’s not a go-get-you fighter,” said Mora to DAZN Boxing.

Strategic compromises exist within that blueprint. Hooking to the body requires closing the gap through the danger zone where Hutchinson’s hand speed can intercept incoming fire. Boxing at range shields Buatsi from check hooks, yet it inevitably caps the number of flush shots he can sink downstairs.

Stabbing jabs into Hutchinson’s chest and solar plexus provides an answer. Buatsi can disrupt breathing without smothering his own reach, keeping the target moving while assessing whether heavier artillery should follow. The body work shifts from an all-out physical press into an earned sequence.

Sharper feints also disrupt a reactive opponent. Buatsi has no obligation to commit fully with every twitch. Subtle level changes and shoulder feints will pull Hutchinson out of his stance, leaving him off balance when he reaches for air.

None of this functions without banking early points. Hutchinson will gladly sit back if he is allowed to dictate the pace from the outside. Mora’s scenario of a stoppage depends on Hutchinson feeling desperate enough on the scorecards to march forward into incoming traffic.

“So if Buatsi can win some early rounds and get Hutchinson to come at him, I could see Buatsi running him into a right hand and hurting him, and dropping him and maybe stopping him,” said Mora.

Securing ring center anchors this entire setup. Forcing Hutchinson to circle eats away at the Scotsman’s legs while preserving Buatsi’s stamina for the late rounds. An active lead hand must continually penalize every reset.

Temperament presents the true obstacle. The moment Hutchinson lands an eye-catching flurry, Buatsi must fight his natural urge to fire back instantly in the pocket. Stepping back behind the jab after tasting leather will reveal whether Buatsi values tactical efficiency over raw violence.

Buatsi faces Hutchinson in a rematch for the vacant WBC light heavyweight title this Saturday, November 7, at Manchester’s AO Arena, live on DAZN.

Sports.title: Outbox or Get Cracked: Shane Mosley’s Bentley Gamble
Sports.content:
Shane Mosley Jr. needed two trips to the scale on Friday, sweating off a stubborn final pound to reach the 160-pound limit after coming in at 161. That extra hour in the sauna creates immediate questions about his legs, particularly against a puncher like London’s Denzel Bentley over 10 rounds at the Copper Box Arena. Bentley checked in right on the mark at 160 on his first try.

Mosley’s stated strategy depends on superior activity and sustained output. With a five-inch reach advantage, his cleanest route to a points win is operating behind a busy, disciplining jab to trap Bentley on the perimeter. But if Friday’s late weight cut robs Mosley of fluid lateral movement, Bentley will not have to work hard to close the distance.

Middleweight madness incoming 👀 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 @2Sharp_D – 160lbs

🇺🇸 @IamShaneMosley – 160lbs 📺 @SkySports + @ParamountPlus | #ZuffaBoxing12 https://t.co/E1Rvtw2vJI — Zuffa_Boxing (@Zuffa_Boxing) November 6, 2026

Mosley made his intentions clear this week, saying that a points victory in hostile territory holds more value for him than an early finish:

“The reason why I feel like it’s even better to beat you on points than to knock you out is because if I can show everybody in here, everybody in the arena that I’m better than you, that’s better to me than knocking you out,” Mosley said to Sky Sports Boxing sit down. “What’s better is if I went to your hometown and in front of your fans and beat you convincingly, where everybody said, ‘Yeah, he won.’ That to me shows greatness.”

Aiming to win a clear decision on British cards requires a dominant volume gap, especially against a hometown fighter. Scraping by on split margins fails the standard of mastery Mosley outlined.

Bentley was initially unfazed by the prediction before recognizing the tactical insult behind it.

“At first I thought, ‘All right.’ I went back and I thought, ‘Wait, I’d rather he say he’d knock me out,’” Bentley admitted. “He’s basically saying he can outpoint me.” His response was blunt: “That’s not happening.”

For Bentley, winning does not require round-by-round territorial dominance. He carries an 82% knockout rate and thrives when opponents throw in prolonged combinations, creating counter-punching lanes for his right hand. If Mosley’s punch output dips in the middle rounds from dehydration, Bentley’s heavy single shots will stand out sharply on the scorecards.

“I want to crack that chin. I want to see if it’s real. Watch,” Bentley said.

Bentley has acknowledged Mosley’s chin and ring experience, so a wild blitz out of the gate is unlikely. Even with the WBO belt absent after Bentley opted for this bout over a mandatory assignment, the terms of the fight are clear: Mosley must execute a disciplined, 10-round boxing clinic at range, while Bentley needs only one sustained opening to punish him on the inside.

Sports.title: Groves Expects Fury vs Joshua Despite Fury Injury Rumor
Sports.content:
George Groves fully expects Tyson Fury to step into the ring against Anthony Joshua, brushing off chatter that an injury could derail the December 11 date. His view is simple. Both men are battle-worn veterans, so expecting either to show up at one hundred percent is unrealistic.

The conversation kicked off after Frank Bruno claimed an insider from Fury’s gym told him an injury could stop the clash from happening. Groves did not have insider details on Fury’s body, yet he cast heavy doubt on the idea that the event is actually in jeopardy.

“I don’t know about any rumors, but there might be a lot of kidology, a lot of rumors floating about. Could have been leaked by anyone,” Groves told talkSPORT Boxing. “I genuinely don’t know, but I’ll be very shocked if that fight don’t happen. I think both guys will fight no matter what.”

Groves offered an unfiltered take on where both boxers stand right now. He views them as past their physical primes, meaning a completely smooth camp is out of the question for either side.

“I don’t think at this stage either one of these two guys who are veterans, way past their best, are going to be in perfect condition going into this fight. That doesn’t matter. They’re going to fight,” Groves said.

It is a harsh reality check for an all-British heavyweight meeting years in the making. Fans are getting the spectacle, but Groves points out that the clock has been ticking the whole time.

Looking back on his own ring days, Groves pointed out that modern training camps are never completely clean. Wear and tear, missed sessions, or personal distractions always creep in, no matter how sharp someone looks at the podium.

Whether Fury carries a genuine knock remains unconfirmed. Bruno’s story is secondhand talk, and Groves made it clear he has no direct intel. Still, Groves remains convinced that both heavyweights will walk through fire to make the bell.

When a guaranteed nine-figure bag is sitting on the table, standard training camp knocks take a back seat.

Walking away from a projected 100 million dollars each over an elbow tweak, sore shoulder, or bruised rib would be professional madness. At this stage of their careers, neither Tyson Fury nor Anthony Joshua has another payday of this magnitude waiting in reserve.

If one pulls out now with a minor complaint, there is zero guarantee the momentum, public appetite, or financial backing survives to reschedule it cleanly.

Both fighters have operated under fire while compromised before. Fury fought through severe cuts and facial trauma, while Joshua has spent years managing the mileage on his body. Every veteran north of thirty-five carries something into the ring; reaching fight night at one hundred percent physical perfection is a myth in modern heavyweight boxing.

Unless one of them suffers a catastrophic structural tear or a medical commission flat-out denies a license, they are walking to the ring on December 11 in Cardiff. At 100 million dollars apiece, you fight through the aches, take your shot, and settle whatever needs healing after the final bell.

Sports.title: Fury: Ryan Garcia Has The Star Power Haney And Shakur Lack
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury believes Ryan Garcia is primed to take over as the premier attraction in American boxing once Canelo Alvarez steps away. Fury points directly to Garcia’s charisma and gift for commanding headlines, putting pure drawing power ahead of pure technical mastery.

While Fury listed talents like Devin Haney, Shakur Stevenson, Abdullah Mason, and Richardson Hitchins, Garcia earned his clear vote. The challenge facing everyone else is something victories in the ring cannot automatically fix: reaching beyond the hardcore boxing bubble.

“Other than Canelo, which Canelo’s obviously on his way out too, then it’s Ryan Garcia in America,” Fury said on Behind the Mic. “He’s got a personality. He talks. He’s entertaining. He’s charismatic.”

Asked if he sees reflections of himself in Garcia, Fury agreed completely, admitting others might possess sharper fundamentals but insisting they cannot generate the same revenue.

It is a crucial division when assessing Canelo’s commercial heir. Observers can debate Garcia’s ring craft against elite competition, yet Fury focuses strictly on ticket sales and viewer attention. Boxing culture often conflates technical brilliance with stardom, even though they demand completely different skill sets.

Garcia keeps the public talking during long layoffs. His unpredictable persona draws viewers who would never bother watching sparring footage or checking divisional rankings. People tune in hoping to see him win or desperate to watch him get knocked out, but either motivation sells pay-per-views.

Fury sounded far more skeptical about the mainstream presence of other top contenders.

“Inside of boxing people know who they are,” Fury said. “Outside of boxing, you go and ask 50 people … they don’t know who they are.”

Haney, Stevenson, Mason, and Hitchins have built formidable resumes. Yet Fury argues that respect from devoted boxing circles will only carry an athlete to a certain ceiling. Becoming the marquee figure who causes general sports fans to clear their weekend calendars demands a bigger presence.

Fury also took aim at modern streaming setups, questioning whether current platforms actually build true mainstream excitement. He recalled previous eras where extensive profile features introduced contenders long before fight night, whereas modern streaming formats often show the event without making casual viewers care in advance.

Because of that shift, self-promotion falls squarely on the fighter. Fury stressed that young talent must chase interviews, drop consistent content, and hustle for their own spotlight instead of waiting for a promoter to do the heavy lifting.

Garcia naturally excels at that playbook. Pure spectacle does not guarantee long-term dominance, since keeping the public invested still requires memorable bouts and dependable results. Even so, Fury’s view holds firm: Garcia knows how to hook an audience before the first bell sounds, while his peers face a much steeper climb proving they can match that commercial reach.

Sports.title: Conor Benn Says Pacquiao Fight Offered For December
Sports.content:
Conor Benn has confirmed he received an offer to square off against Manny Pacquiao this December, but opted against the date to focus on family time and physical recovery. While Benn remains open to meeting the boxing legend in early 2027, major questions remain about which weight class could accommodate both men.

Benn pointed to the brutal toll of his recent cut to 147 pounds, alongside the arrival of his newborn son, as key reasons for passing on the end-of-year window.

“The fight got presented to me for December, and it was just too soon making weight. Got a newborn son,” Benn said to Sky Sports Boxing. “So for me it was really about spending time with my family and just enjoying this period, the festive period, with my family. But if Q1 he wants to get on again, I’m interested.”

While Pacquiao represents a lucrative, marquee target for a return bout, Benn’s physical transformation presents a major hurdle. Having bulked back up to around 185 pounds, Benn insists his days at welterweight are completely finished. He even dismissed campaigning at junior middleweight.

“My future’s at middleweight,” Benn stated. “I thought about light middle. There’s nothing in me at light middle even. That’s how bad the weight cut was.”

Without a designated catchweight, matching an eight-division champion who spent his career far lighter against a fighter settling into middleweight remains an unresolved riddle.

Reflecting on his recent loss to Ryan, Benn admitted that outside noise fueled his miscalculated attempt to hit the welterweight limit.

“I don’t know what I was thinking making 147,” Benn said. “There’s one thing making the weight, and then there’s one thing performing at your best at the weight, and it showed. I paid the price for, say, chasing greatness.”

Still, Benn gave Ryan full credit for landing the decisive blows and finding victory on the night. Though he wanted the chance to battle on after rising from the canvas, Benn refused to fault the referee for waving off the bout, taking full accountability for the outcome.

Facing Pacquiao offers Benn an appealing path forward in 2027, but bridging the massive weight gap will require serious negotiations before anyone can sign a contract.

Pacquiao is a novelty payday trap. Even if Benn wins, nobody gives him real credit for beating a faded icon. If he looks bad winning, he gets ridiculed. If he loses, he is finished at the elite level.

Sports.title: Devin Haney Needs to Stop Living in the Past to Sell Liam Paro Clash
Sports.content:
Devin Haney is digging into his past, using his victories over George Kambosos to hype his December 19 unification clash with Liam Paro at Chase Center. Dominating Kambosos secured undisputed status at lightweight, but rehashing those nights won’t fire up crowds to see him chase another belt.

“My resume speaks for itself,” Haney stated. “I’ve never been afraid to go into a champion’s backyard and put my record on the line. I went to Australia, took George Kambosos’ belts, and became undisputed lightweight champion of the world. Now I’m bringing another Australian world champion, Liam Paro, into my backyard. This time, I plan to take his belt and become a unified welterweight world champion right here at home.”

Rehashing those wins now doesn’t elevate Liam Paro; it just reminds everyone how limited Kambosos actually was. The problem is that nationality is not a fighting style. Paro earned his IBF junior welterweight belt by traveling to Puerto Rico and physically outworking Subriel Matias, a dangerous puncher who was supposed to run through him.

If Haney truly understood how to build a fight, he would talk about Paro traveling to Puerto Rico to derail Subriel Matias or how Paro will actually bring a fight to him. Instead, he defaults to his old comfort blanket because self-promotion has never been his strong suit.

Paro is a tougher, more durable, and fundamentally different stylistic threat than Kambosos ever was. By presenting Paro through the Kambosos lens, Haney actually diminishes his own opponent while making the matchup sound like an easy rerun.

Devin needs to stop pretending the fans only care about belts. Haney should focus on the homecoming angle by promising a style change from his normal pure boxing approach. If he speaks openly about having to stand his ground against Paro’s physical, brawling style, he gives people a reason to watch for drama rather than just waiting on the judges’ scorecards.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury Says Usyk Discussed March Trilogy Fight
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury claims Oleksandr Usyk signaled he could be ready to step into the ring again in March. That float keeps the door ajar for a third encounter, even with the Ukrainian holding two clear victories over him. Fury must handle Anthony Joshua first, yet he is already floating Usyk’s name for his next move.

Fury says the conversation happened when the Joshua matchup still hung in the balance. No paperwork exists for a trilogy, and Fury leaves crucial blanks, starting with whether March remains realistic once he steps out against Joshua.

“I actually spoke with Alexander to say, like, if he doesn’t fight, then we’ll do it. And he said he’s busy. He’s going on holiday with his family, but he could do a fight in March. So, maybe we do that in March. I don’t know yet. One fight at a time,” Fury said to Fighthype.

Booking the pairing again guarantees immense global interest, yet justifying it on merit gets tricky after back-to-back Usyk wins. Fury commands massive crowds, but he cannot claim unsettled business in the ring, no matter how vigorously he disputes the scorecards.

He still speaks as if the two losses solved nothing. When asked about those bouts, he doubled down on his claim that the judges got them wrong.

“I thought I won both fights,” Fury insisted. “I’m not bitter towards Alexander. He’s a good man. Like, he’s a God-fearing family man. I wish him all the luck in the world. But when he looks in that mirror every day, he knows he didn’t beat GK.”

That stance gives him an obvious marketing angle. He can insist he got robbed twice, promising to finish the job inside the distance next time. Spectators who watched Usyk take both contests will need stronger proof to believe a third chapter goes any differently.

Joshua might shatter this entire timeline anyway. Fury must defeat AJ and emerge unscathed for March to stay viable. A grueling war would instantly derail such a tight turnaround.

Fury also brushed aside talk about Usyk dropping down to cruiserweight to face David Benavidez, arguing that a Usyk trilogy offers the premier commercial draw.

“He just wants a big payday, and I’m his man to give him that,” Fury stated.

However, Saudis almost certainly pass on financing a third meeting, and outside of Riyadh, nobody else has the appetite to write those checks. Turki Alalshikh cares about global prestige and spectacle rather than standard event profit and loss, but he avoids financing fights that feel settled or stale. When one man has already collected 24 rounds of undisputed evidence across two fights, the storyline vanishes.

Alalshikh wants legacy events that captivate the sporting world, not expensive reruns where the outcome feels foregone. Unless Tyson Fury delivers an explosive, career-altering win that makes fans demand it again, Alalshikh will look to put his budget behind fresh pairings.

If the Saudis say no, the fight essentially dies right there. Here is why neither traditional promoters nor major streaming platforms would step into that breach:

Traditional promoters like Frank Warren’s Queensberry or Bob Arum’s Top Rank operate strictly on commercial reality. To stage Fury vs. Usyk 3 without Saudi site fees, they would have to fund massive eight-figure guarantees entirely through ticket sales, sponsorships, and pay-per-view buys.

The first two fights showed that pay-per-view numbers alone struggle to justify astronomical purses without state subsidies. Putting together $80 million to $100 million in combined purses on a pay-per-view model for a 2-0 rivalry would be financial suicide for any standalone promoter.

Netflix has entered live combat sports, but its entire strategy relies on massive cultural events and spectacle that drive mainstream global viewership without pay-per-view barriers. A technical chess match between two pure boxers, where the Ukrainian has already dominated the series, does not fit the kind of mass-market spectacle Netflix targets.

If Netflix is going to spend tens of millions on a live boxing broadcast, they will chase crossover draws or a massive domestic clash like Fury against Anthony Joshua, not a redundant third bout between Fury and Usyk.

Sports.title: De La Hoya Says Huge Paydays Hurt Boxing
Sports.content:
Oscar De La Hoya makes a legitimate point about the fallout from boxing’s oversized paydays. The moment an elite fighter lands an exorbitant purse, putting together another significant fight becomes an uphill battle.

A wealthy champion can comfortably afford to stay on the sidelines, waiting around for another monster payday rather than risking a world title against an unheralded, high-risk challenger for standard money.

This dynamic leaves skilled contenders with smaller fanbases stranded. They climb the ranks and secure mandatory status, yet they still struggle to bait a titleholder into the squared circle. Defeating an unheralded contender offers minimal commercial value to an established champion, while an upset defeat destroys their future earnings.

“Fighters are ducking their mandatories and taking forever to fight the very best opponents. Why is that? Because Turki’s paying for this,” De La Hoya argued during his latest Clap Back Thursday broadcast.

De La Hoya aimed his remarks directly at Turki Alalshikh, alleging the Saudi investor overpays competitors who fail to deliver in the ring. While that view concentrates blame on a single financier, the broader problem reaches far beyond whoever signs the checks.

A massive purse quickly morphs into an athlete’s baseline demand. Normal market offers suddenly appear insulting, even when those figures match actual gate receipts and broadcast revenue. Flush with cash, the fighter holds all the leverage to decline fights and sit idle.

The sport simply lacks enough marquee rivals capable of producing record-setting revenues on demand. When several elite boxers freeze their careers chasing the same small pool of opponents, extended layoffs turn into the standard routine. Top contenders get told to stay busy, taking on all the danger while the biggest names bide their time for optimal terms.

The classic rationale of high danger and low reward makes fiscal sense to managers, but fans have grown exhausted hearing about it. Holding a world championship should demand more than cherry-picking matchups that deliver maximum profit with minimal physical jeopardy.

Canelo Alvarez facing the choice between Hamzah Sheeraz and Osleys Iglesias highlights this exact problem. Facing Hamzah Sheeraz guarantees strong ticket sales and broadcast numbers, while Osleys Iglesias poses a dangerous stylistic nightmare that only dedicated purists recognize. The avoided challenger gets passed over precisely because he possesses the skill set to score an upset.

Riyadh Season bankrolling could ideally bridge that gap. If conventional promotional companies cannot guarantee the money required to finalize tough bouts, an ultra-wealthy investor holds the power to make them happen. Throwing massive capital at famous names accomplishes little for the sport unless the matchmaking forces champions into genuine danger.

When fighters realize giant checks arrive regardless of opponent quality, they have zero incentive to accept severe stylistic challenges. Convincing them to take tough fights for less money later turns nearly impossible.

The sanctioning bodies share substantial blame for enabling this cycle. When titleholders receive continual exemptions, mandatory challengers pay the price in lost prime years. Owning a championship belt must carry an ironclad duty to defend it against legitimate contenders, regardless of how many pay-per-view buys those challengers command.

Boxers take immense physical punishment and deserve every dollar they generate. De La Hoya’s point reminds everyone that financial compensation must remain tied to competitive matchmaking. Whenever excessive wealth allows champions to freeze divisions and avoid elite threats, the entire sport suffers long after the money gets spent.

Boxing has reached a state where capital is subsidizing inactivity. In past eras, financial pressure kept fighters active. A fighter made a living by entering the ring three or four times a year. If a champion held a belt, sitting idle cost real money, which meant dangerous mandatory challengers actually got their shot.

Contenders could leverage their number one ranking because champions could not afford to take an eighteen-month vacation waiting for an imaginary windfall. Once an unbacked financial bubble enters the ecosystem, the entire risk calculation collapses. A fighter walks away from one evening with forty or fifty million dollars.

From that moment on, their market value in their own mind is anchored to that unnatural number. An honest domestic or network promoter offering four million dollars to defend against an undefeated, dangerous mandatory looks like an insult, even if four million is the maximum revenue that gate and television rights can actually support. Because the champion is already rich beyond imagination, they hold all the leverage to say no.

They pack their bags, hit the gym casually, post workout clips on social media, and wait by the phone for the next massive check from a sovereign wealth fund or a deep-pocketed financier. The consequences for everyone else in the sport are brutal. Entire divisions freeze due to this problem. When three or four top names in a weight class are all parked on their couches waiting on the same financial patron to call their number, nobody fights each other. The pipeline stalls.

You end up with prime athletes fighting once every twelve to sixteen months, burning away their athletic peaks in hotel lobbies and negotiation rooms instead of under the lights.

The fighters who actually take the hit are the avoided, high-skill contenders. A guy who worked his entire life to become a mandatory challenger suddenly finds himself in an impossible trap. The champion will not fight him for realistic money because the contender does not bring casual pay-per-view buys. At the same time, the champion demands absurd money from outside backers to take on the stylistic hazard. The contender is told to stay busy, fight other dangerous guys for modest purses, and hope the superstar eventually runs out of soft alternatives.

It rewards marketability and name recognition while actively punishing ring ability. The sanctioning bodies completely capitulate, allowing it to happen. Belts exist to mandate competitive fights. Yet because sanctioning bodies take a percentage fee off the total purse, their financial allegiance lies with the massive check, not the integrity of their own rankings.

They gladly grant continuous medical exemptions, voluntary defense allowances, and special championship designations to mega-earners while stringing along the real number one contenders with interim straps. If the four sanctioning bodies had the spine to strip a wealthy champion the second an ordered mandatory defense deadline passed, this holdout culture would vanish overnight.

Boxing used to be built on hungry fighters needing to prove their dominance to sustain their livelihoods. Today, mega-purses have allowed elite fighters to operate like part-time consultants who only show up when the payout is absurd, and the opponent poses minimal threat to their brand.

Until the belts lose their marketing power or the infinite money well dries up, the sport will stay stuck in this loop of extended layoffs, ducked contenders, and synthetic events.

Ghana News.title: Obuasi Beverages CEO donates GH¢120,000 towards 33-year-old man’s brain surgery
Ghana News.content:
The Chief Executive Officer of Obuasi Beverages Company Limited, Dr Amo Collins, has donated GH¢120,000 towards the emergency brain surgery of 33-year-old Edmond Benefo, who has been diagnosed with a brain tumour.

The contribution, equivalent to US$10,000, covers half of the US$20,000 required for Edmond's medical treatment and surgery in India.

Edmond's health challenges reportedly began with complaints of eye problems, which progressively worsened before medical examinations revealed a brain tumour requiring urgent surgical intervention.

His parents, Aron Benefoh and Christiana Graham, have been seeking financial assistance to secure the specialised treatment.

Dr Collins' donation is expected to ease some of the financial pressure on the family as they work to raise the remaining US$10,000.

The family is appealing for further support to meet the outstanding cost of treatment and facilitate Edmond's medical care in India.

Ghana News.title: Newsfile to discuss Traffitech-GH fines, drug busts and Parliament’s continued absence of Asante Akyem North MP
Ghana News.content:
This Saturday’s edition of Newsfile on JoyNews will examine three major issues dominating Ghana’s public discourse, as host Samson Lardy Anyenini leads discussions on road safety enforcement, the fight against drug trafficking and developments in Parliament.

The programme, scheduled for Saturday, November 7, 2026, from 8:00 a.m. to 12 noon, will scrutinise the implementation of the Traffitech-GH system, renewed drug seizures and the continued absence of the Member of Parliament for Asante Akyem North from parliamentary proceedings.

The first major issue will focus on TraffiTech-GH and whether the new automated traffic enforcement system will deliver safer roads or impose unfair financial burdens on motorists. The system, which became operational on November 1, 2026, is intended to strengthen compliance with road traffic regulations through technology-driven monitoring and enforcement.

However, its introduction has attracted criticism from commercial transport operators, who accuse the government of prioritising fines while failing to address the occupation of designated bus stops and pedestrian walkways by traders. The National Road Safety Authority (NRSA) has also raised concerns about faulty traffic lights, missing road signs and faded road markings, warning that these deficiencies could undermine the effectiveness of the system.

With the Ghana Police Service urging motorists to verify traffic violation notices before making payments, the programme will examine whether the system is adequately designed to improve road safety while ensuring fairness and transparency in its enforcement.

The discussion will also turn to the growing number of drug seizures linked to Ghana and questions about the effectiveness of the country's border security systems. Recent developments have renewed concerns about Ghana's role in international drug trafficking networks, particularly following the seizure of 46.7 kilogrammes of cocaine at the Rafic Hariri International Airport in Beirut, Lebanon, in a consignment that originated from Accra.

The Narcotics Control Commission (NACOC) has defended its decision to allow a suspected trafficker to travel to Lebanon, explaining that it was part of a controlled-delivery operation intended to identify and arrest other members of the international trafficking network. Three foreign nationals have subsequently been arrested in Ghana in connection with the shipment.

The concerns have been compounded by a fresh interception of approximately 4.8 tonnes of suspected marijuana by the Ghana Navy at the Volta Lake estuary near Ada, with the consignment allegedly destined for Nigeria.

The Minority in Parliament has meanwhile demanded accountability from President John Mahama over what it describes as failures in the country's border protection arrangements. It has also renewed calls for a parliamentary inquiry into the major drug seizures, raising questions about port security, intelligence coordination and possible institutional weaknesses.

Newsfile will interrogate whether the successive seizures reflect failures in Ghana's border controls or form part of coordinated operations to dismantle international drug trafficking networks.

Another significant issue will be Parliament's resumption for the third meeting of the Second Session of the Ninth Parliament without the Member of Parliament for Asante Akyem North, Ohene Kwame Frimpong.

The MP remains in custody in the Netherlands following his arrest at Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport in May 2026, in connection with a United States extradition request over allegations involving romance scams and money laundering. Two applications for bail have reportedly been unsuccessful, with his extradition hearing scheduled for November 18, 2026.

His prolonged absence has raised questions about the constitutional provisions governing an MP's failure to attend parliamentary sittings and whether his continued detention could put his parliamentary seat at risk.

Private legal practitioner Martin Kpebu has cited a 2008 Court of Appeal ruling involving former Nkoranza North MP Eric Amoateng, arguing that the precedent could have implications for Mr Frimpong's situation, particularly regarding the constitutional requirement for written permission from the Speaker for prolonged absence.

The Majority, however, maintains that the seat should not be declared vacant while the MP remains presumed innocent and has not been convicted of any offence.

The programme will examine the legal and constitutional implications of his continued absence and what it means for parliamentary representation in Asante Akyem North.

With these issues commanding national attention, Saturday's Newsfile promises a robust examination of road safety, institutional accountability, national security and constitutional governance.

Join Samson Lardy Anyenini and his panellists this Saturday, November 7, from 8:00 a.m. to 12 noon on JoyNews and JoyFM 99.7.

Ghana News.title: Before buying AI, businesses need to ask better questions
Ghana News.content:
A recent analysis encouraged Ghanaian entrepreneurs to connect artificial intelligence with practical needs, including customer communication and record-keeping. That is a useful starting point, but it leaves another question: how should a business choose the company providing the technology?

A convincing demonstration should begin a discussion, not end it. Before committing money or uploading customer information, owners need to understand what a service delivers, what remains their responsibility, and how they can leave if it disappoints.

Request a Demonstration of Your Actual Work

Consider a hypothetical printing business in Kumasi comparing two services for preparing quotations. Instead of accepting a supplier's polished examples, the owner could provide a fictional order and an approved price list.

Ask each provider to complete the same task. Include an unavailable paper size, an unclear delivery instruction and a request for an unauthorised discount. Observe whether the system asks questions or invents answers.

Keep the expected result beside the output. Check calculations independently rather than accepting a fluent explanation as evidence.

Also ask whether a spreadsheet or standard template would solve the problem. The purpose is to improve a business process, not buy an AI feature merely because it is fashionable.

Let an employee who missed the sales presentation repeat the exercise using only the supplied instructions. If routine work still depends on the vendor's representative, include the additional training and support required in your evaluation and budget before giving the wider team access.

Establish What Happens to Your Information

Before uploading real records, ask where information is processed, how long it is retained and whether it is used to train models. Request answers covering the particular subscription under consideration.

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre recommends assessing external AI providers and controlling data sent outside an organisation. Its guidance also emphasises limiting access to necessary functions.

For the printing business, an early trial needs neither customer addresses nor unpublished designs. Use fictional examples until appropriate arrangements have been checked.

Ask who can access account history, how departing employees lose access and how deletion requests are handled. Keep the supplier's written commitments alongside your own operating instructions.

Make Clear Communication an Acceptance Test

A useful service should help employees explain the business accurately, not simply produce more words. Teams hoping to humanize AI drafts should preserve prices, deadlines and conditions while improving readability.

Compare a revised quotation with the source document. Has a possible delivery date become a guarantee? Has the deposit requirement disappeared?

OWASP identifies convincing but inaccurate information as a risk in language model applications and recommends verification against trusted sources.

Test messages with the staff who answer customer questions. Where communication involves Twi or another Ghanaian language, include competent speakers rather than judging only the English version.

Ask the supplier how corrections are applied. A mistake should lead to a documented improvement, not another employee repeatedly fixing the same sentence.

Look for Evidence Behind Security Promises

Where an AI-enabled website or business integration needs independent assessment, choose a penetration testing company authorised to provide the relevant services in Ghana. The Cyber Security Authority's licensing framework explicitly includes vulnerability assessment and penetration testing.

Verify the provider's certificate through the authority's verification portal rather than relying on a logo in a proposal.

Agree the scope, written permission, reporting process and arrangements for checking repairs. Do not authorise tests against a supplier's infrastructure without its permission.

Ask what was tested and when. The NCSC cautions that a penetration test provides assurance at a particular time, not a permanent guarantee. Security claims should describe evidence and limitations, not promise invulnerability.

Calculate the Cost Beyond the Subscription

Compare offers using the same workload and number of staff. Ask about setup, training, storage, support, usage limits and charges for connecting other business systems.

The NCSC notes that differently priced cloud licences can include different security features. Confirm that essential protections are included in the quoted package.

Record the time employees spend reviewing outputs and correcting mistakes. Faster drafting is not necessarily faster completion.

Check the billing currency and renewal conditions, then ask how price changes will be communicated. Avoid committing to an annual package before a manageable trial has shown value.

Require a clear support route. Identify who responds when something fails and what assistance is actually included.

Plan the Exit Before Signing

Ask for a demonstration of exporting records in a usable format. Check whether templates, attachments and relevant history leave with them, rather than assuming that a download contains everything.

Keep an independent copy of essential business information. Agree how work will continue during an outage and who can suspend automated actions.

Before renewal, compare results with the original problem. Has quotation preparation become more reliable? Are customers asking fewer clarification questions? Can employees explain and correct the output?

For Ghanaian businesses, successful adoption should strengthen control rather than surrender it. The right supplier is not necessarily the one with the most impressive presentation. It is the one whose promises can be tested, whose responsibilities are clear and whose service remains worth paying for.

Ghana News.title: Nollywood actor Diewait Ikpechukwu dies at 71
Ghana News.content:
Veteran Nollywood actor Diewait Ikpechukwu has died at the age of 71, bringing to an end a career that spanned more than two decades in the Nigerian film industry.

The actor reportedly died on Thursday, November 5, 2026, with the Actors Guild of Nigeria (AGN) confirming his passing on Friday, November 6.

AGN National President, Alhaji Abubakar Sanusi Yakubu, announced the death in a tribute, describing Ikpechukwu as another legend whose memories would remain with the industry.

Ikpechukwu was particularly recognised for his portrayal of traditional rulers and other authoritative characters in Nollywood productions.

His performances in films such as Evil Men, alongside veteran actor Pete Edochie, as well as Python King, The Guilty and Omera, earned him recognition among audiences.

Beyond his work on screen, he played an active role in the Actors Guild of Nigeria, serving as chairman of its Enugu State chapter, where he supported and mentored emerging actors.

His journey into entertainment, however, was not limited to acting. Before establishing himself in Nollywood, Ikpechukwu was an accomplished footballer in the 1970s and reportedly earned an invitation to join Nigeria’s national team, then known as the Green Eagles.

He later ventured into radio broadcasting, working as a sports commentator before pursuing a career in film.

Ikpechukwu is survived by his wife, Gloria, children and grandchildren, who join colleagues, friends and fans in mourning his passing.

His death marks another loss for Nollywood, particularly among the generation of actors whose performances helped shape the Nigerian film industry.

Ghana News.title: Mining Reforms Must Protect Jobs, Investment and Community Interests — Ghana Chamber of Mines
Ghana News.content:
The Ghana Chamber of Mines has called for sustained dialogue and careful consideration of the economic implications of ongoing mining sector reforms, stressing that efforts to deepen Ghanaian participation must also safeguard employment, investment and the industry’s long-term competitiveness.

The Chamber’s Chief Operating Officer, Ahmed Dasana Nantogmah, said recent concerns expressed by mineworkers and host communities highlighted the importance of consultation and a balanced approach to mining policy and regulatory decisions.

His comments follow protests by mineworkers at Akyem Abirem over the directive to transition certain mining operations from owner mining to contract mining. The workers have raised concerns about potential implications for job security, wages, benefits and existing conditions of service.

Mr. Nantogmah acknowledged government’s commitment to strengthening local participation in the mining industry, describing it as an important national objective that the Chamber supports.

“Greater Ghanaian participation in mining is an objective we all share. However, the approach must protect existing jobs, maintain safety and operational efficiency, and ensure that the industry remains competitive enough to sustain investment and create new opportunities,” he said.

He emphasised that significant changes to established mining operating models require meaningful consultation among regulators, mining companies, employees and other stakeholders to ensure that policy objectives are achieved without unintended economic consequences.

Commenting on the ongoing discussions surrounding the renewal of Gold Fields Ghana’s Tarkwa mining leases, Mr. Nantogmah acknowledged the expectations of host communities for greater and more visible benefits from mineral development.

“Mining communities must see tangible improvements in their livelihoods. Equally, investors must have confidence that their rights and obligations will be administered fairly and consistently. These objectives are not mutually exclusive,” he stated.

He stressed the importance of constructive engagement with traditional authorities and other stakeholders, while ensuring that decisions concerning mineral rights are guided by transparent, predictable and lawful procedures.

Mr. Nantogmah also noted the recent regulatory developments involving Adamus Resources and Northern Ashanti Mines, emphasising the importance of continued engagement in addressing such matters.

He acknowledged the responsibility of the Minerals Commission and the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources to ensure compliance with mining laws, while encouraging dialogue, due process and mutual understanding in resolving regulatory concerns in the interest of sustaining investor confidence and protecting Ghana’s mining industry.

The COO further pointed to recent operational and financial results announced by Galiano Gold and AngloGold Ashanti as indications of the industry’s capacity to sustain production and pursue further investment opportunities.

He noted that realising this potential requires a stable operating environment, access to capital and a competitive fiscal and regulatory framework.

“Our collective objective should be to develop mining policies that secure fair revenues for the State, expand opportunities for Ghanaian businesses, protect jobs and deliver lasting benefits to communities, while encouraging the investments needed to sustain future mineral production,” he said.

Mr. Nantogmah reaffirmed the Chamber’s commitment to working constructively with government, regulators, organised labour, traditional authorities and other stakeholders to strengthen Ghana’s position as a competitive and responsible mining investment destination.

Ghana News.title: COCOBOD relaunches free fertilizer programme with new monitoring platform to boost farmer incomes
Ghana News.content:
The government has relaunched the Free Fertilizer and Agro-Input Programme for cocoa farmers under a major intervention to restore productivity, improve farmer incomes, and reset the cocoa sector.

The program is a policy shift from a 50-per cent subsidy to free fertilizer distribution to farmers, which the Ghana Cocoa Board says represents a total reset of how government intends to support farmers and increase cocoa production.

The relaunch of the program has seen the procurement of over 3.5 million bags of granular fertilizer for distribution to cocoa farmers nationwide.

Approximately 1.2 million bags have already been delivered to farmers as a new digital platform has been developed to strengthen accountability and ensure fair distribution.

Speaking at the event, Chief Executive Officer of COCOBOD, Dr. Randy Abbey, described the intervention as a decisive declaration that government, through COCOBOD, is fully committed to relieving the financial burdens of farmers.

He explained the initiative also seeks to restore maximum productivity to the soil and secure the golden future of the cocoa sector.

“We are removing financial barriers to high yields. Free fertilizer is not a handout; it is an investment in farmers, in the soil, and in the foreign exchange earnings of this republic,” Dr. Abbey said.

The relaunch held at Sefwi Wiawso under the theme: “Cocoa Sector Reset: Free Fertilizer for Increased Productivity and Improved Farmer Income,” brought together government officials, traditional leaders, farmers, and other stakeholders in the cocoa value chain.

Farmers with mature and productive cocoa plantations in designated operational district areas are expected to receive fertilizer, whether granular or liquid, as well as insecticides and fungicides.

The COCOBOD will also supply free pneumatic and motorized sprayers to farmers.

Dr. Abbey noted that the board is fully aware of the challenges that plagued previous free distribution systems, highlighting that the good intentions of the state to revamp the sector were rather undermined by diversion, smuggling, favouritism, and unfair distribution.

“Inputs meant for genuine farmers ended up in open markets across the borders and on the farms of the well-connected, while smallholder farmers at the end of the line went home empty-handed,” he noted.

The COCOBOD is rolling out a new digital system to track every input taken from the warehouses to farms to ensure accountability and prevent abuse of the reintroduced initiative.

According to the COCOBOD boss, every beneficiary must register and have their farms marked and captured on the Digital Cocoa Management System (CMS).

The identity of every farmer will be verified at the point of collection through the national identification card or by biometric data.

“This time, we have built the entire distribution around a new digital distribution system that follows every bag or litre of input from the warehouse to the farm. No one can collect the fertilizer and the agro-inputs in another person’s name, and no ghost farmer names can appear on the list,” Dr. Abbey said.

He added that the system calculates each farmer’s entitlement automatically based on the marked size and condition of the farm, and therefore, officers at distribution points cannot add or deduct from the allocation.

Dr. Abbey cautioned smugglers and saboteurs, stressing that any officer, buyer, or individual found diverting or selling the distribution inputs will face the full rigours of the law.

The cocoa industry continues to face significant challenges, including declining productivity, ageing and unproductive farms, rising production costs, labour constraints, soil fertility challenges, persistent threats of capsid pests and swollen shoot virus disease, and the increasing effects of climate variability.

Highlighting the importance of cocoa to the country’s economy, Board Chairman of the COCOBOD, Dr. Samuel Ofosu-Ampofo, noted that these challenges require deliberate, coordinated and sustained interventions.

He noted that the distribution of the fertilizers is in line with the government’s commitment to addressing the challenges confronting the cocoa value chain.

"We cannot expect increased national cocoa production without investing adequately in the farms and supporting the farmers who cultivate them. Equally, we cannot achieve sustainable productivity if we do not address the underlying challenges of soil fertility, pest and disease management, access to improved planting material and effective extension services,” he said.

Additionally, the COCOBOD says 1.8 million litres of liquid fertilizer, 2.3 million litres of insecticide, and 1.5 million kilograms of fungicide have been purchased for cocoa farmers across the country.

Dr. Ofosu-Ampofo said that the government has unprecedentedly supplied about 27,000 new spray machines in a single year, bringing the total number of spray machines available to about 67,000.

To complement the supply of sprayers and chemicals, he also noted that approximately 5.7 million litres of pre-mixed fuel have been supplied to cocoa farmers to support the mechanical application of liquid fertilizer and insecticides.

The board and management of COCOBOD say they remain committed to ensuring a sustainable cocoa economy that provides optimal benefits to farmers, sustains profitable and integrated value chains, as well as promotes environmental resilience and social inclusion.

Ghana News.title: Farmers urged to enroll in insurance policies to protect investments against El Niño impacts
Ghana News.content:
The recent climatic phenomenon, El Niño, is prompting the urgency for farmers to take immediate steps to seek insurance protection for their investments.

Despite the rollout of insurance policies, including the Ghana Agriculture Insurance Pool, for the agricultural value chain, many farmers fail to leverage the avenues to mitigate financial hardship brought about by unpredictable weather conditions and crop diseases.

The Chartered Insurance Institute of Ghana is pushing for farmers to safeguard their investment now against the vagaries of the harsh weather as the world is predicted to further heat up in the ensuing years.

Weather and climate experts predict intense weather conditions in the coming years, exposing uninsured farmers to more threats of loss.

Despite a pool of insurance policies, farmers continue to lose out on their benefits.

The insurers are moving to strengthen insurance products for the agriculture sector to rope in more farmers to safeguard their investments.

Speaking at the annual conference of the Chartered Insurance Institute of Ghana in Kumasi, Chairman of the Insurance Awareness Coordinators Group, Wilson Teye, highlighted challenges confronting the rollout and uptake of the policies by farmers.

“We haven’t had mechanized agriculture. We depend completely on the vagaries of the weather and that is a problem. Even some of our methods, such as deliberately setting fires on farms, are issues. There is also the challenge of bring all the farmers together to understand and appreciate the need for insurance. But regardless, we have brought this to the forefront and are addressing agricultural insurance,” he said.

Agricultural insurance provides protection to key stakeholders in the agricultural production value chain in the event of crop failure ad livestock mortality due to both natural phenomena and human-induced activities.

President of the Chartered Insurance Institute of Ghana, Solomon Nii Amah-Kai Lartey, says the time is now for vulnerable large- and small-scale farmers to secure their produce.

“Make sure you have your insurance now. There is parametric insurance, which does need much assessment after a loss. Once the parameters are triggered, a claim can be made. With the emergence of El Niño, people should get insured now,” he said.

Mr. Amah-Kai also disclosed that farmers and other stakeholders along the agriculture value chain can leverage the dedicated insurance pool for subsidized products.

“The Ghana Agriculture Insurance Pool is available for agriculture stakeholders. This pool is there to ensure that agric insurance premiums are subsidized for people to be able to buy insurance,” he said.

Deputy Commissioner of Insurance, Bernard Ohemeng Baah, emphasized the importance of insurance for agriculture as he revealed that the National Insurance Commission is in its concluding stages to roll out subsidized agriculture insurance for smallholder farmers.

“Because we don’t have data, the price of insurance for farmers tends to be really high. So, many of them don’t patronize it. We are employing innovative approaches to deliver insurance to farmers at a low cost. This will help protect Ghana’s food basket and also ensure that families that depend on agriculture are not exposed to the shocks of the weather,” he said.

Closing the Insurance Gap

The AGM and educational conference of the insurers, held on the theme: “Closing the Gap: From Awareness to Action in Building an Adaptive Insurance Industry,” assembled professional stakeholders in the sector to leverage the opportunity in building a resilient insurance industry.

Ghana’s insurance industry, despite making considerable gains, is still confronted with significant gaps between public awareness, insurance ownership, and effective financial protection.

In 2024, Ghana’s insurance penetration stood at approximately 1.0 per cent of the gross domestic product (GDP). The International Financial Reporting Standards report 0.63 per cent associated with insurance service revenue. But insurers only paid approximately 3.6 billion cedis in claims during 2024.

Mr. Nii Amah-Kai noted that the challenge must extend beyond just raising awareness but must extend insurance protection to more people and businesses and also to ensure that the experience of purchasing and using insurance justifies the public’s confidence in the insurance cover.

“We need to make sure that the awareness we are creating is translating into real insurance take-up. This conference seeks to find answers to whether or not the awareness is properly done and how it is benefiting the Ghanaian people,” he said.

Mr. Wilson Teye says people’s trust and confidence must be heightened to increase their enrolment in insurance policy avenues.

“The bedrock of insurance is payment of claims. If people do not trust that their claims will be paid and on time, they naturally wouldn’t want their money buying insurance. The objective is to address the mistrust and get regulatory intervention,” he said.

As part of the annual activities, the association also visited the T.I. Ahmadiyya SHS in Kumasi to sensitize students on the job prospects in pursuing study programmes in insurance and actuarial science.

The association also invested in the digital infrastructure of the school with the donation of printers and learning projectors to aid academic work, while also providing some souvenirs from member insurance companies.
