Trans Nzoia Governor George Natembeya, however, said Sifuna was best placed to challenge the President and asked Mr Gachagua and Mr Musyoka to back him.

“I want to urge Gachagua and Kalonzo to back Sifuna for the opposition to secure an easy win against Ruto. I want to assure you that there will be no rigging of the election,” he said.

Meru Governor Kawira Mwangaza said Kenyans would reject Ruto at the ballot for failing to honour pledges, including those on women’s empowerment.

Sifuna accused the President of failing to protect the Constitution and the rights of Kenyans. “He has focused more on building houses and markets and failed to protect lives,” he said.

He also claimed the government had issued title deeds for smaller parcels than residents used to own, while land was stolen. He further alleged that the government was plotting to plunder mineral resources at Mrima Hill in Kwale and demanded that an agreement with American investors be made public.

World.title: Musonye to lead AFCON 2027 preparations
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Sports Cabinet Secretary Salim Mvurya with Local Organising Committee (LOC) Standing Committee chairperson Nicholas Musonye on October 29, 2026. [Jonah Onyango, Standard]

Sports Cabinet Secretary Salim Mvurya has unveiled the Local Organising Committee (LOC) Standing Committee for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON PAMOJA 2027), with Nicholas Musonye appointed chairman to oversee Kenya’s preparations for the continental football tournament.

Musonye will be deputised by Hussein Mohammed, while Anthony Lung’aho Inzihuli, also known as Antony Emmanuel Inzahuli Lung’aho, will serve as head of the secretariat and chief executive officer.

The committee is tasked with coordinating Kenya’s preparations, including stadium renovations, infrastructure development, operational planning and logistical arrangements ahead of the tournament, which Kenya will co-host with Uganda and Tanzania.

Mvurya said the committee brings together individuals with experience, professional expertise and leadership to help deliver a successful competition that meets the expectations of football fans, participating teams and the Confederation of African Football (CAF).

“I have unveiled the TotalEnergies CAF Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) PAMOJA 2027 LOC Standing Committee, entrusting its members with the national responsibility of coordinating and overseeing Kenya’s preparations towards delivering a world-class, memorable and successful continental football tournament,” Mvurya said.

He challenged members to move from planning to implementation, emphasising operational readiness, coordination, strategic partnerships, financial accountability and adherence to delivery timelines.

“With less than eight months to kick-off, I challenged the committee to move decisively from planning to execution,” he said.

Besides Musonye, Mohammed and Lung’aho Inzihuli, the listed committee members include Football Kenya Federation (FKF) Vice-President McDonald Mariga and FKF National Executive Committee representative Robert Macharia.

Other members named in the roster are Timothy Nabea, a former FKF NEC member; Gabriel Mghendi; Peter Kamau; Kerubo Momanyi; Benard Lagat; Collins Kalee; Caleb Amwayi; Ken Rungu; and Dan Shikanda, the former AFC Leopards chairperson.

The list also includes Charles Njagi, Thomas Karugu, Evelyn Cheluget, Miriam Chepkoech, Rodgers Chimega, Diana Injendi Manyengo and Collins Were.

The 38 committee members also comprises representation across functional areas, including finance, technical matters, refereeing, legal affairs and youth development.

The committee is expected to coordinate the different aspects of tournament preparation and ensure that the relevant agencies and stakeholders work towards agreed targets.

Kenya’s preparations also include the development of Talanta Sports City, officially known as the Raila Odinga International Stadium, which is expected to strengthen the country's capacity to host major international football matches.

Mvurya said the planned high-profile encounter between German giants FC Bayern München and Dutch powerhouse AFC Ajax, scheduled for January 5, 2027, would provide an opportunity to assess the country’s readiness.

The event is expected to test security arrangements, transport and logistics, crowd management, operational systems and the overall fan experience.

The CS also disclosed that representatives of the two European clubs had visited Kenya to assess its capacity to host the proposed fixture.

He said the government was adopting a whole-of-government approach, involving relevant agencies responsible for security, immigration, tourism, travel and hospitality.

AFCON 2027 is expected to attract thousands of supporters, officials and international visitors, creating opportunities for hotels, airlines, tour operators, transport businesses and other service providers.

The government is also positioning the tournament as an opportunity to promote tourism, attract investment, develop sporting infrastructure and inspire young footballers.

Mvurya said the committee carries the responsibility of delivering an event that would bring national pride while creating a lasting legacy for the country.

“I reaffirmed their mandate and reminded them that they carry the hopes and aspirations of over 55 million Kenyans to deliver a tournament that brings pride and joy to the country while securing a lasting legacy in sports development, tourism, investment and economic opportunities,” he said.

World.title: 2026 CAF Awards shortlist: Egyptian footballers and coaches set to battle for Africa’s top prizes
World.content:
The Confederation of African Football (CAF) has officially announced the shortlist of nominees for the 2026 CAF Awards, which will be hosted in the Nigerian capital, Lagos, on December 7. The final shortlist was marked by the exclusion of Al Ahly and star-studded Pyramids FC from the Club of the Year category.

Club and national team nominations: Zamalek carries Egyptian hopes

Club of the Year: Zamalek SC stands as the sole representative of Egyptian football in this category, bearing the hopes of Egyptian fans to clinch the prestigious continental title amid fierce competition from Arab giants (including Esperance de Tunis, Al Hilal Sudan, USM Alger, CR Belouizdad, FAR Rabat, RS Berkane, and Olympique Asfi) alongside South Africa’s Mamelodi Sundowns and DRC’s Maniema Union.

National Team of the Year: The Egyptian National Team (“The Pharaohs”) leads a strong Arab presence alongside Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia. They will clash with heavyweight contenders such as Ivory Coast, Senegal, South Africa, Ghana, DR Congo, and tournament surprise Cape Verde in an open race for continental dominance.

Coach of the Year: Hossam Hassan and Moatamed Gamal lead the line

Egypt boasts two prominent names in the Coach of the Year category:

Hossam Hassan: Head coach of the Egyptian National Team, nominated following a major resurgence in performance and results with The Pharaohs both continentally and internationally.

Moatamed Gamal: Head coach of Zamalek SC, representing Egyptian domestic coaching alongside elite continental figures such as Walid Regragui and Mohamed Ouahbi (Morocco), Sébastien Desabre (DR Congo), and Pape Thiaw (Senegal).

Interclub and Young Player awards: Trézéguet, Shehata, and Hamza Abdelkarim

Interclub Player of the Year (Based in Africa): Featured several prominent names, highlighted by Mohamed Shehata (Zamalek SC) and former Al Ahly star Mahmoud Hassan “Trézéguet” (currently playing for Saudi Arabia’s Al-Riyadh).

Young Player of the Year: Promising Egyptian talent Hamza Abdelkarim made the final shortlist, competing alongside Algeria’s Ibrahim Maza and Moroccan duo Abdellah Ouazane and Ayyoub Bouaddi.

Goalkeeper of the Year: Shobier and El-Mahdy represent Egypt

In the Goalkeeper of the Year category, an Egyptian duo earned nominations to compete for Africa’s top goalkeeper honors:

Mostafa Shobier: Al Ahly goalkeeper.

El-Mahdy Soliman: Zamalek SC goalkeeper.

Women’s football overview

The Women’s category saw a historic presence for Algeria following their qualification for the 2027 World Cup, with Marine Dafeur nominated for Women’s Player of the Year alongside Morocco’s Hanane Aït El Haj. In the Goalkeeper of the Year category, Algeria’s Chloë N’Gazi and Morocco’s Khadija Er-Rmichi feature among the final candidates.

World.title: Egypt condemns missile attack targeting Medina, reaffirms support for Saudi Arabia
World.content:
On Friday, Egypt strongly condemned in the highest terms the attempt to target Medina in the sisterly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia with a ballistic missile.

In a statement issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation, and Egyptians Abroad, Egypt expressed its deep denunciation of such attacks, which represent a flagrant violation of the rules and provisions of international law, and undermine the security and stability of the region as well as de-escalation and peace efforts.

Egypt reaffirmed its full solidarity with the Kingdom and its stance alongside it in all measures it takes to defend its security, sovereignty, and the safety of its territory and citizens—emphasizing that the Kingdom’s security is closely linked to Egyptian national security and serves as one of the pillars of stability in the region as a whole.

On Thursday, the Coalition to Restore Legitimacy in Yemen announced the interception and destruction of a ballistic missile launched by the Houthi group toward Medina.

Saudi Civil Defense had issued an alert yesterday via the National Early Warning Platform in Yanbu Governorate, located on the Red Sea coast, to warn of a potential threat.

World.title: The wealth of nations in the age of AI: What Egypt must get right
World.content:
Two hundred and fifty years ago, Adam Smith published The Wealth of Nations and challenged the way people understood economic prosperity. A country’s wealth, he argued, was not simply the gold accumulated in its treasury, but the productive capacity of its people.

Today, as artificial intelligence begins to reshape economies, industries and labour markets, Smith’s question has acquired a new urgency: what makes a nation wealthy in an age when machines can perform tasks once considered exclusively human?

This was the central question explored at a conference hosted by New Giza University, marking both the 250th anniversary of Smith’s landmark work and the university’s tenth anniversary. Bringing together academics, policymakers and business leaders, including colleagues from the University of Glasgow, where Smith studied and later taught, the discussions offered an opportunity to reconsider the relationship between markets, government, technology and society.

The most important conclusion was that Smith’s ideas remain relevant, but applying them to today’s economy requires a broader understanding of wealth, responsibility and opportunity.

Adam Smith was never an advocate of an absent state

One of the most persistent misconceptions about Adam Smith is that he believed markets should operate without government intervention, or that the pursuit of individual greed would automatically produce collective prosperity.

Smith was a moral philosopher before he became an economist. His understanding of markets was inseparable from questions of justice, responsibility and the welfare of society.

He recognised an essential role for government in protecting rights, maintaining fair competition and providing the conditions in which economic activity could benefit society.

This distinction matters enormously today.

Artificial intelligence is creating opportunities for productivity and economic growth on a scale that would have been difficult to imagine even a decade ago. But it is also raising serious questions about market concentration, employment, privacy and the distribution of economic gains.

The challenge is not simply to encourage technological innovation. It is to ensure that innovation serves the wider economy rather than concentrating wealth and power in the hands of a limited number of companies or individuals.

In other words, the principles of fair markets must now extend to fair algorithms.

The new wealth of nations

In the industrial economy, national wealth was closely associated with factories, natural resources, infrastructure and physical capital.

These remain important. But a new form of economic capital is emerging, built around data, computing power, artificial intelligence models, specialised talent and public trust.

We described this during our discussions as instrumental capital: the resources and capabilities that enable countries to participate meaningfully in the new technological economy.

Possessing advanced technology, however, is not the same as knowing how to use it productively.

Countries will increasingly be judged not by the number of artificial intelligence initiatives they announce, but by their ability to translate technological capabilities into better services, more competitive businesses, higher productivity and improved living standards.

For Egypt, this distinction is particularly important.

The country does not need to compete with the world’s largest technology companies in every field. It needs to identify where artificial intelligence can address real economic and social challenges, and where investment can produce measurable results.

Financial services, agriculture and water management, logistics, healthcare and public services are among the areas in which focused applications could offer significant value.

The objective should not be technological prestige. It should be practical economic improvement.

Regulation should enable innovation, not prevent it

The relationship between governments and technology companies is becoming more complex.

Governments are no longer merely regulators of economic activity. Increasingly, they are investors, strategic planners and participants in the development of technological infrastructure.

This creates both opportunities and risks.

Excessive regulation can discourage experimentation and investment. But insufficient regulation can expose consumers, workers and businesses to decisions they neither understand nor have the ability to challenge.

Egypt therefore needs an approach to AI governance that protects competition, consumers and financial stability while allowing innovation to develop.

Regulatory sandboxes, including approaches already being explored by Egypt’s Financial Regulatory Authority, offer a useful model. They allow new technologies to be tested under supervision before broader regulatory decisions are made.

Equally important is the principle that citizens should have the right to understand and challenge significant decisions made about them by automated systems.

Technology must not become a convenient way of removing accountability from public institutions or private companies.

The greatest investment is still in people

Perhaps the most difficult challenge presented by artificial intelligence concerns employment.

AI is not simply replacing repetitive manual tasks. It is increasingly capable of performing administrative, analytical and professional functions that have traditionally provided entry-level opportunities for young graduates.

For a country such as Egypt, with a large young population, this development demands particular attention.

Education and training systems cannot continue preparing students for an economy that is already changing.

A national partnership between government, universities and employers is needed to develop the skills required by the emerging labour market.

Such a partnership should involve shared funding, practical training and continuous adaptation of educational programmes.

But technical knowledge alone will not be enough.

The capabilities that will distinguish human beings in an increasingly automated economy include judgement, ethical reasoning, creativity, empathy and the ability to understand complex social situations.

The purpose of education must therefore extend beyond teaching students how to use new technologies. It must prepare them to think independently and responsibly in a world shaped by those technologies.

Social protection systems must also evolve. Rather than merely compensating people for the jobs they lose, they should help workers acquire the skills and opportunities needed to move into new forms of employment.

Safety nets must become springboards.

Public investment must create public value

Artificial intelligence requires substantial investment in computing infrastructure, research, data systems and specialised capabilities.

Not all of these investments can be expected to come from the private sector.

There is a legitimate role for government in developing shared infrastructure, supporting research and making high-quality data available under appropriate safeguards.

For Egypt and the wider Arab world, investment in Arabic-language artificial intelligence is especially important.

Language is not simply a technical consideration. It shapes access to knowledge, participation in economic life and the ability of societies to benefit from technological change.

Yet public investment must be guided by clear principles.

It should be transparent, competitive and open to private-sector participation. Its purpose should be to create opportunities for a broad range of businesses and innovators, not to establish a small group of privileged beneficiaries.

Small and medium-sized enterprises, in particular, need practical support to move beyond isolated experiments and adopt AI tools that improve productivity.

Success should be measured by economic value, not by the number of pilot projects or announcements.

Universities have a central role in this process. They must become active partners in research, policy development and industry collaboration, rather than remaining observers of technological transformation.

Prosperity must be measured by its human impact

There is a danger that the debate about artificial intelligence will become dominated by investment figures, technological capabilities and competition between nations.

These are important, but they are not sufficient measures of success.

Adam Smith offered a more enduring test when he wrote: “No society can surely be flourishing and happy, of which the far greater part of the members are poor and miserable.”

That observation remains as relevant today as it was in the eighteenth century.

Artificial intelligence may generate extraordinary wealth. But if its benefits remain concentrated, if young people find fewer opportunities, or if technological efficiency comes at the expense of human dignity, economic progress will have failed a fundamental test.

For Egypt, the real question is not how much artificial intelligence we can acquire, or how quickly we can announce its adoption.

It is whether we can use it to create a more productive economy, stronger institutions, better employment opportunities and a fairer distribution of prosperity.

Two hundred and fifty years after Adam Smith asked what makes nations wealthy, the answer still begins with people.

Technology may change the instruments through which wealth is created. It should not change the ultimate purpose for which that wealth exists.

World.title: Water rescues, evacuations underway as ‘catastrophic flood event’ hits North Georgia and southern Tennessee
World.content:
Homes are flooded and water rescues and evacuations are in progress as flash flood emergencies — the highest level of flood warning — impact North Georgia and southern Tennessee.

Follow this storm live. Track changing conditions in real time.

The flash flood emergencies are in effect for McCaysville, Georgia, and Copperhill, Tennessee, on the Georgia-Tennessee border.

Record flooding is ongoing there along a river known as the Ocoee River in Tennessee and the Toccoa River in Georgia once it flows across the border.

The river crested just above the previous record flood set in 1990 just after 6:00 a.m. ET in McCaysville and Copperhill, above the level that causes a “catastrophic flood event” in the two towns, according to the National Weather Service.

A state of emergency has been issued in McCaysville, and the city is closed until further notice, according to the city’s police chief Michael Earley.

“We’re actively trying to water rescue people, and we’ve still got several people trapped in homes that we’re trying to get to,” Earley told CNN affiliate Atlanta News First. “The water keeps rising, so just bear with us as much as you can and please say a prayer for them and their families.”

There were still “numerous residents” that needed evacuations in Fannin County, where McCaysville is located, the county’s emergency management said early Thursday morning.

Evacuations were ordered for residents in McCaysville on West Tennessee Avenue and East Tennessee Avenue, where a Georgia DOT camera showed streets and buildings swamped by the flooded river.

“DO NOT DELAY YOUR EVACUATION. LEAVE THE AREA NOW,” Earley said in a social media post.

A separate flash flood emergency was also issued overnight for other parts of Fannin County and Gilmer County in Georgia.

Emergency management in both counties reported “widespread flooding, with multiple homes flooded and some completely surrounded by water” and water rescues.

Flooding in downtown McCaysville, Georgia, as seen on a Georgia traffic cam. Georgia DOT

Widespread rainfall totals of 3 to 6 inches from slow-moving overnight storms were reported across parts of North Georgia, with over 8 inches in isolated spots.

Up to 6 inches of rain fell in just six hours at multiple rain gauges in the area. This equates to at least a 1-in-200-year rainfall — a rate that has only a 0.5% chance of happening in a given year, under normal circumstances.

Such extreme rainfall is becoming more common as planet-warming pollution pushes temperatures higher as warmer air can hold more moisture.

The rain has come to an end across northern Georgia and southern Tennessee. No additional downpours are expected through the weekend, but dangerous river flooding will remain a threat throughout the day.

World.title: Anthropic was founded to answer to humanity. Soon, it will also answer to Wall Street
World.content:
In 2021, a group of employees at OpenAI left to start a new company focused on the safe development of artificial intelligence. They named it Anthropic, a word that means “relating to humanity.” Later this month, that company is expected to make its debut on Wall Street in what could be one of the largest initial public offerings in history. But the move raises a fundamental question: Can a company put humanity first while also answering to Wall Street?

The IPO is a monumental development for the AI boom and will put a spotlight on how investors feel about the maker of the Claude chatbot. The stock market debut also marks a new chapter for Anthropic that will test whether it can balance its mission of safely developing AI with the pressures of being a publicly traded company.

Anthropic has a special ownership structure designed to help the company stick to its original goals, balance profit growth with its mission and keep investors from staging a takeover. The structure includes a group of trustees who have majority control of the board of directors, as well as a special class of shares that ensures the seven founders own a majority of the general shareholder voting power.

With its mission for safe AI and its unorthodox corporate structure, Anthropic’s Wall Street debut can be viewed as a guinea pig for AI frontier labs and how they are received by investors.

The Nasdaq MarketSite in New York on October 16, 2026. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Public benefit corporation

Anthropic is registered as a public benefit corporation, or PBC. These types of companies are legally required to balance the interests of shareholders with the company’s stated mission. It’s different from a traditional company that focuses primarily on maximizing shareholder value.

“The governance structure for Anthropic is very unique,” said Gil Luria, head of technology research at financial services firm D.A. Davidson. “They spell it out. They’re very upfront about it.”

Anthropic described its “tripartite goals” as a PBC in its S-1 filing: “the pecuniary interest of our stockholders, the best interest of those materially affected by our conduct and the Company Purpose.”

Just a fraction of publicly traded companies are PBCs. Patagonia, which is privately held, and eyewear retailer Warby Parker (WRBY) are both PBCs.

PBCs can choose what they want to do with corporate profits and invest as much as they want in safety measures. And investors have little power to do anything about it. Anthropic rival OpenAI became a PBC in 2025.

“Anthropic is explicit about that, that they believe that there will be instances where they choose not to maximize shareholder value because of the judgments that they make, the board and the leadership team,” Luria said.

“Growing the company and enjoying profitability are part of the goal, so it’s not that it’s contrary to the goal,” he added. “It’s just that they’re saying that there may be some cases where that is not the goal, or they seek other goals, even at the expense of growth and profitability.”

Anthropic’s seven founders collectively have 50.1% of the voting rights at the company, which means regular shareholders won’t have any say in its operations. This is a variation of a trend in Big Tech companies in recent years that have had structures where the founders retain majority control, like Mark Zuckerberg at Meta and Elon Musk at SpaceX.

Long-Term Benefit Trust

It’s not just that the founders have majority control. Anthropic in 2023 established the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), which is composed of five subject-matter experts who have no financial stake in the company’s stock. However, they have special non-financial shares with the authority to appoint four directors to the seven-person company board.

The LTBT members include Neil Buddy Shah, CEO at the Clinton Health Access Initiative; and Ben Bernanke, a former chair of the Federal Reserve. There is one vacancy in the LTBT that has yet to be filled.

“The LTBT may have interests that differ from yours, and it may exercise its power in a way with which you disagree or in a way that may be adverse to your interests,” Anthropic says in a filing with the SEC, referring to shareholders.

When a company goes public, there can be more pressure to grow profits and deliver strong results for shareholders. But Anthropic and CEO Dario Amodei have also talked about the risk of AI causing tremendous harm to humanity if placed in the wrong hands. Anthropic’s IPO filing includes more than 90 pages of risk disclosures, varying from how AI can be misused by bad actors to the possibility of existential risk to humanity.

“While this Long-Term Benefit Trust has a lot of power, the founders also have a lot of power. But, you know, in both cases, public shareholders don’t have the power,” said Jay Ritter, professor emeritus at the University of Florida and an expert in IPOs.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei outside the White House on September 29, 2026. He has talked about the risk of AI to humanity if it ends up in the wrong hands. Finn Gomez/Getty Images

What does this all mean?

If there are growing concerns about AI, the founders and LTBT can make decisions for the company that impact the value of shares without any consideration for investors. In theory, it can help the company stick to its mission — but it remains to be seen how the structure will function until an event forces the company to act.

Anthropic’s ownership structure won’t matter as much if profits are strong and it follows its mission of developing safe AI. But it will be stress-tested if earnings aren’t as strong as expected, safety issues arise, or disagreements fester between the board, founders or trustees, Luria at D.A. Davidson said.

“The strangest aspect of Anthropic’s filing is its corporate governance structure,” Jay Goldberg, senior analyst at Seaport Research Partners, wrote in a note. “We believe this is the largest PBC and the full implications of this structure will take time to become apparent.”

“We believe this structure gives the LTBT and the founders effective permanent control of the company,” Goldberg added.

World.title: Republicans quickly turn against Pete Hegseth after midterms rout
World.content:
President Donald Trump may have made the decision to launch the war that tanked voters’ support for the GOP and dealt them a midterm shellacking. But the historic losses are accelerating a push for someone else to take the fall: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

And the House could vote as soon as next week to impeach the Pentagon’s top leader.

Many Republican lawmakers and allies alarmed by Tuesday’s wipeout are moving swiftly to pin blame for the election results on Hegseth, arguing behind the scenes that he played a chief role in convincing Trump to attack Iran with no exit strategy — and no plan for managing the inevitable political fallout.

The knives-out campaign comes despite private acknowledgement from House and Senate GOP strategists that the party’s problems extended far beyond the war, triggering 2008-level losses that will take years to reverse. But for now, party leaders – and many in their ranks – remain unwilling to directly blame Trump for their woes.

Even among House Republicans who survived Tuesday’s onslaught, there’s zero expectation they will suddenly break from the president with two years left in his term. Yet that fealty does not extend to Hegseth, the combative defense secretary who has made few friends on Capitol Hill since taking over command of the Pentagon.

House Republicans are expected to vote to directly repudiate the defense secretary in a matter of days. Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, the famously anti-Trump GOP lawmaker, told CNN he plans to trigger a vote to impeach Hegseth when Congress returns next week — and multiple GOP sources said they expect it to pass.

Rep. Thomas Massie speaks to reporters after delivering a speech introducing a proposal to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, to the House of Representatives on September 16. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

Hegseth, a vocal cheerleader for the war, oversold the US’ ability to win the conflict quickly and easily, multiple Republicans argued to CNN, describing on condition of anonymity why many in their party are now turning against the defense secretary. They accused him of continuing to advocate for escalation despite little sign that continued bombing has brought Iran closer to surrender.

The conflict has since turned into a quagmire, they said, entangling the US in the Middle East indefinitely, worsening the affordability crisis, and triggering voters’ midterm revolt against the GOP. On Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance issued an extraordinary statement that “the reason we lost is the war,” though he did not assign any specific blame for the conflict.

“The pivot is starting” on the war and Hegseth, a former senior Pentagon official said. “This has been primarily a Department of War-led effort because you chose to take military action to resolve a foreign policy matter.”

Still, despite efforts around him to turn up the heat on Hegseth, Trump’s own confidence in his defense secretary hasn’t yet wavered even as he’s continued to survey allies about his performance, multiple White House officials told CNN.

Trump personally likes Hegseth, and has told aides that he believes he should fight back against efforts to impeach him or launch investigations into his decision-making.

“Just two days ago the president was in the room with him, telling him, ‘You’re my best guy. You’re the best guy I have,’” one of the officials said.

Trump may also feel an additional need to keep Hegseth around if he chooses to move forward with additional strikes against Iran, another source familiar with his thinking told CNN, especially with Democrats’ new majority in the Senate likely to complicate any administration efforts to confirm new Cabinet appointees.

Pressed Wednesday on Hegseth’s job status, Trump defended the war effort and denied any plans to fire him, saying he thought the defense secretary was “doing a very good job.”

“If I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again,” Trump said of his decision to go to war.

This video screenshot shows a monitor aboard the USS George Washington, displaying a camera feed of a fighter jet landing on the aircraft carrier’s deck in the Arabian Sea, on September 13. The aircraft carrier was enforcing a US naval blockade against Iran. Ed Ou/Reuters

The White House also decried the prospect of Democratic investigations into the Pentagon, with spokeswoman Lauren Bis arguing in a statement that “if Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.”

But some Republicans feel it may be only a matter of time before Trump looks for someone to blame for the midterm losses, and they view Hegseth as an obvious target.

“If the president is serious about anyone taking responsibility for it, it’s Pete Hegseth,” one Republican close to the White House said of the electoral thrashing. “Pete has been either dishonest or incorrect — neither of which are acceptable — about timelines, goals and objectives since the beginning.”

Trump has not yet signaled plans to fire any top officials. But in the aftermath of the GOP’s midterm drubbing, allies and advisers widely expect him to eventually oversee some level of changes within the administration.

Within Trump’s orbit, some have seized on Hegseth’s likely impeachment as additional justification for making him the fall guy in the wake of an embarrassing rebuke of Trump’s presidency — contending that he’s bound to become a central target of Democrats’ ire over the war anyway.

Hegseth, for his part, has been defiant about his ability to withstand the forthcoming wave of congressional scrutiny.

While he has at times discussed his potential future ambitions with allies — including possibly running for office in Tennessee — those closest to Trump don’t believe that’s an immediate goal of his, people familiar with the discussions said. (Some Republicans on the Hill, in the meantime, privately bristle at the prospect of Hegseth serving in Congress.)

In the immediate aftermath of Tuesday’s midterm election results, one person close to Hegseth told CNN that Trump’s defense secretary still expects to stay in his role and is prepared to fight an impeachment effort.

Hegseth has also communicated to the White House that he’s prepared to own every policy decision and action taken by the Pentagon, the person said, believing that he’s well-equipped to defend those moves in public hearings that would likely grow contentious if Democrats launch them after they take control of Congress in January.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth walks offstage after presenting President Donald Trump during an event at Sparrows Point Shipyard, in Baltimore County, Maryland, on October 6. Eric Lee/Reuters

In a statement, chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said that Hegseth “will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists.”

“We will continue to drive President Trump’s agenda at the Department of War — despite threats of sham witch hunts from Democrats — and Secretary Hegseth is 100% committed to leading the Department until the end of President Trump’s term in office,” Parnell said.

Yet once that congressional scrutiny ramps up, Trump advisers and allies have questioned how long Hegseth’s resolve might last. Even before Tuesday, several White House officials, members of the president’s political operation and Trump allies candidly acknowledged the Iran war was — in their view — their biggest liability for the midterms. And Hegseth, one of the biggest proponents of military action in Iran, is intrinsically linked to that liability, they added.

“I think he probably knows he’s dead but would like an exit sufficiently dramatic that it gives him a launching pad to run for POTUS,” one administration official said.

For skeptics of the administration’s open-ended war in Iran, successfully pushing Hegseth out of the Pentagon would mark a critical victory — but only the first step in a broader effort to bring the fight to an end.

After all, Massie noted, Trump has continued to argue for continuing the war in Iran, no matter the political and economic price paid at home.

“You don’t screw up this badly an election with just one issue,” Massie said. “It was completely avoidable if they’d just broken out of the cultish following of Donald Trump.”

World.title: Top Iranian official mocks Vance after VP blames Iran war for midterm rout
World.content:
A senior Iranian negotiator mocked JD Vance on Thursday after the US Vice President blamed Republican midterm losses on the war in Iran.

Iran’s Speaker of Parliament Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf said on Thursday that Vance showed “losing-gambler energy,” and that he “can’t walk away from the table.”

“Boss is prepping the next war phase while America teeters on an Israel-First cliff. Skip the TED talk. Why not say this to your boss?” Ghalibaf wrote on X.

Trump has admitted that the war in Iran was partly to blame for the Republicans’ losses. Vance was more explicit, saying in a lengthy X post Wednesday that “the reason we lost is the war.”

Ghalibaf has been the main negotiator in US-Iran talks to end the war.

World.title: The world is waging a “Third World War” through Artificial Intelligence – what role can Egypt play?
World.content:
Technology and the struggle for global influence have become increasingly intertwined at a time when Artificial Intelligence (AI) has grown from a mere economic tool into a defining component of national power and countries’ capacity for strategic deterrence.

This has made the development of AI capabilities and the regulation of their use matters of national security, particularly amid the growing military applications of these technologies and documented evidence of their use in the genocidal war waged in the Gaza Strip.

Against this backdrop, New Giza University, in collaboration with the University of Glasgow, hosted a conference titled “The New Wealth of Nations: AI Is Fundamentally Reshaping the Global Economy.”

The event, bringing together a distinguished group of diplomats and academics, examined the implications of the technological revolution for the global balance of power, the future of the economy, and the development of ethical and institutional frameworks to govern the use of intelligent technologies.

Egypt emerged prominently in the conference discussions as a country well positioned to play an influential role in the emerging international order.

This potential stems from its geographic location, strategic weight, and role in managing Middle Eastern crises, as well as opportunities to expand its presence in global trade, investment, and production chains, and contribute to shaping the rules governing cybersecurity and artificial intelligence.

Amid competition among the United States, China, and the European Union, alongside the rise of blocs such as BRICS, participants raised questions about Egypt’s ability to help move countries across the region from a position of vulnerability to international conflicts and transformations to that of active partners in shaping their future.

They stressed that stability in the Middle East remains contingent on a just settlement of the Palestinian issue, while shifts in the global economy are creating new opportunities for Egypt, provided it develops the technological and institutional capabilities needed to compete.

The forum marked the 10th anniversary of New Giza University and the 250th anniversary of the publication of The Wealth of Nations by Scottish economist Adam Smith, widely regarded as the “father of modern economics.”

His ideas on the division of labor and free trade laid important foundations for understanding the growth of production, wealth, and societal prosperity.

The opening session featured discussions among leaders, officials, and academics who drew on Smith’s intellectual legacy to interpret contemporary transformations.

They warned of technology becoming an instrument of conflict among major powers and highlighted the risks of wealth and influence becoming concentrated in the hands of a limited number of companies and countries.

They also underscored the need to redefine the role of the state in regulating markets, protecting people, and ensuring a fairer distribution of the benefits of technological progress.

Adly: AI is a new arena of conflict among major powers, with Egypt at the heart of a changing international order

Egypt’s former ambassador to the European Union in Brussels, Raouf Adly, said that AI had become a new arena of competition among major powers, as international rivalry shifts from traditional military capabilities towards technological ownership, knowledge production, and data processing.

He described the ongoing cyber confrontation as a “Third World War” being waged through different means, warning that the region risks being left out of this equation.

He further cautioned against the use of these intelligent technologies without ethical safeguards to protect humanity.

Adly ruled out the possibility that international relations would remain confined to a bipolar framework dominated by major powers.

Instead, he predicted a growing role for regional blocs and cross-regional alliances, potentially creating opportunities to reinvigorate European partnerships with the Middle East amid tensions between Washington and Brussels.

He stated that Egypt was well positioned to occupy a pivotal place in these emerging dynamics.

Adly based his assessment on the historical turning points that followed the two world wars, noting that the First World War led to the establishment of the League of Nations, while the Second World War gave rise to the United Nations.

Major wars, explained, have historically transformed the structure and institutions of the international system, raising the possibility of another reshaping of international relations in the near future.

Adly also discussed his experience in negotiations over the Egypt-European Partnership Agreement, which was linked to the Madrid Peace Conference and aimed at building economic and trade relations that would pave the way for a broad free-trade area.

However, the stalled peace process prevented this vision from fully achieving its objectives, leaving the agreements closer to a model of “managed free trade” than to the complete liberalization of commercial exchange.

He argued that tensions between the US and Europe could prompt European capitals to redirect part of their economic and strategic relationships towards regions beyond the continent, particularly the Middle East, Africa, Asia, and Latin America. This, he said, would give Egypt an opportunity to strengthen its partnerships, given its geopolitical position and its role in managing regional crises.

Adly added that developments in the Middle East since October 7, 2023, had once again highlighted the importance of Egypt’s role in containing crises.

Cairo’s influence, he said, rests on a measured and precise diplomatic approach, as well as international recognition of its position in regional stability calculations.

He stressed that any vision for the region’s future would remain incomplete without a just settlement of the Palestinian issue.

On economic transformations, Adly cautioned against reducing BRICS to an alliance seeking to overthrow the dollar or confront the United States. Instead, he viewed the bloc as reflecting a broader shift towards international multipolarity and creating opportunities to redirect trade and cooperation across regions.

He cited the dollar’s continued dominance in approximately 80 percent of global transactions and China’s foreign exchange reserves, estimated at around $3.2 trillion, arguing that these figures do not support simplistic assumptions that Beijing intends to abandon the US currency.

Concluding his remarks, Adly linked current transformations to the legacy of economist Adam Smith, arguing that the rise of protectionist policies had harmed international trade and that the global economy was moving towards a more regulated model, which he described as “managed free trade.”

This, he said, reflects a shift away from the concept of the market’s “invisible hand” towards a greater role for the “visible hand” of government policies and organized intervention.

Nazif: Egypt must establish ethical rules governing the use of AI

Former Egyptian Prime Minister Ahmed Nazif linked the transformations that AI is bringing to the global economy with the future of development in Egypt.

He stressed that the diversity of the Egyptian economy and the country’s location at the crossroads of three continents offer opportunities to attract investment and strengthen its presence in international production and trade chains.

He explained that artificial intelligence is not merely an advancement in production tools, but a transformation that is redefining wealth, economic value, and competitiveness.

This, he said, makes it necessary to establish ethical rules governing its applications and protecting people from potential harm.

Nazif called for subjecting AI applications to what he described as “meta-rules”: fundamental ethical principles that should precede the rules governing machines and prevent them from killing, lying, or cheating.

He stressed that any program violating these principles should be stopped.

These rules, he argued, should govern the relationship between AI systems, human beings, society, and the environment, regardless of differences in economic and political systems.

He recalled beginning his studies of AI in 1976, when the field was known as “expert systems.” His doctoral dissertation focused on developing such systems, with particular emphasis on meta-rules.

The current challenge, he explained, lies in transferring the hierarchy of human rules to machines, enabling them to distinguish between fundamental principles designed to protect life and changing economic rules.

Nazif also reviewed his experience in developing Egypt’s telecommunications sector during his tenure as minister, highlighting the establishment of an independent regulatory authority, market liberalization, and opening the sector to private-sector investment.

He considered reducing the government’s direct role in production and service delivery, while strengthening regulation and oversight, an application of free-market principles.

According to his assessment, foreign direct investment in Egypt increased tenfold over a period of five or six years. He noted that approximately half of the investments he referred to came from Egyptian investors, including expatriates and entrepreneurs.

Globally, Nazif said wealth was no longer confined to labor and capital, but had expanded to include intellectual property, brands, quality, and competitiveness.

He cited automotive production chains, whose components and manufacturing stages are distributed across dozens of countries.

He described AI as a new phase following the agricultural, industrial, and digital revolutions, and therefore requiring regulatory frameworks that maximize its benefits while limiting its risks.

He called for strengthening Egypt’s position in this competition.

University of Glasgow Vice-Principal: Egypt featured in Adam Smith’s analysis of national prosperity

In a historical assessment of the foundations of Egypt’s economic prosperity, the Vice-Principal of the University of Glasgow Graeme Roy, said that Egypt occupied a prominent place in Adam Smith’s analysis of the factors behind the prosperity of nations.

He noted that Smith discussed the role of the Nile and irrigation projects in supporting agriculture and manufacturing and strengthening Egypt’s position as an international trading center.

Roy explained that Smith referred in The Wealth of Nations to Egypt’s early advances in agriculture and manufacturing, linking them to major irrigation projects that enabled the distribution of Nile water and supported agricultural and commercial activity.

This historical experience, he said, highlights the importance of infrastructure and institutions in transforming geographic advantages and natural resources into economic opportunities — a principle that remains relevant to Egypt’s development prospects.

Marking the 250th anniversary of the book’s publication, Roy stressed that Smith’s concept of wealth was not limited to gold, silver, or financial indicators.

Rather, it was connected to the extent to which economic activity improved people’s lives.

He emphasized that economic performance should not be assessed solely through gross domestic product, stock markets, or individual fortunes, but also through the impact of growth on society as a whole.

Roy noted that prosperity is closely linked to international production and trade networks, citing mobile phones and medicines whose production involves institutions and individuals from multiple countries.

Such examples, he said, demonstrate how the division of labor has expanded into cross-continental production chains.

He warned against US President Donald Trump’s calls for imposing tariffs and trade restrictions, arguing that addressing inequalities associated with globalization does not require abandoning the benefits of international cooperation.

This is particularly important for economies seeking to attract investment and expand their trade presence, including Egypt, he said.

Regarding AI, Roy stressed the need to prioritize ethics, education, and a deeper understanding of inequality, highlighting the role of universities in knowledge exchange and multidisciplinary cooperation.

Adam Smith’s legacy, he argued, does not provide ready-made answers to the challenges of 2026, but raises a fundamental question: how can societies be empowered to prosper, and how can the benefits of that prosperity be distributed?

Heba Nassar: Combating digital monopolies and reskilling workers are essential to protecting Egypt’s economy

From the perspective of economic justice, Professor of Economics at Cairo University, Heba Nassar stressed the need to combat digital monopolies and prevent major technology companies from imposing their dominance on markets and extracting economic rents at the expense of delivering genuine value to consumers.

She emphasized that rejecting excessive trade protectionism does not mean eliminating the role of the state.

Rather, it requires strong institutions that protect property rights, ensure cybersecurity, and invest in reskilling workers to help them adapt to the transformations driven by algorithms.

Without such measures, she warned, the most vulnerable groups risk being excluded from the development process.

This vision is particularly relevant to Egypt, which faces the challenge of balancing the benefits of emerging technologies with the protection of employment opportunities and the promotion of competition.

Such a balance is essential to ensuring that the technological revolution does not become a tool for concentrating wealth and influence in the hands of a limited number of companies.

New Giza University President: Technological shifts and trade wars require Egypt to rethink its economic future

In a broader assessment of international transformations, the President of New Giza University, Ahmed Sameh Farid, described the global economy as going through an exceptionally complex period, driven by the intersection of rapid technological change and geopolitical instability.

He stressed that addressing current crises requires moving beyond conventional patterns of thinking, citing Albert Einstein’s famous observation: “We cannot solve our problems with the same thinking we used when we created them.”

Farid explained that supply chain disruptions, rapid advances in artificial intelligence and e-commerce, escalating trade wars, and military confrontations have made it increasingly difficult for policymakers to predict the trajectory of the global economy and develop sustainable growth strategies.

He noted that the contemporary economy has become so complex that traditional models alone can no longer explain movements in international markets.

Nevertheless, he said, Adam Smith’s contributions to productivity, exports, the division of labor, and free markets remain relevant, despite the 250 years that have passed since the publication of The Wealth of Nations.

Farid also pointed to the emergence of new variables, including structural inflation and the impact of technology on employment rates, as evidence of the scale of transformation in the global economy.

He cited the contributions of mathematician and economist John Nash to game theory and negotiation theory, emphasizing the importance of thinking beyond conventional and ideological frameworks when responding to economic and geopolitical shocks.

Farid concluded by stressing that bringing together academic, executive, and diplomatic expertise aims to develop practical solutions that can help governments and institutions restructure their tools and build more resilient economies.

The conference discussions reveal that Egypt’s position in the emerging international order will not be determined solely by its geographic advantages or political weight, but by its ability to translate these assets into productive and technological power, develop its infrastructure and institutions, reskill its workforce, and participate in establishing rules for the responsible use of AI.

Amid opportunities for European partnerships, the growing multipolarity represented by BRICS, and transformations reshaping the global landscape of wealth and trade, Cairo appears to have an opportunity to strengthen its position as an influential partner in shaping the future of the global economy, rather than merely a recipient of its consequences.

Five recommendations to harness AI for Egypt’s economy

At the conclusion of the conference, the Dean of the School of Business at New Giza University and Secretary-General of the conference, Khaled Abdel Aziz Hegazy, presented five key recommendations on behalf of the conference, drawing on the discussions from its two sessions.

The recommendations aim to harness artificial intelligence to support Egypt’s economy while balancing technological innovation, economic fairness and the protection of individual rights.

Hegazy opened his closing remarks by revisiting the question posed by Adam Smith in The Wealth of Nations in 1776 – “what makes a nation wealthy?”

Smith’s answer, he noted, was not the gold held in national treasuries, but the productive capacity of its people. The conference revisited the same question in the age of algorithms.

He explained that the first session challenged common misconceptions about Smith’s economic philosophy. Smith did not advocate the absence of the state or praise greed; rather, he envisioned a vital, albeit limited, government that regulates markets, safeguards rights and protects vulnerable groups, ensuring that economic growth translates into broader social well-being.

The second session examined the changing composition of national wealth, which increasingly encompasses data, computing power, AI models, skilled talent and public trust.

Hegazy described these elements collectively as instrumental capital, arguing that the state’s role has also evolved: it is no longer merely a referee in the marketplace, but increasingly an investor and strategic actor in developing technological capabilities.

He stressed that Smith’s principles remain relevant but must extend further in the age of algorithms.

Fair markets, he argued, must now include fair algorithms, the protection of rights must encompass data and human dignity, and social safety nets must evolve into springboards that enable people to participate in the emerging economy.

Public investment in AI, he added, must be assessed against the principles of competition, fairness and genuine public benefit.

The first recommendation called for AI regulation that enables innovation rather than merely restricting it.

This includes governance frameworks that protect consumers, competition and financial stability while allowing room for innovation. It also calls for expanding regulatory sandboxes, drawing on the experience of Egypt’s Financial Regulatory Authority, to test new applications before imposing restrictions.

Citizens should also have the right to understand and challenge significant decisions made about them by algorithms.

The second recommendation focused on turning social safety nets into springboards through workforce development. It called for a national partnership between government, employers and universities, with shared responsibility and funding for upskilling programs.

Particular attention should be given to young people entering the labor market, whose entry-level jobs are especially exposed to automation.

Alongside technical capabilities, education should strengthen human skills that machines cannot readily replace, including sound judgment, ethics, creativity and empathy.

The third recommendation urged businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, to pursue focused and realistic AI adoption.

Rather than relying on scattered pilot projects, companies should move towards specific, measurable applications, beginning with data readiness, identifying high-value uses and measuring actual economic returns rather than simply the scale of technological activity.

Priority sectors identified for Egypt include financial services, agriculture and water management, logistics, healthcare and government services.

The fourth recommendation called for directing public investment towards public goods that markets cannot provide on their own. These include shared computing infrastructure, open and responsibly governed data, scientific research and the development of Arabic-language AI capabilities.

Such investments should be transparent, competitive and open to private-sector participation, helping build an integrated national ecosystem rather than concentrating the benefits among a limited number of companies or privileged beneficiaries.

The fifth recommendation emphasized making universities active partners in technological transformation. Universities should work alongside government and industry on research, policy advice and the responsible use of AI, while updating their curricula to prepare graduates for the emerging economy rather than the one being left behind.

Hegazy concluded by quoting Adam Smith: “No society can surely be flourishing and happy, of which the far greater part of the members are poor and miserable.”

He described this principle as the real test of the AI age, arguing that the central question is no longer how much AI a nation possesses, but how wisely and fairly it deploys it to improve the well-being of all its people.

World.title: Liberia Pays £5.95 Million to IMO, Remains Top Financial Contributor to Global Maritime Body
World.content:
Annual contribution accounts for approximately 15 percent of IMO’s operating budget as Liberia reaffirms commitment to safe, secure and sustainable international shipping.

LONDON, United Kingdom — Liberia has paid £5,946,633 (approximately £5.95 million) in annual assessed contributions to the International Maritime Organization (IMO), reinforcing its position as the organization’s largest financial contributor and one of the leading voices in global maritime governance.

Liberia’s Maritime Commissioner and Chief Executive Officer, Cllr. Neto Zarzar Lighe Sr., presented a symbolic cheque for the amount to IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez during a ceremony in London on November 6, 2026.



Commissioner Lighe said the timely payment underscores Liberia’s commitment to the IMO, its institutional programs and the continued development of international shipping.

As the world’s largest ship registry, Liberia contributes approximately 15 percent of the IMO’s annual operational budget through its assessed financial contributions.

Speaking during the presentation, Lighe emphasized that Liberia considers its financial obligations to the organization a serious national responsibility, particularly given its influence in the international maritime industry.

“Liberia takes its obligations to the IMO as a serious national obligation. As a global maritime leader and Category-A member of the IMO Council, we remain firmly committed to fulfilling our responsibilities promptly and supporting the Organization’s vital mission of advancing safe, secure, efficient, and environmentally sustainable international shipping,” he said.

Receiving the symbolic cheque, Secretary-General Dominguez expressed appreciation to the Liberian Government for meeting its financial obligations on time and maintaining its longstanding commitment to the organization.

Dominguez also recognized that Liberia’s contribution to the IMO extends beyond financial support, highlighting the country’s active participation in the organization’s technical working groups, committees and Council deliberations.

He described Liberia’s representation as effective, efficient and highly engaged, noting its important role in advancing the IMO’s mandate and strengthening international maritime cooperation.

Liberia has consistently maintained an influential presence within the IMO, reflecting the country’s strategic importance to international shipping through its extensive ship registry.

Commissioner Lighe was accompanied at the presentation ceremony by Liberia’s Permanent Representative to the IMO, Ambassador Robert Wilmot Kpadeh; Alternate Permanent Representative, Dr. Harry Conway; and other officials of the Liberia Permanent Mission to the IMO.

The latest payment further reinforces Liberia’s standing as a responsible flag State, a dependable international maritime partner and a major contributor to global maritime governance.

World.title: Liberia: China Signals Readiness to Expand Agricultural Imports, Eyes Investment in Processing Sector
World.content:
Vice President Jeremiah Koung secures commitment from Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang on market access for Liberian cocoa, coffee and dried chili peppers, while Beijing pledges continued development support and encourages Chinese investment.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

MONROVIA — China has expressed readiness to increase imports of agricultural products from Liberia, including cocoa, coffee beans and dried chili peppers, as the two countries explore ways to expand trade, attract investment and strengthen economic cooperation.



The commitment was conveyed by Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang during bilateral discussions with Liberia’s Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung Sr. in Shanghai on November 5, according to a press release from the Office of the Vice President.

Vice Premier Ding identified the submission and approval of eligible Liberian exporting companies as the next practical step toward accessing the Chinese market. He explained that agricultural products such as dried chili peppers, coffee beans and cocoa from African countries, including Liberia, had been granted access under existing market arrangements.

He encouraged Liberia to submit a list of companies interested in exporting these products to China for the necessary approval procedures, after which successful applicants could begin trading.

The discussions followed Vice President Koung’s participation in the opening of the Ninth China International Import Expo, where he called for greater efforts to translate China’s zero-tariff policy into increased exports, domestic processing and employment opportunities for Liberians.

Ding also expressed China’s willingness to strengthen agricultural trade facilitation with African countries and encouraged Liberia to take advantage of the China International Import Expo and other commercial platforms to connect local producers with Chinese buyers.

Welcoming the opportunity, Vice President Koung identified rubber, cocoa, coffee and other agricultural products as priority areas for expanded trade cooperation.

He emphasized that Liberia wants foreign investment to go beyond the export of raw materials by creating opportunities for domestic processing, skills development and employment.

“Our objective is to create jobs, develop Liberian skills, and retain more value within our economy,” Koung said.

He invited Chinese businesses to explore investment opportunities in Liberia’s special economic zones, particularly in rubber processing, agro-processing and light manufacturing.

In response, Vice Premier Ding said China would encourage more Chinese companies to invest in Liberia and called for continued support to facilitate their operations.

He also identified iron ore mining as an important area of bilateral cooperation, expressing China’s readiness to strengthen policy coordination to ensure that investments generate greater benefits for both countries.

China Outlines Additional Development Support

Beyond trade and investment, the Chinese Vice Premier reaffirmed Beijing’s willingness to support Liberia’s development priorities through ongoing and proposed infrastructure and technical assistance projects.

Ding outlined continued cooperation involving the Congo Town overpass bridges, diagnostic laboratory facilities, agricultural machinery, government vehicles and road-related assistance.

He further disclosed that Chinese working teams would visit Liberia to assess proposed projects involving broadcasting facilities and the renovation of the Capitol Building.

China also pledged to continue providing scholarships and training opportunities for Liberian professionals as part of efforts to strengthen the country’s human resource and technical capacity.

Vice President Koung welcomed the assistance but stressed the importance of incorporating training, maintenance and technical support into development projects to ensure their sustainability.

He also highlighted reliable and affordable electricity as a major national priority, identifying opportunities for cooperation in solar energy, battery storage, hydropower and rural electrification.

Other areas raised by the Liberian delegation included clean water, healthcare delivery, digital connectivity and vocational training.

To move the discussions from commitments to implementation, Koung proposed the designation of focal persons and the identification of a shortlist of priority projects for further engagement between the two governments.

He assured the Chinese delegation that Liberia’s Embassy in Beijing and relevant government institutions were prepared to work with their Chinese counterparts to advance the proposed initiatives.

Liberia Seeks China’s Support at UN Security Council

The discussions also addressed cooperation on international affairs, particularly Liberia’s upcoming presidency of the United Nations Security Council in December.

Vice Premier Ding congratulated Liberia on its forthcoming presidency and expressed China’s readiness to maintain close communication and cooperation with Monrovia.

Vice President Koung, in turn, thanked China and other international partners for supporting Liberia’s election to the Security Council for the 2026–2027 term.

He outlined Liberia’s priorities during its tenure, including strengthening the participation of women and young people in peace and security initiatives, addressing the connections between climate change, conflict and natural resources, promoting regional security, and advancing Security Council reform and peacekeeping.

Koung also solicited China’s continued support for Liberia’s December presidency.

Both officials reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening the Liberia-China strategic partnership and translating diplomatic engagements into practical economic and development benefits for their respective populations.

The meeting was held at the Xijiao State Guest Hotel in Shanghai and attended by Shanghai Mayor Zhu Zhongming; Chinese Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs Miao Deyu; Liberia’s Ambassador to China, Dudley McKinley Thomas; and Executive Chairman of the Liberia Special Economic Zones Authority, Prince A. Wreh.

Other members of the Liberian delegation included Samuel Nagbe, Executive Director of the Rural Renewable Energy Agency; Deputy Chief of Staff for Administration Macdonald Metzger; Press Secretary Richmond Neufville; and J. Wesley Washington, Minister Counselor at the Liberian Embassy in China.

World.title: Liberia: The Economy Grew. So Did Poverty. And Nobody Can Say What the State’s 47 Companies Cost
World.content:
MONROVIA — On paper, 2025 was a good year for Liberia. The economy grew 5.1 percent, its strongest pace in the five years the World Bank charts. Inflation ended the year at 4 percent. The budget deficit narrowed, and export earnings leapt by nearly 58 percent on the back of gold and iron ore.

By Rodney D Sieh

Yet by the Bank’s own estimate, more Liberians slipped into extreme poverty — from 34.6 percent of the population in 2024 to 36.1 percent in 2025.



That contradiction sits at the heart of Beyond Growth, the 7th edition of the World Bank’s Liberia Economic Update, released in October. Its diagnosis is blunt: Liberia is growing in the places where few Liberians work, and stalling in the places where most of them do. And it turns a spotlight on an institution that rarely features in growth debates — the state’s own portfolio of 62 government-owned entities, whose finances, the report says, the government itself cannot reliably see.

Growth that skips the household

The 2025 numbers were driven by mines, not markets. Industrial output jumped 10.8 percent, powered by a 42 percent surge in iron ore production as a major project scaled up and a 17 percent rise in overall mining output. Gold, iron ore and rubber now account for 92.8 percent of everything Liberia sells abroad; gold alone is 61.8 percent.

The sectors where Liberians actually earn a living moved the other way. Manufacturing shrank 2.8 percent. Agriculture, which still employs about 39 percent of the workforce, slowed to 2.6 percent growth from 3.4 percent, and farm labour productivity has fallen about 1.1 percent a year since 2014.

The labour market tells the rest. Some 78 percent of workers are in what the Bank calls vulnerable employment — informal self-employment or unpaid family work. Wage jobs account for just 20.9 percent of employment, a share that has barely moved in two decades. About 55,000 people join the labour force each year, but the economy creates roughly 50,000 jobs.

Firms are too small to absorb them. Some 86 percent are micro-sized and nearly 89 percent are one-person operations. Liberia registers about two new limited liability companies per 10,000 adults a year — roughly 165 times below the global average, the report says.

Prices compounded the squeeze. Food inflation collapsed after rice prices fell and the government cut the wholesale price of a 25kg bag from US$16.75 to US$14.00. But non-food inflation climbed to 9.9 percent, driven by services, healthcare and housing — costs that hit urban wage earners hardest. The Bank expects poverty to ease to 33.2 percent in 2026 if farming recovers.

Stability bought with the capital budget

Monrovia’s fiscal numbers improved. The deficit narrowed to 2.1 percent of GDP, domestic revenue rose to US$830 million (15.9 percent of GDP), and public debt eased to 55.1 percent of GDP. Domestic revenue now covers 69.3 percent of public spending, up from 59 percent.

But the Bank is plain about how the books were balanced. As donor grants fell from 7.8 to 4.9 percent of GDP, capital spending was cut from US$406 million to US$297 million — from 8.5 to 5.7 percent of GDP. Interest payments, meanwhile, rose from US$49 million to US$87 million.

Cutting the investment Liberia needs to break its jobs trap, the report says, is “precisely the wrong adjustment.” It points instead to money left on the table: tax exemptions worth about US$240 million in 2024, more than 40 percent of tax revenue; a mining sector from which Liberia captures only 15–20 percent of available fiscal value, against 50–60 percent in peer countries; and a domestic capital budget that has historically been only about one-third executed.

The gap matters because the government’s ARREST Agenda development plan needs roughly US$8.4 billion over five years, at a time when concessional finance is shrinking and Liberia remains at high risk of overall public debt distress.

The black box: 47 state firms, few accounts

The report’s second half is its sharpest. Liberia’s government owns 62 entities — 47 operating, 15 dormant — running power, ports, petroleum, water, transport, hospitals, universities and regulators. They control assets worth roughly a quarter of GDP. Yet in 2024 only 19 submitted financial returns to the state’s oversight bureau, and 26 of the 47 active entities report nothing at all. Just 13 percent file compliant quarterly reports.

Where auditors have looked, the picture is grim. Only 17 of the 47 have had even one General Auditing Commission audit since 2019. Of 36 financial-statement opinions issued for FY20–FY24, 25 were adverse, seven qualified and four clean. All ten compliance audits came back adverse.

The self-reported numbers that do exist flatter the portfolio. The 19 reporting firms booked a combined US$29.0 million profit in 2024, but US$19.7 million of that was pension accumulation at the National Social Security and Welfare Corporation (NASSCORP). Strip out US$15.1 million in government subsidies and a US$16.7 million donor grant to the electricity utility, and the group posted a loss of about US$2.7 million.

The bigger risk sits off the subsidy line. Government on-lent or guaranteed US$423.3 million of state-enterprise debt as of end-2025 — debt that lands on the treasury if a company cannot pay. The report also finds firms that did not remit workers’ income tax for years: the Liberia Civil Aviation Authority paid nothing until a marginal sum in 2024. Auditors found NASSCORP could not link US$4.1 million of 2022 deposits to any contributor.

Governance is part of the problem. A 2023 Bank review of eight state firms found ministers on every board and some directors missing three-quarters of meetings. Presidential performance contracts are signed directly with chief executives, bypassing boards. The old Bureau of State Enterprises oversaw this portfolio on less than US$1 million a year.

Its successor, the State-Owned Enterprises Authority of Liberia (SEAL), formally took over on August 23, 2026. The Bank calls it timely but flags weaknesses: no governing board, three political appointees with loosely defined tenure, and funding from a 0.25 percent levy on the very firms it polices. A House-passed bill barring sitting officials from state boards, reported by FrontPageAfrica in March and cited in the Bank’s report, still awaits Senate action.

LEC: the utility at the centre of the risk

No entity illustrates the problem better than the Liberia Electricity Corporation (LEC). It holds about 77 percent of all liabilities reported by state firms, and its accounts have drawn adverse audit opinions year after year.

LEC reported modest losses of about US$3.5 million over 2022–2024. But that was only after booking roughly US$50 million in grant income. Without it, the Bank estimates, losses would have run US$17–20 million a year. Its equity fell from US$51.0 million to US$30.4 million in 2024, as liabilities climbed to 95 percent of assets.

The utility’s biggest deadbeat is its owner. Of US$34.0 million owed to LEC at end-2025, about 91 percent was owed by government ministries and agencies, most of it more than a year old. In December 2025, core government paid 0.3 percent of what it owed, against about 21 percent for customers overall. The government, the report notes, is at once LEC’s shareholder, regulator, least reliable customer and lender of last resort.

Businesses pay the price. More than 90 percent of Liberian firms now own a generator, up from 73 percent in 2017. Auditors also found LEC operated for at least five years without documented board minutes or adopted by-laws. The planned expansion of the Mount Coffee hydropower plant from 88 to about 130 megawatts by 2028 offers relief — if the utility can be run to use it.

What the Bank prescribes — and what to watch

The Bank is careful not to overclaim. It says it has not established that state firms cause Liberia’s jobs problem. Its argument is narrower and harder to dismiss: without accounts, audits and a register of who sits on which board, no one can say what the portfolio costs, what it delivers or what risk it poses to the treasury.

Its fix is deliberately unglamorous. By end-2027, it wants every entity classified as commercial, public-service or hybrid; a published register of entities and directors; a minimum annual reporting template for all 47 operating firms; and audit firepower focused on the five biggest exposures — LEC, NASSCORP, the National Port Authority, the Liberia Petroleum Refining Company and the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation — with private auditors brought in under the Auditor General’s oversight. By June 2028, it wants government’s tangled money flows with those firms reconciled, public-service obligations costed, the first public aggregate report on state enterprises, and a legal inventory of the 15 dormant companies.

The wider outlook is cautiously positive but exposed. The Bank projects growth averaging 5.3 percent a year over 2026–2028, inflation of 7.0 percent in 2026 and a VAT launch in early 2027. But global growth is forecast to slow to 2.5 percent in 2026 as the Middle East conflict lifts oil prices. A 15 percent fall in gold and a 20 percent fall in iron ore prices would wipe about US$295 million off export earnings, with reserves covering only about two months of imports.

For a country that has heard many reform plans, the test is simple. Growth figures can be announced. Whether the state can account for its own companies — and pay its own electricity bills — will show whether Liberia’s boom is starting to reach the people living through it.
