World.title: Thomas Markle Sr., Meghan's father, arrested in Florida
World.content:
Thomas Markle Sr., the estranged father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, was arrested in Florida on Friday in connection with allegations that he possessed child sex abuse materials in storage units in California, the Justice Department announced.

The announcement came after three sources familiar with the matter confirmed the arrest to CBS News.

The Justice Department said Markle was arrested for allegedly keeping child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, in two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for nearly two decades.

Markle is set for an initial court appearance Friday in Tampa, Florida. It was not immediately known if he has an attorney who can respond to the allegations.

"These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law," Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, said in a statement.

The Daily Mail, a British tabloid newspaper, first reported Markle's arrest.

Last month, it was reported that Markle was under investigation by authorities in the Philippines for alleged possession of child sexual abuse materials. Markle has denied the claims against him, calling them "sick lies."

"I have never downloaded anything like that in my life," he was quoted as telling the Daily Mail.

Thomas Markle Sr. is seen on Aug. 10, 2018, in San Diego, California. MEGA/GC Images/ Getty Images

A spokesperson for the Philippine National Police told CBS News in a statement that they launched an investigation after Markle's personal items were turned over to law enforcement by his son, Thomas Markle Jr.

Markle Jr. told the Sun tabloid last month that he reported the images to police in the Philippines and contacted the FBI.

"I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years — but that stops now," Markle Jr. told The Sun. "I won't speak to my father ever again unless I'm called to give evidence against him."

The Daily Mail reported last week that it alerted the FBI of a cache of child porn found inside a storage unit Markle Sr. had rented near his former home in Rosarito, Mexico.

Mexican authorities seized a storage unit with the belongings of Thomas Markle during a search for alleged child sexual abuse material, in Baja Malibu, on the outskirts of Tijuana, Mexico, Nov. 1, 2026. Guillermo Arias /AFP via Getty Images

In a statement on Friday, the Baja California State Attorney General's Office in Mexico confirmed to CBS News that a search was conducted on Oct. 29 after a report via the 911 emergency line.

"During the operation, three old magazines and VHS tapes containing child pornography were discovered," the office said in its statement. "The evidence and the associated case files were referred to the Attorney General's Office (FGR), which will handle the follow-up to the case."

DOJ's claims against Markle Sr.

According to an affidavit in the complaint filed in federal court, the investigation in the Philippines led law enforcement to investigate two storage units registered to Markle Sr. in the Los Angeles area that he had rented since 2008, with the most recent payments on both made last month by auto-pay.

Inside the units, agents with the FBI seized 78 items, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse materials. In one of the units, agents found at least 18 images that appear to constitute child pornography.

Two of the images found allegedly show an adult man — whom a witness identified as Markle Sr. — with a nude prepubescent girl, the affidavit said.

A third image allegedly shows a nude prepubescent girl in a room that appears to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines. Other photos allegedly show Markle Sr. with children in various stages of undress, the affidavit said.

"Mr. Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement, adding: "This FBI will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide."

If convicted, Markle Sr. would face a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison.

Meghan distanced herself because of allegations years ago

After the reports of the investigation were made public, Meghan, who recently moved back to Britain with her husband Prince Harry and their children, said in a statement sent to CBS News that she had been aware of the allegations against him since 2018 and that the allegations were shared with U.K. authorities at the time.

She said it was based on that information that she and Harry decided to cut her father off from contact with their children.

"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them," she said.

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, on Oct. 15, 2026, in Nottingham, England. Photo by Karwai Tang/WireImage

Meghan also confronted her father last year about the child sexual abuse allegations leveled against him, according to CBS News partner BBC News. Video that the British tabloid the Daily Mail says it obtained exclusively shows Markle accepting a letter sent by his daughter in his hospital room in the U.S. in December 2025.

According to the BBC, in that letter, Meghan wrote that she and authorities "knew he had abused young girls," adding that he would never meet her and Harry's children Archie and Lilibet.

Meghan will not be commenting on the arrest at this time, sources say.

World.title: Trump's global health strategy is emerging. What will the Democratic Congress say?
World.content:
Trump's global health strategy is emerging. What will the Democratic Congress say?

toggle caption i U.S Embassy in Zambia

By all appearances, it was a classic government ceremony. Officials in suits. Big black chairs around a wooden table. A cluster of microphones. It happened on October 8 in Lusaka, Zambia. Amid applause, U.S. and Zambian officials signed a global health agreement, called a Memorandum of Understanding or MOU.

But Mich Coker — the Chargé d'Affaires at the U.S. Embassy in Zambia — said this agreement was anything but classic.

"This MOU represents a fundamental shift," he said, speaking at the signing ceremony . He explained that the relationship between the two countries was moving "from a traditional donor-recipient model to a true partnership, one grounded in Zambian leadership, in Zambian ownership and in shared accountability."

Sponsor Message

Global health experts on all sides of the political spectrum and all over the world agree with Coker that there's been a fundamental shift in the U.S. approach to global health.

"The shift that's currently unfolding is very large and it's very rapid," says Janeen Madan Keller, acting co-director of the Global Health Program at the Center for Global Development.

The story of this fundamental shift starts at the beginning of the second Trump Administration with months of global health turmoil — Madan Keller and other experts say — but has given way to a clearer strategy. One with big goals, a short timeline and a lot less transparency than what came before.

Here is a look at where things stand now and how a Congress controlled by the Democratic Party might impact the new landscape.

First, the "chaos"

President Trump's second term started dramatically. When he dismantled USAID (the U.S. Agency for International Development), citing alleged " fraud, waste and abuse ," everything changed overnight.

"It is a period that is best described as chaos," says Madan Keller. The repercussions were massive and immediate, she says, "for people and communities in some of the poorest countries of the world."

Clinics shut down suddenly. Patients ran out of HIV medications. In Zambia, as well as a number of other countries, many patients who relied on U.S.-supported clinics and programs faced tons of uncertainty and, often, dire health consequences .

Sponsor Message

"For the first half of 2025, there was a complete upheaval," says Jennifer Kates , senior vice president and director of global and public health policy at KFF.

A strategy emerged

Next came a new stage in the history of U.S. foreign aid. "Starting over the summer of 2025 and going into September, there actually was a sort of step back to develop an actual strategy and a plan," says Kates.

What emerged from the State Department was the America First Global Health Strategy with the stated goal of making "America safer, stronger, and more prosperous." The main way this strategy is being implemented is through agreements with individual countries. In the past, the U.S. had done more work through large international organizations or local non-governmental organizations.

Experts say one defining feature of these agreements is that they are transactional. For example, in Zambia "there was a massive scandal because activists were able to show that the agreement was planning to condition access to [U.S. global health] funding on access to [Zambia's] copper and rare earth minerals," says Asia Russell , executive director of the HIV/AIDS advocacy organization Health GAP. Her organization helped expose this situation.

While the part of the agreement about minerals was separated from the global health agreement after the public outcry in Zambia, many of the global health agreements do require the recipient country to share data such as pathogen information.

Big (but not new) goals

Speaking at the signing ceremony in Zambia, Coker ticked off some of the top priorities in the new strategy, including that recipient countries increase their financial contributions to health in the years ahead and that they are transitioned off aid in the near future.

He said in the Zambian MOU, the U.S. would pay $1.5 billion over five years "with Zambia simultaneously committing to increase its own domestic health expenditures by $975 million. We are charting a path toward a stronger, more self-reliant health system."

Sponsor Message

Another priority has been building up a country's own health infrastructure — and not a parallel system run by non-profits and NGOs.

"We are looking to have up to about 40,000 healthcare workers recruited through this support," said Zambian Health Minister Roma Chilengi at the same ceremony.

The priorities in the MOUs — such as recipient countries contributing more and being weaned off aid money — are not new ideas. In the world of global health they have long received bipartisan support. But, up until now, they've been hard to implement. "This approach really does kickstart them in a new way that had not occurred before," says Kates.

But in her view the chaos before this kickstart makes implementing these goals more challenging — as does the fact that everyone's now operating within a greatly diminished U.S. global health system.

The speed of the transition also troubles some. Madan Keller says that the strategy aims to achieve major changes in just a handful of years. "It's happening on a compressed timeline with arguably limited capacity to manage it, and that's where some of the risks and concerns are coming from," she says.

And Russell, for her part, is worried that the main goal of the Trump Administration has been hammering out MOUs rather than setting ambitious health-related goals, such as reducing HIV transmission. The Trump administration is focused on "process indicators — not impact indicators — as its first measure of success, which is basically a loser's gambit when it comes to pandemics," she says. "Rubio crowed about signing documents. That doesn't save lives."

The State Department declined an interview request but said in a statement that most African countries with MOUs now have drawn up implementation plans and "U.S. embassies globally are now focused on operationalizing these implementation plans [and] recipient country governments are also executing on the commitments they have made in the MOUs."

Sponsor Message

"Very hard to get the information"

Another major challenge in assessing the new strategy has been a lack of information provided to the public, says global health experts.

This represents a big break from past U.S. global health initiatives. For example, the U.S.'s flagship program for HIV/AIDS — called PEPFAR – "was a gold standard for collecting data on a regular basis and sharing it transparently — and then using that data to really inform decision making," Ramona Godbole , the former deputy director of policy, planning and programs at the now-defunct U.S. Agency for International Development, told NPR earlier this year.

"Now it's much more opaque and very hard to get the information. The agreements themselves have not been publicly released by the U.S. government," Kates says. Although, the text for some of the agreements have become available through litigation or Freedom of Information Act requests filed by advocacy groups.

There is even less information on the implementation plans, she says, which are supposed to contain detailed goals and metrics for how the money will be spent and what programs will be supported.

Kates says this is true despite the fact that U.S. taxpayers are underwriting the aid, which totals $16 billion committed across the 36 agreements that have been signed. That money comes from U.S. taxpayer dollars that Congress allocated to foreign aid. KFF has calculated that this represents a 34% drop in U.S. global health aid and it has left some countries without an agreement. For instance, Zimbabwe lost U.S. global health aid since the two governments were not able to agree to MOU terms.

In its statement, the State Department said: "Claims of a lack of accountability and transparency are unfounded….We have and will share every signed MOU with Congress."

A new blue Congress

In the wake of this week's midterms, there are new questions about how this fundamental shift in global health will play out. With the Democratic Party returning to the majority in Congress, many expect that lawmakers will demand more transparency.

Sponsor Message

"I think 100% they are going to demand: give us the MOUs, show us the implementation plans, come in and tell us more detail about what you're doing," Kates says.

Another question is whether the new Congress might try to resurrect what was dismantled. Kate says there are still a lot of unknowns about what the new Congress will do after it convenes on January 3 and how the Trump Administration will respond, but she expects lawmakers will first push for the public to get more information on what global health work the U.S. is and isn't currently supporting.

Russell says many global health activists are calling for more oversight — and she is one of them. "Congress needs to slam its feet, both feet, on the brakes unless and until it gets this information, gets this accountability," she says.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: No one knows how many ballots are outstanding in Mississippi's Senate race
World.content:
No one knows how many ballots are outstanding in Mississippi's Senate race

toggle caption i Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images

In Mississippi's too-close-to-call U.S. Senate race, every ballot matters.

But no one can say for sure how many ballots there are left to count.

The razor-thin margin between incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic challenger Scott Colom is shining a light on an election process in Mississippi that is among the slowest and most decentralized in the country.

"Mississippi is not a model of election administration," said Michael Morse, a law professor at the University of Pennsylvania who studies voting.

As of midday Friday, fewer than 2,000 votes separated the two Senate candidates. But information about exactly how many ballots were outstanding was hard to come by.

Sponsor Message

Loading...

The Colom campaign said late Tuesday it was aware of more than 15,000 provisional ballots, which require verification before they're counted. And the chair of the state Republican Party said Thursday he thought there were 20,000 outstanding ballots, including potential absentee votes that can legally be received by officials until Nov. 10 if they were postmarked by Election Day.

Mississippi's top voting official, Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson, said counties run their own elections, and even his office didn't know how many provisionals were left to count. He said midday Friday over 9,000 of them had been processed.

"Until we have the certified results, the individual counties will be the best source of the latest and most up-to-date information," Watson said in a statement. There are 82 counties in Mississippi, and they are not required to transmit election results to the state until next week.

Morse said he was shocked by the lack of good information available for such a high-profile race.

"Right now I would love to know a lot of things about the process and I am struggling to figure out what is unfolding here," Morse said. "I cannot tell you basic things."

Mississippi has a relatively high rate of provisional ballots

What is becoming clear is that the rate of provisional ballots, which are called affidavit ballots in Mississippi, may end up being among the highest in the country this election cycle. Those ballots are cast by people whose eligibility is questionable, according to local officials, so those votes are segregated and officials decide on a case-by-case basis whether they will be counted.

Sponsor Message

If the Colom campaign's estimate of 15,000 affidavit ballots holds true, that would represent roughly 1.5% of the total ballots cast in the Senate race, according to unofficial results.

In the last midterm year, 2022, just four states had a provisional ballot rate higher than that, according to federal data. And Mississippi looks to have a provisional rate close to double of that in North Carolina this year, based on the preliminary data in both states.

One potential reason is an in-the-weeds detail on how Mississippi does voter registration.

In most states, when voters don't cast ballots over a certain number of election cycles, or local officials come across data that indicates a voter has moved or is ineligible for some other reason, they move that voter to what's known as "inactive" status. But the voter is still able to vote normally for a period of a few years, mandated by federal law, before they either confirm their eligibility or are eventually removed.

Mississippi is one of the few states that makes those "inactive" voters have to vote provisionally. That means those voters need to fill out another form and their information needs to be reviewed after the fact by local officials before their votes are counted.

It's unclear at this point why so many voters had questionable eligibility when they showed up to vote, although the local outlet Mississippi Today has reported extensively on the state's experimental use of credit data to cull voter lists.

Morse said that list maintenance technique is garnering attention, but it's not the whole story.

"It's pairing the experiment with credit data, which could introduce some unreliability, with an undermining of the typical procedural process [in many other states], where a voter [marked "inactive"] could cast a regular ballot for at least the next two federal general elections," Morse said.

Sponsor Message

Watson, the Republican secretary of state, has already come out in defense of the state's registration process.

"The extra few minutes it may take to vote via affidavit ballot are well worth the election integrity added by having cleaner voter rolls!" Watson wrote Tuesday in a post on X.

But Kathy Boockvar, the former Democratic secretary of state of Pennsylvania, told NPR that while many people who have to vote with a provisional ballot are likely to be ultimately deemed eligible, the process doesn't breed trust from those who have to interact with it.

"It feels like you have to go talk to the teacher or something in the back room," Boockvar said. "It's a little bit of a suspicious-seeming thing because somebody who's going through it generally thinks that they're eligible to vote and feels like they're being asked to do something other than that."

Boockvar added that the fact that information has been so hard to come by is a sign Mississippi hasn't been in the limelight like traditional battleground states before.

"We all have to be prepared whether we expect it or not," Boockvar said. "Transparency and good data is one of the best solutions we have to combating all the suspicion and distrust."

World.title: Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as Trump's chief of staff
World.content:
Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as Trump's chief of staff

toggle caption i Alex Wong/Getty Images

White House chief of staff Susie Wiles is being replaced by Stephen Miller, President Trump said Friday.

The change comes after Republicans were swept out of power during this week's midterm elections.

Miller currently serves as deputy chief of staff in the White House. Trump announced the change on social media today, saying that Miller will take over on Monday.

Wiles worked with the Trump 2020 campaign in Florida and has served as chief of staff in this White House from day one. She was diagnosed with breast cancer earlier this year, and but it was announced she was cancer free this fall.

Sponsor Message

Miller has been a fixture in Trump's circles since 2016 and is considered an architect of some of his core policies, including immigration.

World.title: Pope Leo begins a 12-day, 3-country South America tour after his cancer surgery
World.content:
Pope Leo begins a 12-day, 3-country South America tour after his cancer surgery

toggle caption i Martin Mejia/AP

MONTEVIDEO, Uruguay — Pope Leo XIV has arrived in South America for a 12-day, three-country journey that will be his longest and most far-reaching trip yet, and his first major overseas visit since undergoing lung cancer surgery.

Along the way Leo will take 12 flights, including two helicopter rides, give 36 speeches and visit 10 cities including Cusco, Peru, which sits more than 11,000 feet above sea level. Even the heartiest of travellers can experience altitude sickness there and may require supplemental oxygen.

Last month, Leo underwent surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung. Vatican officials say he has completed his two-week recovery period and requires no further treatment.

Sponsor Message

The Vatican's new communications chief Maria Montserrat Alvar said the pontiff was eager to begin his journey. "His doctors are very confident and he'll have plenty of medical care on board should something happen," she said.

First stop Uruguay

It's a puzzling choice for the first leg of the pope's anticipated return to South America, where he spent two decades in Peru, first as a missionary then as Bishop of the coastal city of Chiclayo. Uruguay, a small nation of around 3.5 million people, where adoring crowds will be small, is famously Latin America's most secular nation.

When asked why go to Uruguay at all, given the high rate of atheists and strict separation of church and state, Communications Chief Alvarado answered simply, "Why Not?" Adding, "the Gospel is meant to go everywhere."

Few welcome banners are seen throughout the capital Montevideo, except for large posters of a waving Pope Leo adorning city churches. A huge banner drapes down the facade of the Blessed Sacrament Church, in Montevideo's upscale Pocitos neighborhood, where 70-year old retiree Ana Maria Saprissa was heading for quiet prayer.

We are thankful, agradecida, she says that the pontiff is coming to visit. "His visit gives us such joy because …he remembered us all here in this tiny country that has so many needs," she said.

Sponsor Message

Uruguay's tradition of separating religion from government and public life dates back more than a century. Christmas has long been officially referred to as Family Day, while Easter week is given the vacation-friendly name Tourism Week.

Only about a third of Uruguayans identify as Catholics and even less say they practice the religion, according to political analyst Mariana Pomiés , director of the public polling firm CIFRA.

But as a practicing Catholic, Pomies says sometimes Uruguayan and especially officials misinterpret what secularism is. "Secularism is not anti-religion, it's the neutrality of the state in religious matters. But here the neutrality se convirtió en un absoluto… it became an absolute."

toggle caption i Matilde Campodonico/AP

Pope celebrates 'positive secularism.'

Dozens of volunteers cleaned streets, mowed lawns and erected a simple stage outside the tiny brick Our Lady of Guadalupe Church. It's the focal spot for many in the Casavalle neighborhood, a working-class city about a half hour north of Montevideo, where the pope is scheduled to visit on Saturday.

"I am very happy, very glad, very grateful … that eyes have been set here," where many are forgotten and stigmatized, said Father Pablo Coimbra who's served as the community's pastoral leader for the past six years

"For the first time many people live their lives always on the margins, on the margins of opportunities, of possibilities, of the future, on the margins of a loving gaze... well, today they are in the heart, in the center," he said.

A proposed papal address to the parliament triggered a swift rebuke from the public and politicos alike and was quickly scrapped. However, Uruguay's left-wing President Yamandú Orsi will oversee a welcome ceremony outside Montevideo's main cathedral, where Leo will later celebrate evening prayers, vespers with church leaders and laypeople.

Sunday mass will take place in Florida, about an hour outside the capital, a town replete with Catholic and national pride. Every Nov. 8, church goers commemorate the Virgin of the Thirty-five, a symbol of Uruguay's independence movement from the Brazilian empire in 1825.

Sponsor Message

A long awaited Papal return to Argentina

By Sunday, Pope Leo will be in neighboring Argentina, fulfilling a wish of his predecessor, Pope Francis, who had hoped to return to his homeland but never made the trip.

Before his death, Francis had said he didn't want a papal visit to become entangled in Argentina's intensely polarized politics.

Pope Leo's visit to Argentina offers an early test of how he will address the Catholic Church's differences with right-wing populist leaders gaining ground across Latin America. Those tensions have also surfaced in the U.S., where Leo has clashed with President Donald Trump over immigration and the treatment of migrants.

Far-right President Javier Milei's sweeping austerity measures, which have pushed millions of Argentines into poverty, could put him at odds with Leo, who has long championed the poor.

Milei has also embraced data centers and a largely unfettered approach to artificial intelligence regulation, while Pope Leo's inaugural encyclical called for ethical caution and safeguards to protect human dignity in the age of AI.

toggle caption i Guadalupe Pardo/AP

Saving the best for last?

The final leg of the trip will take Leo back to Peru in what has been billed as a homecoming.

As a missionary priest and later appointed Bishop of the coastal city of Chiclayo, Pope Leo spent two decades in the country. He became a naturalized Peruvian in 2015, and has said the country shaped his life more than anything else.

He will visit several cities and towns where he lived and will meet with President Keiko Fujimori, the daughter of former Peruvian dictator Alberto Fujimori.

As a priest during the Fujimori dictatorship, Leo was openly critical of military violence and human rights abuses and supported efforts leading to Peru's Truth and Reconciliation Commission following the return to democracy.

But for many Uruguayans Pope Leo is not very well known. Walking past the huge stage set up for Leo's welcoming ceremony, Juan Martin Guerreiro said he wasn't sure he would attend the pope's speeches.

"He doesn't feel as influential to me … as Pope Francis," said Guerreiro. But he said he's willing to give the new pope a chance because he is South American.

When reminded that Pope Leo was born in Chicago, Guerreiro said he wouldn't hold that against him.

World.title: Health intel-sharing group warns industry in wake of cyberattack on French blood bank
World.content:
Health intel-sharing group warns industry in wake of cyberattack on French blood bank

toggle caption i Helene Rigny/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

In a new security bulletin, the information sharing and analysis center devoted to the healthcare industry, Health ISAC, alerted members to a recent wave of cyberattacks targeting refrigeration controllers — including one incident that affected a major French blood bank.

"This alert is issued for situational awareness, highlighting how recent operational technology (OT) attacks against specific refrigeration brands directly intersect with emerging threats to the health sector," reads the bulletin seen by NPR. Operational technology refers to the machines that control physical processes in the real world, from cooling systems to water pumps.

Sponsor Message

Cyberattacks on grocery stores and food processing plants everywhere from Europe and Israel to U.S. military bases have drawn headlines in recent months, particularly as attacks have resulted in spoiled food, fires, broken machinery, and major business disruptions. Attackers are clearly aware of the vulnerability of these systems and are taking advantage.

However, until news broke that the French blood bank, known as the French Blood Establishment, had also been targeted, there was less public attention focused on the potential consequences of refrigeration controllers failing in other industries, particularly healthcare, where lifesaving implements like blood and vaccines often require finely tuned temperature-controlled environments to remain viable.

"This incident underscores a stark operational reality: cybersecurity in healthcare is fundamentally about patient safety," wrote Errol Weiss, the chief security officer at Health ISAC in an email to NPR. "When threat actors manipulate operational technology like cold-chain storage and refrigeration units holding donor blood, plasma, or critical therapies, they aren't merely stealing data or locking down administrative files, they are directly endangering the physical resources required to sustain human life."

On Thursday, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the FBI, the Department of Health and Human Services, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture published their own fact sheet about threats to industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems, tools they identify as critical to multiple industries from healthcare to chemical production, food and agriculture, and transportation.

Sponsor Message

The FBI Cyber Branch Operations director, Brett Leatherman, said the bureau is tracking bad actors targeting these systems "across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk."

"Industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems protect food, medicine, and other temperature-sensitive products, making them attractive targets for malicious cyber actors," Leatherman said.

Iran, Russia and the search for the culprits

The French blood bank confirmed in a press release Tuesday that one of its vendors used in cold storage rooms was targeted by malicious cyber activity, resulting in the defrost and temperature thresholds being raised dangerously high. The French Blood Establishment ultimately managed to detect the suspicious activity in time to rescue blood samples.

It remains unclear who is responsible for the global attacks on refrigeration controllers, and whether it's multiple actors or groups.

Iran has been linked to at least one incident in Israel earlier in the spring, though that breach involved a lot more sophistication and malicious activity. Investigators probing the disruptions at U.S. military bases are also considering Iran as the potential culprit.

Meanwhile, two pro-Russian hacking groups, NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance, belatedly released videos and posted on Telegram claiming responsibility for the attacks across Europe, publishing a sample of alleged hacked credentials that would've allowed them to access equipment including machines made by the Danish company Danfoss and the American company Copeland. Those machines can monitor and control temperature and other functions. The hacking groups have some history of targeting refrigeration controllers and other operational technology. However, it's unclear if the recent wave of attacks on refrigerators and freezers across Europe even required stolen credentials to execute, a factor that has led some cybersecurity experts to be skeptical of their claims.

Even so, it will require more evidence like access logs, configuration changes, and connections between maintenance accounts on the controllers to make any clear assessments, explained Tom Hegel, who leads threat intelligence research at cybersecurity firm SentinelOne.

Sponsor Message

"Russian-aligned actors are a credible hypothesis because there is a credible precedent, including the refrigeration-related attack DOJ attributed to CyberArmyofRussia_Reborn and NoName's history of politically motivated disruption. But that is only the context, not the missing evidentiary link to these European incidents," Hegel told NPR.

"It's important to note that such Russian threat actors often seek attention and claim to cause incidents even when false," he continued.

Regardless of who's responsible, the incident highlights how these nearly ubiquitous tools used to remotely manage critical systems are vulnerable to attack in several different ways.

For one, thousands of the refrigeration controllers in France alone were exposed to the open internet with almost no protection put in place before unidentified hackers went after them in October. Afterward, experts were still tracking hundreds of devices left unprotected. That's just a fraction of the tens of thousands of exposed operational devices online, many of them embedded in critical infrastructure.

Additionally, many of the major remote management systems used in refrigerators and freezers have security vulnerabilities. After alerting the companies to the problems, cybersecurity firm Claroty published research on vulnerabilities in multiple major refrigeration controllers, including those made by both the American manufacturer Copeland and by Danfoss.

While some of those vulnerabilities have been discovered and the vendors have designed patches to seal the hole, the problems don't stop there.

Experts warn it's difficult to patch operational technology because doing so often requires shutting systems down. In industries like healthcare, even minutes of downtime create extreme risk for patient safety. And for some aging models, it's impossible to patch, because the vendor is no longer offering updates — and companies can't afford to spring for a new model.

Sometimes, executives don't even know what machines are on their networks.

Additionally, for many companies, vendors that work with them demand remote access to systems like refrigeration controllers to regularly service them. It's often a requirement in the contract companies sign.

Sponsor Message

"Industrial chillers operate under vendor contracts that mandate persistent remote access," explained Nic Adams, CEO of 0rcus, a U.S. offensive security firm. "These commercial agreements leave national food and medical supplies defenseless against basic credential abuse."

Finally, hackers are now using AI to find these vulnerabilities faster than ever, and AI is also helping them to better understand the complex machines and the processes they control. Bad actors a world away no longer need to understand individual languages or industries, or even the physics involved to disrupt operations. In recent weeks, cyber incident responders tell NPR they're seeing a massive spike in attacks that are at least in part carried out by AI agents.

The good news is that a lot of these attacks, even if they incorporate AI, are not particularly sophisticated, novel, or stealthy.

Weiss of Health ISAC tells NPR there are basic steps the healthcare industry can take to prevent being a victim of these opportunistic attacks.

That process "begins" by "eliminating public internet exposure," wrote Weiss, then "enforcing strict network segmentation" in order to isolate refrigeration systems "from standard enterprise and guest networks" and finally adding on safeguards "that software overrides cannot bypass" like "hard-wired mechanical cutoffs" and "independent thermal alarms."

In the Health ISAC alert, the industry is urged to separate not just refrigeration controllers from hospital IT systems, but also medical gas monitors, for one, and train staff onsite on how to take physical manual control of machines in an emergency.

Finally, the alert urges hospitals to have offline backups of their systems.

Store managers on the frontlines

Sharing intelligence about these kinds of cyberattacks can help other potential victims avoid disaster.

While Estonian grocery stores were targeted in the most recent wave of attacks, many of those store managers were on high alert thanks to warnings issued by Estonia's Information Systems Authority, RIA. "When one Selver store was attacked on 2 November, the attackers managed to change the refrigeration system's temperature setting to +50°C. However, the service provider reacted quickly and prevented significant damage," said Annika Müür, a spokesperson for RIA. "So while we can't say that Estonia managed to prevent the attacks entirely, I think this case is a good example of the importance of monitoring threats internationally, acting on early warnings and working closely with businesses to minimise the impact."

Sponsor Message

Weiss of Health ISAC also urged companies across sectors that are being targeted by this recent wave of attacks to share information to help others defend themselves.

"The attack highlights why timely, trusted information sharing across borders and sectors is our strongest collective defense," he wrote.

"Rapid intelligence sharing allows hospitals and health facilities globally to recognize emerging attack patterns, verify vendor exposure, and harden critical infrastructure before threat actors can cause physical harm."

World.title: European flights and broadcasters are targeted with another wave of bomb threats
World.content:
European flights and broadcasters are targeted with another wave of bomb threats

toggle caption i Andreea Alexandru/AP

PRAGUE — Officials across Europe reported a fresh slew of bomb threats against multiple flights on Friday, following a string of hoaxes that have caused flight diversions this week. Three broadcasters also received security threats, in a possible sign the menace was spreading beyond the skies.

No suspicious items have been found and no one has been injured, but the threats have raised concern because they came on the heels of other European disruptions — including attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems and drone incursions.

Sponsor Message

Overall, the threats have caused minimal disruption to aviation, according to the European air traffic authority. Eurocontrol said it was aware of bomb threats against 14 flights on Thursday — only 0.05% of all of the nearly 26,300 flights across the European network that day — and seven on Tuesday. The European Union's transportation commissioner, Apostolos Tzitzikostas, said there were 11 more on Friday.

Even so, airlines have to take every threat seriously because they are ultimately responsible for the lives of their passengers, said Robert Jordan, research director at Britain's Royal United Services Institute think tank.

Jordan told the BBC that there are more ways than ever to make threats against flights, and secure messaging apps have allowed for greater anonymity.

"The risk appetite for airlines is always going to be incredibly low," he said, noting the great strides that have been made in airport security in recent years. "It is baked into their safety procedures, and it's baked into their security procedures."

Tzitzikostas said after a meeting with Eurocontrol and the EU's Aviation Safety Agency in Brussels that security experts will meet in the Belgian capital next week to discuss measures needed to deal with the rash of bomb threats.

"Our priority here is clear. The safety of passengers and the smooth functioning of European aviation," he said.

Sponsor Message

Fighter jets are scrambled

In Hungary, the defense minister said fighter jets escorted three passenger planes Friday through the country's airspace within an hour after each received a bomb threat. Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said the escorts were for flights from Brussels to the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, and from Prague to Cyprus and Romania.

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu's office said four bomb threats were made against aircraft flying over France. The planes landed safely at Paris' Orly Airport and bomb disposal experts conducted inspections. The office didn't specify which flights were affected.

Threats were also made against a Prague-to-Bucharest, Romania, flight operated by Romanian carrier Tarom, and a Ryanair flight from the Portuguese capital, Lisbon, to Rome. A WizzAir flight from Prague to Rome was diverted to Venice after a bomb alert, and passengers were evacuated after the aircraft landed.

Eurocontrol said Friday it was monitoring the situation and working closely with airlines, airports, navigation service providers and other groups across Europe "to mitigate any disruption to air traffic flows."

Nine of the affected flights were coming or going from Václav Havel Airport in Prague, airport spokesperson Denisa Hejtmánková said. They included flights from Denmark, Spain and Britain, and departures to the Netherlands and Britain, in addition to the ones to Cyprus, Italy and Romania. Czech police said security measures were taken that had "a minimal impact on the normal operations at the airport."

Diverting and inspecting flights is costly, though.

"I think it's a big problem for aviation that this is happening," Torstein Nymoen, a 52-year-old Norwegian traveler, said at the Prague airport. "It must cost a lot for the companies, the aviation companies. And I think that it's sad that some people are doing this."

In Denmark, police deployed to Copenhagen airport for a second consecutive day as a precautionary measure over threats directed at air traffic, and deemed there was no danger to passengers or others at the airport.

Sponsor Message

No clear evidence on who is behind the threats

More than two dozen flights were affected by threats earlier in the week, with some diverted as authorities scrambled to rule out any danger.

Fake bomb threats are relatively common but it is unusual to see so many in such a short period.

It remains unclear who is behind the airline threats, which come at a time of increased geopolitical tensions and warnings from authorities that Russia may be ramping up so-called hybrid threats in Europe.

Authorities have not attributed the threats to any group or state actor, and no evidence has emerged linking the hoaxes to a government. An email containing the threat sent Thursday to airport authorities in Rome and reviewed by The Associated Press purported to come from a group describing itself as anti-feminist and claiming it was targeting a "feminist regime." Another European airport received a threat with similar wording, but it was unclear if it came from the same sender.

Bomb threats are on pilots' minds and create unnecessary tension, but crews are prepared to respond professionally, said Paul Reuter, vice president of the European Cockpit Association. Pilots review procedures with cabin crews, identify airports where they could divert and may carry extra fuel, he said.

Reuter called the use of civil aviation for geopolitical disruption or hoaxes "totally unacceptable."

Broadcasters also received threats

In Ireland, the Dublin headquarters of national broadcaster RTE was evacuated Friday because of a bomb threat, and live broadcasts were replaced with prerecorded programs. Staff returned to the building after a few hours, once police with sniffer dogs had searched the area and declared it safe.

Ireland's police force, An Garda Síochána, said it has been liaising with Irish media organizations and that the threat will be investigated.

Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin said the threats to RTE and others "just illustrates how relatively simple it can be to cause disruption and to undermine the normal operation of society through unconventional activities of this kind, which are designed to cause fear and anxiety."

Sponsor Message

He said there would be a "very significant security operation" in place next week when Dublin hosts meetings of the European Political Community and European Union leaders.

Separately, U.K.-based broadcaster Sky said it had also received a "security threat." In a statement reported by Sky News channel, it said that "we are working closely with authorities to ensure our people and operations remain secure." Sky News remained on air.

Meanwhile, NOVA TV, a private broadcaster in Bulgaria, said it received an email Friday threatening it with a bomb. It said the sender claimed to be behind the threats to European air traffic, and that the broadcaster implemented its standard safety measures without any interruptions to its TV and radio broadcasts.

World.title: The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult is sentenced to 200 years in prison
World.content:
The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult is sentenced to 200 years in prison

toggle caption i Brian Inganga/AP

MOMBASA, Kenya — The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult linked to the deaths of more than 400 people was sentenced on Friday to 200 years in prison for the murders of 191 people.

The High Court in Kenya's coastal city of Mombasa issued the sentence for Pastor Paul Mackenzie. He was convicted of murdering 190 children and one adult after he ordered his followers to starve themselves to death in order to meet Jesus.

Mackenzie is also facing terrorism and manslaughter charges for the more than 200 other victims, as well as child abuse and torture charges in two other courts.

Justice Diana Kavedza said that Mackenzie, leader of the Good News International Church, bore the "primary criminal culpability" for relocating his followers to a remote location and ordering them to fast to death.

Mackenzie was charged with the murders alongside 28 of his followers, including guards who enforced his fasting directives and gravediggers who helped conceal the mass graves. All denied the charges, except for one person who confessed and pleaded for leniency.

toggle caption i Brian Inganga/AP

On Oct. 19, the court found all 29 of them guilty of the murder of 191 people.

Sponsor Message

In 2023, more than 400 bodies were exhumed from shallow graves on the 800-acre (320-hectare) Chakama Ranch in coastal Kilifi County, where Mackenzie's followers lived in mud huts, away from the scrutiny of local communities and authorities.

More than 60 bodies were positively identified and reburied by their relatives, while many others remain unidentified and unclaimed.

During the sentencing, Kavedza said that 183 victims died of starvation, defined as a complete lack of food, and the deaths of the other eight were classified as murder by direct homicide.

Kavedza said the killings were "cold and calculated" and dismissed claims by some of the accused that the loss of their own children altered the fact that they had participated in the killings of many other children.

The justice said that the perpetrators didn't show remorse and declared they were ready to fast to death as well. During the sentencing, Mackenzie often smiled and chatted with his assistant pastor, Smart Mwakalama, who was sentenced to 160 years in prison.

All of those who were convicted have been granted 14 days to file an appeal.

The prosecution had argued for the death penalty for Mackenzie and life imprisonment for his accomplices.

Defense lawyer Lawrence Obonyo, who represents Mackenzie and several others who were convicted, told The Associated Press that he had already launched an appeal. He said that the decision was "circling around the constitution to give a sentence that is unattainable" since the sentences of between 160 and 200 years amount to life sentences.

A father of seven, Suleiman Ziro, who traveled 120 kilometers (75 miles) for the sentencing, lost six of his children and his wife to the cult in 2023. He said that the sentence wasn't enough especially because he has yet to recover the bodies of his loved ones, calling for the death penalty in the case.

Sponsor Message

Mackenzie's son, Dan Mackenzie, said that he felt sorry for his father over the conviction, but it was "justice served to the victims." He said that he escaped by "rebelling" against his father's teachings and was often punished for it, but was glad he survived. Two of his younger brothers and three sisters were rescued and are currently at a children's home.

Those sentenced to death in Kenyan courts serve a life sentence. Kenya's last execution was in 1987.

World.title: Trump replaces chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller after midterm defeat
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump's top political adviser, chief of staff Susie Wiles, is leaving the White House just days after the Republican Party's resounding defeat in the midterms.

Trump announced Wiles's departure in a post on Truth Social and said she'll be replaced by deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, the key architect of the president's immigration policies.

"I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday," Trump said in the post.

He said Wiles had done an outstanding job and will be "moving over to the Trump Political Operation."

It's not immediately clear what Trump means by his political operation. It could be his MAGA Inc. political action committee, a fundraising organization that had hundreds of millions of dollars at its disposal to back Republican candidates in the midterms and could prove influential in the 2028 presidential campaign.

"I wanted to make a change," Trump told reporters outside the White House on Friday afternoon. "Sometimes in life you have to make moves."

The elevation of Miller to the top post appears to signal that Trump has no intention to back away from the mass deportation campaign that has gone far beyond its promised target of the worst criminals.

Stephen Miller, Trump's new chief of staff, has been the architect of the administration's immigration policy and its efforts to deport one million undocumented immigrants per year. Miller is shown in the Oval Office on Oct. 20. (Jacquelyn Martin/The Associated Press)

Backlash against Immigration and Customs Enforcement detentions of undocumented immigrants who've lived upstanding lives in the U.S. for years was one of the factors that swung many Hispanic voters against the Republicans in the midterms, helping to deliver a U.S. Senate seat for Texas to Democrat James Talarico.

Wiles had for much of the past year signalled that Trump would campaign for the midterms with a focus on affordability.

However the president instead sent voters an inconsistent message — often dismissing concerns about the cost of living while spending significant time in his rally speeches talking about his construction projects in Washington, D.C.

World.title: Your questions about this year's federal budget, answered
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's government unveiled a budget Thursday that covered more than $150 billion in spending, detailed in a 500-plus-page document. As Canadians attempt to parse what the budget means for them, here are answers to some of the questions sent in by CBC readers, viewers and listeners.

What questions do you have about the federal budget? Send an email to ask@cbc.ca.

How will the merger of RRSPs and RRIFs work and when will it start?

The government plans to merge Registered Retirement Savings Plans (RRSPs) and Registered Retirement Income Funds (RRIFs). Currently when Canadians turn 71, they can no longer contribute to their RRSPs and must convert them into RRIFs and begin withdrawing from them.

The "RRSP-for-life" plan would eliminate the need to switch.

The budget says the exact details haven't been ironed out yet, though under the proposal Canadians over 71 would continue to be required to make minimum withdrawals. The government says it is still considering whether the RRSP could be kept open after death by a spouse or common-law partner, and whether the current "rollover" rules could be replaced by direct tax-free transfers.

The changes wouldn't take hold for some time, as they require changes to both federal and provincial legislation. Canadians can send their views on the proposal in writing to the Department of Finance by emailing RRSP-consultation-REER@fin.gc.ca by Jan. 8, 2027.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne delivers the federal budget speech in the House of Commons on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Thursday. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

How does the Canada Housing Benefit work?

The budget renews the Canada Housing Benefit that provides direct monthly rental assistance to low-income renters. The 10-year extension starts at $1.7 billion over the first three years, beginning in 2028-29, and increases to $3.9 billion in future years.

The benefit is cost-shared with each province and territory, so the rules are different depending on where you live.

An aerial view of a residential neighbourhood in Vancouver on Tuesday. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

What does the new tax credit for business income from 'creative artistic works' apply to?

We don't know yet.



The federal government says it will consult with Canadians and the cultural sector on the Canada Creative Credit and provide details in the 2027 spring economic update.

The only details so far are that it would likely take the form of a non-refundable personal income tax credit that, combined with an earner's basic personal amount of tax-exempt earnings, would cover up to $45,000.

WATCH | What the budget means for your taxes: What the federal budget means for your taxes | Hanomansing Live | Duration closed caption 4:29 Thursday's federal budget includes a number of measures aimed at making life more affordable for Canadians. More low-income workers will get benefit payments to help them make ends meet. Those who make a minimum of $3,000 annually get a refundable tax credit under the Canada Workers Benefit, but that threshold is being lowered to $500 for all workers.

Are heat pumps in the budget?

Yes. As the government announced on Oct. 8, the federal government is launching a $2-billion rebate program that it says will help homeowners in Canada lower their annual heating costs while reducing emissions when they install heat pumps in their homes.

The funding will provide rebates for up to 820,000 homeowners over the next eight years, saving them an average of $1,400 a year on their heating bills when they replace existing heat pumps or heating systems.

What's in the budget for seniors ...

The budget document points to about a dozen items that it says will have benefits for "predominantly seniors or the baby boom generation." Those include making the tax credit for home accessibility renovations easier to claim; "modernizing" Canada Post; removing the GST/HST from devices specially designed to treat cancer using alternating electric field therapy; and a new national anti-fraud strategy.

The Bloc Québécois said the budget does not do enough for seniors, particularly in regard to health care.

"It is the people, the seniors, the sick who will suffer," Jean-Denis Garon, the Bloc's finance critic, said in a statement.

WATCH | Bloc pushes back on budget: Liberal budget not grounded in reality, says Bloc critic | Duration closed caption 7:41 The federal government released its 2026 budget, sparking pushback from the Bloc Québécois over federal encroachment on provincial jurisdictions and a lack of unconditional funding for health care and seniors. Power & Politics hears from Bloc Québécois finance critic Jean-Denis Garon.

... and youth ...

The government claims almost 30 items in the budget will have impacts on "predominantly youth, children, and/or future generations."



Those include revitalizing rec facilities and hockey rinks; the new Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission of Canada to enforce the Safe Social Media Act; and funding the Canadian Centre for Child Protection.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said Friday that youth are desperate for homes and jobs and that Carney shows he is out of touch with his spending and immigration policies.

... and for grocery shoppers ...

The budget tops up the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, a pre-existing program that gives quarterly payments to Canadians with low and modest incomes.



The top-up increases the payments by 50 per cent for the 2026-27 benefit year, delivered as a standalone payment early next year. The supplement would provide up to $339 for a single person without children and up to $679 for a couple with two children.



The government says it amounts to $4.1 billion in additional support to more than 12 million people.

... and for small businesses?

The federal budget has zeroed in on business growth with a suite of tax measures and incentives designed to spur private-sector investment, but some business leaders and groups said the budget falls short in addressing the needs of small businesses.

"While there's a mega deduction and there's a focus on mega projects, my takeaway is that this is a mega disappointing budget for small business owners," said Dan Kelly, president and chief executive of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business.

The budget enhances the small business rollover of taxes when capital gains are reinvested in another Canadian small business.

"If you sell your business, but then you invest that money back into a new one, you're not going to get hit with capital gains right away," Kelly said. "It already exists but they're making it a little bit more flexible."

WATCH | Does Carney's budget meet the moment?: At Issue | Does Carney's budget meet the moment? | Duration closed caption 22:25 At Issue this week: Mark Carney's second budget lays out billions to build Canada's sovereignty and tackle the affordability crisis, but will it work? And what does the Democratic Blue-nami mean for Canada-U.S. trade talks?

On entrepreneurship, Ottawa said the Canada Growth Incentive will encourage investors and business owners to reinvest capital gains in Canadian companies.

And on innovation, the budget introduced a $930-million expansion of the Scientific Research and Experimental Development tax incentive program to help businesses develop new products and technologies and bring them to market.

For self-employed business owners, Ottawa plans to simplify tax instalments by allowing a single annual payment instead of quarterly payments.

"All of these pieces put together are supportive of growth and investment in Canada over the longer term," said Randall Bartlett, deputy chief economist with Desjardins Group.

WATCH | 'Big bet' budget has its critics: Budget 2026: Carney makes 'big bet' for investment, opposition blasts affordability moves | Duration closed caption 6:43 The Carney government's second budget lays out over $150 billion in spending to attract investment, accelerate nation-building projects, boost housing and tackle the affordability crisis. The NDP says it favours the rich, while Conservatives call it a 'credit card budget Canadians can't afford.'

What are the debt repercussions of the budget's price tag?

In the budget, the cost to finance Canada's roughly $1.3-trillion national debt will jump from $60.2 billion in 2026-27 to $85.5 billion in 2030-31.

Sahir Khan, the executive vice-president at the Institute of Fiscal Studies and Democracy, said the government's "fiscal sustainability is intact." Canada's sterling credit rating, relatively strong GDP growth and healthy balance sheet mean that, "compared to everybody else, we're looking really shiny," he said.

Carney hopes the budget's massive public investing will have transformed the economy by the time the debt servicing charge has hit 12.5 per cent of the government's expenses, up from about 10 per cent now.

The Opposition is not on board.

WATCH | Poilievre says 'time is up' for Liberals: Carney has allowed economic 'disaster in people's lives,' Poilievre says | Duration closed caption 1:15 Asked by the CBC how long Canadians should give the Liberal government to demonstrate results from their plan to build economic growth, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says 'the time is up.'

Poilievre said the Liberals should have named the budget "mastered by debt" and said their plan will inflate the prices of essentials and make life more unaffordable for Canadians. Adam Chambers, Conservative shadow critic for innovation, science and industry, said the budget is dependent on no major global shocks hitting the economy in the meantime.



"If the government is wrong, then the financial health of the country could deteriorate actually quite quickly," he said.

World.title: Joly asks Competition Bureau to investigate Cleveland-Cliffs purchase of Stelco
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's industry minister is asking the Competition Bureau to investigate Stelco's parent company after its CEO told CBC News that he only bought the Hamilton steelmaker to stop it undercutting his U.S. business.

Mélanie Joly said on Friday she has sent a letter to the competition commissioner asking them to examine whether Cleveland-Cliffs's conduct ran afoul of the Competition Act.

"If negotiations and acquisition were conducted in bad faith, Canadians deserve to know. The company needs to face the consequences," she said in a statement.

Last week, Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves told CBC's Power & Politics with David Cochrane "I bought Stelco because I could not afford anymore having Stelco flooding the market here in the United States to the detriment of my own company."

WATCH | Stelco owner's comments prompt minister to call lawyers: Stelco owner's live TV admission prompts industry minister to call lawyers | Duration closed caption 2:49 Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said she called the government's lawyers after the head of Stelco's American parent company told CBC News that he only bought the Hamilton steelmaker to stop it undercutting his production facilities in the U.S.

Joly called that a "shocking admission" and said she contacted the department's lawyers to see if there should be any consequences.

"It is the commissioner's responsibility to examine this matter thoroughly and, if warranted, take the appropriate measures," she said on Friday.

Goncalves made his comments after Joly's demand that the company reverse its layoffs at Stelco or face potential legal action.

The government says the company agreed when it purchased Stelco to keep the number of unionized employees at 2024 levels through to 2029.

Joly's letter comes as Ottawa's 15-day deadline ends for the company to address the alleged violation of those commitments.

Goncalves's company maintains that it's in "full compliance" with the obligations it made under the Investment Canada Act.

Stelco announced plans on Sept. 28 to lay off up to 500 workers at its Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont., steel mills, citing U.S. tariffs, weak demand for Canadian steel and competition from imported steel products.

However, Cleveland-Cliffs and the union have recently confirmed only 175 workers have been laid off so far, all in Hamilton.

World.title: Tesla will stop making Cybertrucks next year: Musk
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas Gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, after years of persistently weak sales for a futuristic model once touted as a rival to legacy pickup trucks.

The move is a major retreat from what has been one of Musk's pet projects. In an X post, Musk said the wind-down would let Tesla make more of the Cybercab, a robotaxi he has made central to the automaker's autonomous-vehicle ambitions, but one that has yet to prove itself commercially.

The announcement comes at the end of a bruising week for Musk, as his record political spending of nearly half a billion dollars yielded little in Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections, with the vast majority of the Republican candidates he backed losing their races.

Furthermore, his companies were on track to lose more than $180 billion US in combined market capitalization for the week.

A Tesla Cybertruck near the White House last year. (Leah Millis/Reuters)

While it wasn't immediately clear whether Cybertruck production would be moved to another facility or phased out entirely, the automaker's Austin plant is the only known Tesla facility equipped to manufacture the specialized components for the heavy, angular model.

In response to a user on X, Musk called the Cybertruck the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made" and the wind-down the "end of an era."

Tesla has been shifting its focus to robotics and autonomy, a transition analysts say comes at the expense of the electric-vehicle business it helped pioneer as Chinese rivals gain ground.

The U.S. EV maker began delivering the Cybertruck to customers in late 2023. According to automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the company only sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the U.S. last year, down 48 per cent from 38,965 in 2024. Around the start of production in 2023, Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 units.

"It doesn't make sense to keep it going when it's not meeting its targets," said former Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer. "Every rational auto guy would say the same."

"It will no doubt only be a rounding error on Tesla's balance sheet, but the statistics speak for themselves."

Musk's SpaceX was one of the model's biggest customers last year and bought $131 million worth of Cybertrucks from Tesla in 2025 at list price, according to its IPO filing.

WATCH | The Cybertruck's unveiling in 2019: Tesla unveils electric Cybertruck, smashes its 'bulletproof' glass | Duration 1:11 Tesla showed off its upcoming entry into the electric truck market in a lavish launch event last night. An attempt to demonstrate its "bulletproof" glass using a metal ball backfired, however, as the windows shattered. Twice.

'Cybertruck won't go, can't go'

Right from its unveiling in 2019, the Cybertruck was a controversial choice for Musk. Pickup truck purists mocked its angular design, and safety experts predicted it would be hard to gain approval for sale in key markets like Europe.

The unveiling event itself was marred when Musk tried to prove that its windows were shatterproof by having metal balls thrown at them — only to leave massive cracks in two of them.

During Cybertruck's official launch in 2023, Musk touted it as a futuristic competitor to pickup trucks from General Motors and Ford, saying "finally, the future will look like the future."

But the model has struggled to meet those expectations. Tesla has issued 11 recalls for the Cybertruck since it went on sale in late 2023, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. Some vehicles required physical repairs, while others were fixed with over-the-air software updates.

WATCH | Tesla unveiled its latest auto venture last month: Elon Musk shows off redesigned Tesla Roadster that can thrust itself into the air | Duration closed caption 0:55 Elon Musk's car company Tesla debuted its second generation Roadster, which includes a set of cold gas thrusters and a "multi-mode" suction system that can fling the car in the air for short spurts and spin the vehicle mid-flight.

Automotive analyst Felipe Munoz said that although the Cybertruck has been called a failure because of its poor sales, electric pickups from Ford and others have also flopped in the U.S. market.

"All of them lost the competition because electric pickups aren't popular in the U.S.," Munoz said.

But Cybertruck's sharp-edged, stainless steel design limited its prospects in markets like Europe, where EVs are more popular. Regulatory approval was impossible for Europe because of rules there concerning pedestrian impact.

"Anywhere where you have crash regulation that takes into account pedestrian impact, that Cybertruck won't go, can't go," former Aston Martin CEO Palmer said.

World.title: Blue Jays player faces backlash after reposting Islamophobic content on social media following U.S. midterms
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Community organizations and advocates are speaking out after a Toronto Blue Jays player posted Islamophobic content on social media following the U.S. midterm elections.

In a series of Instagram stories that were later taken down, right fielder Anthony Santander reposted one reel featuring video of the newly-elected Michigan Senator Abdul El-Sayed with the caption, "America voted for Sharia last night," and another that said, "Islam is not peaceful."

The reels, originally created by the American Truth Project account and a Gospel of Jesus Christ minister, caused outrage on social media. While Santander's decision to repost them sparked backlash from Canada's Muslim community.

His stories were "hurtful" for many Muslim baseball fans, said Ahmad Al Qadi, a senior advisor at advocacy organization National Council of Canadian Muslims (NCCM).

"It puts them in a position where they're now questioning whether they have a place in the sport, whether they have a place in Canada," he told CBC Toronto. "It's incredibly disappointing to see this kind of rhetoric being displayed by someone like Anthony Santander."

Santander, 32, played 56 games during the Blue Jays' 2025 run to the World Series, but missed the entirety of this past season following shoulder surgery. He previously played eight seasons in Baltimore, including an all-star year in 2024, and is now in the middle of a five-year, $92.5-million deal with Toronto.

CBC Toronto has reached out to Santander and his agency for comment.

Al Qadi said online hate has become all too normalized, but it's up to big corporations like Major League Baseball and the Blue Jays to stand up against Islamophobia. That’s why the NCCM has reached out and is discussing the incident, as well as next steps, with the organizations, he said.

The NCCM is urging Santander to apologize, Al Qadi said, and meet with people in Canada's Muslim community to understand why the posts that he shared "are so hurtful, can cause damage and are causing damage and pain to the Muslim community in Canada."

Blue Jays organization distances itself from posts

In a statement to CBC Toronto Thursday, a spokesperson for the Blue Jays said the team has created an inclusive space where all fans feel welcome.

"Baseball is for everyone," spokesperson Adam Felton said. "Individual comments do not represent our organization’s values and beliefs."

Canada's former special representative on combatting Islamophobia, Amira Elghawaby, said in a post on social media that she expects more from the Blue Jays and Santander, whom she said is a role model and a public figure that many young sports fans look up to.

"His reckless actions have impact, and we have seen anti Muslim hate turn deadly in Canada," Elghawaby said in a post to X Thursday.

Canada's former special representative on combatting Islamophobia, Amira Elghawaby, also took to social media to condemn Santander’s actions. She said he is a role model and a public figure that many young sports fans look up to. (Amanda Margison/CBC)

"Deleting his posts is not enough — Santander owes fans an apology, and the Blue Jays need to take a stronger stand against Islamophobic hate, and be transparent about how they plan to make this right," she added.

In a post to social media platform X Thursday, the Muslim Advisory Council of Canada called on the federal government to address Santander’s actions.

"This issue should not be left solely to Muslim communities to condemn," the non-profit organization wrote. "It is a matter of collective responsibility, and everyone, especially those in positions of leadership, must speak out and take a stand."

The office for Canada's Secretary of State for Sport, Adam van Koeverden, declined to comment.

World.title: Carney's bet on economic growth — and the risks that come with it
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Mark Carney is making a bet.

He believes massive public investing now will position the Canadian economy to grow in spite of the trade war and the shifting winds of global geopolitics.

By the 2030-31 fiscal year, the federal government will shoulder $85.5 billion in annual public debt charges. By then, Carney hopes the bet will have paid off and the economy will have undergone a transformation.

"[Ottawa] is borrowing money for these major projects, hoping that it really jump-starts the economy," said Sahir Khan, executive vice-president of the Institute of Fiscal Studies and Democracy at the University of Ottawa.

Khan says the risk is the economy shifts and macro trends change and leave Canada holding a pile of debt that never actually catalyzed growth or investment or created actual jobs.

"There are no jobs created by MOUs and frameworks. They're done when the projects actually get financed, people get hired and we see economic activity," said Khan.

Why many experts are backing Carney's plan

Most experts, including Khan, believe the government's plan is a good idea. They say Canada has not taken steps to boost investment and productivity in years and it shows.

The economy was weak before the trade war began; in 2022, the Bank of Canada warned productivity was reaching emergency, " break glass" levels.

Carney says his plan will address productivity, bring in investment for major projects that will create revenue and build jobs. He says the cost of that is clear, but manageable.

WATCH | Spending is 'under control,' Carney says: ‘We’ve got spending under control’: Carney on federal budget | Duration 0:40 Prime Minister Mark Carney says the federal government is balancing the operational budget a year early and has spending under control while shifting to invest to be ‘masters of our own destiny.’

The key plank to that is the so-called productivity mega-deduction . That alone is expected to encourage businesses to invest in their companies. It brings Canada's marginal effective tax rate to the lowest in any G7 country.

There's also a new Canada growth incentive , an exemption from capital gains that allows entrepreneurs to avoid taxes on up to $15 million in capital gains if those funds are reinvested in a Canadian business.

But those measures cost a lot of money. The productivity-mega deduction alone will cost some $36 billion over five years.

Carney told CBC News after the budget that his government is already taking measures to bring the deficit down.

"We've got spending under control, shifting to invest to be masters of our own destiny. Opportunity, affordability and sovereignty. Canada's moving forward is a fantastic day for the country," said Carney.

What are the risks of massive spending?

But the risk isn't just that these bets don't turn into shovels in the ground or actual jobs.

Adam Chambers, Conservative shadow critic for innovation, science and industry, worries what happens if some other global event crashes into the economy while we have taken on so much debt to deal with the current crisis.

"There's no question the probability of there being an event is rising. Certainly the debt markets would suggest that there is some volatility happening," he said.

The federal government has touted what it calls Canada's "fiscal capacity." Canada has not borrowed nearly as much as other advanced economies and, as a result, the borrowing costs here are lower than they are in many other jurisdictions.

But the list of unexpected events that have changed the economic landscape and made debt riskier is a long one.

"There's a bet being made that there will be no other significant negative shocks. But if the government is wrong, then the financial health of the country could deteriorate actually quite quickly," he told CBC News.

WATCH | Does Carney's budget meet the moment?: At Issue | Does Carney's budget meet the moment? | Duration closed caption 22:25 At Issue this week: Mark Carney's second budget lays out billions to build Canada's sovereignty and tackle the affordability crisis, but will it work? And what does the Democratic Blue-nami mean for Canada-U.S. trade talks?

Chambers says those rising debt service payments should give everyone pause.

By the end of the budget's projections, the deficit will be lower, the debt to GDP ratio will remain within the government's guardrails. But those debt service payments will be at $85.5 billion and sit as the second largest single expenditure in the budget.

And all that a full two years after the end of Donald Trump's term as president.

World.title: Landslide prompts evacuation order for village of Zeballos on Vancouver Island
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An evacuation order has been issued for Zeballos, a village of about 125 people on the northwest coast Vancouver Island, due to a landslide.
