Emergency Info B.C. says the order affects properties on Pandora Crescent and Maquinna Avenue. It says the landslide is a risk to life and safety and anyone in the affected area must evacuate now.

The Strathcona Regional District says it is "actively monitoring flooding and potential landslide risks in the area."

The district's emergency operations centre has been activated.

"We recognize that this is a concerning situation for the community," the district said on its website.

"Public safety remains the priority, and we will continue to provide updates as more information becomes available."

World.title: Morgan Fairchild, the icy diva you couldn't miss on 1980s TV, joins racy subscriber platform OnlyFans
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Perhaps you remember the icy glam of her primetime TV roles or her scene-stealing turn as Chander Bing's spicy novelist mom on Friends.

But Morgan Fairchild is vowing to share another side of herself as the latest veteran soap vixen to join the racy online subscription platform OnlyFans.

"I'm putting up new pictures and videos. And before anyone asks: no, not that kind," the 76-year-old actress told U.S. media outlets, including People, TMZ and USA Today.

"Mostly, it's just me being goofy and talking about whatever's on my mind."

From left, actresses Linda Gray, Fairchild, Donna Mills, Loni Anderson and Nicollette Sheridan attend a Beverly Hills, Calif., event in 2023. Mills, who starred on Knots Landing, joined Onlyfans in July. (Randy Shropshire/Getty Images for Lifetime / A+E)

A mainstay on TV and in movies in the 1980s and '90s, Fairchild's wide-ranging credits run the gamut from soaps like Falcon Crest, Dallas and General Hospital to her regular cameo spots in episodes of hit shows like Mork & Mindy, Magnum, P.I., The Love Boat, Saturday Night Live, Murphy Brown and Friends.

"People know the characters, the clothes and the big hair... They may not know what a science nerd I am or how easily my sister can make me laugh. I'd love to share more of that," said the Dallas-born actress, who currently hosts the podcast 2 Bitches From Texas with her sister Cathryn Hartt.

She follows in the footsteps of friend and Knots Landing star Donna Mills, who joined OnlyFans this past July and has spoken positively in interviews about her experience thus far. Last spring, Mills went viral on social media with a post clapping back at an age-shaming comment she received.

An online platform where subscribers pay creators for custom photos and videos, OnlyFans is best known for its adult content and as a safer space for sex workers to make a living. It's been singled out amid wider debates about combatting sex trafficking and the exploitation of minors, with the platform announcing a ban of sexually explicit content in 2021, but backtracking days later.

More recently, however, a wider range of people looking to bolster their finances have joined the service, including a growing wave of famous faces aiming to connect with paying fans through tamer, non-explicit content.

American Pie's Shannon Elizabeth, Battlestar Galactica's Tricia Helfer, Drea de Matteo from The Sopranos and multiple stars from Baywatch are among the 1990s and early-2000s Hollywood stars who've signed up.

Elite athletes — including a raft of Olympians — have also turned to the platform as a source of income and financial stability while they navigate the steep costs of a competitive athletic career.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: Peña says he will face his impeachment trial as Argentina denies he has entered the country
World.content:
Peña says he will face his impeachment trial as Argentina denies he has entered the country

6th Friday, November 2026 - 01:56 UTC Full article

“We have no record of him being in Argentina.” Javier Milei’s government, a political ally of Peña, has not commented on the Paraguayan crisis.

Paraguayan President Santiago Peña announced on Thursday night that he will appear before the Senate to defend himself in the impeachment trial against him, after Congress failed for lack of a quorum to consider the resignation he had tendered hours earlier, leaving him formally in office. Argentina’s government, meanwhile, denied any record of Peña entering Argentina, following reports that he might have left Paraguay.

“Given the continuation of the impeachment trial, I will appear and exercise my right to a defence,” Peña said in a message released after the joint session of Congress called to accept or reject his resignation was suspended. The session lost its quorum when deputies of the ruling Colorado Party walked out. The Senate called an extraordinary session on Thursday night to set the impeachment trial in motion, on grounds of “poor performance of his duties”, and another on Friday morning to begin proceedings in the president’s presence, according to the Paraguayan press. The Chamber of Deputies had approved the charges by 78 votes to none. A two-thirds Senate majority is needed to remove him.

Uncertainty over Peña’s whereabouts persisted through the afternoon. Presidential spokesman Guillermo Grance acknowledged he did not know where the president was, according to ABC Color, and the speaker of the Chamber of Deputies, Colorado Party member Raúl Latorre, also admitted not knowing. “While we debate, the media are saying that President Santiago Peña has already set foot on Argentine soil,” opposition deputy Johana Ortega said during the session. In Buenos Aires, official sources quoted by La Nación ruled it out: “We have no record of him being in Argentina.” Javier Milei’s government, a political ally of Peña, has not commented on the Paraguayan crisis.

The reports recalled the departure of former Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, who on October 27 crossed into the Argentine city of Puerto Iguazú and flew from there to Miami after refusing to accept his defeat by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

The dispute between resignation and impeachment has legal consequences. If Congress accepts the resignation, Peña would take a lifetime Senate seat with parliamentary immunity; if the Senate removes him, he would lose that protection. The opposition and much of the ruling party, including Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, back the impeachment. According to the press, prosecutors have announced they are opening proceedings against Peña, although no formal charges have yet been brought.

The crisis erupted on Tuesday with the takeover of Ueno Bank, which froze the deposits of nearly three million customers and hundreds of millions of dollars of public funds. If Peña leaves office, Vice President Pedro Alliana will take over the presidency until August 15, 2028.

World.title: Lula sees his win as “a lesson for the world” after setbacks for Netanyahu and Trump
World.content:
Lula sees his win as “a lesson for the world” after setbacks for Netanyahu and Trump

6th Friday, November 2026 - 01:42 UTC Full article

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva described his October 25 re-election as “a lesson for the world” and linked it to the electoral setbacks suffered in recent days by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump. “In the same week, Netanyahu lost in Israel and I think my friend Trump is losing in the United States,” he said on Thursday in a live broadcast on YouTube.

Lula, 81, spent an hour and a half on a livestream with congressman André Janones, the architect of the digital strategy that helped his electoral comeback, watched by some 600,000 viewers. “I am more afraid than in my first term,” he admitted. “My obsession is back: I cannot fail, I cannot betray them. I have to do better.” The president defended some of his priorities, such as ending online betting, the sovereign exploitation of critical minerals and the importance of the university entrance exam, and promised to find ways for people to take part in government decisions.

Lula said he would speak more often through social media. “I will speak more directly to the people through social media. I will no longer allow the press to interpret what I think,” he said. He also invited Janones to accompany him next week on his first official trip since re-election: the UN climate summit, COP31, in Turkey, and a summit with Southeast Asian countries in Manila.

In Israel’s October 27 election, Netanyahu’s bloc lost its parliamentary majority, winning 53 of the 120 seats, although his Likud party came first; Netanyahu has alleged fraud. In the United States, Democrats regained control of both chambers of Congress on Tuesday. Lula will begin his fourth term on January 5.

World.title: Watchdog publishes a list of 77 clergy accused of abuse in Peru ahead of the Pope’s visit
World.content:
Watchdog publishes a list of 77 clergy accused of abuse in Peru ahead of the Pope’s visit

6th Friday, November 2026 - 01:38 UTC Full article

US-based organisation Bishop Accountability on Thursday presented in Lima a list of 77 members of Peru’s Catholic clergy publicly accused of sexually abusing minors, days before Pope Leo XIV, who lived in the country for more than two decades, begins his tour of South America. Victims and the organisation called on the pontiff to take concrete steps, including setting up a truth commission.

The list, published on the website of the organisation, which documents sexual abuse cases in the Catholic Church, includes priests, brothers, seminarians and consecrated laypeople who have worked in Peruvian parishes and schools, as well as Church officials accused of allegedly covering up complaints. It is based mainly on the book Den of abusers or safe Church?, published this year by Reinaldo Nann, a former bishop of Caravelí in southern Peru who has left the priesthood. Those on the list have been publicly accused; not all have been tried or convicted.

“The Peruvian Church is stubbornly putting children at risk by covering up for abusers,” said Bishop Accountability co-director Anne Barrett Doyle. José Enrique Escardó, president of the Peruvian Survivors’ Network and one of the first to denounce the Sodalitium Christianae Vitae, the Catholic movement Pope Francis suppressed in early 2025 after abuse allegations, said “victims need comprehensive reparation” and that “the most important thing is prevention”.

The organisations made three requests to the Pope: that bishops and religious superiors in Peru publish the names of clergy accused of abusing minors; that a Truth Commission be set up to investigate the cases; and that a universal zero-tolerance rule be enshrined in canon law.

Leo XIV, who holds Peruvian nationality, was bishop of Chiclayo and chaired the Peruvian Bishops’ Conference Commission for the Protection of Minors, where he worked alongside Nann. According to the former bishop, the current Pope was then “more open to listening to victims than the rest of the bishops”, although he considers him “too cautious a man” who is not driving change fast enough. According to El País, the Vatican has announced that the Pope will meet victims during his visit, although the meeting is not yet on the official schedule. There has been no response from the Peruvian Bishops’ Conference to the list.

The Pope will visit Uruguay and Argentina before arriving in Peru, where he will stay from November 11 to 17.

World.title: Big Tech loses a trillion dollars in a day after the Democratic win
World.content:
Big Tech loses a trillion dollars in a day after the Democratic win

6th Friday, November 2026 - 00:51 UTC Full article

Trump blamed the opposition. “The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election. Remember, it wasn’t Republicans,” he wrote on social media

Shares in major technology companies plunged on Wall Street on Thursday and in Asian markets on Friday, in a sell-off that wiped hundreds of billions of dollars of market value, on fears that the Democratic victory in the US midterm elections will slow the expansion of data centres and artificial intelligence. The so-called magnificent seven, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, together lost a trillion dollars in a single session, according to the BBC.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq closed down more than 5.5%, losing an estimated US$2.5 trillion in market value, according to Dow Jones data, and entered what analysts call correction territory, a fall of at least 10% from its recent high. The S&P 500 fell 4.4% and the Dow Jones more than 3.4%, their worst days since 2025. Nvidia dropped more than 9%, losing more than US$400 billion; AMD and Micron fell more than 17%, and Intel 10.3%. Tesla and SpaceX, the companies of Elon Musk, who spent heavily backing Republican candidates, together lost more than US$300 billion.

The sell-off spread to Asia on Friday. Seoul’s Kospi index plunged more than 8.5%, triggering a temporary trading halt; Japan’s Nikkei fell 6% and Taiwan’s Taiex more than 8.3%. Chipmakers suffered the steepest losses: SK Hynix lost more than 11.5%, Samsung nearly 10% and Taiwan’s TSMC about 8.5%.

Democratic candidates across the country campaigned to curb the spread of data centres, criticised for their water and electricity consumption and their impact on local bills, and dozens of local ballot measures sought to restrict them. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa pledged a moratorium on their construction. “Fresh panic over the AI trade has hit Wall Street hard,” said Susannah Streeter of Wealth Club, for whom doubts about the returns on those investments “are now colliding with the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction”. “There is a difference between supporting AI development and allowing infrastructure to expand at any cost or pace,” said Charu Chanana of Saxo.

President Donald Trump blamed the opposition. “The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election. Remember, it wasn’t Republicans,” he wrote on social media. Senator Bernie Sanders, by contrast, called for a “national data center moratorium”. OpenAI president Greg Brockman admitted the backlash had surprised the industry: “You can’t just tweet and say: ‘This is going to be good.’ You need to be in those communities.”

World.title: Paraguay’s Santiago Peña tenders his resignation, but Congress presses ahead with impeachment
World.content:
Paraguay’s Santiago Peña tenders his resignation, but Congress presses ahead with impeachment

5th Thursday, November 2026 - 22:12 UTC Full article

“I have decided to submit my resignation from the Presidency of the Republic. I do so with the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions,” Peña said

Paraguayan President Santiago Peña tendered his resignation on Thursday, cornered by the collapse of Ueno Bank, but minutes later the Chamber of Deputies unanimously voted to impeach him, in an attempt to prevent him from taking up a lifetime Senate seat with immunity from prosecution once he leaves office. The final decision rests with the Senate.

“I have decided to submit my resignation from the Presidency of the Republic. I do so with the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions in mind,” Peña said in a video posted on social media as deputies debated the charges. “My greatest wish is that the return of those funds is guaranteed,” he added, referring to the frozen savings of nearly three million of the bank’s customers. Interior Minister Enrique Riera formally submitted the resignation to Congress at around 1.30 p.m.

Less than an hour later, all 78 deputies present approved the impeachment charges, which now go to the Senate, where a two-thirds majority is needed to remove the president. The chamber rejected impeachment proceedings against Vice President Pedro Alliana, who would take over the presidency until the end of the term on August 15, 2028.

Mensaje del Presidente de la República, Santiago Peña, al pueblo paraguayo. https://t.co/RBz6IfFV9L — Santiago Peña (@SantiPenap) November 5, 2026

The dispute is also constitutional. Under the Constitution, Congress must accept or reject a president’s resignation; if it accepts, Peña would become a senator for life, with parliamentary immunity. If the Senate removes him through impeachment, he would lose that protection. A session of Congress called to consider the resignation was suspended for lack of a quorum, so for now Peña formally remains president, according to Argentina’s La Nación.

Peña’s downfall accelerated when his own party withdrew its support. Former President Horacio Cartes, head of the ruling Colorado Party and for years his main political backer, endorsed the impeachment. “We will not side with the plundering of public and private funds and of pensioners,” he said. According to El País, prosecutors announced they were opening proceedings against Peña, and opposition lawmakers expanded a criminal complaint alleging illicit enrichment, money laundering and influence peddling, among other offences, which also targets Economy Minister Óscar Lovera, former Central Bank president Carlos Carvallo and other officials. No formal charges have yet been brought against the president.

The crisis erupted on Tuesday, when the Central Bank took over Ueno Bank, the country’s largest digital bank by customers, over insolvency and irregular loans to companies owned by its owners, the Vázquez Group, and froze its deposits, including hundreds of millions of dollars of public and pension funds. The bank’s president and other executives were detained. Thousands of savers took to the streets of Asunción demanding their savings and the president’s resignation. On Wednesday, Peña signed a law to speed up deposit guarantee payouts and proposed Raúl Vera Bogado to head the Central Bank, but failed to stem the crisis.

Carvallo, whom Peña appointed Central Bank president in 2023, had been chief executive of Ueno Bank, and Peña himself was a shareholder in Ueno Holding until April 2025. On the eve of the takeover, Alliana had publicly distanced himself from the president.

Peña, a 47-year-old economist who took office in August 2023, becomes the second Paraguayan president since the return to democracy in 1989 to face impeachment proceedings reaching the Senate; in 2012, the Senate removed Fernando Lugo in a fast-track process.

World.title: Ibero-American foreign ministers unanimously back Argentina’s Falklands claim
World.content:
Ibero-American foreign ministers unanimously back Argentina’s Falklands claim

5th Thursday, November 2026 - 07:21 UTC Full article

“The Ibero-American community reaffirms, once again, its support for the Argentine Republic,” said Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno

Ibero-American foreign ministers meeting in Madrid unanimously approved a special communiqué backing Argentina’s sovereignty claim over the Falklands and calling on Argentina and the United Kingdom to resume negotiations, on the eve of the Hamburg hearing on the Sea Lion oil project.

The document, approved at the foreign ministers’ meeting held during the 30th Ibero-American Summit of Heads of State and Government, urges both governments to resume talks on the dispute “as soon as possible” and acknowledges Argentina’s “constructive attitude”. The Ibero-American Conference, which brings together the countries of Latin America with Spain, Portugal and Andorra, routinely adopts such a statement at its summits.

“The Ibero-American community reaffirms, once again, its support for the Argentine Republic,” said Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno, who called the issue “a sacred cause for Argentines” and defended the diplomatic route to end what he considers an anachronistic colonial situation.

The backing comes five days before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea holds hearings in Hamburg on November 10 and 11 on the four provisional measures Argentina requested on October 13 to halt Sea Lion, which is being developed by Israel’s Navitas Petroleum and Britain’s Rockhopper Exploration. According to the tribunal’s schedule, Argentina will present on the first day from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. and the United Kingdom from 3 p.m. to 6 p.m.; on the second day, Argentina will speak from 10.30 a.m. to noon and the UK will close from 5.30 p.m. to 7 p.m. Argentina’s agent is Ambassador Mario Oyarzábal. The tribunal’s 21 permanent judges include Argentina’s Frida María Armas Pfirter, its vice-president, while the United Kingdom, which has no judge of its nationality, has chosen British professor Vaughan Lowe as judge ad hoc.

Argentina is not asking the tribunal to rule on sovereignty, but on rights to maritime resources and the environmental obligations set out in the Law of the Sea Convention. Sea Lion is expected to begin development drilling in 2027 and commercial production in 2028.

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has called Argentine attempts to interfere with commercial activity in the area “unacceptable”. According to Infobae, the British government will activate legislation before the end of the year to protect Navitas and Rockhopper from possible Argentine sanctions. London maintains that it will not negotiate sovereignty unless the islanders wish it.

World.title: One dead and more than 2,000 affected by El Niño flooding in the Galápagos
World.content:
One dead and more than 2,000 affected by El Niño flooding in the Galápagos

5th Thursday, November 2026 - 07:14 UTC Full article

Authorities announced repairs to the road linking the airport with the island and the removal of debris

Heavy rains linked to the El Niño phenomenon triggered a flash flood on Santa Cruz island in Ecuador’s Galápagos archipelago overnight from Friday to Saturday, leaving one person dead and more than 2,000 affected, according to local mayor Fanny Uribe. Water reached up to three metres deep in some neighbourhoods of Puerto Ayora, the island’s main town.

After some ten hours of heavy rain in the highlands of Santa Cruz, water rushed down a ravine towards the inhabited coastal areas. “Rescues were carried out using kayaks and Zodiacs, and most people were brought to safety,” said fire chief Freddy López, who estimated the water reached three metres in the La Cascada and La Unión neighbourhoods. There were no alarms: firefighters, Red Cross volunteers and young residents went door to door to wake people, some of whom had to swim out of their homes. Most took refuge in the Puerto Ayora Coliseum. A local foundation says it has identified at least 500 more people affected who are not on the official register because they are staying with relatives.

Authorities announced repairs to the road linking the airport with the island and the removal of debris. Uribe said she was negotiating housing vouchers with the government for families who lost their homes, was preparing to distribute 1,000 food kits and that the relocation of the La Cascada neighbourhood was being studied. Residents have organised community kitchens and aid networks; a fishermen’s foundation is serving three meals a day to some 1,200 people. According to El País, President Daniel Noboa had not commented publicly on the emergency.

The Environment Ministry said no deaths of giant tortoises or wild birds have been reported as a result of the rains. Farmers in the island’s highlands, whose produce largely feeds the local population, fear for their crops.

Santa Cruz, with about 15,000 inhabitants, is the most populated island in the Galápagos, some 1,000 kilometres from the mainland. Ecuador’s National Risk Management Secretariat declared a nationwide red alert for El Niño on September 29, and its effects are expected to peak in December.

World.title: Paraguay seeks to return part of the savings frozen at Ueno Bank within 24 hours
World.content:
Paraguay seeks to return part of the savings frozen at Ueno Bank within 24 hours

5th Thursday, November 2026 - 07:08 UTC Full article

Paraguay’s Senate on Wednesday approved a reform of the deposit guarantee law that would allow customers of Ueno Bank, taken over by the Central Bank on Tuesday, to receive an advance of up to 40 minimum wages, about 121 million guaraníes, within 24 hours of the bank’s resolution. The bill now goes to the Chamber of Deputies, which was due to consider it on Thursday.

The current law set a deadline of 15 days, extendable by a further 15, for the Deposit Guarantee Fund to pay savers at a failed bank. The approved text specifies that customers with loans from the bank will have only overdue instalments deducted, not their entire debt, and that the advance is a payment on account that does not change the total coverage of up to 75 minimum wages, about 228 million guaraníes per depositor. According to the Central Bank, that limit covers 97% of customers. Above that figure, the Social Security Institute, the pension fund, will be paid before large savers. The Senate rejected a proposal to extend the guarantee to all public funds deposited in the bank.

The Central Bank’s interim president, Liana Caballero, who took over after Carlos Carvallo’s resignation, said a first payment would be up to 10 million guaraníes and that depositors would be divided into three tranches, although there are still no dates, locations or requirements. “The operational side is the problem in paying out,” she acknowledged. The Association of Banks of Paraguay backed the advance but urged caution over using the fund to return money from pension funds.

“The priority of the government of Paraguay is and will be to protect with all our strength the fruit of that effort and to provide concrete, rapid and responsible answers,” President Santiago Peña said in a televised address. Peña cancelled his attendance at the Ibero-American Summit in Madrid. The opposition has said it will push for impeachment proceedings against him and Vice President Pedro Alliana.

The Central Bank took over Ueno after its solvency ratio fell to 5.56%, against a minimum of 12%, and it detected irregular loans to companies owned by the bank’s owners, the Vázquez Group. Eight executives were detained, according to the press. The crisis also affects South American football’s governing body, Conmebol, which has US$14 million deposited in the bank, although it says payment of prize money for the Copa Libertadores and Copa Sudamericana finals is not at risk. The Vázquez Group’s media outlets closed, leaving about 300 employees without pay. Groups of savers gathered outside the Central Bank on Wednesday night to demand their deposits.

World.title: El Jalapeño: California high-speed rail project reaches -25% completion as Mexico line hits 25%
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — Construction on the 102-kilometer Querétaro-Irapuato passenger rail line reached 25% completion this week, just 12 months after breaking ground, creating a stark contrast with California’s Los Angeles-to-San Francisco high-speed rail network, which transit analysts confirmed is currently sitting at -25% complete.

According to data released by Mexico’s Agency for Trains and Integrated Public Transportation (ATTRAPI), crews in the industrial Bajío region have laid physical track, initiated 10 viaducts and begun assembly on railcars in Hidalgo. Meanwhile, across the northern border, project metrics indicate California has managed to regress 25% below its starting line after spending 16 years, US $11 billion and thousands of billable hours untangling lawsuits over land rights that no longer exist.

“When Mexican crews complete 25% of a project, it means a quarter of the actual track is ready for trains,” said Arthur Pendelton, a senior fellow at the Institute for Infrastructure Comparison in Sacramento. “When California logs -25%, it means we have spent enough time in environmental mediation to un-build the preliminary ideas we drafted during the George W. Bush administration.”

The Mexican route forms part of a federal initiative to build 2,500 kilometers of operational track by 2030. Transportation planners in Washington have struggled to interpret the data, noting that under standard U.S. transit models, laying 25% of a line in one year without first commissioning a seven-year feasibility study on environmental noise disruption violates accepted notions of government practice.

“In our system, progress is measured in metric tons of paperwork generated per mile,” Pendelton added, gesturing to a chart showing California’s progress line sloping downward into negative territory. “If you actually pour concrete and build a bridge, you lose the ability to commission a follow-up impact study on the visual aesthetics of the concrete. From a regulatory perspective, Mexico is moving backward by moving forward.”

At press time, California high-speed rail officials announced plans to spend US $2.4 billion to hire an external consulting firm to investigate how Mexico achieved positive momentum on its construction timeline.

World.title: Sheinbaum calls for INE ‘cleanup’ after corruption scandal: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🏛️ Sheinbaum says INE corruption goes beyond Guadalupe Taddei: The president asserted that corruption in the awarding of electoral materials contracts occurred “during the entire period of Lorenzo Córdova,” Taddei’s predecessor as INE president, and “probably before as well.” Taddei resigned as National Electoral Institute president last week amid allegations of corruption.

Sheinbaum recalled the “el INE no se toca” (“don’t touch the INE”) protest slogan and suggested it was used “to hang on to this whole electoral mafia” that allegedly existed before Taddei became INE president. She said the institute must guarantee clean elections, transparency and republican austerity. 🕊️ Sheinbaum condemns murder of Cuernavaca city councilman: She called the killing of Morena councilman Gabriel Rivas Ríos, an environmental activist, “sad and infuriating,” saying there was “no doubt” it was ordered and carried out specifically against him. Rivas had criticized the Alto Verde residential project proposed for Cuernavaca, and Sheinbaum said she asked the Security Cabinet to support the Morelos Attorney General’s Office’s murder investigation. She said Rivas hadn’t requested federal protection.

She called the killing of Morena councilman Gabriel Rivas Ríos, an environmental activist, “sad and infuriating,” saying there was “no doubt” it was ordered and carried out specifically against him. Rivas had criticized the Alto Verde residential project proposed for Cuernavaca, and Sheinbaum said she asked the Security Cabinet to support the Morelos Attorney General’s Office’s murder investigation. She said Rivas hadn’t requested federal protection. 🇪🇸 Sheinbaum explains absence from Ibero-American Summit: She said she skipped the Madrid gathering because she will travel to China for the APEC leaders’ summit later this month. Sheinbaum noted that Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco represented her in the Spanish capital. She will seek a call with Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to discuss the summit’s outcomes.

Why today’s mañanera matters

Alleged corruption in the awarding of National Electoral Institute (INE) contracts to a small group of electoral materials suppliers was a central focus of President Sheinbaum’s Friday morning press conference.

Guadalupe Taddei resigned as president of the INE last week after it came to light that lucrative contracts were awarded to electoral materials companies linked to a businessman with whom she had a close personal relationship. Taddei and that businessman, José Alfredo Hernández Casillas, are reportedly among 25 people who have been added to the Finance Ministry’s Blocked Persons List and who will be investigated by the Federal Attorney General’s Office.

On Friday morning, Sheinbaum asserted that corruption in the INE also occurred when Lorenzo Córdova was president of the institute between 2014 and 2023.

Also of note at today’s mañanera were the president’s remarks about the murder of a Cuernavaca city councilman. Gabriel Rivas Ríos, a Morena party member, was killed on Wednesday in Cuernavaca, capital of the state of Morelos.

Sheinbaum: ‘The INE needs to be cleaned up’

Sheinbaum asserted that corruption in INE’s rewarding of electoral materials contracts predates the 2023-2026 tenure of Taddei as the institute’s president.

Corruption occurred “during the entire period of Lorenzo Córdova,” she said.

“And probably before as well,” Sheinbaum added. “The audit will have to determine that.”

Sheinbaum noted that Córdova and other INE officials participated in various protests against an electoral reform proposal during the presidency of Andrés Manuel López Obrador. She recalled that the slogan of the protests was “El INE no se toca,’ or “Don’t touch the INE.”

“The INE has to be cleaned up. Maybe they said ‘don’t touch the INE’ in order to hang on to this whole electoral mafia that was built with them,” she said.

“The National Electoral Institute is an institute that must guarantee the will of the people, that must guarantee clean elections,” Sheinbaum added.

“In its operation, it must guarantee … transparency and republican austerity,” she said.

Sheinbaum laments murder of Cuernavaca councilman

Asked about the murder of Rivas, Sheinbaum said she knew him and described him as an environmental activist.

She described his murder as “sad and infuriating” and conveyed her condolences to his family and colleagues.

Sheinbaum said that when she heard about the homicide, she requested that the federal Security Cabinet “dedicate time and effort” to supporting the Morelos Attorney General’s Office in its investigation into the crime.

“It was a direct homicide. Some people on a motorbike shot him directly,” she said.

“There is no doubt it was a homicide that was ordered and carried out specifically against him,” Sheinbaum said.

She noted that Rivas had recently been critical of a real estate development in Cuernavaca that could cause “environmental problems.” She was referring to the Alto Verde residential project, whose construction was proposed on a site called La Cazahuatera.

The land where La Cazahuatera is located is “considered one of the last remnants of lowland deciduous forest within the urban area” of Cuernavaca, the news outlet Infobae reported.

In addition to contributing to efforts to solve Rivas’ murder, Sheinbaum said her administration would also work with Morelos Governor Margarita González Saravia “to see what can be done with this [real estate] development that he was fighting against.”

After a reporter noted that many environmental activists have been murdered or attacked in Mexico, Sheinbaum said that a lot of them now have government protection.

“They’ve approached us [to ask for protection],” she said, adding that government protection helps to “avoid” attacks on activists.

Sheinbaum said that Rivas hadn’t requested protection from the federal government.

“That doesn’t mean that we don’t condemn the homicide,” she added.

Sheinbaum explains her absence at Ibero-American Summit in Spain

Sheinbaum told reporters that she decided not to go to this week’s Ibero-American Summit in Madrid as she will travel to China for the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ summit later this month. She said visiting Spain as well as China would mean spending more time outside Mexico than she would like.

Sheinbaum said she advised Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and King Felipe VI of her decision not to travel to Madrid.

“I wrote a letter to them … because they were the ones that invited me,” she said.

Sheinbaum noted that Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco represented her at the Ibero-American Summit, a gathering of leaders and officials from Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking countries.

She said she would seek a call with Sánchez to discuss the outcomes of the summit.

Mexico’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement that “the summit’s four agreements match Mexico’s priorities: care systems, academic mobility, disaster protection, and artificial intelligence that serves people.”

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Bucking expectations, Banxico lowers the interest rate, despite some inflation concerns
World.content:
Mexico’s central bank (Banxico) lowered its benchmark interest rate 25 basis points to 6.25%, surprising analysts, who as recently as this week expected the rate to remain unchanged.

In a split vote, the three bank governors supporting the reduction argued that there are no perceived demand pressures in the economy and that the degree of monetary restriction implemented is still in effect.

In a statement, Banxico adjudged that the disinflationary process has continued, indicating that, “given the prevailing slack conditions, the pass-through of exchange rate movements to prices would be limited.”

In what is viewed as guidance for future actions, the statement added that “going forward, the Governing Board believes that maintaining the rate for an extended period at the level achieved will support the convergence of inflation to its target and will be appropriate to meet external macroeconomic challenges.”

At the same time that Banxico reduced the interest rate, it raised its headline inflation forecast for the fourth quarter from 3.5% to 3.7%, acknowledging that risks remain tilted to the upside.

“This is mainly due to higher-than-anticipated levels for non-core inflation,” the statement said.

The bank also incorporated an upward adjustment to its estimate of core inflation for the last quarter, from 3.6% predicted in September to the 3.7% they now anticipate.

Although the economy continued to expand in the third-quarter, Banxico believes that “slack conditions are still expected throughout the forecast horizon, and downside risks to economic activity persist.”

Still, Banxico believes that its estimate that inflation will reach its target — 3% with a tolerance range of plus or minus 1 percentage point (2% to 4%) — by the fourth quarter of next year.

Banxico’s economic research identified four upside risks to its inflation forecasts: the persistence of core inflation; further depreciation of the peso; disruptions from trade policies or an inflationary impact from geopolitical conflicts; and, climate-related effects and unspecified cost pressures.

Looking ahead, the Governing Board said that maintaining the rate at its current level for an extended period “will support the convergence of inflation to its target and will be appropriate to address external macroeconomic challenges.”

Thursday’s surprise decision — 30 of the 36 institutions consulted by Citi expected the rate to remain unchanged — impacted the currency exchange market immediately.

The reduction pushed the dollar as high as 18.96 pesos during the day, although it later moderated its advance and closed at 18.7499. The peso lost 18.3 centavos, or 0.99%, compared to Wednesday’s close.

With reports from El Economista and El Financiero

World.title: My grandmother spent her life caring for others. Finding care for her changed my direction
World.content:
My grandmother Ene spent decades working as a hospital nurse. She cared for thousands of people she had never met before, then came home and looked after her own family. When my grandfather was struggling with Parkinson’s disease, she nursed him too.

To me, she was simply the best grandmother imaginable. Caring for people was part of her working life, but it was also how I knew her as a wife, mother and grandmother.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by RetireMexico.com (@retiremexico.official)

When she needed care for herself in her final years, I wanted to find somewhere that reflected that. Somewhere she would receive personal attention and feel comfortable living.

The options fell short. The places available felt like hospitals, lacked the personal care I had hoped for and were very expensive. I kept wishing there was somewhere better for her. She had given so much, and I struggled with how little of that seemed to be reflected in the choices available to her.

Ene died in the winter of 2025. Her experience stayed with me and eventually became part of the reason I started RetireMexico.

Making a home in Puerto Vallarta

Before settling in Mexico, I had spent years traveling. Home often depended on where the next flight took me. In 2021, I settled in Puerto Vallarta.

I have worked in marketing and sales since 2013. Along the way, I founded Spring Hub, a coworking space in Tallinn, Estonia, and Vivian Agency, the marketing agency I still run.

Those projects gave me experience building businesses. My grandmother’s final years brought me to a subject I understood much more personally. I had been a family member trying to find care for someone I loved, struggling to find an option that felt right.

When aging loved ones refuse help

Alejandra Arenas, who now co-leads RetireMexico with me, came to this work through experiences of her own.

Alejandra was born and raised in Puerto Vallarta. As a child, she watched her great-aunt live with dementia over six years of summer visits. Her great-aunt had been a pianist. Eventually, as Alejandra described it, she was “just pressing keys.”

Her great-uncle Armando cared for his wife around the clock without outside help.

Later, while in high school, Alejandra volunteered at a senior home on the outskirts of Puerto Vallarta. She helped organize movie nights and art activities. The residents received physical care, but some felt their families had set them aside.

“A home can meet every physical need and still fail the person living in it,” she told me.

Then there was Jim, her mother’s closest friend in Puerto Vallarta. An American who had lived there for more than 25 years, he developed cancer and later dementia. By then, he had no family or old friends left, only his cat.

Jim refused nearly all help, even as strangers began taking advantage of him. Alejandra and her mother became his caregivers, learning as they went how to protect him and manage the responsibilities that came with his declining health. They cared for him until he died in 2019.

For Alejandra, that experience raised a question that sits at the heart of our work. How do you help someone accept support while respecting the independence they still have?

“Finding the right care is only half of it,” she said. “The other half is finding the right moment, and helping someone still largely independent make that move without feeling erased.”

Finding a path forward

My grandmother’s experience and Alejandra’s years of caregiving were different, but they gave us plenty to talk about. We both knew how difficult these decisions could become when someone you loved needed help.

We began building RetireMexico as a free directory of senior living communities in Mexico, gathering information and checking the details with the homes themselves.

The work involves practical questions about staffing, rooms, costs and the care a residence can provide. Our own experiences also keep us asking about daily life. Who notices when a resident is withdrawn? What happens when someone refuses help? Will the person moving in have a say in how they live?

I still wish I could have found a better place for Ene. I cannot change the choices available to her then. But her experience continues to shape the questions I ask on behalf of other families.

Enelin Toneva is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: Beyond its luxury resorts, Riviera Nayarit is facing an education crisis
World.content:
Mexico’s Riviera Nayarit was not always a thriving vacation destination. However, over the past couple of years, ultra-luxury real estate developers have been building multimillion-dollar homes and resorts across the region.

That much is true for Punta de Mita — a jewel of the Riviera Nayarit on Mexico’s Pacific coast — where a strong tourism industry has prompted people with significant purchasing power to settle there. In the second quarter of 2026 alone, Nayarit recorded US $9.28 million in new investment, notching the area the #1 spot for tourism investment in all of Mexico with roughly 20% of the share.

However, that influx of capital does not necessarily translate into equitable living conditions for the local population, says José Antonio Salgado, executive director of the education advocacy organization Peace Punta de Mita

For instance, despite the surge in high-end developments, combined dropout rates among Nayarit students in secondary and upper-secondary education sit at roughly 15%, according to Mexico’s Education Ministry.

While the private sector has made efforts to build decent housing, Salgado believes that’s only half the battle. Proper education for children, he argues, should come first.

According to Salgado, Mexico must address the high dropout rate by examining the root causes preventing students from completing their education, including “economic factors” and a “lack of infrastructure.”

Navigating a deficient education system

To truly effect change in local communities, Salgado embarked on a challenging endeavor: ensuring quality education for children in the Nayarit Riviera.

He spent 26 years in the local education sector and says that “the greatest challenge for the Mexican educational system is to break the vicious cycle of structural inequality and the lack of comprehensive support” from the state.

Today, many of the secondary schools in the area operate under the telesecundaria model, a televised education system for rural communities that the Mexican government first introduced in the 1960s.

Thousands of schools nationwide use the model, reaching roughly 1.3 million students. However, on the whole, it has proven deficient.

“The telesecundaria model serves nearly 20% of the national secondary school enrollment,” Salgado explains. “Despite its vast reach, it frequently operates with a lack of connectivity, outdated materials and absenteeism.”

While the model can be up to 50% cheaper than, for example, a technical secondary school — in terms of both initial investment and operating costs per student — academic achievement remains far below expectations.

What’s more, a single teacher is responsible for instructing all subjects, ranging from mathematics and chemistry to history and English.

To help solve these issues, Salgado began working with PrepaNet, a joint project between Tec de Monterrey (Tec) and Mexico’s Public Education Ministry (SEP). To date, he said, PrepaNet has an internal completion rate of 86.3%.

“This figure is exceptionally high for a virtual model,” Salgado says. “Especially considering that the average completion rate for general upper secondary education in Mexico drops significantly, to 76.3%.”

A new horizon

PrepaNet is part of Peace Punta de Mita, a nongovernmental organization that has expanded its network, providing quality education to local children beyond the telesecundaria model.

Without a comprehensive plan from the SEP to standardize rural and low-income education, PrepaNet is a valuable alternative. Especially, Salgado says, given that “technological or online high school programs often see dropout rates exceeding 50%.”

Enrollment is contingent upon an entrance exam. If accepted, however, students attend the program on a full-ride scholarship.

Over the next two years, they receive training from Tec de Monterrey professors via distance learning, with the support of local faculty members who provide in-person guidance. At the end, students graduate with a dual certificate — jointly endorsed by the Tec and the SEP — which qualifies them for admission to university-level education.

“PrepaNet highlights what is missing from public basic education,” Salgado says. “Technology alone does not educate; it requires the active guidance of a teacher, as well as the involvement of parents who, often due to exhausting work schedules, are unable to provide follow-up support at home.”

To help close that resource gap, the program also offers students free meals, as well as afternoon courses in computer skills, the arts and English.

In a short time, Salgado and his team managed to enroll 23 students, 19 of whom graduated, and 11 of whom have already entered university. Due to the program’s success, it will expand to a three-year high school curriculum starting in 2027.

With more robust in-person care, the program is also working to accommodate children who are neurodivergent.

“It is urgent to design ‘personalized learning pathways’ that leverage intelligent, adaptive diagnostic platforms,” Salgado says.

Education in Mexico by the numbers

An encouraging report from INEGI, Mexico’s national statistics agency, suggests that the country’s educational landscape improved between 2020 and 2025. Despite disruptions brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic, school attendance increased across all measured age groups.

Particularly within the 6-to-14 age group — as children enter primary or secondary school — there was an increase from 92.7% to 96%.

Similarly, the adult illiteracy rate fell from 4.8% to 3.7%. The work of Peace Punta de Mita has certainly played a role in this by providing training in English and computer skills for adults, which in turn broadens their employment opportunities.

Essential tools for better opportunities

PrepaNet considers it vital for local children and adults to acquire tools that will be useful when looking for a job — especially in the Punta de Mita region, as its international tourism profile continues to grow.

For this reason, Mercedes Rubio, coordinator of the program’s English department, says that PrepaNet offers certifications for both children and adults, beginning from the basic A1 level all the way through C2, comparable to a native speaker.

Incidentally, foreign language instruction presents a significant challenge, as students often “have gaps in their native language,” Rubio says, adding “we must adapt to their specific needs.”

Nevertheless, Rubio believes that “speaking English is essential” for getting better job opportunities.

Fostering a safe space for learning

According to Rubio, every school year, PrepaNet’s numbers are getting better and better. Likewise, the students are responding to programs such as “Campeones Jr.” or “Junior Champions,” which she says is “really resonating across the Bay.”

Word is spreading. And so too is the initiative’s impact.

Nowadays, students are arriving from more remote communities, such as Cruz de Huanacaxtle, Sayulita, Bucerías and Mezcales. According to Salgado, even students from nearby telesecundaria schools go to the PrepaNet facilities to improve their reading comprehension and math skills.

“When you ask the little ones what they think of Peace,” Rubio says with pride, “they say it’s their safe place.”

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: Mexican singer-songwriter Silvana Estrada tapped as LA Philharmonic’s first Latin music chair
World.content:
Mexican singer-songwriter Silvana Estrada will help shape the sound of the Los Angeles Philharmonic as its first creative chair for Latin music, expanding her relationship with the orchestra into a role championing Latin American artists and traditions.

The appointment, announced Wednesday, puts the 29-year-old Latin Grammy winner on an artistic leadership team preparing for music director Daniel Harding’s arrival in the 2027-28 season.

Described in 2024 as “the next Mexican global music star” by Mexico News Daily, Estrada will develop programming across Walt Disney Concert Hall, the Hollywood Bowl and The Ford, an intimate amphitheater in the Hollywood Hills.

Her appointment builds on three years of collaborations with the 107-year-old orchestra. She will also collaborate with guest artists and continue working with Youth Orchestra Los Angeles, the organization’s music education program.

“Latin music is not a single sound,” Estrada said in the Philharmonic’s announcement. “To me, it is the soul of an entire continent, an immense and profound richness woven together across generations, with the power to transcend any border.”

Estrada’s piercing lyricism and deeply soulful storytelling come through in her NPR Tiny Desk concerts in 2021 and 2025. Both performances offer English subtitles, allowing viewers who do not speak Spanish to follow her lyrics.

The first was taped at her family’s instrument workshop in Coatepec, Veracruz, during the COVID-19 pandemic and highlighted in the Mexico News Daily article “Regional Mexican music takes over NPR’s Tiny Desk.”

Estrada grew up in the coffee town of Coatepec surrounded by instruments and musicians in her parents’ workshop.

The second was a deeply affecting four-song set in the famously cramped NPR office space, encompassing heartbreak and a defiant message of hope for women facing violence in Mexico.

NPR’s Anamaria Sayre wrote that Estrada brings audiences to tears without extinguishing hope, adding that “her voice finds a way to bend wounds to her will and become whole.”

Her 2022 album, “Marchita,” helped establish her blend of indie folk, jazz and traditional Mexican influences. She won that year’s Latin Grammy for best new artist and received a Grammy nomination for best global music performance in 2024.

Her self-produced 2025 follow-up, “Vendrán Suaves Lluvias,” brought her six 2026 Latin Grammy nominations, including album of the year. The song “Dime” — described by KUTX in Austin, Texas, as “a deceptively lovely song about post-breakup wild rage” — is up for record and song of the year.

The 27th Latin Grammys will be held Nov. 12 at the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas, with Estrada scheduled to perform and Puerto Rican actress Roselyn Sánchez hosting for the 10th time.

“Vendrán Suaves Lluvias” emerged from profound loss. Estrada told NPR that her best friend and his younger brother were murdered in Mexico City in 2022, leaving her to navigate grief while touring internationally.

The Philharmonic also named British composer and conductor Thomas Adès its creative chair for new music, succeeding John Adams, and Bronx-born jazz vocalist Samara Joy its creative chair for jazz, succeeding Herbie Hancock.

With reports from EFE and NPR

World.title: Mexico’s 2026 growth outlook improves in Banxico and Citi surveys
World.content:
Economic growth in Mexico in 2026 is expected to be higher than previously predicted, according to the median forecasts of economists and analysts surveyed by the Bank of Mexico (Banxico) and Citi.

Conducted in late October, Banxico’s most recent expectations survey yielded a median economic growth forecast of 1.5% in 2026, up from a prediction of 1.4% in September. Economists and analysts from 40 Mexican and foreign private sector economic research and consulting groups responded to the survey.

Economists consulted by Citi for its latest expectations survey are more optimistic about Mexico’s 2026 growth prospects. Their median forecast is 1.8% growth this year, up from 1.4% in the previous survey. Economists from 36 banks, brokerages and research organizations responded to Citi’s survey, whose results were published on Wednesday.

The range of 2026 growth estimates among the economists surveyed by Citi went from 0.9% to 2.1%.

According to preliminary data published by the national statistics agency INEGI last week, Mexico’s economy grew 1.9% in the first nine months of 2026 compared to the same period of 2025.

The economy contracted in sequential terms in the first quarter of the year, but expanded in both Q2 (+1.4% compared to Q1) and Q3 (+0.9% compared to Q2, per preliminary data).

President Claudia Sheinbaum said last week that construction, including housing and public infrastructure projects, was helping to drive growth. Sheinbaum also noted that the production of electronic products in Mexico — many of which are exported to the United States — was providing momentum to the economy.

Growth outlooks for 2027

The median forecast of economists surveyed by Banxico is that Mexico’s economy will grow 1.83% in 2027. The prediction is up slightly from 1.80% in the central bank’s previous survey.

The median forecast of economists surveyed by Citi is that Mexico’s GDP will increase 1.9% next year, up from a 1.8% prediction in the bank’s previous survey.

Inflation predicted to approach 4% by end of year

The median forecasts for Mexico’s annual headline inflation rate at the end of 2026 were 3.88%, according to the Banxico survey, and 3.90%, per the Citi survey. The Banxico forecast rose by 0.01 percentage points while the Citi forecast was unchanged compared to the bank’s previous survey.

Inflation increased in September for a second consecutive month, reaching an annual headline rate of 3.45%. The headline rate spiked to 3.62% in the first half of October, according to INEGI’s most recent inflation data.

Despite the recent increase in inflation, the Banxico board decided on Thursday to lower the central bank’s benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 6.25%. Just six of the 36 respondents to Citi’s survey predicted that the bank would cut its key rate after its November monetary policy meeting.

What will the USD:MXN rate be at the end of 2026?

The median forecasts for the USD:MXN exchange rate at the end of 2026 were 18.39, according to the Banxico survey, and 18.50, per the Citi survey. The Banxico forecast increased from 17.50 in the previous survey, while the Citi prediction rose from 18.20.

The Bank of Mexico’s closing USD:MXN rate on Thursday was 18.75. That rate represents a depreciation of 9.9% for the peso since Sept. 4, when it closed at 16.89 to the dollar — its strongest level in over two years.

The MND Peso Index™ determined that the peso was undervalued by 0.7% in early October when it was trading at just below 18 to the US dollar.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: United Airlines cancels all its remaining flights to Tulum starting in January
World.content:
United Airlines has announced it will cease operations at Felipe Carrillo Puerto International Airport in Tulum starting early next year, citing market conditions as the cause.

The announcement comes just two weeks after American Airlines revealed plans to halt its Miami-Tulum route, following similar moves by other domestic and international carriers including Aeroméxico, Volaris, Copa and Avianca.

The final flight for the connection from Newark is scheduled for Jan. 2, while service from Houston will conclude on Jan. 4. The withdrawal will not be immediate; rather, it will take effect after the year-end holiday period, in accordance with the published schedule.

According to United, affected passengers will be able to modify their bookings.

“Customers will have the option to change their booking to flights arriving at nearby airports, such as Cancún (CUN)—which is a 1.5 to 2-hour drive away and serves many of the same tourist areas as TQO—or, alternatively, they may request a refund,” United said in a statement sent to the newspaper El Financiero.

United’s departure marks the culmination of a gradual reduction in its operations in Tulum. Prior to announcing the cancellation of its connections from Newark and Houston, the airline had already withdrawn its services from Chicago and Los Angeles, thereby diminishing its presence at the Quintana Roo terminal.

Industry reports interpret the company’s “market conditions” rationale for eliminating the flights as Tulum’s lower-than-expected vacation demand.

Industry analysts cited by Aviación News blame the tourism decline on high hotel prices in the area and weaker-than-expected demand for leisure travel. Other contributing factors include the massive influx of sargassum and increased fees and other charges on foreign tourists.

The combination of factors has reportedly led airlines to reassess the profitability of their operations and shift capacity to other destinations with higher passenger volumes.

In this context, Cancún International Airport – located 130 kilometers north of Tulum – emerges as the primary beneficiary of the reorientation of supply.

In the meantime, Air Canada, WestJet, and Air Transat have announced that they will resume flights for the winter season. Viva Aerobus continues its operations at the terminal with no announced changes, and state-owned Mexicana de Aviación remains the only carrier offering an increased number of flights.

With reports from Reportur

World.title: France Bans Protests in Two Brittany Cities
World.content:
Saint-Corentin Cathedral, a landmark of Quimper. File photo: WanderingTrad, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

France in Turmoil

Published Friday, 6 November, 2:55 p.m. ET (8:55 p.m. Paris) · Source: Préfecture du Finistère

A French prefect has told protesters to stay out of two Breton city centres on Saturday. Nobody has registered a march.

France’s Finistère prefecture has banned all protests in parts of central Quimper and Brest from Saturday, 7 November, after several calls to demonstrate that no one registered. It is the latest turn in our France protests coverage, and why is France protesting explains the anger over prices behind it.

The prefect, Louis Le Franc, says organisers filed no declaration and made no contact, so police cannot plan routes or safety. Quimper, a city in western Brittany, and Brest, its big naval port, both held large marches on Thursday.

Key Facts What happened. The prefect of Finistère, a western French department, banned protests in central Quimper and Brest for Saturday, 7 November.

When. Quimper from 12:00 a.m. ET Saturday (6:00 a.m. Paris); Brest from 2:00 a.m. ET (8:00 a.m. Paris).

Why. The prefecture says no protest was declared and organisers made no contact with it.

What next. Both bans end at 12:00 a.m. ET Sunday, 8 November (6:00 a.m. Paris).

Prediction markets. Polymarket, a prediction market, puts a French state of emergency by 31 December at about 3% (2:43 p.m. ET, 6 Nov).

This story is part of our coverage of the why France is in crisis. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: Paris Bans Yellow Vest Rally at Concorde
