Hackers also targeted supermarket refrigeration systems in at least seven European countries.

“It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralized or coordinated effort,” the Irish government said in a statement. “However, these threats come on the heels of the ongoing disruption to aviation around Europe caused by similar threats, and it seems likely that this is a coordinated campaign of disruption.”

Bomb threats also targeted at least 18 European flights Friday, after at least 22 the day before, raising concerns that the hoaxes may be part of a coordinated campaign to disrupt air traffic.

Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares told Spanish public broadcaster TVE on Friday that the bomb threats affecting flights could be “an attempt at hybrid aggression and war in some psychological way.” He added that “it cannot be a coincidence that so many identical events occur with the same modus operandi throughout Europe.”

Luis Gallego, CEO of airline group IAG, said: “It is clear that what they [the perpetrators] are looking for is to create chaos and disruption in the different airports.”

World.title: Spain and the Netherlands battle over ECB presidency
World.content:
Exiting European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde gives a press conference in Frankfurt am Main, Germany, on Oct. 29, 2026. | Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP via Getty Images

Pablo Hernández de Cos and Klaas Knot are in the hunt for the top job after Christine Lagarde’s exit.

BRUSSELS — The Netherlands and Spain on Friday submitted candidates to succeed Christine Lagarde, who steps down as president of the European Central Bank on Feb. 7.

Pablo Hernández de Cos, a former governor of Spain's central bank, and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot, a former president of the Dutch central bank, were the only candidates to emerge after the 5 p.m. deadline, as expected.

Their candidacies are part of a larger game of musical chairs that includes France and Germany, as Europe’s four economic powerhouses negotiate how to secure their seats on the ECB’s executive board.

World.title: ‘I don’t know if it reassured or worried them’: European envoys quiz Le Pen over lunch
World.content:
The group of ambassadors from the eight countries that share a border with metropolitan France — Germany, Spain, Belgium, Italy, Luxembourg, Switzerland, Monaco and Andorra — already met with conservative presidential candidate Bruno Retailleau in September. They are planning to host meetings with the other presidential hopefuls, including far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, at their respective embassies in the coming months.

“I don’t know if it reassured or worried them,” said an adviser to Marine Le Pen who accompanied her to the lunch. “What is sure is that they can now report back to their capitals what the National Rally wants to do,” the adviser added.

Le Pen was mainly questioned about her plans to downsize the EU and on bilateral issues, as well as U.S. President Donald Trump after his seismic defeat in the midterm elections.

While in the past, the National Rally has been supportive of Trump, the party has progressively distanced itself from the U.S. president. The National Rally’s Jordan Bardella on Wednesday said his party was not affected by the result and suggested that Trump’s popularity was undermined by the war in the Middle East and its economic consequences.



Le Pen has also been campaigning for a harsher approach on migration, which would involve stricter checks at the borders, potentially impacting countries whose envoys she met on Wednesday. All of them, apart from Andorra and Monaco, are part of the Schengen free-movement area.

“There is a general interest on what would her stance be on the key issues of mutual interest and cooperation on which we are working with France,” said one diplomat from a participating country.

“It was a very frank exchange. She told them what she says everywhere and she was able to elaborate on a number of topics a little more at length than she would do on TV,” the same adviser said, adding that Le Pen regularly meets ambassadors.

Back in December, Le Pen and her No. 2 Jordan Bardella also met with U.S. ambassador Charles Kushner. The far-right leaders are also preparing the ground for a possible election win by meeting top French business executives.

Marcelo Wesfreid and Nicolas Camut contributed to this report.

World.title: Election favorite says Spain should quit as World Cup co-host if Morocco stages the final
World.content:
Feijóo noted that the 2030 World Cup was originally a Spanish-Portuguese bid, until Morocco was invited at a later stage. Despite that chronology, Moroccan officials have been pushing vigorously to stage the final, which is the world’s most prestigious sports event.

Rafael Louzán, Spain’s football chief, told POLITICO in June that he was confident either Madrid or Barcelona would host the final, despite Morocco pouring vast amounts of cash into football infrastructure.

Tensions have flared between the two countries in recent months. Spanish political parties this summer accused Morocco of stoking a migrant crisis in Spain’s North African territory of Ceuta, after 80,000 people surged into the city in late July.

A Sigma Dos poll for El Mundo following the Ceuta crisis found that 84.4% of Spaniards opposed Spain continuing to co-host the World Cup with Morocco.

Leftist party Sumar, the Socialists’ junior coalition partner, said this summer that the World Cup “cannot be shared with a country that uses desperate people for its own geostrategic interests.”

The left-wing party tabled a resolution in parliament that far-right Vox backed in an unusual convergence. The text never made it to a vote because parliament was dissolved ahead of the snap election.

World.title: EU prosecutors open second fraud probe into Spanish high-speed rail
World.content:
The EPPO did not clarify what investigators are looking for or whether any money was misspent, and no findings have been made public. It added that no further details would be released at this stage.

A first probe, opened in March after the Adamuz crash that killed 46 people, covered EU funds for track maintenance on the same line. There has been no public update on its progress.

The EU’s Transport Commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas expressed deep concern at a press briefing on Wednesday over two serious accidents in Spain within a year, calling them “very worrying” and “definitely not something we want to see.” He noted that Spain had reached out to the EU’s railway agency, ERA, to assist with the ongoing national investigation.

Two senior Spanish officials have already stepped down following the Urda crash. Puente resigned Tuesday, calling his decision “a matter of political dignity,” while Adif President Luis Pedro Marco de la Peña quit Wednesday, less than 24 hours later.

Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo is running the Transport Ministry until the Nov. 29 election. The crash took place just weeks before the vote, with Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s Socialists already trailing in the polls and facing further political fallout over the tragedy.

World.title: Mélenchon squares up to Brussels in election manifesto
World.content:
"We will immediately implement our program at the national level. This will therefore require a confrontation with European institutions," according to the manifesto from Mélenchon's France Unbowed. "This also means disobeying rules blocking [us] whenever necessary."

"Our logic is simple. As long as a deal on changing the treaties is not done, we negotiate with our partners and disobey [...] blocking rules in parallel. If we get to an agreement, it will be put to a referendum," the manifesto added.

The proposals, which echo Mélenchon's earlier statements, would likely face tough opposition from France's partners in the European Council, which is currently dominated by more conservative leaders.

The manifesto also said the European Central Bank should be "placed under democratic control and mobilized to fund the ecological and social transition." Mélenchon triggered a flurry of criticism earlier this year when he said he would “set fire” to a large chunk of France's public debt held by the ECB, setting off a nationwide debate on the subject.

France is among the countries hardest hit by a global surge in borrowing costs, with its fiscal situation also limiting the government's ability to soften the impact of higher fuel and food prices, part of a larger cost-of-living crisis on the continent.

With public debt amounting to 117.5% of GDP and a public deficit above 5%, fiscal issues have become a central concern for voters. Presidential candidates are pitching radically different solutions to the problem.

Le Pen has tried to rebrand herself as a responsible steward of the economy unafraid of cuts — despite critics saying her plan is "overly optimistic" and her flagship promises are yet to be funded. Centrist candidates, such as former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe, are pitching themselves as the voice of reason on economic and fiscal issues but are struggling to gain traction.

World.title: Trump appoints immigration hardliner Stephen Miller as new chief of staff
World.content:
US President Donald Trump on Friday appointed Stephen Miller, one of the most influential architects of his hardline immigration policy, as his new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles just days after the Republican Party suffered a major defeat in the midterm elections.

 

Miller, 41, currently deputy chief of staff and homeland security adviser, will assume the position on Monday, November 9, Trump announced on his Truth Social platform.

“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff,” Trump wrote.

Wiles, 69, the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff, will move to Trump's political operation. The president praised her performance, describing her tenure as outstanding.

Wiles confirmed her departure in a statement on X, saying that serving Trump in the White House had been “the honor of a lifetime”. She highlighted the administration's record on border security, tax cuts and its economic policies.

Miller has been one of Trump's closest advisers for more than a decade, dating back to his first presidential campaign in 2016. He has played a central role in shaping the administration's restrictive immigration policies, including its drive to carry out mass deportations during Trump's second term.

His promotion places one of the administration's most outspoken advocates of tougher immigration enforcement at the centre of White House decision-making.

The appointment also comes amid growing scrutiny of the administration's immigration operations, particularly following the fatal shootings of two protesters by immigration agents in Minneapolis in January, which triggered widespread demonstrations and criticism of federal enforcement tactics.

The personnel change follows a bruising midterm election for Republicans, with Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress. The result represents a significant political setback for Trump and is likely to intensify scrutiny of his administration's domestic agenda.

Wiles had been widely regarded as an important organisational force within Trump's inner circle, helping manage competing interests and maintain discipline in the White House. Her departure also follows weeks of speculation about possible personnel changes, although the administration had previously rejected reports that she was about to be replaced.

By moving Wiles to his political operation and promoting Miller, Trump is reshaping his closest circle of advisers at a politically sensitive moment.

World.title: EU rejects Trump’s 'big beautiful' security deal with Russia and 'all of Europe'
World.content:
European leaders have firmly rejected any attempt by the United States and Russia to reshape the continent’s security architecture without their involvement, following President Donald Trump’s suggestion that Washington could be nearing a sweeping agreement with Moscow extending beyond Ukraine to encompass all of Europe.

 

The remarks, made by Trump on Thursday, have raised fresh concerns among Washington’s European allies that the US administration could be moving towards a security arrangement that accommodates Russian President Vladimir Putin’s long-standing demands at the expense of European interests.

Trump described the potential agreement as a “very big” deal involving not only Ukraine but “all of Europe”:

“It’s going to be very big. It’s going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It’s going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone’s going to be thrilled,” Trump said, without going into any details.

His comments came as his special envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, announced that Washington was working on a broader European security architecture intended to create the conditions for lasting peace.

The initiative has immediately drawn objections from European officials, who insist that the continent’s security arrangements are already established and cannot be renegotiated over their heads.

We already have a European security architecture in place Kaja Kallas European Union foreign policy chief

“We already have a European security architecture in place,” European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told journalists in Warsaw on Friday.

“The problem remains that Russia keeps breaking the treaties that underpin it. NATO posed no threat to Russia in 2021, and it poses no threat to Russia at the moment. Putin does not have a veto over European security.”

Kallas also stressed that the European Union would have to be involved in any agreement if it was to be implemented.

Her position was echoed by Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, who warned that any agreement concerning Ukraine and Europe's future reached without European participation would be both politically unacceptable and practically impossible.

“An arrangement about the future of Ukraine and of Europe above our heads would not just be unwise. It is actually impossible,” Sikorski said.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said Moscow could not be regarded as a guarantor of European security, arguing that the priority should be protecting Europe against Russian aggression rather than negotiating spheres of influence with the Kremlin.

“We have to talk about protecting ourselves against Russia, not talking with Russians about spheres of influence in Europe,” Sybiha said.

Sybiha reinforced Kyiv's position following a meeting with EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas in Warsaw, stressing that neither Ukraine's future nor Europe's security could be decided without the direct involvement of both.

Washington pushes for a broader security framework

The diplomatic disagreement comes as the Trump administration intensifies efforts to bring an end to the war in Ukraine, with US representatives preparing for renewed negotiations between Kyiv and Moscow in Abu Dhabi next week.

After months of largely stalled diplomatic efforts, Washington has stepped up its engagement with both sides, seeking a framework that could deliver a lasting settlement.

Earlier this week, American representatives held two days of discussions in Brussels with officials from NATO, the European Union and major European powers. The meetings focused on security guarantees for Ukraine and the future of Europe's wider security arrangements.

Kushner, who participated in the discussions via video link, subsequently outlined Washington's ambition to develop a broader framework.

In a statement posted on the social media platform X, he said the United States was working towards practical arrangements to address the security concerns of all parties and establish the foundations for lasting peace.

The American proposal reflects an attempt to connect the question of Ukraine's postwar security with the wider relationship between Russia and the West.

However, the language has revived longstanding European concerns about Moscow's ambitions to revise the security order established after the end of the Cold War.

Before launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Russia issued an ultimatum to NATO demanding fundamental changes to Europe's security arrangements. Among Moscow's demands was the withdrawal of NATO forces from countries that joined the alliance after 1997.

The Western military alliance rejected those demands, maintaining that sovereign countries have the right to determine their own security arrangements.

Europe demands a seat at the negotiating table

For European capitals, the central issue is not simply whether Washington can negotiate an end to the war, but whether decisions affecting the security of the entire continent can be made without the direct participation of those countries most affected.

Europe has repeatedly called for a greater role in the US-led diplomatic initiative, particularly as discussions increasingly extend beyond the immediate battlefield in Ukraine.

European Commission Chief Spokesperson Paula Pinho said on Friday that considerable work remained before a peace agreement could be reached, stressing that the European Union would determine its own security matters.

NATO, meanwhile, reiterated that Ukraine's allies were working towards a “just and sustainable” end to the conflict.

Kushner sought to reassure European partners that they would not be excluded from the wider process. He said Washington intended to consult closely with them on the sidelines of the Abu Dhabi negotiations and, if progress was achieved, move towards a broader multilateral format involving their direct participation.

Abu Dhabi talks could prove a crucial test

The planned discussions in Abu Dhabi will provide an important test of Washington's ability to reconcile the competing demands of Ukraine, Russia and its European allies.

The United States is seeking to develop proposals that could bring the fighting to an end while establishing security arrangements capable of preventing another war.

However, the fundamental positions remain far apart. Ukraine wants credible guarantees against future Russian aggression, while Moscow has long sought restrictions on NATO's presence and influence in Eastern Europe.

European governments, meanwhile, are determined to prevent any settlement that would reward Russian military aggression or undermine Ukraine's sovereignty and its right to determine its own political and security future.

Washington's efforts to negotiate a broader European security framework with Moscow will have to contend with Europe's firm opposition to any arrangement that could undermine NATO, compromise existing security agreements or limit the sovereignty of European states.

Meanwhile, reactions from Warsaw, Brussels and Kyiv underscore that any deal negotiated primarily between Washington and Moscow would face considerable resistance.

World.title: France's Mélenchon to stage major campaign rally for manifesto launch
World.content:
French presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon published his book and manifesto, "L’Avenir en commun" (A Shared Future), on 6 November, the day before a major campaign rally organised by his far-left France Unbowed party near Paris.

 

Mélenchon is currently polling in second place, with 17.6% of voting intentions ahead of next spring's presidential election. He trails far-right National Rally candidate Marine Le Pen, who is polling at 36%, according to an IFOP poll for broadcaster LCI conducted from 27 to 29 October.

On the question of Europe, the manifesto backs scrapping rules and regulations that do not align with French interests, including those concerning the EU migration pact and European defence.

Mélenchon's party La France insoumise (LFI), known in English as France Unbowed, has also called for reducing France's net contribution to the EU budget by around €9 billion, a proposal reiterated by the party's finance spokesman Eric Coquerel in October.

This eurosceptic stance bears some parallels with that of the National Rally, which has pledged to scrap a number of EU regulations and standards, particularly those tied to the business sector, agriculture, energy and environmental policy.

However, while both parties advocate greater national sovereignty and challenge aspects of European integration, their positions are underpinned by different ideological priorities.

The manifesto gives less prominence to Russia's war against Ukraine than to France's relationship with Israel, accusing the government of allowing "a genocide to be committed" in Gaza and condemning what it describes as "diplomatic double standards".

On Ukraine, the manifesto backs "a diplomatic framework that would make it possible to secure a ceasefire and the withdrawal of Russian troops", as well as a gradual withdrawal from NATO, as part of a broader foreign policy based on military independence and non-alignment.

In terms of domestic policies, the party backs retirement at the age of 60, an increase in the minimum wage, legislation to curb the concentration of media ownership, as well as expanded public services.

France Unbowed also proposes tax increases targeting wealthy individuals and major corporations, alongside the removal of several tax breaks.

The measures are expected to generate an estimated €106.4 billion in additional annual revenue, according to the party's proposed 2027 budget, of which €81.7 billion would finance additional public spending, with the remainder contributing to a reduction in the country's public deficit.

This comes as France faces one of the highest levels of public debt in the eurozone, with its financial situation raising concerns among financial markets and drawing scrutiny from the European Union.

In recent months, Mélenchon's proposal to freeze or effectively cancel part of France's public debt held by the Banque de France, as part of the wider Eurosystem overseen by the European Central Bank, has sparked controversy.

The proposal would require a coordinated decision at European level. Both Banque de France Governor Emmanuel Moulin and ECB President Christine Lagarde have argued that such a move would violate EU treaties, particularly Article 123, which prohibits monetary financing of governments.

World.title: Switzerland: Giant banner targets Big Tech outside data centre site
World.content:
The 676-square-metre display featured images of Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos alongside the slogan "Big Tech Bros suck our water, electricity, data". Drone footage showed campaigners spreading the enormous banner across a field beside a facility being developed by US company STACK Infrastructure. Greenpeace is calling for a nationwide moratorium on new mega data centres until binding regulations are introduced to protect energy supplies, water resources and the public interest.

 

The environmental organisation argues that the rapid expansion of data centres is placing increasing pressure on local infrastructure. According to Greenpeace, the two facilities planned in Beringen could together consume around one and a half times as much electricity annually as the entire canton of Schaffhausen, while requiring substantial amounts of water for cooling.

The group also questions how waste heat will be reused and who will ultimately benefit from the developments. The demonstration formed part of an international campaign against the unchecked expansion of large-scale data centres, with similar actions taking place across Europe. Greenpeace is urging authorities to prioritise environmental protection and public needs over the commercial interests of technology companies.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | November 6th, 2026 – Evening
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Elon Musk's Tesla to 'wind down' Cybertruck production next year
World.content:
Tesla will begin winding down production of its Cybertruck around the middle of 2027, as the company shifts its focus towards autonomous vehicles, CEO Elon Musk announced on his social media platform X on Friday.

 

The decision marks a major shift for Tesla's electric pickup programme, which has struggled to meet the sales expectations set by the world's richest man.

Musk did not clarify whether production would be moved to another facility or whether the vehicle would be discontinued altogether. He also did not address what would happen to outstanding orders.

Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill described the pickup as an "incredible technology development platform" that would live on through the Cybercab.

Musk later reassured owners that the existing Cybertruck fleet would remain on the roads for a long time, calling the production wind-down "the end of an era".

Sales fall short of Musk's ambitions

Unveiled in November 2019, the Cybertruck was presented as a radical departure from traditional pickup trucks, with its angular design and stainless-steel exterior.

Musk initially said the vehicle had attracted around 250,000 pre-orders within days of its unveiling, while Tesla built its Texas production facilities with ambitious plans to manufacture hundreds of thousands of units annually.

However, production was repeatedly delayed, with the first customer deliveries only beginning in late 2023.

The vehicle has struggled to achieve the mass-market appeal Musk had anticipated. According to Kelley Blue Book estimates cited by the Associated Press, US Cybertruck sales fell by 48% in 2025 compared with the previous year, to 20,237 vehicles.

Tesla does not publish separate sales figures for the Cybertruck. Its third-quarter 2026 delivery report showed 8,295 vehicles delivered in its 'Other Models' category, which also includes the Semi and remaining Model S and Model X vehicles.

The pickup has also faced several recalls and quality-control issues, while its unconventional design has divided consumers.

Related Tesla faces fresh blow as regulators recall nearly all Cybertrucks

The Cybertruck never made it to Europe

Despite its high-profile launch, the Cybertruck never entered the European market.

Its heavy construction and angular design have raised questions over compliance with European vehicle safety requirements, particularly rules designed to protect pedestrians and other vulnerable road users.

The truck's sharp-edged stainless-steel body and weight have also fuelled debate over whether such vehicles are compatible with European road-safety standards.

The model has therefore remained largely a North American phenomenon, limiting its potential international customer base.

Its public image has also become increasingly tied to Musk's political activities. The Tesla chief's close association with US President Donald Trump and his role in the administration's Department of Government Efficiency made the vehicle a political symbol for some supporters and critics alike.

Some owners have reported vandalism and harassment, further complicating the pickup's public perception.

Tesla bets on driverless future

The decision to free up factory space for the Cybercab reflects Musk's broader ambition to transform Tesla from an electric-car manufacturer into a company focused on artificial intelligence, robotics and autonomous transport.

A Tesla Cybercab is parked near the White House, Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026, in Washington. AP Photo/Alex Brandon

Unveiled in 2024, the two-seater Cybercab is designed to operate without a steering wheel or pedals and is central to Tesla's plans for a driverless taxi network.

The company has already begun offering limited robotaxi rides in the United States, although the technology remains under regulatory scrutiny.

Tesla has said it intends to make the Cybercab a central vehicle in its future transport network, with Musk arguing that autonomous driving and robotics will become increasingly important to the company's business.

The Cybertruck's production wind-down marks a significant change of direction for a vehicle once presented as one of Tesla's most ambitious projects. Whether it disappears from the company's product line altogether, however, remains unclear.

World.title: Spain: Vintage cars hit the streets of Almería for annual rally
World.content:
Among the highlights was a rare 1905 Vermorel belonging to local collector Pepe Moreno, a vehicle normally displayed in a museum in nearby El Ejido.

 

A century-old Franklin also drew attention, alongside an elegant early 1950s Chevrolet, a late 1920s Nash, vintage Rolls-Royce and Mercedes-Benz models, and a DeLorean DMC-12, the futuristic sports car immortalised by the Back to the Future films.

Spectators watched as owners started their historic engines and drove through the city centre, offering a glimpse of motoring history spanning several generations. For the owners, the rally is as much about sharing their passion as preserving these remarkable machines.

Running from 5 to 9 November, the rally brings together enthusiasts from across Spain for a journey through the landscapes and villages of Almería province, including stops in Enix, Terque and Alsodux. The route also takes participants to Fort Bravo, the famous Western film sets in the Tabernas desert, combining automotive heritage with a tour of southern Spain's cinematic scenery.

World.title: ‘We vote with our money’: What are the biggest commercial opportunities of EU enlargement?
World.content:
It’s been over 13 years since a country last joined the European Union. Now, there are nine official candidate countries, some of which, such as Albania, expect negotiations to conclude as early as 2027.

 

But what does EU enlargement actually mean for the economy and investment opportunities? Does having more members mean more complexities? Does an influx of cheap labour spell disaster for incumbent members? And who stands to gain the most?

In this episode of The Big Question, Angela Barnes is joined by Jan Růžička, Chief External Affairs Officer at PPF Group, a privately held investment group founded in the Czech Republic, to discuss the biggest opportunities and risks of EU enlargement.

What are the biggest commercial opportunities presented by EU enlargement?

When predicting the biggest opportunities arising from this latest wave of accession, Jan looked to past successes. The largest enlargement took place in 2004, when 10 new countries, including his own, the Czech Republic, joined the EU.

Countries with cheap labour, a skilled workforce and traditional industries, such as Poland and the Czech Republic, have boomed over the past two decades. Jan therefore believes that countries like Moldova and Ukraine, which share similar attributes, have good prospects following accession.

“Five-six years ago, people said, ‘Do we need defence? Do we need heavy machinery? Do we need steel factories? Now again, it's very important.”

“In the case of Ukraine, of course, the defence tech, this is something that we don't have so much now in Europe. So I now see, for example, Ukrainians not only asking for investments, but I see Ukrainian investors coming to Europe,” Jan added.

Jan Růžička, Chief External Affairs Officer at PPF Group joined Angela Barnes for the latest epsiode of The Big Question. Euronews

He also stressed the importance of joining the single market, which would allow SMEs to access support.

“Sixty-five percent of our economy, including EU 15, EU 27, candidate countries, are small businesses. They are driving our economies and they are the reason for which we, bigger companies, are successful.”

“EU enlargement will let grow the businesses of small and medium-size companies which then will drive valuation of ourselves as well,” Jan continued.

Are enlargement candidate countries appealing to investors?

PPF Group, the independent, family-owned investment group for which Jan works, already has investments in businesses in the candidate countries of Serbia, Moldova and Ukraine.

“We as PPF, we vote with our money. We are divesting from Asia and investing much more here,” Jan explained.

“Not only because this is a great single market, but rule of law, democracy, predictability, all of this is positive. The European market is the best market in the world.”

Despite Jan’s enthusiasm for EU enlargement and the benefits it could bring to both candidate countries and incumbent members, he acknowledged that the process is not without risks.

He particularly criticised the slow pace at which the Commission is conducting negotiations, arguing that this is discouraging investment.

“I think that the biggest risk is to lose the momentum. [...] Let's not forget that you don't need 27 members to agree. You need 28 as we learned in Iceland, so we need to have some popularity of the EU in those countries and we are losing it,” Jan explained.

(In case you’re not familiar, Iceland was granted candidate status in 2010, with negotiations suspended in 2013. In August 2026, a referendum saw voters reject the resumption of its EU accession process. You can read more about that here.)

To prevent a loss of momentum and enthusiasm during negotiations, Jan suggested granting candidate countries certain limited access rights.

“Maybe it's only the single market, maybe it’s some freight agreement plus, but this is better than to wait for full enlargement.”

The Big Question is a series from Euronews Business where we sit down with industry leaders and experts to discuss some of the most important topics on today’s agenda.

Watch the video above to see the full discussion on EU enlargement and investment.

World.title: Middle East could have big role in Democrats' Trump corruption inquiry
World.content:
After their victory in the US midterm elections, the Democrats have promised to investigate corruption in the Trump administration. Critics say the president's Middle East deals is an area they should focus on.

Several polls of US voters taken around the recent midterm elections show that an overriding concern about the Trump administration is corruption.

Just days after the midterms, senior figures in the Democratic Party were quick to proclaim that they will be investigating corruption accusations when they take their seats in January.

It's highly likely that many of those investigations will center on the Trump administration's and the Trump family's links to wealthy Middle Eastern countries.

"The incoming Democratic majority in Congress will no doubt aggressively use their powers to investigate the administration's alleged wrongdoings," Amy Hawthorne, a non-resident fellow at the Washington-based think tank, the Arab Center, wrote in a commentary after the midterms. "Cases involving the Middle East will be their top targets."

Financial disclosures made by President Trump in the middle of this year showed that during 2025, his businesses made about $2 billion in income. This was triple the income he reported the previous year, observers noted.

"According to the information available … Middle Eastern countries and businesses have directly contributed to the bottom line of Trump's family businesses — more so than any other region of the world," Brian Katulis, a senior fellow and expert in US foreign policy at the Middle East Institute in Washington, wrote in a July text after the presidential disclosure. "Gulf entities paid around $300 million to the president's businesses in 2025."

Billions in cryptocurrency

A lot of the money Trump made in 2025 came from the sale of a stake in a cryptocurrency company, World Liberty Financial, Katulis noted.

The company was founded by the Trump and Witkoff families in 2024 — Steve Witkoff is Trump's special envoy to the Middle East — and in 2025, a large portion of it was sold to an investment firm backed by a senior United Arab Emirates official, Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan. The latter serves as the UAE's national security advisor and is also the brother of the UAE's president.

The deal was done in January 2026 behind closed doors, shortly before Trump's inauguration as president. In May 2026, the US agreed to allow the UAE access to advanced artificial intelligence chips, despite objections from some national security advisers.

Trump's critics allege a connection, the Trump administration denies it.

Trump cryptocurrency: A law suit filed in late October alleges a UAE investment fund chaired by Tahnoon also spent about $2 billion on a World Liberty cryptocurrency to inflate the value of the company Image: Niklas Larsson/BILDBYRÅN/picture alliance

There are also other alleged instances of Trump administration corruption with links to the Middle East.

Trump Towers in the Middle East

Various Trump deals with Saudi and Emirati real estate developers are also being questioned because of possible conflicts of interest.

The Gulf real estate developers, which have close ties to their governments and respective royal families, have agreed to build Trump-branded golf resorts, hotels, mansions, skyscrapers and towers in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar and the Maldives.

In 2025, Trump reported $59.5 million in foreign real estate licensing income, ten times more than he made in 2023, business media outlet CNBC reported in August. Nearly two-thirds of that money came from projects in the Gulf, CNBC said.

Ethics watchdogs argue that, "the deals create conflicts between Trump's political leadership role and private interests" because some of those Gulf states and their developers were also "pursuing major US investments, seeking government permits or pressing for favorable economic and diplomatic relations."

Qatar's flying gift

When the Qatari royal family gifted Trump a luxury jet, worth around $400 million, in May 2025, politicians and ethics experts asked about the propriety of taking such a pricey present from a foreign government.

After his presidency ends, Trump was apparently planning to donate the plane to his Florida-based project, the Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Foundation. Currently, it is unclear whether the Qatari plane will end up there and there's been speculation Trump will try to keep it for personal use.

The luxury plane, described as a "flying palace," had to be retrofitted with additional security for an unspecified cost that's thought to be in the millions Image: Elizabeth Frantz/REUTERS

The library is a non-profit and has received tens of millions in funding — an investigation by the CBS network traced over $100 million in donations — from lawsuits and via corporate donors.

Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has already said the library project would be investigated. "Giant corporations and foreign governments should not be able to buy influence in Washington with donations to the president's library," she told CBS.

Gaza's 'Board of Peace'

Plans for the so-called Board of Peace were created in September 2025 and the body was to facilitate a ceasefire and reconstruction in Gaza.

It was set up to be a kind of multilateral international organization, similar to the United Nations, except that Trump would serve as its chairman indefinitely and member countries donating $1 billion if they want to sit on the board permanently.

The Board of Peace has not achieved much in Gaza, experts say, and there have been several worrying developments.

Four months after its establishment, the World Bank account set up to manage Board of Peace funds was empty, the Financial Times newspaper reported in May . Instead, money had been deposited into a private JP Morgan bank account, over which there was no oversight.

There have apparently been contributions of around $3 million from Morocco and $20 million from the UAE, as well as pledges of $7 billion from board members and $10 billion from Trump.

The board's legal status was also changed to make it into an international non-governmental organization. This change in legal status may aim "to avoid US congressional oversight and keep much of its activity opaque," Zaha Hassan, an attorney and senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, warned in a June commentary . It also "gives Trump ultimate decision-making authority, including over financial matters," she noted.

'Trump crime family'

"The Trump crime family is the top of our investigative priorities," the most senior Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, Robert Garcia, said after the midterms .

And he has already expressed concerns about the behavior of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner in the Middle East.

Most of the issues around Kushner involve potential conflicts of interest. Kushner is acting as a volunteer envoy in the Middle East and has been deeply involved in negotiations to end the Gaza conflict and the Iran war.

Kushner (right) next to Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu and Steve Witkoff (left): Kushner's status as a 'volunteer' envoy means he is not subject to the same scrutiny as an elected official Image: Chen Junqing/Xinhua/IMAGO

In early October, CNN published an investigation that detailed links between Kushner's private equity company, Affinity Partners, and investments into leading Israeli military manufacturers.

It's also been reported that while he was travelling in the region, Kushner was trying to raise billions for his equity firm.

In March, Democratic politicians, including Garcia, wrote letters to the president's office, saying they had "serious concerns about whether the White House is letting Mr. Kushner use his influence for personal financial gain."

The potentially most damaging claims against Kushner come from a recent book, "Prince and Thieves," published late October by American investigative journalist Matthew Cole.

Cole alleges, "Kushner worked with the UAE to shape US policy across the Middle East and that, in the course of this work, he was given access to bank accounts containing roughly $2 billion," the New York Times wrote in its review .

Kushner denies the allegations about any such slush fund held by an Israeli bank and has threatened to sue Vanity Fair magazine, which published excerpts from the book.

But, as the New York Times concluded, "Cole's work is sufficiently calm, detailed and forensic to necessitate a large-scale and urgent congressional inquiry."

World.title: Stephen Miller named by Trump as White House chief of staff
World.content:
Trump said he would be replacing Susie Wiles for the top advisory role. Miller is controversial figure, known as a key architect of the administration’s hardline immigration policies.

US President Donald ‌Trump announced on ⁠Friday ⁠that his ​deputy chief of ​staff and architect of his administration's strict immigration policy, Stephen Miller, will become his new chief of staff.

Miller replaces Susie Wiles, who had been in the post since Trump's inauguration. With the nod, Miller becomes the top aide to the president.

Trump announced the move, saying Miller was "one of my most trusted advisors," adding that Wiles has done an outstanding job, and would be "moving over" to the "Trump political operation."

Wiles also commented on her exit from the White House, saying that her work there was "the honor of a lifetime."

She said she was proud of what the administration had accomplished during her tenure, including "securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First."

The move comes after Trump's Republican Party lost control of the House and Senate after a midterm election rout at the hands of Democrats.

When ICE comes knocking: the fight against Trump's deportations To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

One of Trump's longest-serving aides

Miller's appointment is a signal that Trump intends to continue on with his hardline immigration policies, despite losing control of the House and Senate to Democrats.

The 41-year-old is one of Trump's longest-serving advisers, having joined Trump's longshot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter.

Although his portfolio as Deputy Chief of Staff was wide-ranging, Miller is most responsible for Trump's policies and rhetoric on immigration.

Miller is of the administration's most vocal advocates, frequently making media appearances to defend policies, no matter how controversial they may be. The young aid has never held back in articulating Trump's worldview.

In particular, Miller has defended Trump's aggressive foreign policy towards Venezuela earlier this year, when the Pentagon embarked on striking boats in the Caribbean Sea that they said were carrying drugs and later carried out a military operation to snatch Nicolas Maduro.

"We live in the real world, Jake, that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power. These are the iron laws of the world since the beginning of time," Miller told broadcaster CNN's host Jake Tapper.



Miller also has not held back on attacking the administration's opponents. During the midterm campaign, Miller called Democrats "extremists, freaks and America-hating lunatics" on social media. He also promoted claims about election fraud in California and Alaska, which were not substantiated.

World.title: Ilse Aigner tipped by party allies as next German president
World.content:
German media reports suggest that Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner's chances of becoming the next president are on the up. Long favored by her Bavarian CSU, now it seems Christian Democrats nationwide plan to back her.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (the CDU) and their Bavarian sister party, the CSU, want to nominate a joint candidate to be the next president of Germany when the special "Bundesversammlung" committee that elects one votes at the end of January.

It's long been clear that the CSU favor the current speaker of Bavaria's parliament, Ilse Aigner, for the role.

But on Friday, multiple German news outlets like Spiegel, the Süddeutsche Zeitung and the DPA news agency cited sources in the CDU as saying that party's leadership had also decided on putting Aigner forward.

DPA reported that Merz would officially recommend Aigner as a candidate at a meeting of the CDU's leadership that will convene in Berlin on Sunday and Monday.

On the record, however, party officials would neither confirm nor deny the reports, pointing only to the upcoming meetings on Monday.

Aigner appears to have the backing of both Bavaria's Markus Söder and Chancellor Friedrich Merz, visible in the background on the main stage at the CSU party conference in this photo Image: Peter Kneffel/dpa/picture alliance

Germany's first woman as president?

If chosen, Aigner would be the 13th person and the first woman to take up the role as post-war Germany's head of state, which is a more ceremonial one with primarily symbolic power, while the bulk of the political and legislative power resides with the chancellor.

She would also be the first CSU politician to hold the office.

Aigner, 61, is currently the speaker of the state parliament in Bavaria.

The youngest of four sisters and the daughter of an electrician, she worked in the family business in her early adult life before going into politics. She's a Roman Catholic, single and has no children.

Aigner began her parliamentary career in the Bavarian legislature in 1994, then moved to the Bundestag federal parliament in 1998, before returning to the Bavarian chamber in 2013.

She spent five years as federal agriculture minister under then-Chancellor Angela Merkel.

She would also be the first CSU politician to hold the office.

Current President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, a heavy hitter for years for the Social Democrats before becoming head of state, is nearing the end of his second five-year term in the role, having assumed the office in March 2017.

Aigner is the speaker or president of Bavaria's state parliament at present, she's also a former federal agriculture minister Image: Rolf Poss/IMAGO

What steps remain on the path to Germany picking a new president?

The CDU/CSU's junior coalition partners, the Social Democrats (SPD), have also made it clear they would back a presidential bid from Aigner.

"If the CDU steering committee does indeed officially assert itself on Monday and put forward Ilse Aigner, then on behalf of the SPD I can only say that we would welcome this and support it," SPD chairman Lars Klingbeil said at an event in Berlin.

A large committee known as the Bundesversammlung chooses the German president. It will vote on January 30, 2027.

It's made up of all 630 Bundestag parliament members, and another 630 people assigned to represent the various German states — weighted according to each state's share of the national population.

Most of these are regional lawmakers, but municipal politicians and people from other walks of public life are also sometimes given a vote.

The CDU/CSU and SPD combined have a majority of roughly 50 seats in the special committee.

Beyond this, Merz is expected to try to rope in support for Aigner from the Greens, a party that has long championed more female representation at the top of politics and that would not seem to have a realistic chance of propelling a candidate of its own into the role.

This suggests that if Aigner's nomination were to materialize and solidify, she should have fairly good chances of succeeding Steinmeier.

World.title: Meghan Markle's father arrested in US over child sex abuse material
World.content:
US federal agents arrested Thomas Markle in Florida. The Duchess of Sussex and television actress Meghan Markle, who is estranged from her father, said she was "deeply distressed" by the charges.

Meghan Markle's father, Thomas Markle Sr., was arrested Friday morning by federal agents in Florida on charges related to child abuse, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls,US federal prosecutors said .

Thomas Markle Sr. was charged with one count of possession of child sex abuse imagery, prosecutors said in a statement.

The 82-year-old was arrested outside the city of Tampa on Florida's west coast.

The director of Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Kash Patel, said that "Mr. Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions."

Patel said their agents "moved quickly" to identify and locate the explicit material, and then arrested Markle Sr. in Florida.

Sex abuse images discovered in storage units

First Assistant US Attorney for central California Bill Essayli said federal agents searched two storage units in the Los Angeles area and "seized approximately 78 items, including slides, film negatives, and books" that contained suspected child sexual abuse images.

"Mr. Markle is accused of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs depicting himself with minor girls," said Essayli in a statement. "These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law."

If convicted, Thomas Markle Sr. would face a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison.

Markle Sr. was first reported to the police in the Philippines and to the FBI last month by his son, Thomas Markle Jr, after he claimed to have found child sex abuse material at his father's home in the Philippines, according to reports by the UK newspaper The Sun.

Meghan Markle, the wife of Prince Harry, recently said she was "deeply distressed" by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father's home.

She revealed that a letter containing "troubling allegations" about him had been sent to London police in 2018.

The FBI said last month that it would assist Philippine authorities with the case where possible.

Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, said last month she was deeply troubled by allegations surrounding her entranged father. [FILE: 2021] Image: Photoshot/Avalon/picture alliance

Meghan's father famously didn't attend her wedding at Windsor Castle

Meghan, an American citizen who starred in the US television drama "Suits," married Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018.

Her father did not attend their wedding, prompting extensive coverage in the British media of Meghan's estrangement from her father.

Thomas Markle Sr., a retried television lighting and photography director, was living in the Philippines earlier this year when he suffered a stroke and had his left leg amputated.

That forced him to return to the US.

"I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years — but that stops now," Markle Jr. told The Sun. "I won't speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him."

World.title: Iran war: Gulf tanker attacked, 1 seaferer killed
World.content:
Iran is stepping up attacks on shipping in the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz. A Greek-owned tanker believed to have been struck with a missile, and Iran said two other vessels were on fire.

An explosion believed to have been caused by a missile attack on ‌an oil ⁠tanker in the Persian Gulf left one seafarer dead, the vessel's operating company said on Friday.

Greek management firm Velos Tankers said the ​Marshall Islands-flagged tanker MT Velos Sapphire ​was sailing towards Bahrain when it ‌was attacked.

"The company is ‌greatly saddened to report the ‌death ​of one of its seafarers, who was found fatally injured on board after having initially been ​reported missing in the aftermath of the explosion," the firm said.

The explosion caused a fire to break out in the ship. The crew were able to extinguish the fire without reporting any other injured.

Bahrain's Khalifa Bin Salman Port ultimately took in the ship and now a investigation into the incident will be launched to assess the extent of the damage to the vessel's hull.

Shipping crews caught in the crossfire of the Hormuz conflict To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iran using 'everything it can' to stop oil flows

The incident is the latest in a string of attacks on ships in the Persian Gulf by Iran.

US newspaper The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) cited regional officials, security firms and analysts in a report detailing how Iran is using everything it can to stop the flow of oil leaving the Strait of Hormuz.

According to the report, Tehran has launched bomb-laden undersea drones, fired rocket-propelled grenades and deployed crews to attach limpet mines to ships over recent weeks.

According to data from the UK Maritime Trade Operations Center (UKMTO), October saw the highest monthly number of attacks in the Strait of Hormuz since the war began, with more than 35 incidents.

At least five vessels have been attacked so far in November, UKMTO added.

The increasing attacks coincides with signs of recovery in shipping through Hormuz. US Central Command said last month it had helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil via Hormuz since the summer.

On Thursday, Iranian media reported that five oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

On Friday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two more oil tankers were on fire in the strait, state media reported.

Iran destroys missile over Qeshm island

Meanwhile, Iranian media said ​on Friday ​that Iranian ​air defenses ‌had destroyed a US ‌MQ-1 drone ‌over Qeshm Island in the Strait ​of Hormuz.

The ‌United States did not confirm the incident.

It all comes in the wake of the US launching strikes on Qeshm Island on Tuesday, with Iranian state media reporting five explosions in rapid succession.

A statement attributed to Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned that the Middle East war would widen if the US resumes its attacks.

Khamenei has rejected the notion that Washington will change course after midterm elections dealt a blow to President Donald Trump.

World.title: Tesla to 'wind down' production of flop Cybertruck
World.content:
Elon Musk's electric pickup for the future will start to be consigned to the past next year. The Cybertruck's bulk and crude shape meant it could only pass regulatory standards in more permissive markets.

Tesla owner Elon Musk said on Friday that the company would scale down production of the Cybertruck at its Austin factory in the coming year.

The South African entrepreneur said Tesla would be scaling back production of his futuristic but often-mocked pickup truck and amping up production of what he hopes will soon become a fleet of fully automated taxis.

"Tesla will be winding down production of the cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk said on his X social media site.

The announcement follows a bruising week for Musk amid the US midterm elections, where Republicans struggled despite his major donations, with his companies losing billions in value by market capitalization as investors sought to ditch stock.

Cybertrucks fit on LA's wide roads with relative ease, but that's not the case everywhere Image: Barry King/Alamy/Visually/picture alliance

Why did the Cybertruck fail to attract customers?

Musk later responded to a complimentary user online who hailed the Cybertruck as the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made," and calling it an "end of an era" by saying: "True."

For years he had poured much of his enthusiastic marketing zeal into promoting the Cybertruck, saying during the 2023 launch "finally, the future will look like the future."

However the oversized body, straight lines and stainless steel and the post-apocalpytic vibe these created also met with widespread criticism and even mockery.

The electric powertrain was probably a barrier to sales in the US, by far the biggest pickup truck market, where Musk had hoped to take on some of the country's top-selling gas-guzzling vehicles like the Ford F150 or the Chevrolet Silverado and the Dodge Ram.

Meanwhile, the car's striking shape, weight and size made it impossible for Tesla to try to crack Europe, where electric vehicles are gaining a much larger market share.

Unlike in the US, EU safety regulations place considerable emphasis not just on people in cars in accidents, but also on the dangers posed to pedestrians who might be hit by a vehicle. That meant it was not possible for Tesla to register and sell the Cybertruck for road use in Europe.

Beyond this, the vehicle's size would likely have rendered it impractical and unpopular on many European roads, where space tends to be at more of a premium.

Depending how quick the wind-down proves to be, the Cybertruck's production run could prove shorter than its five-year R&D phase.

The agressive set-square design appealed to some of the more eccentric and well-financed police departments in the US like casino capital Las Vegas Image: Ty ONeil/AP Photo/picture alliance

How far short of Musk's sales targets did the Cybertruck fall?

Given its longstanding issues meeting Musk's very public sales and production predictions, Tesla does not publish sales figures broken down by model.

But according to the automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the company sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down from 38,965 in 2024.

At launch in 2023, Musk had predicted unit sales nearer a quarter of a million.

For orientation, Ford sold more than 800,000 F-Series pickups in the US last year, a slight boost on 2024's numbers. These vehicles start at less than half the list price of a Cybertruck in the US.

The IPO for SpaceX this year revealed that Musk's second-largest company was comfortably the biggest buyer of Cybertrucks in 2025. It bought vehicles worth $131 million and did not even enjoy a bulk-buy or friends-rate discount, paying list prices for the fleet.

SpaceX purchased a vast fleet of Cybertrucks in 2025, perhaps feeling the futuristic styling fits the company's aesthetics, or perhaps as a favor to a friend Image: Charles Briggs/ZUMA/picture alliance

What's the story with the next pet project, the Cybercab?

The Cybercab is a vehicular element in Musk's bid to transform Tesla towards a company focused more on AI and robotics than automobilies.

Rather than just featuring the self-drive or driving assistance programs that Musk has been championing for years, the Cybercab has no steering wheels, pedals or mirrors at all and is designed never to have a human in control.

Musk say the model will be the company's main autonomous model and will supply a global network of Robotaxis.

Starting in the past few months, around 300 such vehicles have been registered and have started operating, on approved roads in the Austin area near Tesla's Gigafactory Texas. They're being added to the existing fleet of autonomous Model Y Teslas being used for the purpose, serving in an area known as a geofence of around 680 square kilometers (264 square miles).

World.title: Data center protesters break into Microsoft site in Amsterdam
World.content:
Protesters are demanding a pause in data center construction in Europe. Campaigners planning protests in 16 countries say the AI building boom threatens water supplies, power grids and climate goals.

Protesters broke into the construction site of a Microsoft data center in Amsterdam on Friday, climbing cranes and hanging balloons while police stood by.

The action opened two days of planned protests in 16 countries, with campaigners demanding a pause in major artificial intelligence data center construction over concerns about electricity, water and environmental damage.

What happened in Amsterdam?

More than 100 activists gathered at the site, marching arm in arm before entering. Some danced or carried placards reading: "Screw your data center."

"These data centers are destroying our world. It's becoming uninhabitable because of all the resources they consume. That's why we're here today," protester Sam van der Beek said.

Image: Koen van Weel/ANP/picture alliance

Site owner Pure Data Centres, which plans to invest more than $1 billion (€890 million) in the project, urged protesters to leave safely and discuss their concerns.

Microsoft said it respected people's right to express their views peacefully but did not condone unlawful actions.

The Stop Dirty Data Centres coalition said other planned actions included a march in Dublin, a protest outside Poland's parliament and a demonstration against another Microsoft data center in Denmark.

Why are campaigners opposing data centers?

The protest group said more demonstrations are planned in several European countries on Saturday, including Ireland, Poland, Denmark, Finland, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, France and the UK.

Campaigners say the facilities strain electricity and water supplies, compete with housing and other businesses for resources and threaten climate goals.

They also raise concerns about job losses and the concentration of power in technology companies.

The coalition said it was not calling for existing data centers to close. It wants governments to establish clearer rules before further large-scale construction proceeds.

Technology companies argue that data centers provide essential infrastructure for AI and cloud services used by businesses, governments and consumers.

The dispute comes amid growing scrutiny of the industry's expansion. A Google project in Finland faces a criminal investigation over land clearances, while Italy and Portugal are tightening environmental rules for data centers.

The Netherlands has about 200 data centers planned, under construction or operating.

World.title: Despite Russia impasse, Germany still hoping to host Men's Ice Hockey World Championship
World.content:
International protests continue after a court ruled that Russia must be allowed to return to international ice hockey. Germany is seeking a solution that will allow the country to host next year's world championship.

A government spokesman has said that, despite talks with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB), the International Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) and others, the impasse caused by last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling remains.

Since the October 30 decision, several leading ice hockey nations — including Finland, Sweden and Czechia — have said they would refrain from playing against Russia in any tournament in which it is allowed to take part. Several key sponsors have also threatened to pull out, should the Russians be allowed to play.

The first tournament to be affected would be the Men's World Juniors, which opens in Canada in late December, followed by the IIHF's premier event, the Men's World Championship, to be hosted by Germany in May.

Hosting Worlds 'practically impossible'

Stefan Kornelius, the spokesman for Germany's government, told reporters in Berlin on Friday that talks held with various stakeholders had made clear that Russia's participation would render the hosting of the World Championship "practically impossible — both from a sporting and an economic perspective."

Kornelius said talks would continue and the government still hoped for a diplomatic solution that would allow Germany to host the World Championship — as planned — in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf in May.

"Our goal must be to hold the tournaments as scheduled," he said. "However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore — through dialogue — how we can still ensure the tournament takes place."

Following the CAS ruling that the IIHF must allow Russia to return to international play, DEB chairman Frank Lutz had conceded that Germany may be forced to consider withdrawing as World Championship host.

German visa restrictions on Russians in place

Asked at Friday's press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, an Interior Ministry spokesman declined to answer categorically, but did indicate that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," Martin Giese said.

Earlier this week, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney categorically ruled out Russian players taking part in the World Juniors in Alberta.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he said.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors," he said, "the Russians will not be there."

Consensus remains elusive

President Vladimir Putin has also weighed in on the issue, accusing countries opposing Russia's return to international sport of violating the rights of his country's athletes

The IIHF Council had originally called two days of meetings, on Monday and Tuesday, to try to reach a consensus on how to respond to the CAS decision — before extending discussions for a third day, on Thursday. By Friday, its members had evidently still not reached a consensus.

This comes as the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship, which is not affected by the CAS decision, opened in Denmark — and with the clock ticking toward the start of the World Juniors in Alberta on December 26.

World.title: Última hora de la actualidad política, en directo | Sánchez defiende la gestión tras el accidente de Urda: “Hemos dado la cara con transparencia”
World.content:
Junts descarta investir a Feijóo e insiste en un candidato del PSOE alternativo a Sánchez

La candidata de Junts al Congreso, Miriam Nogueras, ha descartado negociar la investidura del líder del PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, y ha insistido en que, para plantearse apoyar un futuro Gobierno liderado por el PSOE, exigirían a Pedro Sánchez que se apartara y que los socialistas propusieran un candidato alternativo.

Así lo ha dicho este viernes en una entrevista en SER Catalunya, en la que ha garantizado que el PP, “uno de los partidos más catalanófobos que hay en el panorama español, no tendrá los votos de Junts”, y ha señalado que los populares “ya han decidido que su socio se llama Vox”.

“Esta decisión ya la tomamos en 2023. Quiero recordar que en 2023 ganó el PP y el PP no gobierna gracias a Junts. En cambio, en 2016 el PP gobernó gracias al PSOE. Por tanto, aquí quienes pueden reincidir son los que ya lo han hecho”, ha subrayado.

Nogueras ha incidido en lo que desde su partido han bautizado como la vía Starmer: “El PSOE debe decidir si quiere y prefiere al señor Sánchez, una persona que ha demostrado que no tiene capacidad para gestionar consensos, o pone por delante el partido que dice defender, y el país que dice defender”.

Con todo, la candidata de Junts ha advertido de que su formación no está en el Congreso “para abrir las puertas de Moncloa y cerrarlas”.

“Estamos aquí porque, mientras no seamos independientes, lo que sí tenemos que conseguir es que en Madrid no se pueda lograr absolutamente nada si no es con Cataluña”, ha dicho.

La también vicepresidenta de Junts ha sostenido que los ciudadanos quieren un “cambio” y ha añadido que su formación busca impulsarlo desde la “centralidad”, lejos de los “extremos” que para ella representan tanto Vox como el Frente Amplio. “Con nuestros votos, ni Abascal será ministro ni Colau será ministra”, ha reiterado.

Preguntada por si cree que estos dos espacios son lo mismo, ha dicho que su responsabilidad es “hacer leyes” y que los extremos “están arrastrando la política” lejos de la centralidad y las propuestas: “Y es más atractivo que uno insulte al otro”, ha lamentado.

En cuanto a la relación con ERC en Madrid, Nogueras ha asegurado que con los republicanos “se entiende” y habla con ellos, aunque su candidato, Gabriel Rufián, “ha decidido que su enemigo es un partido catalán”, Junts.

Preguntada por si se identifica como una política de derechas, Nogueras ha respondido que se considera una política “trabajadora”.

También ha asegurado que el partido que “más veces” ha votado con PP y Vox esta legislatura “se llama PSOE”: “El bloque contra Cataluña es el que más hemos visto”.

En cuanto al regreso del expresidente Carles Puigdemont a Cataluña, ha dado por hecho que será después de las elecciones del 29-N, en los términos en los que él mismo explicará una vez sea amnistiado por el Supremo.

La huelga general y el papel de los sindicatos

Sobre si secundará la huelga general del 11 de noviembre, Nogueras ha defendido que “los sindicatos convocan huelgas” y la responsabilidad de los políticos es “aportar soluciones” ante un coste de la vida “elevadísimo” y la crisis en el acceso a la vivienda.

“Lo que pasa es que me da la sensación también de que los sindicatos que convocan esta huelga son sindicatos que están al servicio de los partidos que han tomado estas malas decisiones”, ha apuntado. (Efe)

World.title: La Fiscalía Europea investiga un presunto fraude en las obras de la alta velocidad tras el accidente de Urda
World.content:
La Fiscalía Europea ha puesto en marcha una investigación por un posible fraude en la utilización de fondos de la Unión Europea en las obras de renovación y mejora de la seguridad, señalización y sistemas de comunicaciones en la línea de alta velocidad entre Madrid-Sevilla, según han informado fuentes cercanas a la investigación y ha confirmado el ministerio público de la Unión Europea, órgano independiente encargado de investigar los delitos que atenten contra los intereses financieros de la UE. La Fiscalía Europea ha informado que la investigación arranca por iniciativa propia a raíz del trágico accidente del 28 de octubre de 2026 en Urda (Toledo) en el que murieron 69 personas.

Dentro de esta investigación, agentes de la Unidad Central Operativa (UCO) de la Guardia Civil se han desplazado a las 9.30 de este viernes a las sedes del Administrador de Infraestructuras Ferroviarias (ADIF), de la Agencia Estatal de Seguridad Ferroviaria (AESF) y del Tribunal de Cuentas en Madrid a requerir documentación con la que determinar si se produjo malversación de fondos europeos en varias obras de mantenimiento de la vía de alta velocidad realizadas en los últimos años y que fueron cofinanciadas con los fondos NextGeneration UE y el Fondo Europeo de Desarrollo Regional (Feder). Según detallan fuentes cercanas a las pesquisas, los agentes han recabado, entre otros, los expedientes de tres licitaciones que supusieron un desembolso total de 136,4 millones de euros.

El de mayor importe es el contrato que Adif adjudicó en septiembre de 2021 para la renovación del sistema de seguridad LZB —que impide que dos trenes coincidan en el mismo punto— por el ERTM, más moderno, así como la mejora de las instalaciones de señalización y telecomunicaciones fijas de la línea Madrid-Sevilla. El presupuesto inicial superaba los 131 millones de euros con IVA, aunque finalmente se adjudicó el contrato a Thales España GRP por cerca de 94 millones. Fue precisamente la caída del sistema LZB a las 8.31 del pasado 28 de octubre la que provocó que se paralizaran los siete trenes que en ese momento circulaban por el tramo de más de 63 kilómetros de la vía de alta velocidad afectada por el fallo. A las 9.53, un tren de Renfe al que se le había autorizado reemprender la marcha con normalidad embistió a un convoy de Iryo que aún estaba parado y provocó el siniestro. El entonces ministro de Transportes, Óscar Puente, aseguraría después que el sistema LZB se había caído en 170 ocasiones en lo que iba de 2026.

La segunda licitación investigada es la del contrato para la renovación de 63 desvíos de los 319 existentes en la línea Madrid-Sevilla. Entre ellos, los de Urda, la localidad donde se produjo el choque entre los dos trenes el 28 de octubre. El contrato fue finalmente adjudicado por 21 millones de euros en su primera fase a una unión temporal de empresas (UTE) integrada por Ferrovial Construcción, Grupo Azvi, Convensa y Agrupación Guinovart. Azvi es una de las constructoras a la que la Guardia Civil acudió el pasado jueves para hacer un requerimiento de información en su investigación sobre la trama de corrupción del denominado caso Koldo. El tercer contrato, adjudicado por 21,5 millones de euros también a Thales España, tenía como objeto la renovación de los circuitos de vía ―el sistema que permite detectar la presencia de un tren en un tramo concreto del recorrido― tanto de la línea Madrid-Sevilla como del ramal La Sagra-Toledo.

No es la primera vez que la Fiscalía Europea inicia unas pesquisas sobre las obras en ese tramo de la alta velocidad española. El pasado 30 de enero abrió otras por un posible fraude en los fondos europeos destinados al mantenimiento de esta misma infraestructura. Entonces las pesquisas se iniciaron 11 días después del accidente ferroviario de Adamuz (Córdoba) de enero de este año, en el que fallecieron 46 personas. Tanto la investigación sobre la supuesta malversación de fondos por el accidente de Urda como la de Adamuz discurren en paralelo a las que por su parte tienen abiertas un juzgado de Orgaz (Toledo) y otro de Montoro (Córdoba) para determinar las causas de ambos siniestros y si hay responsabilidades penales. En los dos casos, el epicentro de las pesquisas es determinar el destino que España dio a las subvenciones que Bruselas dio para renovar a fondo esta línea ferroviaria entre Madrid y Sevilla, que es la más antigua de la alta velocidad española.

La Fiscalía Europea tiene un modelo de instrucción parecido al de numerosos países de la UE, en el que los fiscales llevan la batuta de la investigación y el juez designado en España únicamente se encarga de supervisar que el procedimiento avanza con las garantías legales, supervisando medidas restrictivas de derechos fundamentales como órdenes de entradas y registros en domicilios o intervenciones telefónicas. Para las pesquisas del caso de Adamuz, la Audiencia Nacional designó al juez José Luis Calama para ejercer este papel de magistrado de garantías. Otro magistrado se encargará de las ahora iniciadas por el de Urda.

World.title: Saber qué hacer con el dinero: la importancia de aprender a tomar decisiones financieras
World.content:
En tiempos donde se multiplican las opciones de inversión (y los peligros de consejos dudosos en redes sociales), “una sociedad con mayor cultura financiera es más resiliente y sostenible”, como defienden desde Mapfre. Para educar al respecto, apuestan por campañas en todos los canales y formatos novedosos

La gestión del dinero es una preocupación cotidiana. Ahorrar para comprar una casa, preparar la jubilación, hacer frente al coste de los estudios de los hijos o asegurar que el patrimonio no se devalúe son objetivos por los que uno puede hacer mucho más que guardar dinero en su cuenta corriente. Pero, eso sí, con la asesoría apropiada “para planificar bien el futuro y tomar decisiones más responsables”, como explica Mónica Zuleta, Directora Corporativa de Sostenibilidad de Mapfre.

Cuanto más complejo sea un asunto, más urgente resulta encontrar palabras claras y sencillas para explicarlo. Nuevos lenguajes y formatos que lleguen a todo el mundo. Porque si bien hace tiempo invertir fue una actividad reservada a una minoría con grandes patrimonios y conocimientos específicos, hoy el abanico es amplísimo, con opciones aptas para cada bolsillo.

“Hace décadas las opciones eran limitadas y estaban reservadas a perfiles concretos; ahora existe una enorme oferta de productos, información y plataformas. Se ofrecen más oportunidades, pero se genera más confusión”, explica Zuleta, que recalca que “la mejor manera de navegar en ese entorno no es tratar de convertirse en expertos de la noche a la mañana”, ni mucho menos fiarse de la guía de gurús hallados en mentideros de las redes sociales.

“Entender los conceptos básicos y conocer el nivel de riesgo que cada cual está dispuesto a asumir sigue siendo la mejor brújula para tomar buenas decisiones”, afirma Zuleta, que resume algunas de las muchas iniciativas que Mapfre lleva años poniendo en marcha para divulgar sobre estos aspectos y proporcionar formación apropiada: “Hemos promovido herramientas pioneras como Empatía, un asistente de Inteligencia Artificial que permite resolver dudas a través de WhatsApp y que ha logrado solventar en tiempo real el 100% de las consultas que hacen los clientes”.

Juego de mesa de educación financiera de Fundación Mapfre.

Fundacion Mapfre desarrolla juegos de mesa diseñados ad hoc para la impartición de talleres, como Play Pension, escape rooms [juegos de escape] de temática financiera, como Finexit. Mapfre impulsa otro tipo iniciativas como aplicaciones de internet, vídeos formativos adaptados al tipo de comunicación imperante en canales como Instagram o TikTok o incluso una serie de cuatro capítulos, titulada Vecinos a todo riesgo. Ningún formato posible se les escapa
