World.title: Participants of Azerbaijan NGOs Cooperation Forum addressed President Ilham Aliyev
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 2. Participants of the Azerbaijan NGOs Cooperation Forum adopted an address to President Ilham Aliyev.

Trend presents the address:

“Esteemed Mr. President, Victorious Commander-in-Chief!

We, the more than 400 civil society representatives at the Cooperation Forum of Azerbaijani Non-Governmental Organisations, take great pride in extending this address to you on the eve of the sixth anniversary of November 8 – Victory Day, which stands among the most glorious milestones in our nation’s history!

You are the Commander-in-Chief who brought the Azerbaijani people a historic victory, ensured the full restoration of the territorial integrity and sovereignty of our state, revived our people's national pride and dignity, and fulfilled the testament of National Leader Heydar Aliyev. Your determination, political will and strategic vision turned into reality the dream of victory that our people had cherished for decades. This triumph was not merely a military success; it was also a victory of national will, the determination to uphold statehood, people-government unity and historical justice. The triumph achieved under your command in the 44-day Patriotic War elevated Azerbaijan to a new stage in its history, creating a solid foundation for the country's future development.

Esteemed Mr. President!

Today, Azerbaijan is not merely a country that has liberated its territories and restored its sovereignty. It has become a country shaping the region’s political and economic landscape, making its voice heard and asserting its position in the international relations system, while steadily emerging as a middle power with expanding capabilities and growing influence. The fact that Azerbaijan, having secured victory in the war, has taken the initiative in advancing the peace agenda stands as a major historic achievement of your political leadership. The extensive reconstruction and development projects being carried out in the liberated territories, the implementation of the Great Return programme, and the establishment of modern cities and villages embody victorious Azerbaijan’s forward-looking vision. The revival of life in Garabagh and East Zangezur demonstrates the lasting and irreversible outcomes of our victory.

Esteemed Mr. President!

Azerbaijan's strength is not measured solely by its economic and military capabilities. At the core of this power lie the idea of Azerbaijanism uniting us, our national and moral values, our historical memory, and our nationwide solidarity. In this regard, preserving national ideological security, safeguarding society against foreign influence and disinformation, and promoting national interests, historical truths, and national-spiritual values are of paramount importance.

In recent years, major international events hosted by our country under your leadership, including COP29, the World Urban Forum, the World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue, and others testify to Azerbaijan’s growing global role, organizational capabilities, and international trust. These achievements also inspire us to protect and defend our values.

As active civil society representatives, Azerbaijani NGOs recognize their responsibility in this area and affirm their readiness to continue contributing to the protection of the national interests, as well as moral and constitutional values of our country.

Dear Mr. President!

We, the NGOs of Azerbaijan, stand by you and remain fully committed to contributing to the achievement of the strategic goals defined by you for the sake of our state’s development, the protection of our national interests, and the unity and solidarity of our people. Watching the amputee football match featuring landmine victims during the Forum held in Ganja reconfirmed our conviction that no landmine and no war wound can shatter the invincible spirit of the Azerbaijani people. The willpower, enthusiasm for life, and determination demonstrated by these individuals on the pitch served as a vivid manifestation of the fact that our Victory is forever etched in the hearts of our people.

Esteemed Mr. President!

On the eve of this remarkable occasion, we reaffirm that Azerbaijani NGOs fully support the policy pursued under your leadership and look to the future of an independent and powerful Azerbaijan with immense confidence.

Victory is the pride of our people, our sovereignty is the eternal asset of our state, and our national unity based on the idea of Azerbaijanism is the guarantee of our future triumphs!”

World.title: Azerbaijan and Bulgaria hold sixth round of political consultations (PHOTO)
World.content:
Photo: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 6. The sixth round of political consultations between the Ministries of Foreign Affairs of Azerbaijan and Bulgaria was held in Sofia.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Azerbaijan said in a report.

According to the ministry, the delegations were headed by Deputy Foreign Minister Elnur Mammadov and Bulgarian Deputy Foreign Minister Ivanka Tasheva, respectively.

During the political consultations, the current state of strategic partnership relations between the two countries and prospects for their development were discussed in detail, along with issues of cooperation in the political, economic and energy sectors, including green energy corridors, transport and logistics, and other areas.

The sides also held a detailed exchange of views on diversifying trade turnover and promoting mutual investments. The importance of continuing mutual support and coordination within international organizations was emphasized at the meeting.

In addition, opportunities to expand ties in the humanitarian, cultural, scientific and educational fields were considered. It was noted that cooperation in these areas constitutes an important component of bilateral relations.

As part of the visit, Bulgarian Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova-Chamova met with Elnur Mammadov. The meeting focused on issues of mutual interest.

The Deputy Minister also met with Rusi Ivanov, Adviser to the Prime Minister of Bulgaria on Foreign Policy. The sides exchanged views on expanding bilateral ties and prospects for developing cooperation.

Subsequently, the Azerbaijani delegation held a meeting at the National Assembly of Bulgaria with members of the Bulgaria-Azerbaijan Interparliamentary Friendship Group and its Chairman, Hamid Hamid, as well as members of the Foreign Policy Committee and the committee's Deputy Chairman, Slavi Vasilev. During the discussions, the important role of interparliamentary relations in promoting parliamentary diplomacy, intensifying contacts between legislative bodies and developing bilateral ties was emphasized.

During the visit, Elnur Mammadov also delivered a lecture to attendees of the Diplomatic Institute of the Bulgarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and members of the Student Diplomatic Club of Sofia University St. Kliment Ohridski.

World.title: Woodside to cut over 500 jobs globally as part of cost reduction drive
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 6. Woodside Energy plans to reduce its global workforce by more than 500 positions as part of its structural cost reduction program, according to the company's Capital Markets Day 2026 presentation.

The workforce reduction is one of the measures the company listed for reaching its target of cutting $400 million in annual structural costs from 2028. The others are AI-enabled maintenance planning, supply chain optimisation, and risk-based contracting processes.

Woodside said that $130 million of the targeted savings will come from streamlined processes, $170 million from external spending and $100 million from portfolio optimisation.

Woodside Energy, headquartered in Perth, is Australia's largest independent oil and gas company and is listed on the Australian Securities Exchange and the New York Stock Exchange. Its portfolio includes LNG and domestic gas operations in Australia, deepwater oil in the US Gulf of America, the Sangomar oil field in Senegal, and the Trion project under development in Mexico. Woodside said its enablers include a 'One Team' culture, digital and AI innovation, and critical capabilities. The structural cost reduction target excludes contractor spending on major capital projects such as Scarborough, Trion, Louisiana LNG and Beaumont New Ammonia. Woodside held its Capital Markets Day 2026 in Sydney on November 5 and will hold a second event in New York on November 12. At last year's Capital Markets Day, in November 2025, the company set out its growth plans to 2032.

World.title: Cooking classes help cut cost of living and boost social connection
World.content:
Cain Stanley tends to a collection of garden beds housing a wide spread of homegrown fruit and vegetables that are destined for a meal he will help prepare the same day.

The 28-year-old has found time in this garden, clearing away overgrown leaves and removing older plants, is now something he looks forward to each week as part of a regular cooking class.

Mr Stanley has been taking part in the Cooking Outside the Box program at Berri in South Australia's Riverland for a few months and is excited about developing his cooking skills.

Cain Stanley helps maintain the garden at the back of the Berri Community Centre. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

Run by local not-for-profit ac.care and supported by Foodbank, it gives people confidence cooking on a budget and helps them find connection.

"It's just me and my dog at home, so it's good to get out and actually speak to people," Mr Stanley said.

"I've done some of the pasta meals that we've made [at home], and they were good."

The centre grows a range of fresh fruit and vegetables for general community use. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

Cooking through cost-of-living crisis

Berri Community Centre coordinator Sue Dayman meets people all the time who are doing it tough.

The centre runs programs throughout the week and Ms Dayman said many encouraged people to be creative and make meaningful relationships.

She said giving people tools to reduce financial pressure had been rewarding.

"If the cost of cooking can be brought down, children may be able to join a sport [or] other things in the community," Ms Dayman said.

Sue Dayman says Cooking Outside the Box has economic and social benefits for isolated Riverland residents. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

"Everything costs so much these days [and] often we'll find that even those basic vegetables are such a cost."

While the program and ac.care's garden offer many of the ingredients used, different cultural cuisines are included in meal preparation and participants are welcome to add their own ideas and tastes.

"Everything's just evolved out of what the need is, and then people have really owned it," Ms Dayman said.

"We don't really run it; basically, the group runs themselves."

Portia Priori regularly attends the cooking class. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

Building up social confidence

Alongside the cooking, movement and fun are encouraged.

One of the centre's volunteers recently added a Zumba session to help the participants work up an appetite while waiting for the culinary creation to be ready to plate.

Ms Dayman said the group was made up of people from a range of ages, abilities, backgrounds and cultures and it had been special to watch their bond deepen over time.

"It's so good to see the connection, and people feel like they belong here," she said.

" We want it to be like a family … that they can come here with no judgement. "

Janet Becker, who started in the cooking group a year ago, is now proud to help lead the group, which has grown over time.

Janet Becker says being in the class has made a huge difference to her mental health. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

"When I first started, there was only a small group of us; [now] some days we have 20 people here, which is amazing," she said.

" I've made some really good friends, and it gets me out of the house and helps with my mental health. "

Ms Becker said the class had inspired her to cook for herself more at home and be mindful of helping the wider community.

"[Once we] made a lot and we were able to feed the whole group plus some for the homeless out the front," she said.

World.title: Anger over Tungkillo data centre should have Labor on red alert
World.content:
Data centres have become so politically toxic that they've managed to bind together the Greens and One Nation.

The two ideological opposites stood side by side at a community rally in Mannum last weekend, speaking out against a Melbourne developer's bid for a hyper-scale data centre in Tungkillo, roughly 40km east of Adelaide, over concerns about the environment, energy and water use.

The Liberal Party was there too, demanding that locals who are fiercely opposed get a genuine say. Mid Murray Council Mayor Simone Bailey, who ran for Labor at the March state election, told the ABC it was "really hard to understand the benefits" of the proposal.

Mid Murray Council Mayor and former Labor candidate Simone Bailey speaking at the Tungkillo data centre protest. (ABC News: James Wakelin)

Popular independent federal MP Rebekha Sharkie is also against it, posting on Facebook that "Data Centres do NOT belong on prime agricultural land".

The broad coalition that's forming in Tungkillo comes with the backdrop of the US midterms, where Americans used their ballots as a sledgehammer against pro-data centre proposals and politicians.

Labor in SA should be on red alert.

No data centres for the sake of data centres, premier says

The bulk of the anger in Mannum over the weekend was directed at Quantum DC, a company that has had — to put it mildly — a few hiccups with its community consultation process.

But Labor copped plenty of criticism as well, accused by both Greens MLC Robert Simms and One Nation's Carlos Quaremba of "rolling out the red carpet" for data centres.

One Nation's Carlos Quaremba has accused Labor of "rolling out the red carpet" for data centres. (ABC News: James Wakelin)

The government has reason to dispute that characterisation.

It has drafted new laws proposing tougher energy and water requirements on the computing facilities, with Premier Peter Malinauskas declaring "if they're not in our interests, they're not happening".

US voters overwhelmingly rejected data centres The US midterms cemented the issue of data centres as politically toxic. But now the industry will be looking for a new place to call home.

The premier appears to have taken plenty of lessons from the US, criticising their "let it rip" approach.

"They have let data centres be built next to residential homes, they have let data centres be built without any reference to new generation coming on board, we've seen blackouts, we've seen price increases, it's madness," he said.

"If it's going to happen in Australia, it cannot happen like that."

Quantum DC is also yet to lodge its planning application for Tungkillo, with the government saying it doesn't want to "pre-judge" the project.

"I don't even know who these people are, like they haven't even applied," Mr Malinauskas said of the Tungkillo proposal.

"And it's causing an awful amount of community anxiety over a process that no one's ever started formally.

"That doesn't represent the sort of way we want to go about engaging with this."

Mr Malinauskas said he wanted to see a "proper regulatory and legislative environment" that allows his government to "stop data centres from happening unless they comply with our standards".

At the same time, however, the premier and his state development minister, Chris Picton, seem to be the only state politicians who this year have offered anything resembling positive commentary about data centres.

Peter Malinauskas stood alongside Firmus co-founder Oliver Curtis to spruik new AI development in June. (ABC News)

The political wisdom of standing alongside Firmus co-founder Oliver Curtis in June to spruik new AI development in SA is quite easy to question in hindsight, particularly given the spectacular collapse of Firmus' IPO four months later.

Not to mention the government's data centre strategy has plenty of verbs in it like "accelerate" and "streamline" to send a chill down the spine of data centre opponents.

"We are proactively engaging global and domestic AI companies and data centre developers to land major investments, build capability, and create high-value jobs for South Australians," the strategy states.

These are all elements that, fairly or unfairly, could come back to haunt Labor should more unpopular AI proposals lob in other marginal seats.

Because currently, there appears to be far more votes to be won leaning into concerns about data centres than courting their arrival.

Rigorous process or concerning gap?

The government's messaging on Tungkillo has also been curious.

On Saturday, Planning Minister Nick Champion spoke to the media to provide some reassurance to the Mannum community, noting the government controlled the planning pathway for the Tungkillo data centre.

"Whatever the pathway, the process is rigorous," he told reporters.

"There is a very rigorous test on power, they cannot jeopardise our grid, they cannot jeopardise the stability or the power capacity of our grid, they have to pass a test on water, and they have to pass rigorous tests in the planning system."

SA's AI data centre push The South Australian government is pushing for the state to become home to billions of dollars' worth of artificial intelligence data centres.

Yet by the time we got to Thursday, the premier was talking about the urgent need for law reform.

"At the moment, data centres can apply for development applications and the like and we don't necessarily have the controls that we desire to be able to ensure that they do bring their own energy, that they do comply with environmental standards," he said.

"We need to be able to restrict these things from happening unless they do it in circumstances that is in the state's interests."

Labor will soon need to pass its data centre legislation through the upper house of parliament, where it does not hold a majority.

Instead, they will need to negotiate with their political opponents who are leaning into data centre angst.

Don't be surprised to see that Greens and One Nation alliance pop up again.

World.title: Voters in Melbourne's south-east concerned by crime and community safety
World.content:
Crime is front of mind for the businesses on Berwick's main strip.

The butcher has suffered four break-ins in three years and the cafe around the corner suffered two attempted firebombings in recent weeks.

Besima Goga had only been working at the jewellers for two weeks when three masked men came into the shop in the middle of the day with hammers, raiding the store and leaving her boss with a head injury.

Loading...

The men have since been charged and faced court, but Ms Gogo said the jewellers now keep the doors of the shop closed.

"Now, even when I go to shopping centre, I am always looking [around] because I am scared with what happened here," she said.

The local City of Casey Council, in Melbourne's outer south-east, has found in resident surveys the top answers to what council could do to boost safety included increasing security, police and CCTV.

Berwick in Melbourne's south-east has historically been a Liberal electorate. (ABC News: Gabriela Rahardja)

The state seat of Berwick takes in the older suburbs of Berwick and Beaconsfield Upper, and south of the Princes Freeway the booming area of Clyde North.

Monash University political scientist Zareh Ghazarian said the electorate's voters were concerned about local infrastructure, as well as how the government is dealing with crime, the cost of living and housing affordability.

Dr Ghazarian said Berwick, held by the shadow minister for police and former Liberal leader Brad Battin on a margin of 4.7 per cent, would normally be seen as a marginal seat.

The Walk It Out women's only walking group meets every week in the Wilson Botanic Park. (ABC News: Gabriela Rahardja)

But this time, it is part of a swathe of seats in south-eastern Melbourne, including Labor-held Narre Warren North and Narre Warren South, that could be a critical path to a Coalition victory.

"This is going to be critical to see on election night," he said.

Zareh Ghazarian says Berwick is a key seat to watch at the 2026 Victorian election. (Supplied)

The incumbent Labor Party has promised to recruit 1,500 more police officers if elected, and open a second police academy in Melbourne's west.

The Coalition opposition has pledged to reopen 40 police stations and recruit an extra 3,000 police officers, and overhaul the bail system.

Still, Casey council's survey of 450 residents across 2022, 2024 and 2025 found that community and family connection was the top factor for making people feel safer in their neighbourhood.

Police patrols and CCTV ranked lower.

Casey mayor Michelle Crowther said increasing safety through community connectedness was a key priority for council.

"I feel that safety is not just the physical feeling, but it's actually the relationships and the connections," she said.

" It's built through time and people feeling that they belong. "

Building connections

Gia Felix has joined a women's walking group at the Wilson Botanic Park, partly because there are local parks where she would not want to walk alone.

"With all the increasing violence in Victoria … I feel hesitant or think twice before I go," she said.

The green trees and calm lake sceneries in Wilson Botanic Park Berwick make it a great place for nearby residents to meet up. (ABC News: Gabriela Rahardja)

Ariana Te Arihi founded the Walk It Out walking group out of the pandemic in hopes to create a safe space for women to connect with one another.

The group started with one member and quickly grew to a troop of women walking twice a week.

"Loneliness, disconnection and isolation is prevalent in our community … [I am trying] to combat that," Ms Te Arihi said.

When Taznim Moideen moved to Melbourne from Singapore four years ago, she joined the Berwick Neighbourhood Centre to attend prayer events in the community hall on Fridays.

Taznim Moideen says she has made many friends by joining events hosted by her local neighbourhood house. (ABC News: Gabriela Rahardja)

She is now a stallholder at the neighbourhood house's twice-annual community market, where locals sell baked goods, crafts and plants while fostering a sense of togetherness.

"It's a beautiful community. I've got friends from different walks of life," she said.

" I feel extremely safe. "

Manager Kim Peterson said the centre was a "safe haven" for many people in Berwick.

"Everyone is welcome, all inclusive.

"If they've had an incident or a situation, there's someone there to back them up."

"Once you've created community, you recognise other people, you form relationships and they go beyond the perimeters of these buildings," she said.

Loading...

However, Neighbourhood Houses Victoria CEO Keir Paterson said state government funding for local neighbourhood houses was falling behind costs with their operating capacity reaching a 10-year low.

"Nearly half of the 400 neighbourhood houses in Victoria have run at a loss for each of the past three years," he said.

Mr Paterson said he hoped whoever won government after November 28 would restore funding for a service that was essential for communities in outer suburbs.

"Neighbourhood houses are particularly important in new growth areas," he said.

"We know that loneliness and social isolation is particularly a problem in Melbourne's growth areas."

The ABC asked the major parties for their policies on neighbourhood houses but did not hear back by deadline.

World.title: Reefs' new name echoes the legacy of the 'Bingil Bay Bastard'
World.content:
When a Far North Queensland farmer wanted to make fertiliser from coral on the Great Barrier Reef, a local poet emerged as his fiercest opponent.

It was the 1960s. The reef was much less understood and scientists were loath to weigh into a political debate about its future, which was just starting to heat up as Joh Bjelke-Petersen swept to power in Queensland.

Enter John Büsst, the man his opponents came to call the "Bastard of Bingil Bay".

Much of John Büsst's campaigning centred on Ellison Reef, which was under threat from drilling. (Supplied: Christopher Tilt, Birds Eye View Drone Services)

He saw a great threat to the natural paradise that surrounded his home on the Cassowary Coast, between Cairns and Townsville, and so he wrote more than 4,000 letters agitating for its protection.

"He'd fly from Mission Beach to Melbourne to catch up with his buddy [prime minister Harold Holt] to say a few words," marine scientist Adam Smith said.

"He was really an unknown hero.

John Büsst (standing) was a personal friend of Harold Holt. (Supplied: Friends of Ninney Rise)

"When he saw others trying to damage or destroy [the reef], such as the proposed mining of Ellison Reef for coral, or the proposed drilling for oil — which was actually proposed by the Queensland government — he thought he would oppose it."

Two years ago, Dr Smith proposed two unnamed reefs be named in Büsst's honour, recognising his legacy in securing Commonwealth protection.

That naming process concludes this weekend with a celebration at Büsst's old home, Ninney Rise, and an expedition to what are now known as John Büsst Reefs.

1967: The year the reef was nearly bulldozed This is a story about a farmer, an artist, Harold Holt, and the dawn of Great Barrier Reef conservation.

"It must have been a huge undertaking to take on government with very little information," Dr Smith said.

" He persevered, he built a coalition, he got some good science behind him and he won. "

Ahead of his time

Büsst's death in 1971, at the age of 62, came four years too early for him to see former prime minister Gough Whitlam declare the Great Barrier Reef one of the world's largest protected marine areas.

Acclaimed marine scientist Charlie Veron said Büsst, along with the late Judith Wright, was "essential" in championing the reef's protection when academics did not.

Fish and coral at Ellison Reef on the Great Barrier Reef, off Mission Beach. (Supplied: Australian Institute of Marine Science)

"If scientists had done that at the time, things would've moved quicker, I would think," Dr Veron said.

"But there were very few scientists who were able to speak out about the Great Barrier Reef."

Dr Smith said Büsst's campaign pre-dated the dive tourism industry and institutions like the Australian Institute of Marine Science and James Cook University.

"It was actually some of John's ideas that helped form those amazing organisations," he said.

From left to right: John Büsst's wife, Allison, prime minister Harold Holt, an unknown man and Mr Holt's wife, Zara. (Supplied: Friends of Ninney Rise)

Dr Smith said Büsst was also instrumental in campaigning for protection of Far North Queensland's tropical lowland rainforest.

" Every schoolkid, I believe, should know about what he did and how he did it. "

Dr Smith said he would remember Büsst's legacy this weekend while diving in the waters that now, officially, bear his name.

"That's where the magic happens: when you put your head underwater, you look at the coral, you look at the fish, maybe we'll even see a shark," he said.

"[You] go, 'Wow, this is really special.'

"And thanks to … John Büsst's actions 60 years ago, we're enjoying this today."

World.title: Fine line between boxing and barbarism breached in 'frightening' KO
World.content:
The reaction from those watching the replays of Nelson Asofa-Solomona's sickening knockout of Paul Gallen speaks volumes.

Former Cronulla Sharks teammate of Gallen, Michael Ennis, looked desperately shaken as he admitted he found it hard to watch.

Tim Tszyu called it "frightening".

In real time, it was even worse.

"Oh jeez, oh no!" cried experienced caller Ben Damon on Main Event's commentary as the footage showed Asofa-Solomona's fist detonating onto Gallen's expressionless features.

"The last one was the worst one boys," Danny Green cried.

"That was the one he didn't need, he added, as Damon said, "that's no good," over the top of him.

"The last one was a bad one," Green reiterated.

"That's hard to watch," a shaken Damon summarised.

Nelson Asofa-Solomona crushed Paul Gallen inside the opening round. (Supplied: No Limit Boxing)

The fight only lasted two minutes and 56 seconds.

In that time, Asofa-Solomona both proved he was capable of taking another step in his quest to climb boxing's Penrose stairs, and similarly unsuitable to do so.

After a steady start, a thunderous right hand from Asofa-Solomona staggered the 45-year-old Gallen back towards the ropes.

Then another left-right combination put him right back against them.

Asofa-Solomona saw Gallen's head roll back, his arms flailing and glimpsed the opening for an upper cut.

He promptly delivered, landing a blow with such hideous force that Gallen was sent to the brink of unconsciousness.

A second upper cut unquestionably delivered him into that foul abyss.

Paul Gallen was left stricken on the canvas. (Supplied: No Limit Boxing)

But Asofa-Solomona wasn't done.

An unnecessary third grazed Gallen's granite chin as he sank to a seated position, his legs folded under him like a grotesquely discarded marionette.

Still, Asofa-Solomona wasn't done.

As referee Chris Condon threw himself between the fighters, a black-shirted angel of deliverance from the punishment Gallen had already endured for too long, Asofa-Solomona aimed another, sickening blow into the head of his stricken rival.

Few will understand this sanctimonious sermonising about such a despicable blow taking place amidst the wanton violence of a boxing bout.

This was boxing, wasn't it?

Hadn't Paulo Aokuso landed such a sweetly-timed left hand onto the head of Mobin Khahrazeh earlier in the night that it had observers positively purring?

Paulo Aokuso delivered a lauded statement KO in his bout. (No Limit)

Isn't it the point to knock your opponent out, to inflict such damage to a fellow human's brain that they lose consciousness in the pursuit of entertainment?

Yes, oddly enough, it is.

But even within the sanctioned barbarism of modern blood sports, there are rules in place to limit the hurt inflicted on a helpless opponent without being accused of hypocrisy.

It's there in almost every rule book you can care to find.

For example, the Australian National Boxing Federation:

55. Some fouls for which a referee may penalise or disqualify a boxer are: (a) Hitting an opponent who is down or is rising from a knockdown.

There can be caveats.

It took eight seconds from the first of those crushing Asofa-Solomona punches to land before referee Condon stopped the fight, but the four punishing upper cuts all came in the space of two-and-a-half horrific seconds.

It's barely enough time for anyone to react, not least a man who is on the charge and fighting for his future as a novice boxer.

But Gallen was clearly down.

Not only that, he was clearly out.

Nelson Asofa-Solomona delivered a devastating quartet of upper cuts. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Hundreds of boxers around the world have learned when enough is enough and to stop.

Hitting an unconscious opponent is beyond the pale, an unacceptable sin that breaches the unique brotherhood two fighters join when touching gloves with one another in the squared circle.

But Asofa-Solomona was clearly fired up.

His ill-advised leap into the crowd moments later proved that.

There is a caveat there, too.

Although making no illusion to it in the ring, Asofa-Solomona added context to his mad dash towards a punter in his post-fight press conference, telling reporters at the TikTok Entertainment Centre that he had been subject to a racist taunt.

Nelson Asofa-Solomona was heckled by someone in the crowd and lowered himself to challenge them directly. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"Someone was doing an ape gesture. I stood on the ropes and it looked like someone threw something at me," he was reported as saying.

"If I had my time back, I would, because that's not on. But what that guy did to me, in terms of that gesture, is not on either.

"I'd just seen red."

Nobody should ever be subject to such foul, vindictive and uneducated slop and nobody should ever deign to suggest how someone should react if they are.

But his calamitous dash into the not-so-cheap seats added to the chaotic conclusion of the fight, meaning his indiscretion at its sickening conclusion was largely overlooked.

Asofa-Solomona proved to most onlookers that he has some skill in a ring on Friday night.

But the next time he delivers a knockout blow, he'd do well to stop before he risks inflicting any further damage.

World.title: Endangered crayfish return home months after Victorian bushfires
World.content:
In a rugged corner of Victoria's High Country, two scientists are making their way slowly through fire-scarred bushland that is slowly returning to life.

They are travelling with precious cargo: a group of endangered alpine spiny crayfish that are heading back to their home waterway near Lucyvale.

Tree canopy is recovering at Lucyvale after 2026 bushfires. (ABC News: Erin Somerville)

The scientists were here in the immediate aftermath of the January bushfires that tore through the region, and they salvaged 11 endangered crayfish that were at risk of suffocating in the stream from debris and sediment.

The alpine spiny crayfish are restricted in their movement and found in small, isolated pockets that make it tricky for scientists to find, adding to the pressure of rescue efforts as water quality declines after a fire.

"If they aren't rescued they can disappear from these areas," Arthur Rylah Institute senior scientist Will Sowersby said.

Scientists prepare to capture alpine spiny crayfish. (ABC News: Erin Somerville)

The alpine spiny crayfish were taken to the Snobs Creek conservation hatchery, which is run by the Victorian Fisheries Authority near Eildon, where they were cared for until water quality improved post-bushfires.

It is the first time the endangered species has been taken into captivity, and it proved a learning curve for staff.

"It's a new process for us," Snobs Creek's senior conservation hatchery officer Dylan White said.

"They are a bit feisty so we have had to separate them, and we have kept them separate this whole time because they will attack each other."

Spiny crayfish being weighed at Snobs Creek hatchery. (ABC News: Andrew Mangelsdorf )

Giving nature a hand

As the Victorian High Country starts to spring back to life from the Walwa-River Road bushfire that burnt around 121,000 hectares, scientists are continuing to monitor the alpine spiny crayfish's habitat and ponder their future.

Loading...

Conservationists hope the endangered crayfish can be included in a future captive breeding program at the Snobs Creek hatchery to help bolster numbers and geographical diversity.

But with another summer on the horizon, Mr Sowersby predicts their work is far from over.

"We know that bushfires are increasing in their frequency and their intensity, so we suspect it's going to be more and more important that we rescue species post-bushfire and that we also establish new populations to (prevent) the risk of an extinction event due to a catastrophic fire," he said.

A hub at the hatchery

It has been a busy year for Snobs Creek hatchery staff who carry out important conservation work with vulnerable species, especially after natural disasters.

Dylan White is surrounded by rare species at the hatchery. (ABC News: Andrew Mangelsdorf)

"Most of these species we have here are so critically endangered they have never been kept in captivity before, so it's really new for everyone," Mr White said.

"The important thing is we are experienced and we are putting that knowledge and skill set towards caring for them and learning more about them."

Some of the species at the facility are found nowhere else in the world.

That includes a special type of galaxias fish that only exists in a sole tributary of the La Trobe River after experiencing a major population collapse in the past decade, and the critically endangered blackfish that were rescued after bushfires tore through the Grampians region.

A blackfish at Snobs Creek hatchery. (ABC News: Andrew Mangesldorf)

Some species rescued after Victoria's summer bushfires have already been re-released, including more than 100 Macquarie perch and trout cod taken from Seven Creek after the Longwood bushfire.

"It was quite challenging to look after a large number of trout cod at the same time due to their aggressive nature …took up a lot of space," Snobs Creek head of fish production Chris Mullins said.

The species' stay at the facility can be hard work for staff, who have to manage unique diets, water temperature, lighting, and behavioural issues.

Scientists comb an alpine stream for endangered species. (ABC News: Erin Somerville)

With Australia predicted to face more natural disaster as climate change progresses, staff value the significance of the hatchery.

"Every year (natural disasters) seems to be getting more and more, so we have got to have a facility here that we can take some of these species as quickly as we can," Mr White said.

"If we weren't doing it no one would be."

World.title: Trump to replace chief of staff with hardline deputy Stephen Miller
World.content:
Donald Trump has announced that his chief of staff Susie Wiles will be replaced by her hardline deputy Stephen Miller on Monday.

The US president made the announcement on Friday, local time, in a social media post.

Mr Trump thanked Ms Wiles for doing an "outstanding job" and said she would move to a different role in his "political operation".

In reality, the switch sidelines one of his most senior staff members, whom he said as recently as last month had "zero chance" of replacing.

White House chief of staff Susie Wiles will leave the chief of staff role. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

"I want to thank her for her service as chief of staff," Mr Trump's post read. "She has done a great job!"

Later, Mr Trump told reporters at the White House he "wanted to make a change".

It has been widely speculated on Capitol Hill that Mr Trump would reshuffle his administration after his Republican Party's disastrous performance at this week's midterm elections.

The GOP lost control of both the House and Senate in what has been described as an emphatic rebuke of Mr Trump's second term so far.

In March, Ms Wiles announced she would be taking time away from her role after being diagnosed with breast cancer.

Conservative voices, including former MAGA heavyweight Steve Bannon, have previously called for Ms Wiles to resign, although more moderate Republicans view her as a stabilising force in the White House.

Analysts have told the ABC they believe Mr Trump's administration lost its way after Ms Wiles's health battle began.

Loading

"Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honour of a lifetime," Ms Wiles said in a social media post on Friday, local time.

"I'm so proud to have been a part of what we've accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First."

Mr Miller is best known as the architect of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.

The 41-year-old has long helped shape immigration policy in the GOP.

He was Mr Trump's chief immigration advisor during the president's first term.

Before that, Mr Miller worked for Senator Jeff Sessions, who was renowned as one of the chamber's loudest and most uncompromising voices on the subject.

Most recently, Mr Miller has driven the push for mass deportations, pressing ICE leadership to raise arrest numbers and publicly telling officers they would have "federal immunity in the conduct of your duties".

"Stephen gets it, he'll do a great job," Mr Trump said.

World.title: Convicted rapist Brand facing at least four more investigations
World.content:
If Russell Brand was at all worried about being found guilty in his four-week rape and sexual assault trial, he was not showing it.

I was standing a few people behind the British actor and comedian in the queue for security checks outside London's Southwark Crown Court on Wednesday, when he broke briefly into song.

"Sweet Caroline," he sang to a woman beside him in the line, quoting the famous Neil Diamond hit.

The woman had introduced herself to the star as Caroline, and the pair chatted jovially while waiting to move forward.

Inside court, just minutes later, the jury began its second day of deliberations.

Loading...

On other mornings, as Brand was greeted at court by a flurry of camera flashes, journalists asked how he was feeling.

"Blessed," was always the reply.

Throughout the trial, the comedian-turned-born-again Christian influencer continued to make social media videos with his wife, Laura, for their millions of followers.

As the court heard harrowing, graphic and often tearful accounts from Brand's six accusers, he did not flinch.

When he gave evidence himself, he did so standing up unnaturally straight.

Russell Brand giving evidence during his trial. (Reuters: Julia Quenzler)

At crunch time — when the guilty verdicts were read out on Thursday — the comedian stood to attention like a soldier on parade and showed no emotion.

When his lawyer applied for bail ahead of sentencing on Monday, he said his client wanted time to say goodbye to his wife and three children over the weekend.

Outside court and in, this was a defendant who did not seem to think he would go to jail.

Entitled entertainer who used women

Brand has been on trial since mid-October for seven historical sex offences relating to six women spanning a decade from 1999 to 2009.

After eight and a half hours of deliberations, the jury of four women and eight men found him guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

British newspapers cover the opening of Russell Brand's sexual assault trial. (ABC News: Alex Parsons)

He was acquitted of a further two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

On the steps of Southwark Crown Court afterwards, police praised the "extraordinary courage, resilience and determination" of the women, while pulling no punches about Brand.

"Russell Brand used his influence, status, and fame to prey on and exploit women. As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement," Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy, from London's Metropolitan Police Service, said.

" I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be. "

New details about high-profile trial

During the trial, journalists could only report what was said and done in front of the jury, but with verdicts returned and restrictions lifted, we can now give more detail from one of the most high-profile criminal trials in recent British history.

Brand is no longer a mainstream comedian and actor, and instead styles himself as a Christian influencer, broadcasting online prayer videos and sermons to millions.

Russell Brand was found guilty of raping a woman at his house in 2009. (Supplied: Metropolitan Police)

His faith was on full public display from day one of the trial. When he was first shown into the dock before jury selection, he went down on one knee and appeared to pray.

During the trial he wore crucifixes of different sizes, he sometimes carried a bible with sticky notes marking pages, and at least one day he was handling what looked like prayer beads.

Unusually for a defendant in a criminal trial, he posted repeatedly on social media — not about the evidence but about his feelings, his faith, and his disdain for the mainstream media.

It can now be reported that Brand's legal team tried to have the case thrown out, before the trial had even begun because of negative press about him.

Brand tells jury friends won't defend him over sex crime allegations Russell Brand told the court he did not commit the crimes and believed sexual consent was "fundamental, essential, necessary" and "more important than sex itself".

Barrister Ian Winter KC argued his client could not receive a fair trial because of 2023 media reports with allegations about Brand — allegations that prompted the women who would ultimately be the complainants in this trial to come forward.

Mr Winter's application was denied, but he would go on to say during the trial that the 2023 reporting had "poisoned the well".

The 2023 allegations in the media were not part of the trial.

In an extraordinary moment in the corridor at the end of proceedings, Mr Winter launched a tirade at Sunday Times Chief News Correspondent Rosamund Urwin, who worked on the 2023 investigation.

"I hope you are pleased with yourself," Mr Winter said.

Ms Urwin responded that she was "pleased justice has been done".

Mr Winter replied, "Well, it wasn't. You f***** it. Congratulations."

On Friday, the top silk reported the exchange to the Bar Standards Board.

Photographers greeted British actor and comedian Russell Brand and his wife Laura at court every day of the trial. (Reuters: Toby Melville)

There were other moments of courtroom drama during the trial.

On day one, lawyers for People Magazine in the US were hauled before Judge Joel Bennathan to explain why the magazine had reported the attempt to have the case thrown out, when a court order had been made to keep that out of the public domain.

Judge Bennathan then put journalists in court and beyond on notice that he would not be lenient if there were further contempt of court risks.

Another day, police arrested a blogger who had identified one of Brand's accusers, all of whom are granted lifelong anonymity by the court.

The man, who had been sitting in the spillover court watching proceedings on a large video screen, was detained for 12 hours, cautioned, and forced to amend his blog posts.

Police appeal for other women to come forward

There are more allegations about Brand that we can now report too.

The Metropolitan Police revealed its detectives are currently investigating allegations of rape from two more women in the UK, while there are two civil claims afoot against Brand relating to his time in the US.

Metropolitan Police Commissioner Mark Rowley said more accusors were likely to come forward. (Reuters: Chris J. Ratcliffe)

The head of Scotland Yard, Sir Mark Rowley, has said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations. He has appealed for them to do so.

Brand, meanwhile, is spending his first weekend behind bars.

Judge Bennathan denied his bail application saying that while he regrets the impact on the 51-year-old's children, their father had the resources to be a flight risk.

Russell Brand during one of his police interviews. (Supplied: Metropolitan Police)

"I think there are substantial grounds to fear he might in the end not feel able to come along and face his sentence," Judge Bennathan said.

The verdict marks a massive fall from grace for the entertainer; once a swaggering exhibitionist performing to huge crowds, now a convicted rapist in a prison cell.

For the rape and three sexual assaults he was found guilty of this week, Brand will be sentenced on Monday.

The judge has already flagged the rape conviction alone will mean a "significant custodial sentence".

New York: President Donald Trump has named hardline homeland security adviser Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles just three days after the Republicans’ midterm election rout. Trump said Miller, currently a deputy to Wiles and “one of my most trusted advisers”, would start in the top job on Monday. White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller. AP “Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff,” the president wrote on Truth Social. There had been mounting speculation in recent weeks that Wiles would leave the White House and that Trump was sounding out potential replacements.



Miller, a long-time Trump adviser, was a key architect of the Trump administration’s crackdown on illegal and irregular immigration. He is widely regarded as one of the most hardline, conservative figures in the administration, particularly on border security, immigration and American nationalism. Miller was homeland security adviser and the deputy chief of staff for policy at the White House. AP Photo/Alex Brandon The 41-year-old is a ruthless political operative, highly active in the media, and known for his vicious, often hyperbolic attacks on Democrats and the left, which frequently involve accusations of electoral “cheating”. “The Democrats have nominate[d] a slate of candidates who are all extremists, freaks and America-hating lunatics,” he wrote on X two days before the midterm election. “The entire Democrat agenda is humiliating, subjugating and dispossessing Americans.”



Miller’s style contrasts with that of the departing Wiles, a veteran political operative from Florida, who was credited with running a far more stable and united White House than in Trump’s first term. Susie Wiles, a veteran political operative and aide to Donald Trump, will depart the White House for a “political role”. AP Wiles rarely spoke publicly, preferring to remain behind the scenes. She previously said she viewed her role as facilitating the president’s vision, not trying to control or influence his agenda. “Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honour of a lifetime,” she said on Friday (US time). “I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.

World.title: Zach wanted to prevent childhood blindness. Now his sights are set on millions of patients
World.content:
NationalQueenslandMedicine Zach wanted to prevent childhood blindness. Now his sights are set on millions of patients Courtney Kruk November 7, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It was there in plain sight for Dr Zachary Tan. A career in medicine? Or in technology? Enrolling in the University of Queensland’s School of Medicine, he pursued a field that would satisfy both his passions. “I’m a huge nerd,” Tan says. Dr Zachary Tan co-founded Optain Health, a global software and medical technology company using AI to screen for eye conditions. “I was always drawn to ophthalmology because of the large role technology has to play in transforming that area of medicine, both in how we diagnose and treat eye diseases.



“But like so many areas of healthcare, the challenge of ophthalmology is really around access.” Related Article Research Bhabisara’s blood is so rare, most people have never heard of it. Soon it could be grown in this Brisbane lab A little more than a decade after accepting his graduation certificate, Tan now sits at the helm of a company that’s raised $US50 million, and has ambitions to revolutionise access to eye care and retinal disease detection. Tan is speaking from his apartment in New York, where he splits his time between Brisbane. “One of my favourite anecdotes that I like to share with my American colleagues is Queensland is 2½ times the size of Texas.



“People with eye diseases don’t just live in Brisbane; they’re spread all throughout the state,” he says. “And something I’ve been so passionate about since my medical school days is: how can we use technology to really democratise access to ophthalmology services?” Tan hasn’t wasted time trying to answer that question. Optain Health’s device combines technology and AI to screen for common eye diseases. While studying, he helped develop an AI algorithm to screen for retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), a disorder that can cause blindness in premature babies.



The project centred on bringing screening services to patients, particularly in remote areas, rather than requiring them to travel to specialists. Related Article Healthcare Doctors almost sent Kris home with a migraine. Then her whole face went numb This idea became the genesis for Optain Health, a global medical device and software company that uses AI to screen for common retinal diseases, including glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration and cardiovascular disease. Since Tan co-founded the company three years ago, its screening tool is now installed in 500 sites around the world, including Queensland. “In the past 12 months, we screened 150,000 patients and 20,000 patients with some form of disease,” he says.



“I think the potential is huge for AI in healthcare … and one of the things that I feel really passionate about is clinicians having a front-row seat in shaping how we use AI in healthcare.” Related Article AI Your GP is probably already using AI. Now it could talk to you about your medicines When Tan joined UQ’s School of Medicine – an institution that recently celebrated its 90th year – AI was an esoteric concept in contrast to its modern application. But even back then, Tan says the school fostered “a feeling of possibility”. “You could build technology or do research and not just have that be in a lab, but able to translate, from bench-to-bedside,” he explains. “And 2010 was really when we started to see the incredible impacts of Gardasil, the HPV [human papillomavirus] vaccine, which was invented at UQ.



“You’d have your professors and teachers giving lectures, but these were the same people who had functionally now cured cervical cancer.” Tan likens Optain’s tabletop screening tool to an Oculus, the headsets used to create virtual reality. Inside is a fast-working robotic camera that can capture retinal images in less than a minute. “Based off these images, we have specially trained AI, which has been approved by the TGA [Therapeutic Goods Administration], which can look at the different features in the image to provide us with a diagnosis at the point of care.” University of Queensland alumni Tan and Dr Mark Loane in New York. University of Queensland School of Medicine About a week ago, former Wallabies captain and prominent eye surgeon Dr Mark Loane visited Tan in New York, peering into the device to test the technology for himself.



Loane, another UQ alumnus, has spent more than 40 years treating eye conditions, and is renowned for his work in regional and remote Queensland. In 2014, Tan introduced Loane when he presented UQ’s Errol Solomon Meyers Memorial Lecture – a reflection on 20 years of remote eye health. “In the 1980s we had the digital revolution, and ophthalmology itself really benefited from all of that,” Loane says. “Much of the resolution of problems has already been invented, so now it’s about how do you roll out those delivery systems to people all over country … to provincial areas of Queensland or Australia? “[Zachary] has come a long way from 2014 … to meeting again, where he is starting to wrestle with many of the questions which I asked in that lecture about how we deliver services to populations of people and in remote areas. It’s a wondrous closing of circles.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Meghan’s father Thomas Markle charged with possessing child sexual abuse material
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaCrime Meghan’s father Thomas Markle charged with possessing child sexual abuse material Michael Koziol Updated November 7, 2026 — 5:34am ,first published 2:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. New York: Federal US agents have arrested Thomas Markle snr – the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex and wife of Prince Harry – and charged him with possessing child sexual abuse material. Markle, 82, was arrested in Florida on Friday morning (US time) and appeared in court in Tampa later the same day. If convicted, he could face up to 20 years in prison. Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, and her estranged father Thomas Markle snr. AP A criminal complaint alleges Markle possessed “sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls in two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for nearly two decades”, the Department of Justice said. In a court affidavit, a special agent with the FBI said the bureau received reports from different witnesses last month. One witness, understood to be Markle’s son, said they had discovered suspected child sexual abuse material among Markle’s possessions in the Philippines, where he had been living.



Another witness told the FBI that Markle rented a storage unit in California. When the FBI raided two such units registered to Markle since 2008, they discovered suspected child sexual abuse material in both, the affidavit said. Officers found and seized approximately 78 items, including slides, film negatives and books. Some of the film negatives were converted into colour digital photographs and found to contain suspected child sexual abuse material. The affidavit contained detailed descriptions of some of the images, which allegedly featured pre-pubescent girls. “To date, I have identified approximately 18 images that appeared to constitute child pornography,” the FBI agent said in the affidavit. “The investigation is active and ongoing.”



Bill Essayli, assistant US attorney for the Central District of California, said three of the images described in the affidavit featured Markle and minor victims. “These allegations are serious and disturbing,” he said. “We intend to prosecute Markle to the fullest extent of federal law.” The October 24 front page of The Sun, which carried a report of the allegations against Markle snr. Getty Images British tabloid The Sun reported last month that Markle’s son, Thomas Markle jnr, had reported his estranged father to authorities in the Philippines for allegedly possessing “hundreds, if not thousands” of underage sexual images in four large boxes at his home in Cebu. Meghan Markle recently said she was “deeply distressed” by those allegations. She also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about him had been sent to London police in 2018.





Markle jnr told The Sun in October that he reported the images to police in the Philippines and contacted the FBI. “I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years - but that stops now,” he told the newspaper. “I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.” Meghan recently said she had been given assurances that the “troubling and disturbing allegations” made about her father in a letter to London police in 2018 were investigated at the time. “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them.” With AP, Sarah McPhee Read more royal news:

World.title: Victorian election hot seats: Melbourne’s west promised $400m in new transport services
World.content:
For people living in Melbourne’s fast-growing western suburbs, one of the most common and longest-running complaints has been a lack of buses, with some schoolchildren facing half-hour walks to the nearest stop – and an additional wait for a service to show up.

For Sydenham locals, Labor’s $400 million pledge to rewrite west Melbourne’s bus routes with services running on key routes every 10 minutes if re-elected on November 28, will no doubt be appealing.

Under the proposal, about two thirds of pre-existing routes will be upgraded to ‘turn-up-and-go’ services, with a bus promised every 10 minutes, seven days a week. Labor will also create a series of new routes across the west that will connect to train stations.

World.title: How to turn your Christmas shopping into 55,000 frequent flyer points
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingLoyalty programs Opinion How to turn your Christmas shopping into 55,000 frequent flyer points Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor November 7, 2026 — 5:10am

November 7, 2026 — 5:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It’s just under six weeks to Christmas, a fact that might be as distressing as last week’s interest rate rise was for mortgage holders. But this year – just in time for Christmas – I’ve honed my points hacking, and I’m ready to start stacking them from the silly season. It’s a simple strategy: buy gift cards that come with a bonus points offer and use them, instead of cash, to buy things. Indeed, you can start in the Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales, when Aussie shoppers are expected to spend an average of $346, an increase of $22 from last year’s event, according to Shopify. Gift cards might be the new best way to stack frequent flyer points. Let me add the crucial upfront caveat, as I often do, that this is for money that you were going to spend anyway. As if any of us has any to spare! But with necessary, planned spend, why not deploy my proven tactics this year to max the points hacks? Visa/Mastercard gift cards – 10,000 points

Now, this is not my favourite strategy but let’s start here and work up to the best; the reason is that these gift cards charge a $5.75 to $7.95 activation fee per card. Any fee comprehensively erodes the value of the points you earn.



The advantage of these cards, though, is that they can be redeemed just about anywhere. But let’s back up and explain that the common theme in the gift-card hack is to buy them on boosted points. It’s simply adding an interim step that nets you cherry-on-top potential travel. The other thing to realise is that sweet new gift-card deals come up all the time. After the expensive Christmas season, the gift-card points hack could see you with a motherlode of points. For example, a few months ago I snared Visa gift cards for 10 times the number of points per dollar spent – 10,000 points for $1000. Apple gift cards – 20,000 points

Now we move into the straight-up sweet deals with no activation fees. I upgraded my iPhone a few months ago. But I waited and watched first. What I waited and watched for was a very common – indeed, often every two months – deal where Apple gift cards offer points up to 20 times the dollar value.



Sometimes you need to purchase them in person, rather than online. There are usually limits on how many you can buy, so be sure to always read the fine print on any gift-card deal. I only purchased $1000 worth, so only received 20,000 points. But, in fact, I could have doubled that if I’d used gift cards to pay the cost of the phone in full. These can be redeemed even for Apple subscriptions on apple.com. You can use up to eight gift cards per purchase, and it’s really an easy process. Multipurpose, multi-merchant gift cards – 22,250

There are a bunch of these that often go on bonus points, up to 20 times again. I have just bought replacement furniture for my daughter’s decrepit old bedroom setting. But I did so only after I could snare gift cards that worked at IKEA, under the brand Ultimate Home. These are also on offer for other multi-merchant products, such as those grouped for Her/Him/Kids. There are hundreds of retailers in such gift-card grouping. The limit this time was $250 per Flybuys account because this deal was just so generous: 2000 bonus points per gift card, even on low $50 denominations. So I bagged 10,250 points (which includes the base $1 per point rate) for $250 spend.



That wasn’t enough to purchase the furniture, so I lurked a little longer and waited for IKEA cards themselves to go on bonus – then I also purchased three $200 dollar cards at 20 times points: 12,000. So the transactions all up netted me 22,250 Flybuys points. Editor's pick Opinion

Superannuation Super funds are finally overhauling retirement. Here’s what’s changing Bec Wilson Money contributor But note that unlike with a straight 20 times points deal, as with Apple above, with 20,000 points from $1000 spend, these 22,250 points were only for parting with $850. Everyday Wish gift cards – 3000 points

It is also often possible to purchase grocery vouchers themselves, for say three times points from the grocery store itself of via Qantas Marketplace (and watch the latter for other gift-card deals too). I bought $1000 worth of Everyday Rewards cards a few months back for triple points. Extra hacks to stack points

Of course, when you pay for gift cards at a supermarket, you need to swipe your rewards membership card to get any offered bonus points. (And realise that when you buy groceries with a grocery gift card, you also get the points on offer on your purchases, so long as you swipe.)



And, if you have such a thing, the gift cards themselves could be purchased with frequent flyer credit cards, to add whatever you accrue per dollar spent. That’s the triple stack that true points hackers love. How many points did I earn? 55,250 in just a few months. These gift card deals are common, changing weekly, often advertised in the supermarket’s physical catalogue or the digital version (check the apps) only. So after the expensive Christmas season, the gift-card points hack could see you with a motherlode of points – which you can use for money off future shopping – too. Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon is author of How to Get Mortgage-Free Like Me, available at nicolessmartmoney.com. Follow her on Facebook, X and Instagram. World.title: Super funds are finally overhauling retirement. Here’s what’s changing
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementSuperannuation Opinion Super funds are finally overhauling retirement. Here’s what’s changing Bec Wilson Money contributor November 7, 2026 — 5:09am

November 7, 2026 — 5:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

There are currently between 150,000 and 200,000 Aussies entering retirement every year, as the Baby Boomers and the Gen Xers converge on this exciting stage of life. That’s potentially 2 million people who are heading towards some of the biggest financial decisions of their lives, often with a blindfold on. And I need to tell you the truth. If you leave retirement planning until you’re 65, by the time you’re sitting down with an adviser or your super fund, many of your biggest retirement decisions have effectively already been made for you, whether you like it or not. The way you interact with your super is getting a refresh. Simon Letch How much you have saved, how your money has been invested, and how much choice you have about your lifestyle in the years before and after, all matter earlier. You might not have consciously made those choices, but by putting them off, you’ve narrowed your options. That’s why I think more Australians need to understand their pre-retirement and retirement choices earlier, get help to work out what they can do to improve their position, and have the confidence to act while they still have time to make a difference.



But that requires two things: better quality advice that really does act in the consumers’ best interests, and super funds that step up and provide practical, affordable retirement planning services, and good support for people who don’t need or can’t afford to be paying thousands of dollars a year on comprehensive advice. Particularly when that advice may come with a recommendation to moving their money onto an investment platform with ongoing adviser fees. For many Australians retiring in the next decade, retirement income will come from a combination of super and the age pension. And, there’s some encouraging news on that front. Over the last 12 months, some of Australia’s super funds have made significant improvements to the help they’re offering members approaching and entering retirement. And if you’re within 10 years of retirement, it’s worth knowing what’s changing because some of these services could make a real difference to the choices you have ahead of you. The improvements have become clear through the annual assessments for the Epic Retirement Tick, which I developed in partnership with research house, Chant West, who independently assesses the funds.



Until recently, most Australians have had little or no understanding of the services their super funds have offered, let alone what they could reasonably expect. But that’s changing, and consumers are gaining more power to demand better help too. Editor's pick Opinion

Superannuation Millions of retirees are paying super tax they could avoid Bec Wilson Money contributor We’re seeing better retirement education, with funds moving beyond the old-fashioned, poorly attended super seminars and boring technical websites towards more engaging online webinars, courses and structured education programs that help people better understand their choices. There are more videos, more real life case studies, and less dense text to wade through. There’s also a welcome improvement in age pension education. More funds are creating dedicated sections on their website explaining how the age pension works, who might qualify and how it interacts with super and what people need to think about when applying. This is important, and it recognises that for many Australians retiring in the next decade, retirement income will come from a combination of super and the age pension and understanding one without the other isn’t enough.



We’re also seeing more useful online retirement planning tools, where you can experiment with different scenarios, test what happens if you retire earlier or later, explore the impact of going part-time before you stop working altogether, and see how your super and the age pension might work together to provide an income throughout retirement. These aren’t just tools for people who are about to retire. They’re potentially even more valuable if we could get them into people’s hands 5 or 10 years beforehand, when you’ve still got time to do something with what you learn. And importantly, more funds are introducing calculators specifically for people who are already retired. These help retirees understand how long their savings might last, what happens if they increase or decrease their spending and how their income might change over time. It’s a crucial improvement because retirement planning shouldn’t stop the day you retire. People need help managing retirement, not just help getting into it. Another really encouraging development is the growing availability of more affordable retirement advice from funds. Some funds are expanding their digital advice services, while others are making it much easier to speak to someone about retirement income, investment choices and how the age pension might fit into your plans.



Some are also starting to recognise that retirement planning is most often a household decision for anyone who is not single, and are finding ways to include a partner’s circumstances. Editor's pick Opinion

Money psychology Why working harder won’t make you rich – and what to do instead Paridhi Jain Money contributor This stuff matters because frankly, not everyone needs an expensive and comprehensive financial plan. Sometimes you just need help to understand whether you can afford to retire at 62 instead of 65, whether you should change your investment mix, or how much income you could realistically expect to draw from your savings alongside the age pension you might be eligible for. There’s also been some pretty decent improvements behind the scenes in some funds on complaints handling and call centre services. Funds are putting more resources into making it easier for members to speak to someone who can actually help, get questions answered and navigate the paperwork and processes involved. And when things go wrong, we’re seeing improvements in how quickly complaints are handled and resolved, rather than leaving members waiting weeks for answers.



Importantly, there’s much more attention being paid to fraud and cybersecurity risk this year. Knowing your fund has strong cybersecurity protections and multifactor authentication might not be the most exciting part of retirement planning, but with AI making scams more sophisticated, you want to know your life savings are properly protected. But not everything is moving as quickly - funds are taking much longer to develop more sophisticated digital advice offerings and lifetime income retirement products. Ian Fryer, general manager of Chant West, says he expects considerably more activity in these areas over the next two years. And there’s one area where there’s clearly more work to be done: helping people who are retiring and are already retired know how much they can afford to spend. Too many retirees simply draw the legislated minimum drawdown when they could comfortably afford more. Funds are getting better at providing calculators, but relatively few are proactively helping members make those spending decisions. So, if you’re within 10 years of retirement, don’t wait until you’re ready to stop working to find out what your super fund offers. Get onto its website, explore the tools, book in for some education and ask what else is available. You might be surprised by how much you can do now to improve your retirement later.



Bec Wilson, bestselling author of How to Have an Epic Retirement, is a retirement educator and founder of the Epic Retirement Institute. She writes a weekly newsletter about modern retirement at au.epicretirement.net. She has various commercial arrangements with a range of organisations, including superannuation funds.
