World.title: Trump is a false idol and his local franchisee is dumping the brand
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS election Opinion Trump is a false idol and his local franchisee is dumping the brand Peter Hartcher Political and international editor November 7, 2026 — 5:04am

November 7, 2026 — 5:04am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Barnaby Joyce was planning to make the pilgrimage to the Mar-a-Lago shrine to Donald Trump midyear. He’d been invited on an all-expenses-paid trip. His wife, Vikki Campion, had another idea. Woolbrook Public School was due to hold its community barbecue at the local Bunnings and Barnaby and Vikki were rostered to work it. “Your children go to Woolbrook Public School,” Barnaby recounts Vikki telling him. “You’re not going.” He cancelled the trip to the US. Pauline Hanson has taken many of her cues from Donald Trump. Are those days over? Michael Howard Now that the American electorate has repudiated Trump, the decision is looking especially smart. The national swing against his Republican Party across all House elections tallied to 8 per cent, according to the News24 numbers man Tom Connell. For scale, that’s double the size of the swings in the previous three US midterms. The last time there was a swing of 8 per cent was in reaction to the economic devastation of the global financial crisis, when Barack Obama was in the White House. It’s only the fourth time since World War II that both the US House and Senate have flipped from one party to another in the same midterms.



Donald Trump suddenly is more radioactive than an Iranian nuclear reactor. Across the world, right-wing populist parties are backing away from him. In Australia, Pauline Hanson’s One Nation quickly and quietly removed from its website an article offering itself as the local franchisee of the Trump brand: “Want Trump’s action and style, then it’s One Nation you need”, ran the headline. Reinforcing the close identification was a photoshopped picture of the two great leaders, Hanson and Trump, together. Oops. It must have seemed so clever and exciting at the time it was published, January 23, 2025, the week Trump was inaugurated for his second presidency. Illustration: Matt Davidson The midterms pronounced a harsh verdict on Trump’s affiliated billionaires, too. The Republican billionaires on the ballot, Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio and Rick Jackson in Georgia, lost to Democrats. And Elon Musk’s record campaign funding for Republicans of some half a billion dollars was powerless against the popular will. Musk proved more useful to the Democrats as a loathed campaign target than to Republicans as a generous campaign support. So it’s not surprising that another Australian acolyte of Trump’s, billionaire Gina Rinehart, has gone very quiet since the midterms. In Europe, France’s National Rally, Germany’s AfD, Italy’s The League and Futuro Nazionale parties, and Spain’s Vox all distanced themselves from Trump in comments after the midterms. Neither did Britain’s Nigel Farage of the Reform UK party try to defend the Republicans’ “complete and utter rout”.



Is the right-wing populist franchise bust? Trumplike leaders in five countries have lost national elections in the past year and a half. All were populist right-wingers with autocratic tendencies. All had proudly affiliated themselves with Trump. Related Article Opinion

US midterms Trump crashed on his own shores of discontent, but the blue wave doesn’t deliver certainty Waleed Aly Columnist, author and academic In Poland, Hungary, Serbia and Brazil, the Trumplike leaders failed. Trump’s Brazilian buddy, Flavio Bolsonaro, cried “fraud” and took political asylum in the US. Serbia’s Aleksandar Vučić lost to an upstart student-led movement that didn’t even have a leader. The Student List party had to hold discussions to decide which of them would claim victory on election night. Trump’s Israeli ally, Benjamin Netanyahu, lost his parliamentary majority, though he remains in office while negotiations over a new government continue. “The Trump brand is lost,” says Stanford University political scientist Francis Fukuyama. “Donald Trump has become toxic. No foreign political party is going to want to get close to him. “The main issue that united them was immigration but that’s gotten under control in most areas and it’s no longer the same burning issue. What holds populist nationalist together now is the style, more than anything else, that allows them to be racist and insulting.“



And, in countries where they’ve held power, “these populist parties aren’t good at governing. Hungary used to be one of the richest countries in Europe; Viktor Orban ran it into the ground with cronyism and corruption.” Yet while the Trump franchise may be bust, Fukuyama says that it’s too early to dismiss right-wing populists as a force. He points out that Marine Le Pen is poised to win the presidency of France in April. Italy is due for election next year, too, with potential gains for the far right. “We may have a couple more moves in that direction,” Fukuyama tells me, “but a lot of wind has come out of the sails of the populist nationalists”. The implications in Australia are several. We shouldn’t lose sight of the very big picture. Despite fears to the contrary, liberal democracy is alive and well. The world has been in a “democratic recession” since the global financial crisis. The number of democracies has been shrinking. The Economist Intelligence Unit’s annual democracy index surveys 167 nations and counts only 26 as full democracies. It has not counted the US as a full democracy since 2015; it classifies it as a “flawed democracy”. Trump tested the limits of the system. In his last term and again this term. In the US, elections are administered by the states, as the Constitution stipulates, and not the federal government. But, in recent months, Trump strained to seize election powers from the states so that Washington DC could control the outcome of the midterms. But Congress refused to pass his so-called SAVE America bill. State governors and legislatures resisted his efforts. The courts dismissed Trump’s attempts to litigate his way to control over the ballots. The media remained robustly untamed. The checks and balances were under pressure yet held.



The greatest check, however, was the American public, who turned out strongly and voted decisively. Trump accepted the result. This concession is not personally painful to him. He still has his post, his profile, his billions and opportunities to make billions more, and considerable power. Related Article US midterms ‘The reason is obvious’: Bloodletting begins over Republicans’ electoral wipeout It’s too early to declare US democracy safe. We’ve yet to see how Trump behaves when his time in the White House ends. But, for now, the world’s most important democracy has reasserted its credentials as a functioning democracy. The Democrats now have the opportunity to put “liberal” back into US liberal democracy, by which I don’t mean leftist policies; I mean the restoration of citizens’ rights and constitutional limits on executive power. All of this acts as a deterrent to politicians in other nations, including Australia, to mimic Trump’s worst autocratic instincts. For the Australian political parties? First, One Nation. It realises that it has overstepped. “The core message is that performative charlatanry has a shelf life and will be exposed ultimately,” says politics professor emeritus at Monash University, Paul Strangio. One Nation’s vote share stalled in June. The US midterms “must punch a hole in One Nation to a degree”.



What lessons does Barnaby Joyce’s draw for One Nation? “Don’t go too far,” he tells me, before quoting Tacitus: “From wisdom comes moderation”. Related Article High Court of Australia Pauline Hanson, the High Court and the judges’ war of words Yet the party retains some policies that are far from moderate. Its immigration policy, for instance, promises a net outflow of people for three years. This is impractical for the functioning of the economy. But One Nation’s shuffling embarrassment over its Trump fetish is not any sort of salvation for the Albanese government. Because while Trump’s politics and policies are in another universe to Labor’s, they share one big feature in common – both are incumbents. Incumbency is a liability in a time of inflationary discontent. It is a destroyer of governments. Labor needs to show that it can help to solve inflation, not just find scapegoats for it. “They need to show that they have a plan,” advises Strangio. Senior Labor figures agree. The Liberals are Australia’s biggest potential beneficiaries of this post-midterms politics. As one senior Liberal puts it: “The slavish devotion of some on the Australian political right to right-wing populism – that we must do what they’re doing if we want to win – has been completely blown up.



“The US elections show that economic performance is still the most important credential. The rubbish about Trump being a uniquely gifted politician is exposed. The laws of politics are immutable – if you make people’s lives worse, they will punish you. “To focus on economic competence is a very good pathway for us to take if we want to return to government. We don’t have to do crazy things.” Liberals, get off your knees. Trump is a false idol. And his local franchisee is dumping the brand; you can stop trembling at her feet. Can you recover your standing as the most credible economic manager? The opportunity is before you. Will Barnaby accept a future invitation to Mar-a-Lago? “I’ll have to check the barbecue schedule”. Peter Hartcher is political editor and international editor of The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: A cruise boom is about to hit some of our favourite Asian destinations
World.content:
InspirationCruises A cruise boom is about to hit some of our favourite Asian destinations Brian Johnston November 7, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. This year is proving a treat for Asian cruises, with maiden appearances of ships from companies such as Norwegian Cruise Line and Carnival, more Royal Caribbean itineraries from homeports in Hong Kong and Singapore, and many other cruise lines sailing bumper Asian seasons. British small-ship operator Swan Hellenic sailed into Asia for the first time this year on itineraries to Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, the Philippines, South Korea and Japan. Cruise and river ships continue to extend their reach in Asia including Ha Long Bay, Vietnam. iStock APT Luxury Tours, which has long offered river cruises on the Mekong, launched a luxury three-day cruise experience on Ha Long Bay in Vietnam as part of its extended journeys in the region. Meanwhile, Italian company Explora Journeys is inaugurating Asian journeys in 2027 aboard Explora III. Over the 2027-28 season, the luxury ship will make 28 journeys across Japan, South Korea, China and South-East Asia.



The sailings include overnight stays in key destinations such as Tokyo, Osaka, Hong Kong, Shanghai, Ha Long Bay, Ho Chi Minh City and Bali. 



Oceania Riviera and Oceania Vista will be sailing Asia too. And if you want to splurge, then Silversea’s Silver Muse is sailing a 51-day Grand Voyage across 28 destinations in seven Asian nations. Meanwhile, Silver Cloud is sailing in South-East Asia and Japan. Japan is the destination of the moment and has seen a corresponding surge in cruise operations. Silversea announced its first-ever Japan summer season on voyages to the big port cities but also to lesser-known alternatives such as Akita, Shimizu and Amami Oshima. Related Article Cruises Asian cruise companies are offering fresh alternatives for Aussies The summer season is timed to take in local celebrations such as Kyoto’s Gion Matsuri – one of Japan’s most famous festivals, which features ornate floats – and Tokushima’s Awa Odori, which celebrates dance and music. Windstar’s new ship Star Seeker will sail a maiden Japan season in 2027, and in spring 2028 Seabourn will have several Japan sailings. Also coming up for Seabourn are a new 16-day Shanghai and Seoul cruise, a 12-day Shanghai and Taiwan voyage, and eight South-East Asian itineraries.



All this is just a sampling of the cruise range and choices now available in Asia. Just 4.5 per cent of Australian cruisers holidayed there in 2025, but surely more of us should start looking north.

World.title: Trump promotes hardliner Stephen Miller as new White House chief of staff
World.content:
Breaking WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Trump promotes hardliner Stephen Miller as new White House chief of staff Michael Koziol November 7, 2026 — 6:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. New York: President Donald Trump has named hardline homeland security adviser Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles just three days after the Republicans’ midterm election rout. Trump said Miller, currently the deputy chief of staff for policy and “one of my most trusted advisers”, would start in the top job on Monday. White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller. AP “Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff,” the president wrote on Truth Social. There had been mounting speculation in recent weeks that Wiles would leave the White House and that Trump was sounding out potential replacements.



On Friday, US news outlets including Axios and Semafor reported that Wiles submitted her resignation Thursday night in a reshuffle led by Trump, who put some of the blame for the midterm election drubbing on Wiles. Miller, a long-time Trump adviser, was a key architect of the Trump administration’s crackdown on illegal and irregular immigration. Miller was homeland security adviser and the deputy chief of staff for policy at the White House. AP Photo/Alex Brandon He is widely regarded as one of the most hardline, conservative figures in the administration, particularly on border security, immigration and American nationalism. The 41-year-old is a ruthless political operative, highly active in the media, and known for his vicious, often hyperbolic attacks on Democrats and the left, which frequently involve accusations of electoral “cheating”.



“The Democrats have nominate[d] a slate of candidates who are all extremists, freaks and America-hating lunatics,” he wrote on X two days before the midterm election. “The entire Democrat agenda is humiliating, subjugating and dispossessing Americans.” Miller’s style contrasts with that of the departing Wiles, a veteran political operative from Florida, who was credited with running a far more stable and united White House than in Trump’s first term. Susie Wiles, a veteran political operative and aide to Donald Trump, will depart the White House for a “political role”. AP Wiles rarely spoke publicly, preferring to remain behind the scenes. She previously said she viewed her role as facilitating the president’s vision, not trying to control or influence his agenda. “Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honour of a lifetime,” she said on Friday (US time).



“I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First. Related Article US midterms ‘Use the nuclear option’: What happens next after the Democrats’ blue tsunami? “More than anything, I’m grateful for the extraordinary people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside. While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will.” Wiles, 69, recently underwent treatment for breast cancer, and said in September that she was now cancer-free. She worked throughout the treatment. Miller’s appointment was welcomed by several administration figures, including Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, whose future is also under a cloud.



“Patriots in control,” Hegseth said on X. He also posted a photograph of himself with Miller captioned: “Stand. Fight. Defend the Republic.” White House communications director Steven Cheung praised Miller as a “Trump OG”, meaning original, who had been with the president since the beginning. “There is no bigger advocate for the Trump agenda than Stephen, and he will help the administration deliver on monumental victories for the rest of this historic second term,” Cheung said. Miller is broadly despised by Democrats. Trump said this week he wanted to work with Democrats in Congress following their seismic election wins, but the appointment of Miller will call that into question. David Axelrod, a former chief of staff to Barack Obama, said few people did more to contribute to the Republican electoral rout than Miller. “The backlash to his brutal ICE raids and nativist rants can be seen in returns all over the country,” Axelrod wrote on X. “And for that he’s PROMOTED?!

World.title: Zach wanted to prevent childhood blindness. Now his sights are set on millions of patients
World.content:
NationalQueenslandMedicine Zach wanted to prevent childhood blindness. Now his sights are set on millions of patients Courtney Kruk November 7, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It was there in plain sight for Dr Zachary Tan. A career in medicine? Or in technology? Enrolling in the University of Queensland’s School of Medicine, he pursued a field that would satisfy both his passions. “I’m a huge nerd,” Tan says. Dr Zachary Tan co-founded Optain Health, a global software and medical technology company using AI to screen for eye conditions. “I was always drawn to ophthalmology because of the large role technology has to play in transforming that area of medicine, both in how we diagnose and treat eye diseases.



“But like so many areas of healthcare, the challenge of ophthalmology is really around access.” Related Article Research Bhabisara’s blood is so rare, most people have never heard of it. Soon it could be grown in this Brisbane lab A little more than a decade after accepting his graduation certificate, Tan now sits at the helm of a company that’s raised $US50 million, and has ambitions to revolutionise access to eye care and retinal disease detection. Tan is speaking from his apartment in New York, where he splits his time between Brisbane. “One of my favourite anecdotes that I like to share with my American colleagues is Queensland is 2½ times the size of Texas.



“People with eye diseases don’t just live in Brisbane; they’re spread all throughout the state,” he says. “And something I’ve been so passionate about since my medical school days is: how can we use technology to really democratise access to ophthalmology services?” Tan hasn’t wasted time trying to answer that question. Optain Health’s device combines technology and AI to screen for common eye diseases. While studying, he helped develop an AI algorithm to screen for retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), a disorder that can cause blindness in premature babies.



The project centred on bringing screening services to patients, particularly in remote areas, rather than requiring them to travel to specialists. Related Article Healthcare Doctors almost sent Kris home with a migraine. Then her whole face went numb This idea became the genesis for Optain Health, a global medical device and software company that uses AI to screen for common retinal diseases, including glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration and cardiovascular disease. Since Tan co-founded the company three years ago, its screening tool is now installed in 500 sites around the world, including Queensland. “In the past 12 months, we screened 150,000 patients and 20,000 patients with some form of disease,” he says.



“I think the potential is huge for AI in healthcare … and one of the things that I feel really passionate about is clinicians having a front-row seat in shaping how we use AI in healthcare.” Related Article AI Your GP is probably already using AI. Now it could talk to you about your medicines When Tan joined UQ’s School of Medicine – an institution that recently celebrated its 90th year – AI was an esoteric concept in contrast to its modern application. But even back then, Tan says the school fostered “a feeling of possibility”. “You could build technology or do research and not just have that be in a lab, but able to translate, from bench-to-bedside,” he explains. “And 2010 was really when we started to see the incredible impacts of Gardasil, the HPV [human papillomavirus] vaccine, which was invented at UQ.



“You’d have your professors and teachers giving lectures, but these were the same people who had functionally now cured cervical cancer.” Tan likens Optain’s tabletop screening tool to an Oculus, the headsets used to create virtual reality. Inside is a fast-working robotic camera that can capture retinal images in less than a minute. “Based off these images, we have specially trained AI, which has been approved by the TGA [Therapeutic Goods Administration], which can look at the different features in the image to provide us with a diagnosis at the point of care.” University of Queensland alumni Tan and Dr Mark Loane in New York. University of Queensland School of Medicine About a week ago, former Wallabies captain and prominent eye surgeon Dr Mark Loane visited Tan in New York, peering into the device to test the technology for himself.



Loane, another UQ alumnus, has spent more than 40 years treating eye conditions, and is renowned for his work in regional and remote Queensland. In 2014, Tan introduced Loane when he presented UQ’s Errol Solomon Meyers Memorial Lecture – a reflection on 20 years of remote eye health. “In the 1980s we had the digital revolution, and ophthalmology itself really benefited from all of that,” Loane says. “Much of the resolution of problems has already been invented, so now it’s about how do you roll out those delivery systems to people all over country … to provincial areas of Queensland or Australia? “[Zachary] has come a long way from 2014 … to meeting again, where he is starting to wrestle with many of the questions which I asked in that lecture about how we deliver services to populations of people and in remote areas. It’s a wondrous closing of circles.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

New York: Federal US agents have arrested Thomas Markle snr – the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex and wife of Prince Harry – and charged him with possessing child sexual abuse material. Markle, 82, was arrested in Florida on Friday morning (US time) and appeared in court in Tampa later the same day. If convicted, he could face up to 20 years in prison. Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, and her estranged father Thomas Markle snr. AP A criminal complaint alleges Markle possessed “sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls in two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for nearly two decades”, the Department of Justice said. In a court affidavit, a special agent with the FBI said the bureau received reports from different witnesses last month. One witness, understood to be Markle’s son, said they had discovered suspected child sexual abuse material among Markle’s possessions in the Philippines, where he had been living.



Another witness told the FBI that Markle rented a storage unit in California. When the FBI raided two such units registered to Markle since 2008, they discovered suspected child sexual abuse material in both, the affidavit said. Officers found and seized approximately 78 items, including slides, film negatives and books. Some of the film negatives were converted into colour digital photographs and found to contain suspected child sexual abuse material. The affidavit contained detailed descriptions of some of the images, which allegedly featured pre-pubescent girls. “To date, I have identified approximately 18 images that appeared to constitute child pornography,” the FBI agent said in the affidavit. “The investigation is active and ongoing.”



Bill Essayli, assistant US attorney for the Central District of California, said three of the images described in the affidavit featured Markle and minor victims. “These allegations are serious and disturbing,” he said. “We intend to prosecute Markle to the fullest extent of federal law.” The October 24 front page of The Sun, which carried a report of the allegations against Markle snr. Getty Images British tabloid The Sun reported last month that Markle’s son, Thomas Markle jnr, had reported his estranged father to authorities in the Philippines for allegedly possessing “hundreds, if not thousands” of underage sexual images in four large boxes at his home in Cebu. Meghan Markle recently said she was “deeply distressed” by those allegations. She also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about him had been sent to London police in 2018.





Markle jnr told The Sun in October that he reported the images to police in the Philippines and contacted the FBI. “I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years - but that stops now,” he told the newspaper. “I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.” Meghan recently said she had been given assurances that the “troubling and disturbing allegations” made about her father in a letter to London police in 2018 were investigated at the time. “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them.” With AP, Sarah McPhee Read more royal news:

World.title: Victorian election hot seats: Melbourne’s west promised $400m in new transport services
World.content:
For people living in Melbourne’s fast-growing western suburbs, one of the most common and longest-running complaints has been a lack of buses, with some schoolchildren facing half-hour walks to the nearest stop – and an additional wait for a service to show up.

For Sydenham locals, Labor’s $400 million pledge to rewrite west Melbourne’s bus routes with services running on key routes every 10 minutes if re-elected on November 28, will no doubt be appealing.

Under the proposal, about two thirds of pre-existing routes will be upgraded to ‘turn-up-and-go’ services, with a bus promised every 10 minutes, seven days a week. Labor will also create a series of new routes across the west that will connect to train stations.

World.title: How to turn your Christmas shopping into 55,000 frequent flyer points
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingLoyalty programs Opinion How to turn your Christmas shopping into 55,000 frequent flyer points Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor November 7, 2026 — 5:10am

November 7, 2026 — 5:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It’s just under six weeks to Christmas, a fact that might be as distressing as last week’s interest rate rise was for mortgage holders. But this year – just in time for Christmas – I’ve honed my points hacking, and I’m ready to start stacking them from the silly season. It’s a simple strategy: buy gift cards that come with a bonus points offer and use them, instead of cash, to buy things. Indeed, you can start in the Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales, when Aussie shoppers are expected to spend an average of $346, an increase of $22 from last year’s event, according to Shopify. Gift cards might be the new best way to stack frequent flyer points. Let me add the crucial upfront caveat, as I often do, that this is for money that you were going to spend anyway. As if any of us has any to spare! But with necessary, planned spend, why not deploy my proven tactics this year to max the points hacks? Visa/Mastercard gift cards – 10,000 points

Now, this is not my favourite strategy but let’s start here and work up to the best; the reason is that these gift cards charge a $5.75 to $7.95 activation fee per card. Any fee comprehensively erodes the value of the points you earn.



The advantage of these cards, though, is that they can be redeemed just about anywhere. But let’s back up and explain that the common theme in the gift-card hack is to buy them on boosted points. It’s simply adding an interim step that nets you cherry-on-top potential travel. The other thing to realise is that sweet new gift-card deals come up all the time. After the expensive Christmas season, the gift-card points hack could see you with a motherlode of points. For example, a few months ago I snared Visa gift cards for 10 times the number of points per dollar spent – 10,000 points for $1000. Apple gift cards – 20,000 points

Now we move into the straight-up sweet deals with no activation fees. I upgraded my iPhone a few months ago. But I waited and watched first. What I waited and watched for was a very common – indeed, often every two months – deal where Apple gift cards offer points up to 20 times the dollar value.



Sometimes you need to purchase them in person, rather than online. There are usually limits on how many you can buy, so be sure to always read the fine print on any gift-card deal. I only purchased $1000 worth, so only received 20,000 points. But, in fact, I could have doubled that if I’d used gift cards to pay the cost of the phone in full. These can be redeemed even for Apple subscriptions on apple.com. You can use up to eight gift cards per purchase, and it’s really an easy process. Multipurpose, multi-merchant gift cards – 22,250

There are a bunch of these that often go on bonus points, up to 20 times again. I have just bought replacement furniture for my daughter’s decrepit old bedroom setting. But I did so only after I could snare gift cards that worked at IKEA, under the brand Ultimate Home. These are also on offer for other multi-merchant products, such as those grouped for Her/Him/Kids. There are hundreds of retailers in such gift-card grouping. The limit this time was $250 per Flybuys account because this deal was just so generous: 2000 bonus points per gift card, even on low $50 denominations. So I bagged 10,250 points (which includes the base $1 per point rate) for $250 spend.



That wasn’t enough to purchase the furniture, so I lurked a little longer and waited for IKEA cards themselves to go on bonus – then I also purchased three $200 dollar cards at 20 times points: 12,000. So the transactions all up netted me 22,250 Flybuys points. Editor's pick Opinion

Superannuation Super funds are finally overhauling retirement. Here’s what’s changing Bec Wilson Money contributor But note that unlike with a straight 20 times points deal, as with Apple above, with 20,000 points from $1000 spend, these 22,250 points were only for parting with $850. Everyday Wish gift cards – 3000 points

It is also often possible to purchase grocery vouchers themselves, for say three times points from the grocery store itself of via Qantas Marketplace (and watch the latter for other gift-card deals too). I bought $1000 worth of Everyday Rewards cards a few months back for triple points. Extra hacks to stack points

Of course, when you pay for gift cards at a supermarket, you need to swipe your rewards membership card to get any offered bonus points. (And realise that when you buy groceries with a grocery gift card, you also get the points on offer on your purchases, so long as you swipe.)



And, if you have such a thing, the gift cards themselves could be purchased with frequent flyer credit cards, to add whatever you accrue per dollar spent. That’s the triple stack that true points hackers love. How many points did I earn? 55,250 in just a few months. These gift card deals are common, changing weekly, often advertised in the supermarket’s physical catalogue or the digital version (check the apps) only. So after the expensive Christmas season, the gift-card points hack could see you with a motherlode of points – which you can use for money off future shopping – too. World.title: Super funds are finally overhauling retirement. Here’s what’s changing
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementSuperannuation Opinion Super funds are finally overhauling retirement. Here’s what’s changing Bec Wilson Money contributor November 7, 2026 — 5:09am

November 7, 2026 — 5:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

There are currently between 150,000 and 200,000 Aussies entering retirement every year, as the Baby Boomers and the Gen Xers converge on this exciting stage of life. That’s potentially 2 million people who are heading towards some of the biggest financial decisions of their lives, often with a blindfold on. And I need to tell you the truth. If you leave retirement planning until you’re 65, by the time you’re sitting down with an adviser or your super fund, many of your biggest retirement decisions have effectively already been made for you, whether you like it or not. The way you interact with your super is getting a refresh. Simon Letch How much you have saved, how your money has been invested, and how much choice you have about your lifestyle in the years before and after, all matter earlier. You might not have consciously made those choices, but by putting them off, you’ve narrowed your options. That’s why I think more Australians need to understand their pre-retirement and retirement choices earlier, get help to work out what they can do to improve their position, and have the confidence to act while they still have time to make a difference.



But that requires two things: better quality advice that really does act in the consumers’ best interests, and super funds that step up and provide practical, affordable retirement planning services, and good support for people who don’t need or can’t afford to be paying thousands of dollars a year on comprehensive advice. Particularly when that advice may come with a recommendation to moving their money onto an investment platform with ongoing adviser fees. For many Australians retiring in the next decade, retirement income will come from a combination of super and the age pension. And, there’s some encouraging news on that front. Over the last 12 months, some of Australia’s super funds have made significant improvements to the help they’re offering members approaching and entering retirement. And if you’re within 10 years of retirement, it’s worth knowing what’s changing because some of these services could make a real difference to the choices you have ahead of you. The improvements have become clear through the annual assessments for the Epic Retirement Tick, which I developed in partnership with research house, Chant West, who independently assesses the funds.



Until recently, most Australians have had little or no understanding of the services their super funds have offered, let alone what they could reasonably expect. But that’s changing, and consumers are gaining more power to demand better help too. Editor's pick Opinion

Superannuation Millions of retirees are paying super tax they could avoid Bec Wilson Money contributor We’re seeing better retirement education, with funds moving beyond the old-fashioned, poorly attended super seminars and boring technical websites towards more engaging online webinars, courses and structured education programs that help people better understand their choices. There are more videos, more real life case studies, and less dense text to wade through. There’s also a welcome improvement in age pension education. More funds are creating dedicated sections on their website explaining how the age pension works, who might qualify and how it interacts with super and what people need to think about when applying. This is important, and it recognises that for many Australians retiring in the next decade, retirement income will come from a combination of super and the age pension and understanding one without the other isn’t enough.



We’re also seeing more useful online retirement planning tools, where you can experiment with different scenarios, test what happens if you retire earlier or later, explore the impact of going part-time before you stop working altogether, and see how your super and the age pension might work together to provide an income throughout retirement. These aren’t just tools for people who are about to retire. They’re potentially even more valuable if we could get them into people’s hands 5 or 10 years beforehand, when you’ve still got time to do something with what you learn. And importantly, more funds are introducing calculators specifically for people who are already retired. These help retirees understand how long their savings might last, what happens if they increase or decrease their spending and how their income might change over time. It’s a crucial improvement because retirement planning shouldn’t stop the day you retire. People need help managing retirement, not just help getting into it. Another really encouraging development is the growing availability of more affordable retirement advice from funds. Some funds are expanding their digital advice services, while others are making it much easier to speak to someone about retirement income, investment choices and how the age pension might fit into your plans.



Some are also starting to recognise that retirement planning is most often a household decision for anyone who is not single, and are finding ways to include a partner’s circumstances. Editor's pick Opinion

Money psychology Why working harder won’t make you rich – and what to do instead Paridhi Jain Money contributor This stuff matters because frankly, not everyone needs an expensive and comprehensive financial plan. Sometimes you just need help to understand whether you can afford to retire at 62 instead of 65, whether you should change your investment mix, or how much income you could realistically expect to draw from your savings alongside the age pension you might be eligible for. There’s also been some pretty decent improvements behind the scenes in some funds on complaints handling and call centre services. Funds are putting more resources into making it easier for members to speak to someone who can actually help, get questions answered and navigate the paperwork and processes involved. And when things go wrong, we’re seeing improvements in how quickly complaints are handled and resolved, rather than leaving members waiting weeks for answers.



Importantly, there’s much more attention being paid to fraud and cybersecurity risk this year. Knowing your fund has strong cybersecurity protections and multifactor authentication might not be the most exciting part of retirement planning, but with AI making scams more sophisticated, you want to know your life savings are properly protected. But not everything is moving as quickly - funds are taking much longer to develop more sophisticated digital advice offerings and lifetime income retirement products. Ian Fryer, general manager of Chant West, says he expects considerably more activity in these areas over the next two years. And there’s one area where there’s clearly more work to be done: helping people who are retiring and are already retired know how much they can afford to spend. Too many retirees simply draw the legislated minimum drawdown when they could comfortably afford more. Funds are getting better at providing calculators, but relatively few are proactively helping members make those spending decisions. So, if you’re within 10 years of retirement, don’t wait until you’re ready to stop working to find out what your super fund offers. Get onto its website, explore the tools, book in for some education and ask what else is available. You might be surprised by how much you can do now to improve your retirement later.



Bec Wilson, bestselling author of How to Have an Epic Retirement, is a retirement educator and founder of the Epic Retirement Institute. World.title: Trump is a false idol and his local franchisee is dumping the brand
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS election Opinion Trump is a false idol and his local franchisee is dumping the brand Peter Hartcher Political and international editor November 7, 2026 — 5:04am

November 7, 2026 — 5:04am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Barnaby Joyce was planning to make the pilgrimage to the Mar-a-Lago shrine to Donald Trump midyear. He’d been invited on an all-expenses-paid trip. His wife, Vikki Campion, had another idea. Woolbrook Public School was due to hold its community barbecue at the local Bunnings and Barnaby and Vikki were rostered to work it. “Your children go to Woolbrook Public School,” Barnaby recounts Vikki telling him. “You’re not going.” He cancelled the trip to the US. Pauline Hanson has taken many of her cues from Donald Trump. Are those days over? Michael Howard Now that the American electorate has repudiated Trump, the decision is looking especially smart. The national swing against his Republican Party across all House elections tallied to 8 per cent, according to the News24 numbers man Tom Connell. For scale, that’s double the size of the swings in the previous three US midterms. The last time there was a swing of 8 per cent was in reaction to the economic devastation of the global financial crisis, when Barack Obama was in the White House. It’s only the fourth time since World War II that both the US House and Senate have flipped from one party to another in the same midterms.



Donald Trump suddenly is more radioactive than an Iranian nuclear reactor. Across the world, right-wing populist parties are backing away from him. In Australia, Pauline Hanson’s One Nation quickly and quietly removed from its website an article offering itself as the local franchisee of the Trump brand: “Want Trump’s action and style, then it’s One Nation you need”, ran the headline. Reinforcing the close identification was a photoshopped picture of the two great leaders, Hanson and Trump, together. Oops. It must have seemed so clever and exciting at the time it was published, January 23, 2025, the week Trump was inaugurated for his second presidency. Illustration: Matt Davidson The midterms pronounced a harsh verdict on Trump’s affiliated billionaires, too. The Republican billionaires on the ballot, Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio and Rick Jackson in Georgia, lost to Democrats. And Elon Musk’s record campaign funding for Republicans of some half a billion dollars was powerless against the popular will. Musk proved more useful to the Democrats as a loathed campaign target than to Republicans as a generous campaign support. So it’s not surprising that another Australian acolyte of Trump’s, billionaire Gina Rinehart, has gone very quiet since the midterms. In Europe, France’s National Rally, Germany’s AfD, Italy’s The League and Futuro Nazionale parties, and Spain’s Vox all distanced themselves from Trump in comments after the midterms. Neither did Britain’s Nigel Farage of the Reform UK party try to defend the Republicans’ “complete and utter rout”.



Is the right-wing populist franchise bust? Trumplike leaders in five countries have lost national elections in the past year and a half. All were populist right-wingers with autocratic tendencies. All had proudly affiliated themselves with Trump. Related Article Opinion

US midterms Trump crashed on his own shores of discontent, but the blue wave doesn’t deliver certainty Waleed Aly Columnist, author and academic In Poland, Hungary, Serbia and Brazil, the Trumplike leaders failed. Trump’s Brazilian buddy, Flavio Bolsonaro, cried “fraud” and took political asylum in the US. Serbia’s Aleksandar Vučić lost to an upstart student-led movement that didn’t even have a leader. The Student List party had to hold discussions to decide which of them would claim victory on election night. Trump’s Israeli ally, Benjamin Netanyahu, lost his parliamentary majority, though he remains in office while negotiations over a new government continue. “The Trump brand is lost,” says Stanford University political scientist Francis Fukuyama. “Donald Trump has become toxic. No foreign political party is going to want to get close to him. “The main issue that united them was immigration but that’s gotten under control in most areas and it’s no longer the same burning issue. What holds populist nationalist together now is the style, more than anything else, that allows them to be racist and insulting.“



And, in countries where they’ve held power, “these populist parties aren’t good at governing. Hungary used to be one of the richest countries in Europe; Viktor Orban ran it into the ground with cronyism and corruption.” Yet while the Trump franchise may be bust, Fukuyama says that it’s too early to dismiss right-wing populists as a force. He points out that Marine Le Pen is poised to win the presidency of France in April. Italy is due for election next year, too, with potential gains for the far right. “We may have a couple more moves in that direction,” Fukuyama tells me, “but a lot of wind has come out of the sails of the populist nationalists”. The implications in Australia are several. We shouldn’t lose sight of the very big picture. Despite fears to the contrary, liberal democracy is alive and well. The world has been in a “democratic recession” since the global financial crisis. The number of democracies has been shrinking. The Economist Intelligence Unit’s annual democracy index surveys 167 nations and counts only 26 as full democracies. It has not counted the US as a full democracy since 2015; it classifies it as a “flawed democracy”. Trump tested the limits of the system. In his last term and again this term. In the US, elections are administered by the states, as the Constitution stipulates, and not the federal government. But, in recent months, Trump strained to seize election powers from the states so that Washington DC could control the outcome of the midterms. But Congress refused to pass his so-called SAVE America bill. State governors and legislatures resisted his efforts. The courts dismissed Trump’s attempts to litigate his way to control over the ballots. The media remained robustly untamed. The checks and balances were under pressure yet held.



The greatest check, however, was the American public, who turned out strongly and voted decisively. Trump accepted the result. This concession is not personally painful to him. He still has his post, his profile, his billions and opportunities to make billions more, and considerable power. Related Article US midterms ‘The reason is obvious’: Bloodletting begins over Republicans’ electoral wipeout It’s too early to declare US democracy safe. We’ve yet to see how Trump behaves when his time in the White House ends. But, for now, the world’s most important democracy has reasserted its credentials as a functioning democracy. The Democrats now have the opportunity to put “liberal” back into US liberal democracy, by which I don’t mean leftist policies; I mean the restoration of citizens’ rights and constitutional limits on executive power. All of this acts as a deterrent to politicians in other nations, including Australia, to mimic Trump’s worst autocratic instincts. For the Australian political parties? First, One Nation. It realises that it has overstepped. “The core message is that performative charlatanry has a shelf life and will be exposed ultimately,” says politics professor emeritus at Monash University, Paul Strangio. One Nation’s vote share stalled in June. The US midterms “must punch a hole in One Nation to a degree”.



What lessons does Barnaby Joyce’s draw for One Nation? “Don’t go too far,” he tells me, before quoting Tacitus: “From wisdom comes moderation”. Related Article High Court of Australia Pauline Hanson, the High Court and the judges’ war of words Yet the party retains some policies that are far from moderate. Its immigration policy, for instance, promises a net outflow of people for three years. This is impractical for the functioning of the economy. But One Nation’s shuffling embarrassment over its Trump fetish is not any sort of salvation for the Albanese government. Because while Trump’s politics and policies are in another universe to Labor’s, they share one big feature in common – both are incumbents. Incumbency is a liability in a time of inflationary discontent. It is a destroyer of governments. Labor needs to show that it can help to solve inflation, not just find scapegoats for it. “They need to show that they have a plan,” advises Strangio. Senior Labor figures agree. The Liberals are Australia’s biggest potential beneficiaries of this post-midterms politics. As one senior Liberal puts it: “The slavish devotion of some on the Australian political right to right-wing populism – that we must do what they’re doing if we want to win – has been completely blown up.



“The US elections show that economic performance is still the most important credential. The rubbish about Trump being a uniquely gifted politician is exposed. The laws of politics are immutable – if you make people’s lives worse, they will punish you. “To focus on economic competence is a very good pathway for us to take if we want to return to government. We don’t have to do crazy things.” Liberals, get off your knees. Trump is a false idol. And his local franchisee is dumping the brand; you can stop trembling at her feet. Can you recover your standing as the most credible economic manager? The opportunity is before you. Will Barnaby accept a future invitation to Mar-a-Lago? “I’ll have to check the barbecue schedule”. Peter Hartcher is political editor and international editor of The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

This year is proving a treat for Asian cruises, with maiden appearances of ships from companies such as Norwegian Cruise Line and Carnival, more Royal Caribbean itineraries from homeports in Hong Kong and Singapore, and many other cruise lines sailing bumper Asian seasons. British small-ship operator Swan Hellenic sailed into Asia for the first time this year on itineraries to Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, the Philippines, South Korea and Japan. Cruise and river ships continue to extend their reach in Asia including Ha Long Bay, Vietnam. iStock APT Luxury Tours, which has long offered river cruises on the Mekong, launched a luxury three-day cruise experience on Ha Long Bay in Vietnam as part of its extended journeys in the region. Meanwhile, Italian company Explora Journeys is inaugurating Asian journeys in 2027 aboard Explora III. Over the 2027-28 season, the luxury ship will make 28 journeys across Japan, South Korea, China and South-East Asia.



The sailings include overnight stays in key destinations such as Tokyo, Osaka, Hong Kong, Shanghai, Ha Long Bay, Ho Chi Minh City and Bali. 



Oceania Riviera and Oceania Vista will be sailing Asia too. And if you want to splurge, then Silversea’s Silver Muse is sailing a 51-day Grand Voyage across 28 destinations in seven Asian nations. Meanwhile, Silver Cloud is sailing in South-East Asia and Japan. Japan is the destination of the moment and has seen a corresponding surge in cruise operations. Silversea announced its first-ever Japan summer season on voyages to the big port cities but also to lesser-known alternatives such as Akita, Shimizu and Amami Oshima. Related Article Cruises Asian cruise companies are offering fresh alternatives for Aussies The summer season is timed to take in local celebrations such as Kyoto’s Gion Matsuri – one of Japan’s most famous festivals, which features ornate floats – and Tokushima’s Awa Odori, which celebrates dance and music. Windstar’s new ship Star Seeker will sail a maiden Japan season in 2027, and in spring 2028 Seabourn will have several Japan sailings. Also coming up for Seabourn are a new 16-day Shanghai and Seoul cruise, a 12-day Shanghai and Taiwan voyage, and eight South-East Asian itineraries.



All this is just a sampling of the cruise range and choices now available in Asia. Just 4.5 per cent of Australian cruisers holidayed there in 2025, but surely more of us should start looking north.

World.title: 'Shared values' see Pacific Forum increase partnerships with Middle East countries
World.content:
The Pacific Islands Forum chair says shared values are why the regional body is increasing partnerships with Middle Eastern countries, including Israel.

The Forum's chairman, Surangel Whipps Junior, and secretary-general, Baron Waqa, are on the road in the Middle East to lobby for investment in the Pacific's Resilience Facility for coping with climate change impacts.

Whipps, who is Palau's president, spoke to media late Friday in an online press conference from Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates, after meeting with the leadership of the UAE.

Whipps said the UAE has offered to help support the Pacific region's resilience to climate change.

"So it's about financing, it's about oceans, bringing the ocean and climate access to the forefront.

"It's about renewable energy, delivering projects, and that's why we talked about the perspectives that carry that forward."

Asked how the Forum could justify its recent move to partner with Israel's government when the Benjamin Netanyahu-led regime is accused of serious abuses of international law, Whipps gave the following answer:

"We are a long ways away from this region, but I think it's important for us to be able to engage as a partner because we have shared values of interest in climate impacts, building resilience and sustainability, and oceans.

"One of the things that we share with the UAE, for example, is our love and care for the oceans and protecting them. Same thing with Saudi," he explained.

"So we want to take these opportunities to engage not only in those areas but on a broader level."

The Forum is justifying its new drive to forge closer ties with countries in a region mired in conflict by emphasising its goal of building the PRF.

The PRF is a Pacific-led financing mechanism designed to provide grants directly to communities dealing with climate change impacts.

Whipps echoed comments by Fiji's representative at this week's Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in St John's, Antigua and Barbuda, urging the international community to support the PRF.

"The Pacific has also invested in it. In fact, we've raised US$200 million to date. US$100 million of that comes from Pacific Island Forum members," Whipps explained.

The Forum has a US$500 million target for the Facility by end of the year.

"At the end of the day, the people want to see action, and that's why PRF is an important part of that," he said.

World.title: Explainer: Why you won’t hear much about the election on election day
World.content:
Explainer - Today is election day. But you won't be hearing much about it until after the polls close at 7pm.

New Zealand has mandatory rules about how much campaigning is allowed, and you could possibly be hit with a fine of up to $20,000 if you ignore them.

What can't I do?

On election day, you are no longer allowed to do any campaigning or anything that would influence voters. This includes signs, demonstrations and posts on social media.

"I think there is a good argument for giving voters a bit of peace and quiet on election day," said Mona Krewel, a senior lecturer on comparative politics at Victoria University of Wellington Te Herenga Waka who has been tracking the role of social media in previous elections.

"At this point, the campaign has been going on for long enough, and all parties have had a fair opportunity to inform voters about their policies and candidates," she said.

Download the Electoral Commission's full guide to rules on election day here.

What are the penalties?

According to the Electoral Act 1993, interfering with or influencing voters can lead to a fine of up to $20,000.

Is there any campaigning allowed at a polling place?

It's strictly forbidden to do anything anywhere that might influence voters until the polls close at 7pm.

During early voting, any campaigning or advertising was prohibited at voting places or within 10 metres of their entrance.

Can I keep that election hoarding up on my front fence?

No. All election signs and hoardings must be removed by midnight the Friday before election day. Vehicles with election signs, bumper stickers and other political advertising must be out of public view as well.

Political parties and MPs can leave fixed signage at their offices and headquarters if they were up before election day and aren't explicitly part of the campaign.

Can I post a selfie online with my ballot telling everyone to vote like me?

Heck no. On election day from midnight to 7pm, you can't post or share any content on social media about your vote.

"Don't post anything to social media or a website on election day that could influence voters," the Electoral Commission warns.

There is no exemption for "the expression of personal political views online" according to the Electoral Commission, so in other words, no matter how you feel really, really strongly about your personal party vote, keep it to yourself for a few hours.

In 2023, the Electoral Commission said it reported 20 people referred to police over social media posts on election day.

Social media posts on election day can violate the rules. ROBIN UTRECHT / ANP MAG / ANP via AFP

Do I have to take down everything I've ever written in the past about the election?

No. You're not required to remove existing material on websites or social media as long as you don't update it on election day or advertise it, or repost old material on election day, and as long as it's only available to people who choose to access it.

Even things like having your profile picture promoting a party or candidate could be considered an offence, so check your socials carefully.

"The Electoral Commission does not ask people to completely remove stuff from social media or websites on election day, as long as people are not actively being pushed towards that content and only see it when they decide to access it voluntarily," Krewel said.

"Asking for everything to be removed entirely is probably also unrealistic these days."

There is an argument that restrictions laid out in the Electoral Act 1993 aren't quite fit for purpose in 2026, and that plenty of influencing still goes on during early voting.

"With advance voting becoming increasingly popular and many New Zealanders casting their ballots well before election day, the regulation is becoming somewhat outdated," Krewel noted.

"We essentially have a situation where some voters are still exposed to active campaigning right up until the moment they cast their vote, while those who vote on election day get a campaign-free environment. So the original rationale for the restriction is becoming less convincing as voting habits change."

Many people probably aren't even aware of the restrictions on election day posting, Krewel said.

"Most people probably know the basics, but I doubt that many are aware that something as seemingly harmless as posting 'Vote for [whichever party]!' on their personal social media account on election day could constitute a breach of electoral law."

Krewel said the restrictions "strike a fair balance" as people can still seek out previous information online on voting day if they wish, but they also give voters a break from a feed full of election hype on the day itself.

As you head to the polls this week, there's some rules you need to be aware of. RNZ/Nosiphi Mapukata

Can I just take a cool TikTok of the people who are voting?

Absolutely not. The Electoral Commission asks people to respect the privacy of others.

Publishing photos or videos of someone filling out their ballot is a potential offence.

Some permissions can be granted by electorate managers for photo ops, like a candidate casting their vote or media coverage of voting.

Enforcement of the social media rules are difficult, though, Krewel said.

"The Electoral Commission does not actively monitor everyone's conduct on election day, and realistically, it couldn't possibly police everything people post online. Instead, it largely relies on complaints and responds when potential breaches are brought to its attention."

There are rules about conduct around voting places, too. RNZ/Nosiphi Mapukata

Can I give away free sausages outside polling places to everyone voting?

Nah, mate.

Last year, the government moved to strengthen the offence of "treating" by creating a 100-metre buffer around polling stations where free food, drink and entertainment are not allowed.

Any place acting as a voting place that would ordinarily be providing food is allowed to - such as refreshments at a tangi or tea and coffee in a school staffroom.

Can I poll people leaving about who they voted for?

Nope. You can't do that on election day or during advance voting.

"Our processes ensure people have a positive experience, and that their privacy and other rights are protected," the Electoral Commission notes.

Aggressive behaviour will not be tolerated at the polls. RNZ / Nick Monro

Can I just hang out at the voting place for a while afterwards to soak up the vibes?

"Once you have voted, we ask that you don't linger and leave the voting place straight away," the Electoral Commission advises.

The Electoral Commission has also warned people that aggressive behaviour won't be tolerated - a concern particularly high this year.

"Members of the public who are disruptive or causing a disturbance will be told to leave the voting place. Failure to comply with this direction is an offence and may be referred to police."

Can I stand out in front of the polling place with a megaphone telling everyone to vote for my candidate?

That's a definite no, for all the reasons mentioned above.

Can I at least wear my party colours or badge?

According to the Electoral Commission, you may wear a party lapel badge or rosette with party colours, a party name and branding, but not a candidate name. Any lapel badge or rosette you wear must include a promoter statement. You can also wear party colours, but only on people or vehicles.

Can I remind people to vote or help them get to the polls?

You are allowed to contact people to offer help or a reminder, but must not influence how they vote.

If you need help to vote, the Electoral Commission also offers several special services for those with disabilities or in need of support.

Last question - can I bring my dog?

Of course, although they can't vote if they're not enrolled, and it's strictly up to the polling place's rules itself if they're allowed inside.

Who do I complain to if someone is breaking those rules?

You can start with the Electoral Commission. If they believe an offence has been committed, they'll refer people to the police. They can't enforce the law or prosecute offenders themselves.

Krewel said she didn't see the election day restrictions as any real kind of freedom of speech issue.

"People have plenty of time to express their political opinions throughout the election campaign and can freely do so again immediately after election day," she said.

World.title: Drones, AI helping Tongariro National Park regeneration efforts after destructive fires
World.content:
Audio player for " Drone and AI tech helping regeneration after Tongariro fires " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/environment/2394212%2Fdrones-ai-helping-tongariro-national-park-regeneration-efforts-after-destructive-fires

Drone and AI tech helping regeneration after Tongariro fires Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Drone and AI technology is helping regeneration efforts in the central North Island's Tongariro National Park after two fires tore through.

The first, most damaging, blaze flared a year ago this Sunday and closed the popular Tongariro Crossing track for more than a week.

A smaller blaze a month later caused further damage to the same area.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407983771112

Keeping out invasive weeds and animals

Look closely into the dull grey colouring of the charred Mangatepopo Valley and some green shoots are visible.

Department of Conservation (DOC) principal ranger Dan Van Der Lubbe is leading the recovery efforts there.

"It took out 3000 hectares of tussock grassland and regenerating alpine scrub. What we can see now is the natural regrowth after one year," he said.

Red tussock and flax were coming back, while larger celery pines were dead, their black outlines slowly rotting.

A 10-year restorative rāhui introduced by Ngāti Hikairo ki Tongariro is in place on the damaged land, with the hope it will prevent people from unwittingly bringing in invasive weeds. DOC also asks Tongariro Crossing trampers to check their gear so they're not bringing any seeds in.

Stopping the likes of gorse and heather from spreading, as well as keeping out animals such as rabbits, hares, deer and even wallabies, would allow the land to recover naturally, Van Der Lubbe said.

There are all sorts of programmes to help achieve this, including managing mites that eat heather and broom in the wider area.

"These fires have happened here repeatedly over the last thousands of years. In the last 150 years there have been about three fires in this area, so it's just natural regeneration that occurs."

DOC principal ranger Dan Van Der Lubbe is in charge of the restoration efforts. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

RNZ had a look around the fire damage at the Mangatepopo end of the Tongariro Crossing. The colour of the untouched vegetation is in contrast to the fire-damaged land, which leaped over the access road.

It's closed the Mangatepopo Track, which Van Der Lubbe said was under repair.

He was part of the firefighting efforts last year and helped bulldoze fire breaks.

Up at the car park, where tourists are dropped of to begin their walk, firefighters put in a huge shift to protect newly opened facilities and a newly installed pou.

"This was put in a within a month or so of the first fire. It signified the protection that Ngāti Hikairo and Tūwharetoa have over the national park.

"We are very lucky it didn't get destroyed in the fire. He got a little bit charred down by his feet," Van Der Lubbe said.

Flames licked the base of this pou at the Tongariro Crossing entrance but were kept away. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Tech at the forefront of recovery

After the fire the government announced $3.5 million of funding for the recovery.

The work that came out of that was at least a silver lining, Van Der Lubbe said.

For this, DOC used iwi contractors where possible, and brought in specialists when needed.

"Funding from this project has allowed us to investigate new technologies to make our work more effective and more efficient.

"We've started using drones to monitor gorse and broom and wilding conifers. The drone comes in, takes photographs and then they use their AI platform to find all the plants.

"Rather than me sending a helicopter into a block and saying, 'Just search the whole area', I can give them a pinpoint of where the weeds are and they just go and hit those."

Interpine's Dave Herries uses drone and AI tech to find weeds, so they can be removed easily. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

The company behind that is Rotorua-based company Interpine. Its chief technology officer Dave Herries, who has worked there for 27 years, also volunteers for firefighting efforts and was on the ground last year.

He led an intelligence team, which used drones to identify hot spots. Firefighters use an app through their phones to see where these are, so they can put them out.

It's similar for the weed identification efforts.

"After the fire had settled we came in to take imagery of the fire ground for the recovery process and subsequently have been back on a regular basis, capturing snapshots over time."

The company had undertaken three large aerial surveys of the fire zone, and would do another one in December, Herries said.

These provided a visual record of changes to the site.

The AI tech made for efficient use of time.

"[It lets] the Department of Conservation, their contractors and their rangers to be able to identify those weed invasions and target them specifically.

"When we're talking about a fire ground which reached over 3000ha we do need to optimise the use of those ground resources."

The blaze in 2025. Supplied / Alister McDermid and Joanna Finlayson

Nervousness remains

In nearby Waimarino tourist-reliant businesses initially lost bookings.

Tongariro Crossing Lodge owner Louis van Wyk said last summer quickly returned to normality, although he fielded calls from overseas for a while asking if the crossing was closed.

This year lodge guests who walked the track didn't even mention the fire damage.

Van Wyk is a volunteer firefighter, who helped with last year's efforts to contain the blazes. He's still relieved that a change in weather helped avert a bigger disaster last November.

"I'm grateful, but at the same time quite apprehensive that something like that could happen again.

"It just showed with the dry spring we had - and that's in the forecast again for a dry summer - that with a little bit of human error and carelessness those kinds of things can happen again, and that makes me a little bit nervous."

Tongariro Crossing Lodge owner Louis van Wyk says the dry forecast makes him nervous. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Ruapehu mayor Weston Kirton said the fire took a toll.

"The figures are always difficult to work through, but any disruption with people coming into the area is quite significant in terms of accommodation and cancellations of activities and the like," he said.

"So, people are scared off by just the image of fires, for example. There was certainly an impact on the economy, there's no doubt about that."

Kirton said various agencies learnt a lot from their responses to the fires, which would help for future events.

World.title: Country Life: Calves, callouts and 75 years of country vetting
World.content:
New Plymouth Vet Group has many life-long clients like Jordan who have kept up the connection over generations.

"I was a little one at the cow shed when the vets were calling," she said.

Founded in 1951 by farmers, the group has expanded alongside New Plymouth into a mixed practice caring for livestock and pets.

The practice celebrated 75 years in November.

Farmers make up the board and there are about 75 to 80 dairy, sheep and beef official farm members of the "club".

The practice reinvests its small profit back into the clinic and aims to keep its prices as low as possible, catering for companion animals for urban clients as well these days.

Its central New Plymouth premises also cares for injured wild birds.

At the Jordan farm, Mitchell is gloved up with his stethoscope around his neck, checking on one of the heifer calves nestled in the calf shed.

Jordan told him calving had gone well so far with only a couple of bigger calves in the last couple of days.

Good spring weather had helped get their mum's colostrum into them, she said, upping the antibodies and guarding against sickness.

Jordan is one of the vet group's board members and praised the valuable service, particularly during busy times like calving.

Vet Ben Mitchell with days-old calves in the calf shed RNZ/Sally Round

"They drop and run and you can't really get any other professionals in any other industries to do that for you …you ring, the team triage you and where we're situated, you can have a vet on farm in 20 minutes if it's an emergency," she said.

With advances in genetics and more on-farm technology monitoring animal health, things have changed, even during Mitchell's time working as a vet.

"There's so much with genetics and with farm management plans and things," he said.

"I've only been out eight years, but I feel like even in that time, that we're calving [fewer] cows than we used to and so we are seeing some noticeable improvements."

He said work had moved more towards consultancy, education and guidance.

"We try to be very proactive and avoid problems before we see them."

Jordan said breeding for traits like easy calving and teat placement had created fewer problems which would necessitate a vet call-out.

"But you've still got to feed a cow well all year round to be able to get them in calf back in spring or whatever.

"There's no luck in farming. We've got to plan ahead and that's where the relationship with our vets comes in, whether that's nutrition or minerals, anything like that."

Vet Ben Mitchell and dairy farmer Amanda Jordan RNZ/Sally Round

Vets are also an important bulwark for farmers during tough times, Jordan said, such as during a tuberculosis outbreak in the herd.

"The well-being of your animals is so important [...] them standing beside us and talking us through what would be next, it was fantastic."

She said vets and a trusted vet-client relationship were a crucial part of rural communities.

"They can be some of the first people to notice that there might be an underlying issue on a farm. It might be skinny cows or calves aren't quite going well because they're not getting the time because [farmers are] overwhelmed."

Mitchell agreed a huge part of the job was building relationships over time with farmers who often work in isolation.

"Being or trying to be a friendly face, come out and see them and have a chat and just kind of connect on that personal level can provide just a little bit of connection."
