World.title: One dead, four injured in Wellington crash
World.content:
One person has died and four others injured after a crash in Wellington early Saturday morning.

Police got the call to the single-vehicle crash on Brandon Street about 2.10am.

"Sadly, one person was pronounced deceased and four others were injured and transported to hospital."

Police said the Serious Crash Unit had also been at the scene.

Road closures were put in place overnight at the meeting of Brandon Street and Customhouse Quay.

World.title: The stand-off that sank Netball NZ’s privatisation deal with Anna Mowbray and Ali Williams
World.content:
Netball NZ may have ended up paying to hand over control of its elite domestic competition under the privatisation deal negotiated with investors Ali Williams and Anna Mowbray.

As first reported by RNZ, Netball NZ last week abruptly pulled the pin on negotiations with the high-profile couple, just eight weeks after signing a term sheet in which the parties agreed to work towards establishment of a new privately-owned league in 2027.

The collapse has left players facing renewed uncertainty over their professional futures and raised uncomfortable questions about Netball NZ's handling of the process.

The dispute has largely been framed as about control, with the Williams and Mowbray camp questioning whether Netball NZ were truly willing to commit to handing over the keys to the domestic competition.

However, concerns about the balance of the proposed deal were not confined to Netball NZ. One team official told RNZ the feedback from potential franchise investors was that the terms "were too weighted in the league owners' favour".

RNZ understands at the heart of the dispute is a disagreement over whether Mowbray and Williams were taking over the licence to operate the league on a "concession arrangement" or taking ownership of the competition outright.

A concession agreement would grant a private party the licence to operate the league for a set period. The operator makes money through team-licensing fees, commercial deals and broadcast uplift, but also take on the risk, if things don't go well.

It is understood Netball NZ were offering an initial 10-year deal, with a 10-year right of renewal, later increased to 15 + 15 years, while Mowbray and Williams sought a deal in perpetuity.

From the investors' perspective, if they were committing their capital and expertise to building the competition, they needed confidence they would have the security to see that investment through. A fixed-term licence, even with the option of renewal, left open the possibility that Netball NZ could take the competition back, after Williams and Mowbray had put in the work and money.

"Imagine buying a house and the owner puts in the agreement that we can nick it back after 10 years," said one insider. "Who would agree to that deal?"

However, others have questioned the fairness of a deal that would have seen Netball NZ effectively pay the investors to take the league off their hands.

Netball NZ chief executive Jennah Wootten told RNZ the national body would not have received any payment for the league licence and, instead, would have had to contribute money to help establish the competition.

"The proposal would not have seen Netball NZ receive any money as a result of the transaction and, instead, was prepared to invest into the venture," Wootten said. "That ultimately couldn't be made to work in a way that protected the future of netball in New Zealand.

"We cannot get into the details of the arrangements for commercial reasons."

Netball NZ boss Jennah Wootten announced in September the organisation was backing a proposal by Ali Williams and Anna Mowbray to privatise the elite domestic league. Eight weeks later, the deal was off. RNZ / Nick Monro

The news that the national body was pulling the pin on negotiations came a week after Williams and Mowbray provided an update to the Netball NZ board in a meeting that lasted three hours.

Williams told RNZ that, in that meeting, Netball NZ drilled into the details.

"We were transparent around it all," he said. "We made it pretty clear what we believed the potential losses could be to build these things."

When questioned what he meant by losses, Williams responded: "There's a lot of investment that goes into it, that's probably a better word.

"[Netball NZ] understood the investment that we were prepared to put in and it required investment from their end as well, but that was purely around 2027, because it had taken so long to get to where we were and the timeframes we were operating under."

Netball NZ's decision to privatise the elite domestic league was intended to bring in much-needed capital and commercial capability into a competition the national body could no longer afford to run in its existing form.

In July, the organisation revealed the ANZ Premiership ran at a $3.7 million deficit this season. About $1.2m could be attributed to the broadcast costs, after Netball NZ agreed to cover production costs in its deal with TVNZ to get the sport back on free-to-air television.

Privatisation would have allowed Netball NZ to offload the costs of running the competition, but one sports business expert told RNZ that did not mean the proposed deal represented good value for the sport.

"There's no doubt that this is a distressed asset that [Mowbray and Williams] would be taking on, and it would take significant investment on their end to build the league into a strong commercial asset and get that broadcast revenue uplift.

"Regardless, the value of the deal changes significantly, depending on whether it is a concession arrangement or an equity arrangement. If you were talking in housing terms, it's the difference between leasehold and freehold, if you like.

"I sense Netball NZ have done the right thing here in walking away. The terms of that deal, if you're not getting any money for the competition licence... that doesn't make a whole heap of business sense."

Ali Williams and Anna Mowbray emerged as saviours of netball, when the high profile couple put in a proposal to privatise the elite domestic league. RNZ

How the two parties could have reached this point without agreement on such a fundamental question as what was actually being sold remains unclear.

Explaining the shock decision to walk away from negotiations, Wootten said the investors had strayed from what was set out in the original term sheet signed by the parties.

Few details have been provided of what was in the term sheet, but at the time of the announcement, Netball NZ said the "long form agreement would see the licence for the competition and competing teams held by the investors, with Netball New Zealand assuming a governance role on the board that will be established to govern the new league".

Williams maintains the position of the investors has never changed.

"From our point of view, the intention was never changed, so the intention of us coming in and doing all these things was still the same. They always knew what our intention was, but from there to signing the long form, that fell over."

Ambition heavy, detail light

The disagreement over ownership and control was only one part of the problem. There were also significant questions about whether the proposed competition's financial model would work - particularly for the teams expected to foot much of the bill.

Former Mainland Tactix general manager Kate Agnew, who was involved in trying to put together a bid for a Christchurch-based team, said the feedback from investors was that the proposed model was weighted too heavily in favour of the league operators.

Under the proposed arrangement, teams would have been required to pay a significant fee to secure a licence, then cover their own operating costs, including player salaries, travel, accommodation and support staff - costs previously covered through broadcast rights and sponsorship at competition level.

"In some cases, that is a model that a lot of leagues follow, but usually there's either a greater certainty of return and being able to offset those costs, or there's more investment coming in from the league itself to help support the owners with paying those costs," said Agnew, who previously worked at Netball NZ.

"That was a lack of clarity for the investors - did it mean they were going to end up having to foot an awful lot of costs, but with little prospect of return?"

Agnew said there had been some "really positive conversations" with potential investors, but not enough detail or certainty in the proposal for them to confidently commit.

"There were still quite a lot of gaps in the information and the certainty of the proposal to be able to put to investors for them to have real confidence that they understood what they were buying into.

"Ali [Williams], for example, has said he had broadcast deals and that's great, but what's the detail of the broadcast agreements - is every game going to be broadcast? What times and days?

"What broadcast channel and, therefore, what kind of reach and visibility could investors expect for the product?"

Former Tactix general manager Kate Agnew said it would not be feasible for the team to enter the new league under the model proposed. © Photosport Ltd 2026 www.photosport.nz

Williams told RNZ he had secured sponsors, and had a broadcast deal lined up with both Sky and TVNZ, but these could not be signed until the long form agreement with Netball NZ had been reached.

"Unfortunately, I couldn't give them more detail, which I would have loved to and that would have come out, but we can't go down those paths, until things are all signed up."

The financial model also presented a significant hurdle for the existing franchises - three of which (Northern Stars, Tactix and Waikato-Bay of Plenty Magic) were already run by Netball NZ.

The national body had underwritten most of the competition's costs this season, after broadcast revenue dried up, but the proposed model would have shifted that financial responsibility to individual teams.

An official involved with one of the franchises put the cost of running a team at about $1.2m a season, while RNZ understands the buy-in cost for a franchise licence was $500,000 - a figure Williams said was "about right".

Magic liaison manager Gary Dawson told RNZ the financial model didn't "stack up" for the Waikato-Bay of Plenty side.

Of the three teams that stand on their own feet financially, RNZ understands only one - Southern Steel - were close to being able to pull together the funding required, but even that "wasn't a done deal".

Wellington-based Central Pulse said it would have been challenging for the franchise to put a bid together, while Northern Mystics chief executive Phil Vyver said, when Netball NZ pulled the pin, they were still a fair way off from being able to secure a team.

"We would have required a private investment of our own or a significant increase in commercial sponsorship revenue to be able to afford it," Vyver said. "On face value, the Netball Northern Zone don't have the reserves to be able to put towards it.

"Over the last couple of months, we've been looking for investment into the team. When the decision was made [by Netball NZ], we hadn't had anything secured, plenty of conversations, but nothing was 100 percent locked in place."

However, there was no requirement that the teams in the new competition would be aligned with the existing zones. The investors could have established five entirely new teams.

Speaking to RNZ on Tuesday, Williams said he had private investors for three teams lined up "and then the rest we were working on, but that then sits with us, right?"

Asked if that meant the couple were prepared to take on some of team licences themselves, Williams responded: "We promised what we promised, that's how it has to work."

Ali Williams and Anna Mowbray own a 15 percent stake in A-League club Auckland FC, and hoped to bring the team's fan-centric model to netball. Andrew Cornaga/www.photosport.nz

Williams acknowledged the proposed model would not have worked for everyone, but he said the investors were looking to take a different approach to how the sport was run.

"I respect the zones, I respect their elements, but you also have to respect the fact that we needed to look at things in a different light," he said.

Williams said the proposal was about finding investors who bought into a broader vision for the sport, rather than simply looking at the immediate financial returns.

"There were people that could see the vision and understand what we were trying to achieve, and then there were others that it was hard and I'm not going to deny that.

"This is not for everyone, so yeah, I can understand their position, but there's also a reality around being able to do something and wanting to do something."

Silver Ferns shooter Martina Salmon is among a handful of national players left without a contract heading into 2027 - a World Cup year. AAP / Photosport

A future left hanging

The abrupt change of direction from Netball NZ has taken a huge toll on the players, coaches and support staff, who have endured a prolonged period of uncertainty over their professional futures.

While 18 players will head overseas next season, predominantly to Australia's Suncorp Super Netball competition, several current Silver Ferns remain without a deal.

They include Peta Toeava, Parris Mason, Martina Salmon, Laura Balmer, Taylah Earle and injured defender Catherine Hall. Recent internationals Phoenix Karaka, Maia Wilson and Whitney Souness are also without contracts.

There is hurt and frustration among the playing group, particularly over the lack of warning that Netball NZ was considering walking away from negotiations.

The players' association has repeatedly called for the athletes to be included in discussions, believing they could help find a way through the impasse.

General manager Pippa Moore said the players had become the collateral damage in a commercial dispute they had very little influence over.

She added the association still hoped a compromise could be reached and wanted an opportunity to bring the two parties together.

"We've repeatedly said to Netball New Zealand 'bring the players in'," Moore said. "The players can be used to assist.

"Bring us into the conversation and let's work together collectively to find a solution.

"We'd really love an opportunity to take part in a mediation with Netball New Zealand, and Ali and Anna, and perhaps we can find a solution we're all happy with."

World.title: Wairarapa police concerned about increased illegal firearm use
World.content:
Police say they are concerned about increased illegal firearm use in Wairarapa after two incidents involving guns within the last week.

Detective Senior Sergeant Philip Skoglund said one man was arrested in Martinborough early on Friday morning.

"About 12.30am, Police were called to a private address on Malcolm Street, following reports of a firearm being discharged," he said.

"The shooting allegedly occurred following a confrontation between two groups.

"Two shots were reportedly fired, one in the direction of a person. No injuries were reported, but a vehicle was hit."

A 22-year-old man was charged with discharging a firearm with intent to intimidate and was due to appear in Masterton District Court on 7 November, he said.

The other incident happened in Masterton last weekend.

Skoglund said a man was denied entry to a private party on Judds Road about 2am on Sunday, 1 November.

A fight broke out on the road and the man left in a taxi, making verbal threats as he left.

"First into the air, then in the direction of a group of people outside the address, putting everyone in the area in danger."

No one was injured, he said, though some partygoers were shaken.

A 31-year-old man was arrested and charged with unlawfully possessing a firearm, two counts of reckless discharge of firearm and driving while disqualified.

World.title: Country Life: The Kiwis growing fungi from fairytales
World.content:
An evening wander through the Richmond Community Garden's Fungi Farm might send chills down your spine - if you don't know what you're looking at.

Tattered books wrapped in flax can be found tied around tree branches, or hidden in the ground cover.

It's not some mysterious ritual, but what will happen to these books over time is magic all the same.

Audio player for " Growing mushrooms from fairytales " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/country/2392751%2Fcountry-life-the-kiwis-growing-fungi-from-fairytales

Growing mushrooms from fairytales Country Life Download MP3 14m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

If the weather plays ball, and the books stay warm and moist enough, edible mushrooms will begin to protrude from their pages.

Country Life joined the garden's last Fungi Whānau workshop of the year, held on the aptly named Fungi Farm.

The workshops, run by Inga Robinson of the Foraging and Growing Corner, share facts about native fungi, and how some of them can be grown to eat - like native phoenix oyster mushrooms (Pleurotus pulmonarius).

An old attempt at mushroom growing at the Richmond Community Garden. RNZ/Anisha Satya

"Mushrooms are just the babies [of fungi]," she said.

"It's like fruit. It's like an apple from an apple tree."

Growing mushrooms starts with a seed, literally. A bag of grain spawn - barley or similar seeds that have been inoculated with mycelium (the root-like structure of the original fungus) - get sprinkled into the growing medium of choice.

The fungi grows out of its host seed, in the book, and eventually grows those tasty mushroom morsels.

It has to be something porous, that retains moisture, and stays relatively warm. Egg cartons and straw bales are commonly used, but Robinson has opted for something less conventional: books.

"It's an experiment from Melrin Sheldrake's book; It's called Entangled Life.

Fungi workshop attendees soak some old books to use for oyster mushroom growing. RNZ/Anisha Satya

"He fed his own book to oyster mushrooms. And I thought it was hilarious to repeat it in the garden."

Attendees used old books donated from the Shirley library, soaked them in water, and scattered grain spawn through their pages.

The mushrooms will be ready to pick in three to six months' time, depending on the weather.

Richmond Community Garden director Morgane Honoré said it felt a "bit criminal" to treat books that way but the activity made use of books that would otherwise end up in the bin.

"They're old books, nobody reads them anymore. So, we're giving them a new life."

An old attempt at mushroom growing at the Richmond Community Garden. RNZ/Anisha Satya

Giving life to empty spaces is the garden's purpose. Twelve years ago, volunteers came together to reestablish a vegetable garden which had been destroyed in the earthquakes.

"A lot of the land that we're standing on was red-zoned. Our board of trustees who are still the same people to this day, 12 years later, advocated for this piece of land to be used by the community."

World.title: Khawaja claims all players knew about Sandpapergate ball tampering
World.content:
All players and staff knew about the ball tampering during the infamous 2018 Cape Town Test, Usman Khawaja has told Nine newspapers ahead of the release of his book.

In an explosive claim in his new book Sabr, Khawaja says sandpaper was also used in the previous Test in Port Elizabeth, now known as Gqeberha.

"It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us," Khawaja told Nine newspapers.

"I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now."

The claim is at odds with Cricket Australia's assertion that only Cameron Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner knew about the tactic. Bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitch Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon also denied publicly in 2021 that they knew about it.

Bancroft was banned for nine months after being caught using sandpaper on the ball during the third Test of the series in South Africa, while captain Smith and vice-captain Warner copped 12-month bans for their parts in the scheme.

Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith front the media after Bancroft was caught using sandpaper to tamper with the ball. (Gallo Images via Getty: Ashley Vlotman)

In the book, Khawaja claims that lighthearted discussions about the use of sandpaper at St George's Park led to Smith walking out of the rooms and saying that he didn't want to know about it.

He claims Bancroft then volunteered to use sandpaper in the first innings at Gqeberha, where the ball swung significantly, and that he sat next to Bancroft at Newlands and saw who spoke to the young batter during the Test that would see the Australian team caught out.

Khawaja has been promoting his book across various media outlets over the past weeks. However, the claims made in the ball tampering chapters had been redacted until today. He said he had dedicated the chapter to Bancroft, Warner and Smith because he had seen how the saga had weighed on all three players.

Khawaja told ABC Radio National's Conversations program that revisiting the 2018 series for the book was particularly difficult.

Loading...

"Everyone in that team, one way or another, was affected and we still are affected by that to this day," he said.

"For me, writing that chapter was more about what I thought was the right thing to do. … I still struggle to talk about it in a lot of respects. There's no easy way to talk about what happened over there. There's no easy way to write about that period of Cricket Australia and that period of my life.

"It's just about telling my story. and what my feelings were particularly at that time and what I saw."

Khawaja said it was a culmination of seven years of playing with a "win at all costs" mentality that made the rest of the cricket world hate them.

He said that started after the 2011 Argus Review, which came in the wake of the team's first home Ashes series loss in 24 years, during which Khawaja made his Test debut as England won by an innings and 83 runs to complete a dominant 3-1 series victory.

"The way we were playing, we were disrespecting other players and I talked to other players in other teams I was friends with and they were just like 'yeah, we hate your boys'," he said.

Usman Khawaja reveals illness he kept secret his entire Test cricket career Cricket great Usman Khawaja could barely walk and thought he had a terminal illness when he was just starting out his Test career. He was soon diagnosed with a crippling disease, which he has kept secret for 17 years.

"This all manifested during that time with sandpaper, and no-one had our backs after that either because why would they? We just acted like idiots for the last seven years."

Khawaja's childhood coach and mentor, Bill Anderson, told Australian Story last month: "Usman actually tried to coerce them all to say 'we all knew what was going on' and some of them wouldn't buy into that. Ussie's view being, 'they're not going to sack us all'."

The 39-year-old told Conversations that if he could have his time over again, he would have stood his ground more resolutely.

The silver lining of the whole affair, Khawaja said, was that it forced the Australian men's team to have a long, hard look at its playing style.

"The best things come out of the worst times. I genuinely believe, for the Australian cricket team, the best thing that came out of Sandpaper is we found humility again," he said.

"JL [Justin Langer] came in as coach and he was honestly probably the best coach we could've had at that time. He put humility back in the Australian cricket team.

"It was just lovely to see. It was beautiful. I really enjoyed it. I really enjoyed seeing where the Australian team went from that point onwards and obviously Pat Cummins, who ended up becoming the captain, was a part of that process and journey."

World.title: Asofa-Solomona leaps into crowd, apologises after 'frightening' Gallen KO
World.content:
A furious Nelson Asofa-Solomona has leaped into the crowd in sensational scenes following his knockout victory over fellow former NRL star Paul Gallen in Sydney.

Gallen, returning to the ring for the final time, was knocked out with 10 seconds remaining in the first round of their five-round heavyweight bout at the TikTok Entertainment Centre.

The 45-year-old was hit with a thunderous right that sent him back against the ropes, before four devastating upper cuts, the last of which was landed despite Gallen already being down.

As Gallen lay stricken on the ropes in considerable distress, Asofa-Solomona leaped onto the corner ropes to celebrate his win.

Then, incredibly, the 200cm, 137.5kg giant leaped over the ropes and ran to someone in the crowd.

Footage appeared to show the former Storm forward swing a wild punch towards a spectator, who was later led out the building by police.

Nelson Asofa-Solomona was heckled by someone in the crowd and lowered himself to challenge them directly. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"I just want to apologise for what I did, I acted like a bloody idiot," Nelson Asofa-Solomona said in the ring.

"I just got in a bit of the heat of the moment.

"I should not behave like that, I'm sorry."

Gallen, meanwhile, who surrendered a 20cm height advantage and more than 33kg in weight, was able to sit up.

He was later shown laughing with his shaken son in the dressing room, seemingly recovered.

Former world champion Tim Tszyu said the knockout was "frightening", while Gallen's former Sharks teammate Michael Ennis was in a state of shock at the sheer violence meted out on his friend.

Paul Gallen was left stricken in terrifying scenes. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"That was really hard," Ennis said.

"It was really hard to watch."

George Rose, promoter of No Limit Boxing, did not criticise Asofa-Solomona, but was adamant that attending his shows was safe.

"One thing that we love with our shows is that we like to make it a safe and enjoyable and entertaining experience for everyone," Rose said on Main Event.

"We want to make sure that it's something that people can be a part of and feel safe to come and enjoy."

Asked later, Asofa-Solomona said: "Someone was doing an ape gesture. I stood on the ropes and it looked like someone threw something at me.

"If I had my time back, I would, because that's not on. But what that guy did to me, in terms of that gesture, is not on either.

"I'd just seen red."

Earlier in the night, Paris Olympian and Commonwealth Games medallist Callum Peters, despite being slightly off colour, maintained his unbeaten record with a unanimous points win against rugged Colombian Juan Diego Ortiz.

Meanwhile Paulo Aokuso delivered a statement knockout to beat Mobin Khahrazeh in the second round of their IBF Inter-Continental light heavyweight title fight.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Ex-CFMEU boss admits to illegal tirade against AFL umpiring boss
World.content:
Former construction union boss John Setka is unapologetic for breaking workplace laws, with his barrister saying he did not "deliberately" wage a public campaign against an ex-building regulator and AFL umpiring chief.

Mr Setka, the former powerful Victorian secretary of the CFMEU, faces a fine of up to $18,730, but could be hit with a much heftier legal bill because the union has refused to indemnify his court costs.

The Federal Court on Friday heard Mr Setka admitted breaching the Fair Work Act by trying to coerce the AFL into sacking its head of umpiring Stephen McBurney in mid-2024.

Mr McBurney was the Australian Building and Construction Commissioner and participated in more than 50 court cases against the union between 2018 and 2023.

Mr Setka's barrister Margo Harris said her client should not receive a severe penalty.

She said he was now retired, in the middle of a divorce, and spent most of his time looking after his elderly mother.

"He doesn't express any remorse but he has made an admission that what he did was wrong," Ms Harris said.

Mr Setka was not in court for Friday's hearing.

Former union boss admits to breaching law

The development comes three days before the start of hearings in Victoria's Royal Commission into the state government's "Big Build" construction projects, which have been dogged by claims of widespread corruption and crime.

Mr Setka, who left the CFMEU weeks after his verbal attacks on Mr McBurney, is also facing separate criminal charges over alleged harassment of the union's administrators.

In the Fair Work case, Mr Setka was still union boss when he made social media posts and gave media interviews over a two-week period, threatening that the CFMEU would disrupt or delay AFL building projects if it did not get rid of Mr McBurney, the court heard.

"This is going to cost the AFL a lot of f**king money. I hope it's worth it," Mr Setka said.

"Projects without our full co-operation are going to be a f**king misery for them. They will regret the day they ever employed him."

John Setka left the CFMEU weeks after his verbal attacks on Stephen McBurney. (ABC News)

The Fair Work Ombudsman (FWO) prosecuted Mr Setka and the CFMEU, alleging the demands to sack Mr McBurney were made because of his lawful work as ABCC commissioner.

On Friday, barristers for Mr Setka and the CFMEU admitted to the breaches.

Ms Harris said there was no evidence Mr Setka "actively sought" media attention, even though he made statements to newspapers, and appeared in radio and television interviews where he said the AFL should sack Mr McBurney.

Ms Harris also said Mr Setka did not "deliberately" engage in a media campaign against Mr McBurney, prompting Federal Court judge John Snaden to clarify what she meant.

"When I say deliberate, there's a range of deliberateness. It's not a question of being pregnant or not pregnant," she replied.

"It comes in the stream of the interview. There's a question asked of him, he answers it."

However, FWO barrister Marc Felman said Mr Setka was not forced to give interviews.

"There can be no question that this is a media campaign," he said.

During one press conference, Mr Setka said of Mr McBurney: "He's a zealot. He hates unions. He hates workers in general."

He also put up a social media post depicting Mr McBurney in a mock poster containing the words: "(Not) Wanted Dead or Alive".

Penalty to be set for Setka and CFMEU despite claims of new regime

Mr Felman said Mr Setka's breaches of the Fair Work Act were "very, very serious".

He said Mr Setka wasn't the first person to call for the sacking of an AFL umpire, but it became illegal because the demands were connected to Mr McBurney's lawful work in an old job.

Mr McBurney, who has umpired four grand finals, was backed by the AFL at the time and remains the league's head of officiating.

Stephen McBurney adjudicated 401 AFL games and is still employed as the league's head of officiating. (AFLUA Hall of Fame)

The CFMEU, which has since been taken over by administrators, could be fined up to $93,900.

Barrister Andrew White, for the CFMEU, called for the penalty to be moderated because the union's new regime no longer saw breaking the law as "the cost of doing business".

He said the cultural shift had occurred following hundreds of Setka-era officials being removed or leaving their jobs.

"A new culture of lawful but robust unionism is taking hold," he said.

Justice Snaden will set the penalty for Mr Setka and the CFMEU at a later date.

World.title: Baseballer loses sight in one eye in 'horrific freak accident'
World.content:
Adelaide's baseball community is rallying around a "tough cookie" player who lost sight in one eye after a "horrific freak accident" during a weekend game.

Veteran member of the Adelaide Angels Baseball Club, Tyler Forney, was struck in the eye by a foul ball off his own bat, during a double-header against Woodville on Saturday.

Close friend and long-time teammate Chris Congdon said Mr Forney was in the batter's box during the second game when the incident happened.

"His ball ricocheted off his bat and basically collected his right eye," Mr Congdon said.

"[It] resulted in him getting taken off to hospital by ambulance in a bad way and having significant eye surgery that evening.

"However, he's permanently lost vision in his right eye as a result of that.

"Anyone I've spoken to around the club that was there was just really mortified by the accident … it's a really horrific freak accident."

Mr Congdon said Mr Forney was an integral member of the club since joining back in 2016, after moving from Arizona in the United States.

He said Mr Forney had a gifted athletic ability which he had honed while playing college baseball.

"He's a really really tough cookie, Ty — I'm sure he played through a broken hand for parts of last season," Mr Congdon said.

"He was a walking highlight reel, he would make plays at shortstop that just no one else could make.

"He just stuck with us and [he's] a massive reason why the last five years we've had huge success."

'So grateful' for support

A GoFundMe page has since raised more than $16,200 by Friday afternoon to cover Mr Forney's medical fees.

"He [Mr Forney] did not realise how much of an impact that he has had on people — not only in our club, but the wider baseball community," Mr Congdon said.

" He's a very humble person, but this has really, really taken him taken by surprise and he's just so grateful. "

Mr Congdon said Mr Forney was being supported by his partner, two children and three stepchildren as he recovers.

He said while Mr Forney's playing career may have come to an end, the club is already talking about ways to transition him to a coaching role.

"He's the sort of person that is quite private and reserved, but when he speaks and he does, everybody listens, so I think he wouldn't have thought about coaching," he said.

"He had so much left to do as a player and still so valuable as a player."

World.title: Man sues former AFL players Dion Prestia and Steven May
World.content:
A man is suing former AFL players Dion Prestia and Steven May over an alleged brawl on Victoria's Mornington Peninsula.

The two players were previously charged over an alleged streetside altercation with another group in the coastal town of Sorrento on Boxing Day in 2024, but the charges were dropped in May 2026.

Mr Prestia, a former Richmond premiership player, had been charged with recklessly causing serious injury and affray, while Mr May, an ex-Demons player who retired this year, was charged with affray.

The incident left two men in hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

Previously, both Mr Prestia and Mr May strenuously denied their involvement in the alleged incident.

A personal injury claim is now underway in the Supreme Court over the alleged assault.

It is understood medical costs are among the damages being sought by a single plaintiff, who claims he was assaulted.

His name has been restricted by the court.

Court documents containing the exact details of the claim are yet to be released.

At a directions hearing in the Supreme Court on Friday, lawyers confirmed two more defendants were being added to the civil case alongside Mr May and Mr Prestia.

Their criminal matters remain before the court which means civil action is unlikely to commence before their cases are finalised.

Mr Prestia played 254 games for Richmond and Gold Coast and is a three-time premiership player.

It was recently announced he would join Hawthorn's coaching line-up for the 2027 season as an AFL development coach.

Mr May played 251 AFL games for Melbourne and Gold Coast and was a member of the Demons' 2021 premiership-winning squad.

He retired suddenly on the eve of the 2026 season.

Mr Prestia's employer and Mr May have been contacted for comment.

World.title: Aussie Calleja ready for winner-takes-all world championship weekend
World.content:
The biggest weekend in karting is here, with nearly 200 drivers descending on south-east Italy for the FIA Karting World Championship.

This weekend's event is the grand final of international karting, with drivers from around the world qualifying throughout the year for a chance to become world champion.

The OK (Original Kart) and OK-Junior world championships will be decided this weekend at the World Circuit La Conca in Muro Leccese, Italy.

F1 records broken by Kimi Antonelli in 2026 Kimi Antonelli sets numerous benchmarks that are likely to stand for some time.

There will be three Australians among the 194 competitors set to enter this weekend's racing.

William Calleja, Jenson Burns and Chris Lowe will all compete in the OK class, while Australian-born female racer Ava Jean Lawrence is in the OK-Junior event.

Calleja enters this weekend's world championship with a genuine chance of winning after a terrific season in the European Karting Championship.

The teenager from Victoria finished fourth in the championship, dominating the final round of the season in Kristiansand, Sweden, where he was fastest in qualifying and went on to win the final.

"It's great to have an FIA win under my belt, and I go into this very important race with winning experience in my hands," the Victorian said.

"The level of competition is the highest in the world in this category of motorsport, so winning any race at this level is a high achievement. I'm feeling good and looking forward to showing my best at La Conca."

The weekend's racing begins on Friday. Drivers go through qualifying sessions and heats in a bid to make it to Sunday's final race, which decides the world champion.

"It's a very mentally challenging race, and it will require proper preparation," Calleja said.

"I need to block out external noise and keep my eyes on the job ahead of me, not focusing too much on the end result but performing well in each stage throughout the weekend is what matters."

Burns, 16, from the Gold Coast in Queensland, placed 26th in the OK-N karting class at the FIA World Cup last month.

Lowe, from Melbourne, won a Victorian state title at his home track, Oakleigh, last year.

Meanwhile, Ava Jean Lawrence will compete in the junior class this weekend.

Despite racing under an Emirati licence, Lawrence is very much an Australian driver on the rise. She was signed to the Aston Martin F1 Academy program earlier this year.

World.title: Lynn's secret drugs ban revealed on BBL eve
World.content:
Big Bash League record-setter Chris Lynn's one-month suspension for a positive drugs test has been revealed, two months after he served the ban.

The revelation comes just days after the former Brisbane and Adelaide BBL big-hitter was linked with a move to the Melbourne Renegades for the season, which begins next month.

The 36-year-old was handed the suspension in August, after he tested positive on the day of England's T20 Blast finals in July, having helped Northamptonshire to the title.

After tests revealed an adverse analytical finding for cocaine's metabolite benzoylecgonine, Lynn admitted to using the drug days earlier.

The findings noted Lynn did not have a therapeutic use exemption for cocaine and that the cricketer had successfully argued his drug use amounted to an out-of-competition violation unrelated to sporting performance.

He was given a one-month ban, backdated to the period of between July 31 and August 30.

Lynn was set to play in Sri Lanka after the T20 Blast, but after one appearance he was ruled out with an unspecified leg injury on July 29.

Any further punishment would be at his BBL club's discretion, with Lynn available given he has served his penalty and is not on a Cricket Australia contract.

Lynn is the BBL's leading run-scorer and six-hitter, and has also played four one-day internationals and 18 T20 internationals for Australia.

He has also played for at least 25 different T20 franchises around the globe.

AAP

World.title: How a toy giraffe helped the AFLW Bulldogs rise back into finals
World.content:
Each week, Western Bulldogs fan-favourite Elaine Grigg looks forward to the side's player meetings.

It has been a good year for the Dogs, with eight wins from 12 games, finishing seventh on the ladder and back playing finals since 2022.

But reviewing the side's victories isn't the only reason Grigg likes getting together.

"This year, we've had a little mascot. Its name is Sawya, and it's a pet giraffe," Grigg told ABC Sport.

"Every week we spin a wheel, and someone has to take Sawya during the week … You have to make a video of what you do with it. So every Monday you present that, and it has been a really good laugh every week."

The "little mascot" a player takes home every week. (Supplied: Elaine Grigg)

Grigg, who joined the club as a high-profile draftee in 2023, said it has been a great way to get to know teammates and who they are off the field.

When she took Sawya, she said it was mostly work (as a student support officer at a school) and recovery, including a lot of time in the sauna. However, it has given away some teammates' hobbies, such as goalsneak Sarah Hartwig's creative side.

"That really surprised me," Grigg said. "How many different things she can do … She sews, she bakes, she does all these different things. I'm like, 'Twiggy, you need to start a business.' She makes all these different clothes as well."

More than bonding for the fun of it, Grigg said it's part of the Bulldogs's focus on building team connection, which has helped them immensely on the field.

Elaine Grigg is quickly becoming one of the personalities of AFLW. (Getty: Quinn Rooney)

In 2023, the club hit rock bottom with a last-place finish, resulting in a review of its program and the appointment of a new coach, Tamara Hyett.

From there, it was a slow and steady climb back up the ladder. In both 2024 and 2025, the Dogs finished 12th.

This year, however, they fired back with a 26-point win over fellow finals team Gold Coast.

The Bulldogs' great AFLW turnaround The team's turnaround from rock bottom to the AFLW finals seems rapid but has been many years in the making. This is how they did it.

Many AFLW pundits and commentators have remarked on the side's new feel, particularly the excitement and "fun" factor.

"We know we need to lock in when we're at the club (and) when we're out on the footy field. But then it's the balance of having fun and also when it's time to be serious, to be serious as well," Grigg said.

"The connections that we have with everyone, it actually helps on the footy field."

The Western Bulldogs with their "little mascot" in Sawya. (Supplied: Elaine Grigg)

The side also dances before every game, with a new player picked each week to lead.

"That came about in our off-season trip. We were having a pool party and that dance, we did it, and that's carried on to our pre-game," she said, citing teammate Ellie Blackburn as the main instigator.

"It just shows how much fun we can have as a group, even before a game, to just let loose and be really connected with each other … It's something you look forward to and brings us closer as a group."

There was a lot of excitement around Elaine Grigg when she was drafted to the Bulldogs in 2023. (Getty: Quinn Rooney)

On the field, Grigg said one of her favourite moments this year was Emma McDonald kicking a fourth-quarter haul against Sydney in round four, handing the Swans their first loss of the season.

"She went on a rampage to kick her three goals and to get us up and about," Grigg said.

"But it was her first one (liked the most). It was a team goal."

Grigg will hope for a similar finish this Sunday, when the Bulldogs face the Swans in an elimination final at Henson Park.

Tech.title: All the latest updates on AI data centers
Tech.content:
Massive new data centers are the physical foundation for tech companies’ hopes and dreams for AI. But the rush to expand warehouses full of energy-hungry servers has also kicked up fights across the world over their impact on power grids, utility bills, nearby communities, and the environment.

Data centers were a major bipartisan issue ahead of the 2026 midterms, and voters largely opposed data center expansion at the polls. Tech giants like OpenAI and Amazon are promising to work more closely with local communities and cover their data center energy costs. But following the election, Democratic leaders are calling for further data center restrictions and slowdowns that the AI companies will have to grapple with.

Tech.title: Shure’s popular podcasting and streaming mic is almost $50 off
Tech.content:
is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

While the Shure Mv7 Plus is popular with streamers and podcasters, it’s equally good at impressing your friends and coworkers on meetings and Discord calls. It’s currently marked down to $255 at various retailers, including Amazon, Guitar Center, and directly from Shure. That’s almost $50 lower than its usual price, and just a few dollars off Amazon’s all-time low. If you don’t already have a stand, both Amazon and Shure are offering a bundle that includes the mic and a desktop stand for $269, and the white model is also discounted at Amazon.

When our team shared some of our favorite audio gear in late 2024, we noted that the Mv7 Plus was the mic we send to podcast guests for remote interviews. It’s known for its crisp and clean audio quality, with auto-leveling and denoising, so you can use it without touching an equalizer.

The MV7’s unique shape and sonic profile is inspired by the Shure SM7B (also discounted), a microphone that’s often used in professional recording. This version is meant as a more budget-friendly variant for content creators looking for a simpler setup, with both an XLR output and USB-C, letting you wire into an audio interface or directly to a computer.

Tech.title: Lame-duck Congress might actually do something: speed up energy projects
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A massive permitting bill that could help energy projects come online much quicker and potentially lower utility bills for Americans is advancing with bipartisan support. And while it could be a catalyst for lots of clean energy, it could also speed up polluting projects and limit oversight of new data centers.

With data centers demanding more electricity for AI, environmental advocates fear that developers could take advantage of the reforms to evade public scrutiny and rely more heavily on fossil fuels. The bill sacrifices caution for speed, limiting environmental reviews and preventing communities from stopping a project from moving forward by taking it to court.

“Whether it is permits to bulldoze wetlands, the fast-tracking of gas pipelines or general environmental review, with this legislation, data centers would not need to answer to the concerns of local communities,” Christy Goldfuss, executive director of the nonprofit Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), says in an email to The Verge. “People would be shocked to realize their representatives are rushing such a consequential decision.”

The bill sacrifices caution for speed

“They swung big with this bill. It’s a really good bipartisan compromise,” Xan Fishman, executive vice president of the Energy Program at the Bipartisan Policy Center, tells The Verge.

Four senators calling themselves the “four corners” — Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Mike Lee (R-UT), and Martin Heinrich (D-NM) — introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on September 30th. “If we can pass this bill, we will flood the grid with clean, affordable energy and make data centers start paying their fair share,” Whitehouse, a climate hawk, said in the press release.

The announcement simultaneously garnered support from climate and renewable energy groups, as well as fossil fuel interests. “Pass the frickin’ bill so we can start building things again,” the US Oil & Gas Association said in a statement.

The Senate could vote to move the bill forward as early as next week, teeing it up for potential passage before the end of the year, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. Fishman expects President Trump will want to sign the bill if the current Republican-controlled Congress acts, adding in an email that the White House has been “very involved” in negotiations. Newly empowered Democrats, however, could decide to drag out debate on the bill until next year in order to make fewer concessions to Republicans.

“Sometimes, bureaucratic processes that are created with good intentions kind of spiral out of control.”

If it becomes law, the bill would limit the reach of bedrock laws (stemming back to the 1970s environmental movement) that protect water resources and endangered species and give the public an opportunity to weigh in on large projects that might impact public health. Over the years, however, reviews that once took months at most might take several years or even decades, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. Fishman attributes the delays largely to lengthy legal battles. Now, agencies have to spend more time preparing for lawsuits as they consider permitting applications, Fishman says. That holds up development on all kinds of infrastructure projects, including cleaner energy alternatives to fossil fuels.

Fishman expects BAAJA to be very effective in amending outdated permitting rules that have become burdensome to projects across the board, even those that might ultimately have a net positive impact on the environment. “Sometimes, bureaucratic processes that are created with good intentions kind of spiral out of control,” he says. “You want to protect the environment, you want to protect people, but you want to get to a yes or no [on a permit application] in a reasonable amount of time and you don’t want to have this endless litigation cycle.”

The bill would set a 45-day deadline for a lead agency to issue a decision on a project after completing an environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). In many cases, NEPA review is the only opportunity for nearby residents to weigh in on large projects that involve the federal government. And it’s been a key tool for opponents to high-profile projects including the Dakota Access and Keystone XL pipelines. BAAJA narrows the scope of projects subject to NEPA, creating exclusions for transmission upgrades and certain pipeline expansions, to name a couple. Many projects receiving federal loans or grants or that have already been through a similar state environmental assessment would no longer trigger NEPA review.

The bill also sets a strict new 150-day limit for anyone to challenge a project in court over alleged violations of NEPA, the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, or National Historic Preservation Act. And BAAJA strips away a court’s ability to halt a project altogether even if it finds that a federal agency violated NEPA; it would simply force the agency to correct any issues.

The Clean Water Act allows the Army Corps of Engineers to issue general permits to projects that discharge dredged material into US waters as long as they’re deemed as having “minimal adverse environmental effects.” BAAJA could make it easier for large projects including data centers to qualify for those permits.

Some environmental groups are concerned that those general permits would take away public participation requirements for individual projects, especially when it comes to data centers that use a lot of water. The proposals in BAAJA amount to “rubber-stamping permits under the Clean Water Act” and “blocking interference from States and Tribes,” according to the environmental organization Earthjustice Action.

“It will enable fast delivery of gas to fuel the data center build-out.”

They’re also concerned that BAAJA aligns with the Trump administration’s push to deregulate industry and weaken environmental protections in order to swiftly build out more data centers and fossil fuel infrastructure to power them. Data center energy demand has led to a surge of new gas projects in the US, and the bipartisan bill could help streamline reviews for new pipelines delivering fuel for data centers.

“One very big reason why passing BAAJA is such a high priority for the gas industry is it will enable fast delivery of gas to fuel the data center build-out,” Earthjustice Action President Abigail Dillen said in a Thursday blog. “BAAJA delivers a precision strike for developers of dirty data centers.”

Long pipeline delays slow data center development, according to energy research firm Wood Mackenzie. Permitting reform could benefit data center developers building out their own gas generation rather than relying solely on the grid, so-called “behind-the-meter” projects, by ending regulatory delays when it comes to connecting pipelines. Reforms would also speed grid-connected gas generation, Wood Mackenzie says in a recent news release.

“I don’t think we’re seeing it as this bill helping one type of technology over the other. I think it clears the way for all technologies to get onto the grid a little quicker,” Siddhant Warrier, research analyst for North American Power for Wood Mackenzie, tells The Verge.

Notably, the bill is supposed to protect bipartisan interests by preventing any single administration from attacking a particular project type — such as the Biden administration attempting to phase down oil and gas in the power sector or the Trump administration issuing stop work orders to wind farms. BAAJA aims to provide “project certainty” by barring federal agencies from canceling or suspending permits they’ve already approved in most cases. It even allows developers to take agencies to court for “disparate treatment” to sue for damages incurred from project delays.

“This part of the legislation could also lead to a slew of industry lawsuits that result in taxpayers paying billions of dollars to private industry,” the NRDC warns in its analysis of the bill. It could also prevent communities from challenging projects, including data centers, that wind up having unforeseen consequences for the environment and public health.

Despite those concerns, the NRDC and other advocacy groups are optimistic about the bill boosting renewable energy and enabling power grid upgrades needed to meet rising demand while keeping costs down.

BAAJA could shorten the time needed to build a new transmission line nearly in half — from 10 years or more to around five or six years, the NRDC estimates. Transmission lines that carry electricity across long distances — key to getting electrons to urban centers from far-flung solar and wind farms — are particularly tricky to build because of the patchwork of permitting processes they’re subject to across different jurisdictions.

Two separate reports project that the permitting bill would increase renewable energy capacity in the US and cut greenhouse gas emissions as a result. It also points to modest reductions in energy costs as a result of BAAJA passing compared to a baseline reflecting the status quo. The average annual cost of producing electricity would fall by as much as 7 percent by 2041, according to modeling by think tank Resources for the Future. Household electricity bills would lower by $50 to $78 per year by 2040, according to an analysis by research firm Rhodium Group. The White House put out its own analysis in October claiming that the average household could see their electricity bills fall by as much as $251 each year as a result of BAAJA.

One of the ways BAAJA aims to keep utility bills from rising is to force data center developers to pay more for transmission costs. Current law prevents utilities from charging them for costs stemming from both new builds and existing infrastructure, which inadvertently shifts costs to other customers to fill in the gap. The bipartisan bill mandates what’s called “and pricing” so that data centers and other large electricity customers would be on the hook to pay for both added and existing infrastructure.

The bill would also require utilities to disclose electricity sales to data centers. It would force large data center developers to make financial assurances to utilities before they break ground, as well as make them responsible for covering costs of new energy projects even if the data center shutters before the infrastructure is paid off.

Unfortunately, the bill may only solve part of the problem since utility rates reflect more than just transmission costs. Increasing electricity demand from the data center boom can still raise prices for fuel and gas turbines, for example. And the bill doesn’t address other issues that have sparked backlash against data centers, like noise and air pollution from generators on site.

Still, without permitting reform, gas and power prices would likely continue to climb as new energy projects keep hitting bottlenecks, according to Wood Mackenzie. Even environmental groups concerned about some of the provisions in BAAJA are holding out to see if Congress can amend the bill to strengthen environmental and consumer protections.

The bill has become a sort of Rorschach test for its backers, one expert speaking on background tells The Verge. They’re all optimistic that their energy source of choice, be it oil and gas or solar and wind, will ultimately come out on top — as long as it gets the green light to build.

Tech.title: Meta’s Muse AI can create custom ‘spaces’ for the version of the app you need right now
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta will now allow you to build customized, app-like experiences within Muse. The new feature, called “spaces,” allows its AI assistant to build things like a shopping hub, school dashboard, music tracker, trivia game, and more, which you can interact with directly in the Muse app.

Meta says you can create a new space by describing it. If you connect an outside app to Muse — like Gmail, Google Calendar, OpenTable, Notion, and others Muse works with — the AI assistant will continuously pull information from them, allowing it to update pricing, dates, and other information in your space in the background. You can also interact with elements inside your spaces by checking things off, adding notes, and making edits.

Related Muse has a voice mode now

You can also change the placement of your spaces in the Muse app, too, as Meta lets you keep them in the sidebar, move them into your main tab, or schedule when you see them. “For example, keep your weekly planner up front during the workweek, then swap it for your weekend plans on Saturday,” Meta says.

Meta also announced that it’s bringing new “Active Memory” and “Active Focus” capabilities from its Muse Wonder AI model into the Muse app and its Meta AI chatbot. This will allow Muse to understand when past information becomes relevant during conversations, as well as make it better at working toward goals.

Meta is rolling out spaces to all Muse users. The company is also looking into ways to share your spaces with other users and collaborate with them.
